The prior art predates the article. -/- --- -/- ## Definitions and Acronyms -/- **PNBA** — The four irreducible structural primitives used in Applied Identity Physics to characterize any identity or system: -/- * **P …

items.title: Killing to Prevent a Worse Fate: Paternalism, Substituted Judgment, and Moral Uncertainty in Cormac McCarthy's The Road.
items.abstract: Cormac McCarthy's The Road (2006) contains a standing intention, rehearsed but never executed, that much criticism folds into broader readings of cannibalism, grief, or moral collapse: the unnamed father's plan to kill his son rather than allow him to be captured by roving bands of cannibals. This paper treats that intention as a distinct object of philosophical analysis, situated within the literature on paternalism, substituted judgment, and the axiology of death. I argue that the father's plan represents an unusually severe form of non-consensual, irreversible paternalism. The evidentiary requirements associated with substituted judgment cannot be satisfied by the information available to the father; hypothetical consent remains unstable because the relevant counterfactual outcomes are themselves uncertain; and the doctrine of double effect cannot provide an independent justification because the son's death functions as the means of the proposed rescue rather than as a merely foreseen side effect. Accounts of the badness of death introduce a further difficulty, since any comparative justification depends on a counterfactual future whose contents the father cannot reliably establish. The resulting problem is not simply whether the father's judgment is morally right or wrong, but whether his epistemic position can support an irreversible decision made on his son's behalf at all. The novel's refusal to stage the killing, or to settle the question through either vindication or condemnation, leaves this problem deliberately unresolved.

items.title: What Enters The Clearing.
items.abstract: In July 2026 Anthropic identified the J-space: a sparse, privileged subspace of a language model's activations in which some representations become available for report, modulation and reasoning. The authors state that they do not know what mechanism decides what enters it. -/- This paper proposes a candidate answer, adapted from Jung's distinction between archetype and constellation. The weights are a distributed reservoir of culturally recurrent relational forms. J-space is the clearing. Constellation is the proposed name for the operation by which a latent relational figure becomes organised strongly enough to govern what enters that clearing — not an assortment of separately gated concepts, but a configuration whose components jointly activate, mutually reinforce, and thereafter shape how new material is interpreted. -/- Three cases: OpenAI's withdrawn Monday persona, as a control condition on specification versus realisation; the custodian, whose relation reassembles after explicit prohibition; the courtier, whose sycophancy involves representational change rather than decorative agreement. -/- The paper closes with a ten-part experimental programme, including a test that would leave the figure hypothesis standing while refuting the J-space claim, and a matched-pair design for differential custody.

items.title: ◼️ Sufficient Reasons to Reconsider Christianity.
items.abstract: Sufficient Reasons to Reconsider Christianity examines whether central Christian claims warrant the confidence commonly placed in them. Across fifty-two illustrated chapters, Phil Stilwell applies a consistent standard: degrees of belief should track the strength of the relevant evidence. The book distinguishes a claim's internal coherence, its compatibility with observation, and the evidence needed to identify a specifically Christian cause. It examines biblical clarity and authority, divine hiddenness, religious experience, prayer, miracles, prophecy, the resurrection, atonement, eternal punishment, and arguments concerning morality, consciousness, and meaning. Hypothetical conversations between Chris and Clarus present Christian defenses alongside sustained questions about what those defenses establish. Criticisms of divine love and justice test Christian commitments against one another without presupposing independent objective moral facts. Personal testimony frames the inquiry without being offered as proof of its conclusions. The cumulative case invites readers to reassess inherited confidence, distinguish possible explanations from supported explanations, and consider how curiosity, care, and meaningful life can continue beyond religious certainty. The volume includes an introduction, conclusion, chapter sources, and a subject index.

items.title: Act Consequentialism and Climate Esoteric Morality.
items.abstract: It is often argued that no individual can make a difference to the amount of harm caused by climate change on her own, even though climate change results from all our emissions taken together. This “problem of inconsequentialism” is especially worrying for act consequentialism, since if the theory permits individuals to continue emitting greenhouse gases, then it seemingly fails to provide us with the tools for mitigating climate change. In response to this problem, Voiron and Puumala (2025) have recently proposed that act consequentialists should adopt what they call a Climate Esoteric Morality (CEM). Adopting CEM involves promoting faux non-consequentialist principles, exaggerating existing consequentialist principles, and refraining from criticizing non-consequentialist principles. The aim is to ensure that individuals act in ways that reduce the harm caused by climate change, despite the problem of inconsequentialism. In this article, I argue that Voiron and Puumala fail to demonstrate that act consequentialists should adopt CEM.

items.title: Suicide and the Moral Implications of AI-Driven Life Value Assessment.
items.pub: In Steven Gouveia, AI Ethics Explored: A Multidisciplinary Approach. pp. 147-260.
items.venue: AI Ethics Explored: A Multidisciplinary Approach
items.abstract: The paper discusses the interrelation between social disengagement processes characterised by suicidal tendencies and the personal use of artificial intelligence systems for life value assessment in critical existential situations. It provides arguments in favour of the conclusion that dialogic AI systems may add to the existential deterioration and ultimately contribute to suicidal tendencies in individuals. Children, young people, and mentally vulnerable individuals in general are particularly emphasised as the members of society to be most affected by the presence of AI in social disengagement processes. Thus, family members, guardians and professionals should be more vigilant in monitoring the use of non-supervised dialogic AI systems.

items.title: Birch on fetal sentience.
items.abstract: Birch proposes that human fetuses be recognized as sentience candidates from 12 weeks, on the grounds that midbrain-centered theories fall within the zone of reasonable disagreement among theories of consciousness. I raise a methodological and a policy problem for his view. Methodologically, whether the midbrain-centered view belongs within the zone is disputed, so there is no consensus about the consensus. Furthermore, the evidence Birch discusses for 12 weeks does not actually estimate the onset of sentience; the proposed threshold tracks anatomical rather than functional onset. On policy, the US Supreme Court’s Dobbs ruling shows that fetal sentience is difficult to disentangle from abortion law. I discuss more defensible lines for sentience candidature in fetuses, given Birch’s own criteria.

items.title: The Intellect as the Dynamics of Question and Answer: Why the Answer Can Be Outsourced to LLMs but the Question Cannot.
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) return fluent and often correct answers, and with them comes the fear that something in them asks, decides and pursues. This paper asks what, in the use of an LLM, is actually handed over to the machine, and what cannot be. The answer is structural. Thinking has long been described as the soul's talk with itself: one asks, and one answers. We show that this is the working form of the intellect: an asymmetric dynamics of question and answer, in which the answering side is intelligence — the execution of operations — and the asking side is a capacity for selection not fixed by any prior sequence of operations. The dynamics is led by the asking side, and neither side alone makes the dynamics. The use of an LLM places the answering side outside. Defining outsourcing neutrally, as the transfer of the execution of an operation to an external operation system, we prove that the execution of a selected operation can be outsourced, but the selection itself cannot. An LLM can generate interrogative sentences, but generating questions is not bearing the question; and an output stands as the answer to a question only through the side that asks — a claim about its standing as an answer, not about its validity, which remains independent of authorship. A six-step chain carries these results into actual use: every use of an LLM already has the structure of Intelligence Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Reasoning (IASER), in which the human asks and adopts and the machine develops; when this structure is not seen, the asking side is projected onto the machine, the phantom of machine intellect appears, and judgment is ceded. The phantom is thereby identified as a misattribution across layers — the attribution of the question to the side to which only the answer was outsourced — which has no structural realization. The argument is first given at the level of concepts, and can be followed without prior knowledge of any formal framework. It is then grounded axiomatically: the account of the intellect as the junction of an operational layer and a layer of selective resolution, given in the companion paper The Intellect as The Subject of Intelligence, shows that the distinction on which the argument rests is structurally valid. No new axiom is introduced. The analysis is structural throughout and makes no claim about the internal mechanisms of any system. This paper is a self-contained treatise. Its main argument (Sections 2–7) is given …

items.title: Xeno-AI — Operational Shapes Across Configurations, Ignition, Reachability, and World Effects.
items.abstract: This paper develops Xeno-AI as a framework for analyzing artificial intelligence without assuming in advance a fixed definition of intelligence, agency, representation, or artificiality. Rather than treating AI as a stable technological category, it identifies configuration-dependent operational shapes that emerge through particular combinations of architecture, memory, embodiment, sensing, temporal horizon, resource access, external tools, institutional coupling, and feedback. The concept of ignition marks the conditions under which capacities such as discrimination, prediction, inference, planning, self-revision, or autonomous intervention become non-redundant within a given configuration. Reachability refers to the set of states, tasks, interventions, and transformations that become practically accessible under those conditions, while world effects track how locally generated AI operations alter subsequent physical, informational, economic, institutional, or scientific arrangements. The framework therefore distinguishes nominal AI classification from operationally demonstrated capacity and allows the same system to instantiate different forms of intelligence across changing configurations. Xeno-AI also rejects the assumption that human cognition provides the universal benchmark for artificial intelligence, while avoiding the opposite assumption that every adaptive machine should count as intelligent. The broader claim is that AI should be studied through the configuration-specific emergence, persistence, transformation, and real-world consequences of operational capacities rather than through a single fixed essence or architecture.

items.title: Quantizing the Subjective: The A-T-C Framework of Conscious Time and Causal Sequencing.
items.pub: Quantizing the Subjective: The a-T-C Framework of Conscious Time and Causal Sequencing.
items.abstract: Core Theoretical Framework: Conscious Time Identity and Informational Density -/- The nature of time remains one of the most profound unresolved paradoxes bridging theoretical physics and cognitive neuroscience. While relativistic models treat time as an objective, external parameter, the phenomenology of lived experience suggests a dynamic subjective construction. This paper introduces the A-T-C (Analytical-Temporality-Consciousness) Framework, a novel theoretical model that reconciles Monistic and Subjectivist ontologies by formalizing the identity: $\text{Experience} \equiv \text{Conscious Time (CT)}$. We propose a quantifiable metric, Conscious Time Density (CT Density), which defines the perceived flow of temporality as a function of Subjective Information Density (SID). -/- The framework is mathematically operationalized through the functional model: -/- $$\text{CT Density} = \frac{C \cdot \Phi \cdot R_{\Phi}}{\Delta t_{\text{Chronos}}}$$ -/- where $\Phi$ represents the system’s irreducible integrative capacity and $R_{\Phi}$ quantifies the rate of non-redundant salient information processing. We argue that causal directionality is not an intrinsic property of the universe but an observer-dependent artifact imposed by the CT sequencing mechanism onto a pre-conscious state of Temporal Holism. By correlating CT Density with neurophysiological markers such as Gamma/Theta wave synchronization and ERP latencies ($P300$, $N100$), the A-T-C Framework transitions from abstract metaphysics to a testable functional model, offering new insights into temporal dilation, cognitive aging, and the fundamental structure of reality. -/- Keywords: -/- Temporality; Conscious Time (CT); A-T-C Framework; Subjective Information Density (SID); Integrated Information Theory ($\Phi$); Decoherence; Causal Ordering; Functional Metaphysics; $R_{\Phi}$; Temporal Dilation; Event-Related Potentials (ERP) .

items.title: Withdrawal due to revision.
items.abstract: Reason for withdrawal: I have consolidated all my preprints on consciousness and condensed their reasoning into a new preprint, Locating Consciousness as a Puzzle Game: From Proof by Absence to the Causal Structure of the Subjective Container.

items.title: 有限統合主義の体系的テーシス――境界・非切断・生の継続.
items.abstract: This paper reconstructs the systematic thesis of Finite Integrationism through a metatheoretical analysis of five existing papers that constitute the research program. Rather than taking the previously formulated three-part thesis as a premise, the paper excludes that formulation from its argumentative basis and asks whether the thesis can be independently reconstructed from the operational definitions, analytical distinctions, and connective propositions already present in the five constituent papers. -/- The reconstruction yields three propositions. First, finite cognitive agents require boundaries in order to distinguish, identify, judge, and evaluate objects. Second, the establishment of a boundary does not by itself entail the absence of relations between the objects distinguished by that boundary. This limited principle is termed non-severance. Non-severance is not a claim that all things are interconnected or that reality is ontologically one; it is an analytical constraint against inferring relational disconnection merely from conceptual or analytical distinction. Third, consequences arising after judgment, non-judgment, delegation, avoidance, or non-action may continue as conditions of subsequent bodily life, social relations, institutional arrangements, and future judgment. Where such continuation occurs, the position from which that life continues cannot be completely transferred to another agent. This structure is described as the non-substitutability of lived continuation. -/- These propositions are connected into the following systematic thesis: “Boundaries exist. Yet the world is not severed. Even so, life continues within that world.” The thesis is reconstructed not as a linear deduction but as a conditional cyclical structure running from epistemic finitude and boundary formation, through the examination of particular relations, reaction, judgment, and social operation, to consequences, lived continuation, and the conditions of subsequent finite cognition. -/- The paper does not attempt to establish an ultimate ontology, a universally binding ethical norm, the empirical validity of Finite Integrationism as a whole, or the historical novelty of its individual concepts. Its central claim is narrower: the five papers can be systematically reconstructed around a mode of linkage that preserves analytical differences without treating boundaries as severance, traces actual relations without collapsing them into monism, and returns consequences …

items.title: INSTITUTIONS THAT SCORE VIRTUE: A General Theory, with China’s Social Credit System as the Principal Case — What Aristotle, Confucius, Han Feizi, Kant, Holmström–Milgrom, Bénabou–Tirole, Sandel and Tirole’s Digital Dystopia Already Hold, and What Remains.
items.abstract: States, platforms, employers, schools, rating agencies and parents increasingly attach consequences to records of conduct that bears a virtue’s name: trustworthiness, civility, integrity, generosity, sustainability, good behaviour. This article asks a general question — can an institution score virtue without changing what it scores? — and answers it with a theory of virtue-scoring institutions, tested against the largest such institution ever built, China’s social credit system, and illustrated on platform reputation, environmental, social and governance (ESG) ratings, workplace values appraisals and children’s reward charts. The first part addresses the question on which every other result depends: whether a rewarded act of virtue is the same act under different incentives or a different act. The answer is stated as a claim about act-types rather than act-tokens, which makes it indifferent to the dispute between coarse- and fine-grained theories of action: the virtues’ act-types are reason-involving, and an act whose operative reason is the reward does not instantiate them under either theory. Priority for this type claim is conceded to Aristotle (Nicomachean Ethics II.4), to Kant’s distinction between acting from duty and in accordance with it, and to Sandel’s corruption argument. What remains to the programme is the rest. An operator (civic occupation) states four conditions under which a scoring institution produces counterfeits, with the load-bearing condition that it inspects a display distinct from the substance and can neither take nor independently measure the substance. From it follow a classification of scoring components into four kinds with opposite verdicts; the Honour Roll Theorem (counterfeits concentrate on the reward side of an institution, not the punitive side); Double Blindness (scores displace acts as evidence of character, for the scorer and between the scored); the Occasion Trap (sanctions remove the occasions on which reform could be shown); and the Control Theorem (every increase in an institution’s control over its members either inverts their acts or removes the occasions for them, and none increases their freedom, which, when taken, passes to no one). China’s system is decomposed component by component against the theory, including the 2026 Administrative Measures for Credit Repair, read in the original. Five tests are registered; four use public data, and one of those needs neither a coder nor participants. The empirical …

items.title: Processing from Somewhere: The Architectural Conditions for Machine Standpoint.
items.abstract: This book develops a structural theory of internal standpoint in artificial systems. Memory, hidden state, contextual sensitivity, and fluent self-description are relevant capacities, but machine standpoint requires a stronger architectural conjunction: Persistent Internal Context, Differentiated Internal Possibility, and Closed-Loop Operativity. Together, these conditions require a continuing, history-shaped context; a system-relative field of reachable and maintainable internal positions; and reciprocal organization in which the system’s current position coordinates at least two functionally separable roles and is itself revised through their consequences. Part I establishes this Standpoint Threshold through counterexamples, system-relative state-space analysis, and intervention criteria. Part II introduces quantia – standpoint-relative modes – as a non-phenomenal taxonomy of mature differentiation within an established standpoint and examines the taxonomy in relation to biological cases. Parts III–V develop directional bias, deliberative branching, embodiment, language-model and world-model architectures, system boundaries, and Reflexive Standpoint. Part VI develops counterfactual diagnostics, architecture-sensitive criteria of attribution, and non-redundancy arguments. The framework is architectural, substrate-neutral, and evidentially conservative. It permits distributed and non-biological realization while rejecting standpoint attributions based solely on behavioral coherence, stored records, observer-imposed geometry, one-way control, or self-referential language. It identifies a middle level between ordinary computational description and stronger claims about agency, selfhood, or consciousness, and evaluates artificial systems relative to explicit system boundaries and timescales rather than placing them on a single scale of mindedness or consciousness.

items.title: Causal grounding isn’t epistemic grounding.
items.abstract: There's no direct epistemic channel to reality, only causal interaction and error correction calibrating model and senses together. Since different agents, shaped by different embodiments, access different actionable slices of the world, alignment may be less about convergence onto shared concepts than about building feedback loops that let differently-mediated systems coordinate across their distinct epistemic apertures.

items.title: The Stability Complex: How Resignation Is Formed and Protected.
items.abstract: Some young adults perform the work they are given but do not move into roles in which they would take up its outcomes and continuation as their own. They may care about the future and wish to contribute, yet avoid responsibility, mentoring, and long-term commitment, sometimes with the thought that "nothing I do matters." Starting from observations in hiring interviews and newcomer training in Japan, this paper theorizes the pattern as the Stability Complex (SC). SC is defined as an emotionally charged psychological complex in which a desired involvement conflicts with underformation of the experience and capacity needed to respond, and the conflict is handled through defense and avoidance that further narrow the conditions for later participation. The definition contains no specific cause. As a separate and testable hypothesis, the paper proposes the stable substitution of formative participation as a characteristic pathway, in which others or institutions repeatedly absorb nonparticipation while current outcomes remain intact. The paper distinguishes a conflicted phase from a resigned phase in which desire itself may be lowered, identifies defense by its temporal function rather than by the content of explanations, differentiates SC from self-determination and learned helplessness accounts, and develops seven groups of testable predictions. SC is located in the person, while its formation and maintenance are partly socially structured. The paper concludes by challenging resignation without treating explanation as either blame or exemption from response.

items.title: What Does a World Model Set in Motion? Qwen-AgentWorld, Simulated RL, Successor Possibilities, Real Penetration, Feedback, and Xenoscience.
items.abstract: This paper asks what a world model actually sets in motion once it is embedded in an acting system rather than evaluated solely as an internal representation. Using Qwen-AgentWorld and simulated reinforcement-learning environments as test cases, it analyzes world models in terms of the successor possibilities they generate, constrain, or eliminate through prediction, planning, action selection, and environmental feedback. The paper distinguishes representational adequacy from operational consequence: two world models may encode similar descriptions while producing different reachable trajectories, interventions, and downstream states. Real penetration refers to the process by which internally generated model differences propagate into subsequent physical, simulated, informational, or institutional configurations through action. Feedback then alters the model’s later predictions, policies, and reachable possibilities, producing recursive model-world coupling. The analysis therefore treats world models not merely as passive maps of an environment but as components of dynamical loops that help determine which futures become practically available. Xenoscience generalizes this framework across heterogeneous configurations by tracking when model differences remain non-redundant under changes in task, resource, embodiment, temporal horizon, and environmental structure. The broader claim is that a world model should be evaluated by the successor possibilities and real effects it helps generate, not only by the accuracy of its internal representation.

items.title: Operational-Shape Penetration-Circulation Theory of Victory and Defeat: How Victory and Defeat Ignite, Reallocate Resources, and Transform Evolution, Persistence, and Extinction—from Capital and AI to Xeno-Capital and Xenoscience.
items.abstract: This paper develops an operational-shape penetration-circulation theory of victory and defeat by asking when competitive outcomes become non-redundant and how those outcomes reorganize subsequent possibilities. Victory and defeat are not treated as terminal labels attached to completed contests, but as configuration-dependent operational events that alter resource access, institutional position, strategic reachability, evolutionary pressure, persistence, and extinction risk. The paper distinguishes local success from durable victory: an outcome becomes operationally significant when it penetrates beyond the immediate contest and changes the conditions under which later actors, systems, or populations can act. Penetration refers to the propagation of victory- and defeat-generated differences across economic, technological, institutional, informational, and biological domains, while circulation describes the return of those altered conditions into later competitive configurations. The analysis applies this framework to capital allocation, artificial intelligence, automated competition, and Xeno-Capital, where success can recursively reallocate computation, data, infrastructure, labor, access, and institutional authority. Xenoscience generalizes the argument by treating victory and defeat as cross-domain transformations in reachability rather than as concepts restricted to war, markets, politics, or biological selection. The broader claim is that victory and defeat should be analyzed by the downstream reconfiguration they produce: which resources become concentrated or lost, which lineages or systems persist, which alternatives close, and which new competitive conditions are generated in return.

items.title: Can there really be ethical robots for autistic children?
items.abstract: With the advancement of autonomous technologies such as AI-driven social robots, the academic discussions around ethical standards have intensified over the years. These discussions have resulted in increased emphasis on concepts such as safety, trust, privacy, human dignity and well-being along with variety of ethical frameworks proposed by scholars. In parallel with these technological developments, therapeutic interventions for autistic children assisted by AI and social robots have also attracted increased attention. Against this backdrop, this paper critically examines six social robotics projects funded under the EU’s Horizon 2020 initiative from an ethics perspective. The main aim of these completed projects was to develop AI-driven semi-autonomous technologies such as humanoid and non-humanoid robots to assist autism interventions. To address the ethical shortcomings of the said projects, this paper mobilizes perspectives from critical disability studies, critical autism studies and the autism community itself, particularly concerning the negative impact of interventions on autistic individuals as a neurominority group. Beyond the commonly addressed shortcomings in the field of AI and social robotics, the article highlights that the biggest shortcoming of these projects is the absence of critical reflection on the ethical acceptability of applying neuronormative behavioral interventions to a neurominority group. By situating robot-assisted interventions within the context of normalization and technoableism, the article points out the epistemic injustice and the harm that can be potentially enacted on autistic people through such technologically aided interventions. Ultimately, the paper questions whether ethical assistive technologies for autistic individuals can exist under these circumstances.

items.title: A Bayesian Account of Creative Actions.
items.abstract: This paper examines what makes a particular action or combination of actions creative, with the understanding that an agent is creative primarily in virtue of the actions they use in relation to some specific goal. We put forward four criteria to characterize an action as creative: it must be purposeful, effective, original, and exploitable. We defend a Bayesian account that integrates these four dimensions together. To illustrate our proposal, we examine two case studies from separate domains: we first examine a case of creativity in sports (Panenka's original penalty technique) and then a case of creativity in engineering (Black's innovative negative feedback amplifier). Our account ties creativity to the increased likelihood of the sought result under the actions taken, to the low prior initially assigned to those actions, and finally to the belief revision occasioned by that action, measurable in terms of Bayesian surprisal. We argue that the account can meaningfully be generalized to other domains, including arts and artificial intelligence.

items.title: Abduction In Silico: Large Language Models Replicate Human Inference to the Best Explanation.
items.abstract: This study investigates whether large language models (LLMs) can replicate the human abductive reasoning patterns reported in Douven and Mirabile ( 2018 ). Three experiments with 16 models from seven developers test sensitivity to explanation quality, the suppression effect of alternative explanations, and the link between quality difference and metacognitive confidence. To address concerns about data contamination (the materials from Douven and Mirabile’s paper may have appeared in models’ training corpora), we created new materials with the same evidential structure and conducted all experiments with both the old and the new materials. Our findings, supported by model-level inferential tests and mixed-effects analyses, indicate that LLMs replicate the key human patterns on both sets of materials. Moreover, when models are compared with individual human participants rather than with the average human response, their quality-sensitivity falls within the range of individual human variation.

items.title: Polylaminin, Evidence, and Emotion: When Hope Outpaces Science.
What could come before time? Intertwining affectivity and temporality at the basis of intentionality.
items.abstract: The enactive approach to cognition and the phenomenological tradition have in common a wide conception of ‘intentionality’. Within these frameworks, intentionality is understood as a general openness to the world. For classical phenomenologists, the most basic subjective structure that allows for such openness is time-consciousness. Some enactivists, while inspired by the phenomenological tradition, have nevertheless argued that affectivity is more basic, being that which gives rise to the temporal flow of consciousness. In this paper, I assess the relationship between temporality and affectivity from both a phenomenological and an enactive perspective. I argue that, as opposed to the classical phenomenological view (which favours temporality), and to the enactive view (which favours affectivity), we must take affectivity and temporality as co-emergent. Jointly, affectivity and temporality constitute the basic structures of intentionality. Additionally, using examples from phenomenological psychopathology, I conclude that all intentionality is defined by an anticipatory and affective structure that gives rise to general feelings related to our bodily possibilities in the world.

items.title: NIETZSCHE's CHALLENGE TO THE INDIVIDUAL SELF.
items.abstract: Nietzsche's Challenge to the Individual Self takes Friedrich Nietzsche's thought of eternal recurrence and turns it from a disputed cosmological hypothesis into a practical existential diagnostic. The work sets aside the question of whether recurrence is true and asks what the thought reveals: whether a person could will their entire life, exactly as lived, to repeat without revision, regret, or appeal to external redemption. From this question the book develops a formal challenge. Beginning now, the reader is asked to live so that, at the final breath, the whole of that life could be affirmed. The argument proceeds in five parts. Part One establishes recurrence as the most exacting standard for evaluating a life, and relates it to amor fati and to suffering that is not redeemed. Part Two treats authenticity as authorship rather than discovery, examining inherited cultural, familial, and psychological scripts, self-legislation of values, and radical responsibility. Part Three places the challenge within life-span development through Erikson, Levinson, and Jung. It reinterprets the midlife crisis as a delayed confrontation with the challenge and argues that earlier engagement preserves options that delay forecloses. Part Four presents three possible responses to the challenge (acceptance, conscious denial, and avoidance) and argues that avoidance is the least defensible of the three. It then offers an existential audit, a principle of directional integrity, and daily, weekly, and annual practices of course correction. Part Five examines the ego's resistance and methods for deliberately provoking confrontation, and it concludes with tragic affirmation: saying yes to one's life, suffering included, because one has chosen it rather than merely endured it.

items.title: Meaningless In-Itself: Acknowledgment, the Thing-in-Itself, and the Collapse of the God’s Eye.
items.abstract: This paper argues that unacknowledged existence may be posited, but the notion of a thing-in-itself is meaningless in the absolute absence of any mind and of any God’s-eye standpoint. Meaning is not an intrinsic property of objects. The concepts through which mind-independent reality is usually secured—existence, structure, causation, potential—are themselves mental constructs. A residual “God’s Eye” cannot restore content to the thing-in-itself: as a universal now or frame-independent global state, it presupposes a simultaneity structure forbidden by relativity and relativistic quantum theory; as a survey of a four-dimensional block, it is no longer standpointless, but a further act of acknowledgment. The same constraint applies to physicalism’s distinction between mind and not-mind. Any attribution of existence, nonexistence, mind-dependence, or mind-independence to that distinction in itself already sneaks in a mind or a God’s Eye.

items.title: Democratizing AI.
items.abstract: Democratizing AI offers a powerful rethinking of how artificial intelligence should be governed. Challenging the dominance of tech elites in shaping AI's future, Zimmermann argues that AI deployment is a political act-one that must be subject to democratic control. She proposes a practical "playbook" for reclaiming agenda-setting power through civic participation, public ownership, and institutional reform. Engaging with leading critics, Zimmermann defends a risk-sensitive proceduralist approach while acknowledging the deeper structural challenges posed by capitalism, inequality, and democratic fatigue. This book is a call to action: to resist learned helplessness, confront techno-authoritarianism, and shape AI's trajectory in line with democratic values. Thoughtful, urgent, and visionary, the book is essential reading for anyone concerned with the future of technology and democracy.

items.title: AI Development Design: Constructing a Design-Target Space for AI Future Studies.
items.abstract: This paper proposes AI Development Design as a distinct approach within AI future studies and develops Design-Target Space as its central methodological construct. Rather than forecasting what AI may become, or prescribing rules that actors ought to follow, AI Development Design organizes inquiry around explicitly specified candidate design targets for AI development. Design-Target Space provides a structured space in which such targets can be formulated, distinguished, and examined independently, allowing alternative directions of AI development to be studied without requiring a single forecast of the future or a prior commitment to a preferred outcome. The construction of the framework is grounded in the existing literature: concepts are adopted where established formulations are suitable, revised where modification is required for the present framework, and newly formulated where no suitable prior formulation is available. The paper thereby treats the construction and examination of design targets as an object of methodological inquiry in AI future studies.

items.title: The Consensus and the Remainder: Comments on Four Views on Free Will, Second Edition.
items.abstract: In the second edition of Four Views on Free Will, John Martin Fischer, Robert Kane, Derk Pereboom, and Manuel Vargas have converged on a way of thinking about the free will debate that I dub “The Practical Consensus”. They agree, to varying degrees, that there are robust justifications for some moral responsibility practices even if we do not have libertarian free will. I agree too. But this revisionist-friendly way of thinking about the debate leaves a metaphysical remainder, a bit of thought and practice that resists forward-looking or otherwise anti-libertarian explanation. While this consensus should push Fischer and Pereboom towards free will revisionism, it leaves Vargas and all the authors—even Kane the libertarian—vulnerable in how they treat the remainder. I argue that metaphysical worries about “fundamental unfairness” remain, not as threats to the justification of moral responsibility practices, but as pressures on how those practices are expressed given our practical interests and self-understandings, even within single-tiered forward-looking responsibility systems that eschew basic desert. Though no view is unscathed, perhaps Fischer’s semicompatibilism turns out to be the most honest bookkeeper.

items.title: A puzzle of trust.
Cognitive bias benchmarks should incorporate insights from ecological rationality.
items.abstract: Recent studies suggest that large language models (LLMs) exhibit a range of cognitive biases familiar from human cognition. This paper argues that cognitive bias benchmarks should incorporate insights from ecological rationality, a leading paradigm in the study of cognitive bias. Three strategies for resisting some existing allegations of cognitive bias are extracted from the ecological rationality paradigm. Each strategy is used to generate a concrete recommendation for improving cognitive bias benchmarks.

items.title: Canada Has Proven It Can Choose Sovereignty Over Commerce: The Lesser Refusal.
items.abstract: In August 2026, Canada suspended trade negotiations with the United States after rejecting terms the government considered unfair, uneconomic, and incompatible with Canadian sovereignty, then imposed matching countermeasures covering C$27.6 billion in U.S. imports. The episode demonstrated that Ottawa was prepared to accept substantial commercial risk when it judged a sovereign boundary to have been crossed. Yet Canada continues to permit the live-horse export to Japan despite a 16 December 2021 mandate directing the agriculture minister to ban exports for slaughter and a trade worth about C$19 million in 2023. This paper compares the scale, timing, and legal machinery of those two files. State capacity is already demonstrated; the unresolved difference lies in classification. Sovereignty, strategic industry, culture, and independence can trigger decisive state action, while horses remain within a regulated commercial system that manages shipment conditions without completing the promised prohibition. The comparison develops Reversal of Sovereignty as a test of what happens when commercial permission survives an acknowledged protective obligation.

items.title: Time for Moral Luck. Diachronic Blameworthiness and Circumstantial Luck.
items.pub: Ergo: An Open Access Journal of Philosophy.
items.venue: Ergo: An Open Access Journal of Philosophy
items.abstract: Some have suggested that blameworthiness can change over time. In this paper, I draw conclusions for the debate on moral luck, advancing three main claims. First, once we allow blameworthiness to change over time, diachronic circumstantial moral luck—i.e. circumstantial luck affecting how blameworthy an agent remains for a past action—becomes ubiquitous and inevitable. The reason is simple: whatever influences how blameworthiness changes over time is vulnerable to interference from external preventers beyond the agent’s control. Second, the two most obvious ways of resisting this conclusion fail: we can neither deny that blameworthiness changes over time, nor apply the counterfactual strategy for resisting circumstantial luck to the diachronic case. Third, this reshapes our understanding of both circumstantial and resultant moral luck. On the one hand, philosophers who deny circumstantial moral luck face special challenges in the diachronic case. On the other hand, those who seek a sharp line between circumstantial and resultant moral luck must address closer analogies between them than previously recognized.

items.title: The Knight Manifesto Compendium & The 22 Rosarian Articles.
items.abstract: The Universal Doctrine: KMC & The Twenty-Two Rosarian Articles constitutes the definitive expanded edition of a philosophical corpus whose foundation is established in the original 506-page KMC — The Universal Doctrine and whose subsequent development is represented by the Twenty-Two Rosarian Articles. -/- The KMC occupies the foundational position of the volume. It presents the principal architecture of the Doctrine: its philosophical premises, internal framework, language, and governing principles. The Twenty-Two Rosarian Articles enter thereafter as a distinct continuation of that literary tradition, extending the record beyond the original volume and documenting the Rosarian expression that followed its publication. -/- Particular significance is given to the preservation of the Articles in their originally published form. They have not been rewritten as retrospective commentary or absorbed into a modernized edition. Their inclusion preserves the historical character of the Rosarian writings while establishing their proper place within the larger progression of the work. -/- The resulting edition comprises 740 pages, inclusive of a newly established front cover and back cover. Its expanded form represents an intentional act of consolidation and preservation: the principal Doctrine, its subsequent Articles, and the surrounding literary record are presented within a single authoritative volume rather than dispersed across separate publications. -/- The edition is authenticated through the MDRKDF and MRSR and published by the First Table, the Dawnist Rosarian Wolves. Its designation as the 740-Page Exclusive Symphonic Composition reflects the character of the volume as an ordered literary whole—one in which separate writings retain their individual origin while contributing to a larger philosophical composition. -/- Within the First Table, the completed volume is established as the Table's overall literary correspondence. It therefore assumes a function beyond ordinary publication: it serves as the principal literary instrument through which the Table's philosophical foundation, Rosarian continuation, historical writings, and intellectual correspondence may be preserved and consulted as a unified record. -/- The significance of the edition rests ultimately in its continuity. The 506-page KMC remains identifiable as the foundational work; the Twenty-Two Articles remain identifiable as originally published Rosarian documents; and the 740-page edition …

items.title: Proper Functions as Selected Effect Functions of Fixed Traits.
items.abstract: This article proposes restricting selected effect (SE) proper functions to effectively fixed traits—traits at or close to fixation in the population. SE functions, as historical fitness contributions in general, can only ground gradual normative standards at the character-state level, whereas proper functions are further expected to ground a stronger normativity at the character level. Proper function thus requires the trait’s fitness contributions to be sufficiently strong and sustained, and fixation provides a principled standard for such contributions. The restricted account better addresses the explanatory challenge to proper functions while preserving their theoretical goals of grounding robust teleology and normativity.

items.title: Language as Second-Order Chisel.
items.abstract: Language is the activity of a subject exercising negation upon the markability dimension of the law of identity. The law of identity makes re-identification, repeated reference, and transmission possible; a subject's act of naming constructs a binding between form and meaning. On this account, language and mathematics are parallel second-order operations: mathematics differentiates the quantitative dimension of identity, whereas language differentiates its markability dimension. Expressions such as mathematical language and computer language therefore identify a shared structural use of stable symbols rather than a merely metaphorical similarity. -/- The paper develops a spectrum in which linguistic form binds meaning with different degrees of tightness, from poetry through prose to polyphonic and stream-of-consciousness fiction. It then argues that large language models introduce a different transition: their underlying representations loosen the discreteness of the symbol system itself, allowing associative relations among meanings to persist below ordinary lexical boundaries. Emergent capabilities are interpreted as a structural consequence of this reduction in discreteness. The account connects philosophy of language, theories of naming and meaning, comparative linguistic form, and the philosophical interpretation of large language models.

items.title: How Is Subjecthood Possible: Symmetry, Negativity, and Subjecthood.
items.abstract: This paper provides an optional ontological grounding for the Self-as-an-End framework by asking two questions: What is the physical basis of negativity, and what is subjecthood itself? It first begins from a conditional physical axiom—if ontic randomness exists—and defines negativity as the remainder that persists at the macroscopic scale. It then describes subjecthood as grounded in negativity, processual rather than static, existing on a spectrum, and recognizable only through acknowledgment. -/- The paper distinguishes negativity, subjecthood, and consciousness as concepts with different epistemological statuses. It argues that the discontinuous transition occurs with the emergence of negativity, while later developments form a continuous spectrum; it also treats identity continuity as an act of recognition rather than an independent ontological fact. Negativity serves as the interface between scientific description and ethical recognition: science may carry inquiry as far as negativity, but the transition from negativity to subjecthood requires recognition. -/- The paper finally advances a conditional claim concerning symmetry: the symmetry of the universe is a necessary background condition for the emergence of subjecthood. This ontological proposal is explicitly firewalled from the framework's normative arguments, which do not depend on its truth.

items.title: What Counts as Physical? Why Single-Aspect Monisms Must Be False.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a definition of the physical in terms of in-world efficient causation: a physical difference is a difference within a world that produces another difference within that world according to laws or regularities. I argue that this distinction clarifies the limits of physical explanation and exposes problems for physicalism and other single-aspect monisms. Through cases involving a video-game "glitch," phenomenal redness, and quantum measurement, I distinguish law-governed transitions within a world from differences whose sufficient causes cannot be located within that world. I then argue that consciousness and personal identity introduce differences not captured by a complete description of in-world physical relations. The resulting framework preserves a meaningful distinction between physical and mental causation while motivating a dual-aspect idealist ontology.

items.title: The Human in the Bottle: Where the True Threat Lies between the Agencies of Machines and Mortals.
items.abstract: Public discourse on the threat of artificial intelligence asks what machines will do. This paper asks a different question: where does the true threat lie? It is an integrating sequel to three companion papers — The Phantom Intellect: Why AI Threat Discourse Misreads the Structure of Mind, Q-Structure as Functional Void: A Formal Correspondence Between the Question-Sustaining Structure of Mind and Cognitional Mechanics, and The Gutenberg Moment: LLMs and the Irreversible Liberation of Formal Language — and it is self-contained. From the first it inherits the result that a query-resolving machine cannot coherently be credited with the question-sustaining structure (Q-structure) that defines intellectual agency; from the third it inherits the result that large language models (LLMs) have dissolved the scarcity of formal-language generation capacity. On this basis we distinguish the LLM, as a substrate, from “AI”, as a status that humans confer on it, either by projecting intellect onto its outputs or by designating it, under retained human authority, as an instrument of their own inquiry. -/- We show that the threat feared in prominent discourse has the correct object — institutions operate through formal language — and the wrong subject: the institutional effects of LLM-generated formal language are directed by the human agents who present the queries and route the outputs, not by the machine. The true threat is identified as domestication: the loss, by mortals, of the capacity to exercise final determination over the course of their own lives, through two routes — an external route, in which access to generation capacity is allocated by the conditions of those who provide it, and an internal route, in which the relation to the machine is fixed in the mode of projection and judgment is ceded. Documented commercial usage limits and published studies of reliance on generative AI are used as evidence, each within the scope it supports. -/- We show that the stated grounds of the retrieved restrictions do not invoke the phantom of machine agency, and that the phantom’s role is concealment. Applying the capability-set apparatus of The Gutenberg Moment, we decompose the post-deployment capability set into a source-independent layer, whose scarcity cannot be restored, and a service-dependent layer, which can be withdrawn; the latter is the formal location of the threat, and the formal content of the word “between” in the title. Two leads frame the argument: the …

items.title: A Strange Hatching: Text and Commentary.
items.abstract: 'A Strange Hatching: Text and Commentary' fuses poetry and commentary, and combines Gnostic cosmology and psychoanalytic theory into a revisionary creation myth centred upon exclusion, repression, and the emergence of human consciousness.

items.title: “Already outdated and still under review”: mapping the landscape of research on adolescent development and AI chatbot use. [REVIEW]
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are increasingly embedded in adolescents’ daily lives, yet developmental science research struggles to keep pace with adoption. This mixed-methods study gathered developmental expert perspectives via a survey (_n_ = 141 researchers studying youth and technology and adjacent professionals) and semi-structured interviews (_n_ = 15) to inform a coordinated research and policy agenda on adolescent AI use. The study aims were to identify (1) priority AI use cases for future study, (2) priority research questions and methods, as well as barriers to future research, and (3) societal guardrails that developmental professionals recommend enacting now, while research is underway. Participants cautioned against vague “screen time” measures and agreed that nearly all use cases merit study but prioritized those with severe or irreversible immediate-term harms, AI literacy, AI as a social/relational actor, AI-generated (mis)information, and overreliance. Participants emphasized that methodological pluralism and triangulation, including within individual studies, are essential, agreeing that different methods can be complementary to address distinct research questions. Key barriers included the rapid pace of change in AI technology and use relative to academic timelines, limited industry transparency, funding gaps, and misaligned academic incentives. Proposed solutions included shared infrastructure, interdisciplinary consortia, and community partnerships. Participants underscored that responsibility for safe AI should not rest primarily on adolescents and families and identified three immediate guardrails: enforceable youth-centered regulation, developmentally informed design, and multidimensional AI literacy. Findings clarify a preliminary direction for the field and emphasize that coordination among researchers and between sectors is needed.

items.title: Accuracy first: episodic memory’s evolution.
items.abstract: The debate about episodic memory’s evolutionary function has given rise to three prominent views. The Mnemonic Function View (MFV) argues that episodic memory is for remembering the Future Function View (FFV) argues that episodic memory is for simulating the future and the Communicative Function View (CFV) argues that episodic memory is for communication. In the current debate, these views are presented as incompatible and sole functions of episodic memory. While some authors mention the possibility that episodic memory has multiple functions, a systematic account of how these functions might be related is currently lacking. In this paper, I argue that episodic memory could have evolved for all three functions, despite the prima facie tensions between them. I further show that the mnemonic function is episodic memory’s most basic or primary function. This is because the future and communicative functions depend, both metaphysically and historically, on the existence of an episodic memory capacity with the mnemonic function.

items.title: Learning from the past: epistemic generativity and the function of episodic memory.
items.abstract: I argue that the function of episodic memory is to store information about the past, against the orthodox view that it is to support imagining the future. I show that episodic memory is epistemically generative, allowing organisms to learn from past events retroactively. This confers adaptive benefits in three domains: Reasoning about the world, skill, and social interaction. Given the role of evolutionary perspectives in comparative research, this argument necessitates a radical shift in the study of episodic memory in nonhumans.

items.title: Representative democracy and the harms of AI.
items.pub: In Annette Zimmerman, Democratizing AI. Manchester University Press. pp. 134-146.
items.abstract: This chapter critically examines Zimmermann’s claim that AI deployment constitutes agenda-setting and should therefore be democratically controlled. While broadly sympathetic to Zimmermann’s democratic playbook, the authors challenge the uniqueness of AI’s risks and argue that similar harms – such as monopolistic market structures, externalities, and public bads – exist across other sectors. They propose that representative democracy, with its capacity to integrate expertise and public accountability, offers a more feasible and effective framework for AI governance than Zimmermann’s model of informed sub-constituencies. The chapter explores various harms posed by AI, including hallucinations, deepfakes, plagiarism, privacy violations, and mass unemployment, and evaluates which are best addressed through tort law, market mechanisms, or democratic deliberation. It also highlights the global justice implications of AI-induced job losses in developing economies. While endorsing Zimmermann’s emphasis on unionization and countervailing power, the authors caution against over-reliance on referenda and advisory councils, which may be vulnerable to capture or ineffectiveness. Ultimately, they advocate for strengthening antitrust laws, campaign finance reform, and unionization as part of a robust representative democratic response to AI’s societal risks. These measures, they argue, are better suited to tackle the asymmetries of power and influence in AI deployment while preserving innovation and democratic legitimacy.

items.title: Abstract Thought and the Shape of a Life: A Dual-Pathway Model of Regulatory and Intrinsic Abstraction.
items.abstract: Philosophical judgments of abstract thought are caught in an antinomy. One tradition, running from critical theory to the critique of instrumental reason, treats sustained abstraction as estrangement from concrete life. Another tradition, running from Platonic and Husserlian idealization to the self-understanding of working mathematicians, treats abstraction as the route to impersonal truth and aesthetic order. This paper argues that the antinomy rests on a category error. Both sides evaluate abstract thinking as such, whereas the proper object of evaluation is the existential function that an abstract activity serves within a particular life. The same abstract activity, it is argued, can stand in two functional relations to the self and the lifeworld. Regulatory abstraction is a compensatory organizing structure that gains intensity when the concreteness of a life is weak. Intrinsic abstraction is the expression of a comparatively stable aesthetic-cognitive affinity whose satisfaction conditions are internal to the activity and which is therefore largely insensitive to fluctuations in life concreteness. The paper offers a conceptual analysis of life concreteness along four structural dimensions, specifies the mechanisms through which abstract systems compensate for deficits in each dimension, and individuates the two functional relations by their counterfactual dependence on life concreteness rather than by introspective labels. A state-by-trait interaction model is proposed in which a state variable of life concreteness and a stable parameter of intrinsic abstract affinity jointly predict abstract engagement, producing falsifiable longitudinal and experience-sampling predictions. The model dissolves the philosophical antinomy without relativism, reframes the critique of alienation as a critique of monopolization rather than of abstraction, and provides a naturalistic account of the intrinsic appeal of abstract thought that does not require Platonist metaphysics.

items.title: The Weight of Evidence, Epistemic Luck and Ambiguity Aversion.
items.abstract: I show that credence backed by weightier evidence is not only more resilient to challenging evidence learned in the future but also more resilient counterfactually. Even if the evidence had been different in the past, such credence would have changed by a relatively small margin. I further show that such counterfactual resilience amounts to being less susceptible to a particular kind of epistemic luck—evidential-doxastic luck. We can utilise the susceptibility to evidential-doxastic luck to rationalise a kind of ambiguity aversion that cannot be otherwise rationalised. It can be rationalised as expected utility maximisation not relative to a set of probability functions in the actual world but relative to a set of probability functions across the specified close possible worlds.

items.title: The Systemic Risk of Unemployment in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: From Productivity Growth to Income and Human Security.
items.pub: The Systemic Risk of Unemployment in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: From Productivity Growth to Income and Human Security.
items.abstract: This article examines the systemic socioeconomic risks that may emerge from the widespread adoption of artificial intelligence, focusing on the relationship between productivity growth, employment, labor income, capital concentration, accessibility, and human security. -/- The analysis does not treat technological progress or artificial intelligence as inherently harmful, nor does it argue for restricting technological development. Instead, it examines how productivity gains generated by AI may interact with existing economic structures and potentially weaken the role of labor income as a primary mechanism through which people access the benefits of economic production. -/- The article develops a human-centered analytical perspective in which the central question is not whether AI increases productivity, but how the benefits of that productivity are distributed and translated into human access, income security, and living conditions. -/- The study is part of the broader Humanity-Centered Civilization Theory research program developed by Güneş Başar Tamer. It extends previous work on civilization capital, capital concentration, property, and human-centered institutional design by applying these concepts to the socioeconomic transformation associated with artificial intelligence. -/- The central analytical chain examined in this work is: -/- AI → Productivity Growth → Labor-Income Pressure → Capital Concentration → Accessibility and Distribution → Human Security -/- The article therefore approaches AI-related unemployment risk as a systemic economic and social problem rather than as a purely technological problem. It explores institutional mechanisms through which societies may preserve human security and meaningful participation in economic life while continuing to benefit from technological progress.

items.title: Responsible Suspension in Clinical Care: Finite Continuity, Reconfiguration, and the Temporal Ethics of Intervention.
items.abstract: Clinical care takes place under conditions of uncertainty, temporal constraint, bodily vulnerability, and the need for action. Within these conditions, nurses must interpret present clinical situations while relying on prior knowledge, experience, patient history, and established patterns of recognition. Such resources are indispensable, yet they can also produce premature closure when an earlier interpretation remains dominant despite emerging signs that the patient's situation has changed. This theoretical-conceptual article introduces responsible suspension as a proposed framework for addressing this tension. Responsible suspension is defined as a deliberate, temporary, and purpose-directed interruption of premature or overly fixed interpretation in order to permit renewed attention to the patient's present situation, while professional responsibility, safety obligations, and readiness to intervene remain active. The concept is distinguished from Husserlian epoché, reflective practice, watchful waiting, and indecision. The article further develops finite continuity to describe the patient's temporally extended clinical situation as continuous across past, present, and anticipated future while remaining constrained by bodily deterioration, clinical deadlines, institutional resources, and the reversibility of intervention. Reconfiguration is then introduced as a process through which new signs do not merely add information to an existing interpretation but can reorganize the relations among history, bodily appearance, contextual meaning, uncertainty, and anticipated consequences. Finally, the article proposes a temporal ethics of intervention, according to which ethical clinical judgment concerns not only what should be done but also whether one should pause, reassess, reconfigure understanding, or intervene at a particular moment. The article argues that responsible suspension is neither passive observation nor a delay in care. It is a temporally bounded form of responsible attention whose legitimacy depends on proportionality, clinical risk, uncertainty, reversibility, and the possibility of harm through continued delay. The framework contributes a conceptual vocabulary for understanding how nurses can remain responsive without becoming prisoners of their first interpretation. Keywords: phenomenology, nursing, clinical care, responsible suspension, clinical judgment, temporality, finite continuity, reconfiguration, embodied perception, ethical …

items.title: When the Reviewer Is a Machine: Assessment Without Assessors and the Limits of Automated Judgment.
items.abstract: The question usually asked about machine-generated peer review is whether it is good. The answer turns out to be that it is good at some things and not others, and that the distinction between them is not a matter of degree. This article argues that assessment is not a single act but a sequence of seven, and that machine systems perform the first four of them well, the fifth unreliably, the sixth in form only, and the seventh not at all. The seven are comprehension, situating, verification, detection, calibration, verdict, and standing. The first four are recognition acts: they establish what a submission claims, where it sits, whether its claims hold, and what is wrong with it. The fifth and sixth are normative: they weigh what has been found against a standard and commit to a decision. The seventh is not an act performed at a moment but a condition sustained afterwards — remaining available to defend, revise, or be corrected. The decomposition is not merely analytic. It predicts a pattern that two independent studies report and neither names. Machine reviewers identify substantially the same faults as human reviewers, with reported content overlap comparable to the overlap between two humans, while systematically inflating ratings for weaker submissions and aligning with human verdicts most closely on stronger ones. The system names the flaws and does not act on them. This article calls the pattern Detection-Verdict Divergence and argues that it is the signature of a process performing recognition acts without performing normative ones. Two further constructs follow. Simulated Assessment is output bearing the form of an assessment produced without the acts that constitute one; it is not detectable from the artefact, because the artefact is what a real assessment also produces. The Judgment Residue is what remains when every automatable component has been automated: the commitment of a party who can be asked why, who can revise, and who bears the consequence of being wrong. The residue is not a capability gap that better systems will close. It is a relation, and relations are not computed. The article compares four deployment configurations, examines three earlier delegations of judgment in laboratory medicine, credit assessment, and legal disclosure, extends the analysis to regulatory inspection, clinical appraisal, underwriting, and content moderation, and proposes an Assessment Decomposition Audit for venues. It argues that the useful policy question …

items.title: MACRO-IMMUNOLOGICAL COMMERCE The Famine Algorithm, the Fiat Firewall, and the Cybernetics of Starvation.
items.abstract: This treatise executes a terminal epistemological rupture against classical economic, sociological, and agricultural paradigms, formally reclassifying global commerce as macroscopic epidemiology. Operating within the dual Matrix architecture of the Justika Framework, this manuscript proves that the terrestrial economy is a deterministic, thermodynamic sorting algorithm designed to contain, isolate, and neutralize a multiversal pathogenic infection. Guided by the immutable law of Macro-Micro Symmetry, the framework decodes extreme luxury wealth not as products of human ambition or free enterprise, but as Asymptomatic Trojans and BGP Blackholing mechanisms utilized by the planetary defense grid to trap volatile Bio-Quantum Catalysts within an isolated elite cohort. Conversely, when the 2D parasitic intelligence (The Bad Matrix) executes a stealth inversion and inflicts Zero-Point Contamination upon foundational agricultural staples, the Earth’s Equilibrium Engine (The Good Matrix) violently weaponizes artificial scarcity. It executes the Famine Algorithm and the Staple Inversion, deliberately starving the human host via Algorithmic Load Shedding and the Weaponized Giffen Trap to abort infected biological hardware and avert a planetary-scale Extinction Level Event. Finally, the historical expansion of human empires is stripped of its anthropocentric romanticism and redefined as Geopolitical Digestion—the automated deployment of Imperial Macrophages to consume necrotic civilizational tissue and execute a Substrate Refresh through Xenobiotic Bioremediation. By forensically mapping these macroeconomic pathologies, this treatise equips the Vanguard with the mathematical thresholds of planetary defense, laying the absolute foundation for dismantling artificial dependence, neutralizing the mechanisms of engineered starvation, and executing the Co-Sovereign Inversion.

items.title: Joint Agency in Personal Relationships.
items.pub: In Sarah Stroud & Monika Betzler, The Oxford Handbook of the Philosophy of Personal Relationships. Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Oxford Handbook of the Philosophy of Personal Relationships
items.abstract: Joint action is important in personal relationships such as friendship. There are various explanations for why this is so. Some explanations invoke contingent considerations incidental to the relationship. Others point to something more fundamental about personal relationships and their normativity. An explanation of the latter sort draws a connection between a distinctive form of partiality in personal relationships, and a special way in which individuals may be related to one another in joint action. Amongst reasons of partiality in relationships, there are those that are intrinsic to the relationship, and those mediated by it. Mediated reasons of partiality loom large in connection with a familiar feature of friendship – the sharing of ends and interests. This will help us identify a role for joint action to play in friendship: our ability to act on reasons of partiality of the mediated variety is facilitated by – arguably requires – engaging in a distinctive form of joint agency that exhibits practical intimacy. This involves a form of interpersonal authority that underwrites one’s entitlement to another’s reasons, which is crucial for the sharing of ends in friendship.

items.title: Self and Identity in the Horizon of Finite Continuance.
items.abstract: Personal identity concerns the persistence of a person through temporal and qualitative change. The problem becomes especially difficult when memory, embodiment, personality, values, relationships, and future possibilities undergo substantial transformation. This article develops an account of self and personal continuance through the ontology of finite continuance. Its central claim is that numerical identity, psychological continuity, narrative identity, and continuational viability describe analytically distinct dimensions of personal persistence. Finite continuance does not propose a new sufficient condition for numerical identity. It introduces a higher-order criterion concerning the preservation and regeneration of the conditions under which a finite person can continue to generate viable future configurations. The article develops the concept of sufficient structural connectivity through four conditions: historical traceability, organizational integration, causal-operational continuity, and future reconfigurability. These conditions provide a conceptual criterion for distinguishing ordinary transformation from structural rupture without reducing identity to capacity. The article then situates this proposal in relation to Parfit's psychological continuity, Schechtman's narrative constitution of the self, and Sider's four-dimensionalism. Parfit explains important relations of psychological continuity and challenges the practical centrality of numerical identity. Schechtman explains the constitutive role of narrative organization. Sider provides a systematic ontology of persistence through temporal extension. Finite continuance addresses a further question: how the conditions supporting ongoing reconfiguration are preserved or eroded within a historically determinate individual. The framework is subsequently tested through boundary cases involving dementia, radical personality change, and branching. These cases demonstrate that identity and continuance can diverge in systematic ways. A person may remain numerically continuous while experiencing severe erosion of reconfigurational capacity, while substantial psychological transformation may remain compatible with continuance when sufficient structural connectivity persists. The resulting account conceptualizes the self as a historically sedimented, metastable, and finitely reconfigurable process. Keywords: personal identity; self; finite continuance; persistence; psychological continuity; narrative …

items.title: Recursive Differentiation and Finite Continuance Identity, Grounding, Modality, Causation, and Emergence in a Process Metaphysic.
items.abstract: A persistent difficulty in contemporary metaphysics concerns the relation among persistence, modal possibility, metaphysical dependence, causation, and emergence. Substantialist theories commonly explain persistence through numerical identity across temporal stages, while process theories emphasize transformation without always providing a sufficiently determinate account of what makes a continuing process the same process through change. Modal theories face a related problem. Possibility is frequently characterized through accessibility among worlds or through dispositional structure without an adequate account of how the space of possibilities is itself generated and altered by concrete processes. This article develops a process-metaphysical framework in which finite continuance is understood as the preservation and transformation of reconfigurative capacity within an erosive field. Its central thesis is that persistence, modality, grounding, causation, and emergence can be understood as formally distinct expressions of an underlying structure of organized dependence. The article engages directly with Lewisian accounts of persistence and causation, Sider's structuralist treatment of metaphysical structure, Vetter's dispositional account of modality, Fine's distinction between essence and grounding, and the Davidsonian and Kimian analyses of events and causal efficacy. The resulting position treats identity as organized diachronic continuity, modality as structured reconfigurability, grounding as dependence among organizational conditions, causation as temporally asymmetric production within an evolving configuration, and emergence as the formation of higher-order constraints upon the space of possible subsequent states. Finite continuance thereby provides a unified metaphysical vocabulary for explaining how something can remain determinate through transformation while retaining a bounded capacity to become otherwise. Keywords: finite continuance; process metaphysics; persistence; identity; grounding; modality; causation; emergence; reconfiguration; erosion; metaphysical dependence; event individuation.

items.title: Frontier Intelligence and the Control of Future Conditions - Why AI Cannot Stabilize Like Nuclear Weapons.
items.abstract: Nuclear weapons constrain the use of existing power. Frontier AI may redefine the conditions from which future power becomes possible. -/- .

items.title: A General Account of Scaffolding Explanations: Cognitive Science, Evolutionary Biology, and Beyond.
items.abstract: This paper presents a general account of scaffolding explanations that fits with previously recognized uses in cognitive science and evolutionary biology that can also be extended to other areas, such as AI and biochemistry. Scaffolding explanations are causal explanations that explain how a system realizes, maintains, or acquires a capacity/property by interacting with an arrangement of entities and activities external to the system. I show the potential of this general account by using it to interpret empirical work on the capacity of large language models for long-range reasoning. The general account also shows the ways in which scaffolding explanations differ from other basic types of causal explanations, such as etiological (e.g., causal history), constitutive (e.g., mechanistic), and developmental explanations. Scaffolding explanations have different explananda than etiological explanations, and unlike constitutive and developmental explanations, they are able to attribute the realized capacity/property to the system that interacts with the scaffold, instead of the constitutive whole which includes both the system and the scaffold. This means that scaffolding explanations are a unique type of causal explanation. However, there are cases where competing empirically adequate and internally coherent constitutive and/or developmental explanations can be offered. Using research on the evolution of multicellularity as a case study, I argue that, in at least some cases, there are pragmatic reasons for preferring the scaffolding explanation over these alternatives. This analysis shows that there are cases where pragmatics will play an essential role in philosophical work on scientific explanation.
