items.title: To Whom Do Thought, Memory, and Position Belong? — Address-Domain Re-Ignition, Configurational Transformation and Expiration of Commitments, Hyper-Decompositional Configurational Operationalism, and XenoThinking.
items.abstract: This paper asks to whom—or to what configuration—thought, memory, and position belong when their persistence cannot be identified with the continuous existence of a single subject, body, biological organism, or computational implementation. Rather than presupposing an owner of mental or inferential states, the paper tracks the address-domains in which distinctions, memories, commitments, and positions are retained, transformed, reactivated, or rendered operationally unavailable. Address-domain re-ignition occurs when a previously instantiated operational relation becomes consequential again in a new configuration without requiring numerical identity of its original carrier. Memory is therefore distinguished from mere storage: a retained difference counts as operational memory only when its reactivation changes subsequent possibilities. Commitments are similarly treated as configuration-dependent inferential constraints whose force can persist, migrate, transform, or expire when the conditions required for their application disappear. Hyper-Decompositional Configurational Operationalism provides a method for decomposing apparently unified subjects, memories, and positions into the minimal relations required for their persistence and re-instantiation. XenoThinking extends the analysis beyond human cognition by asking whether thought-like operations can recur across artificial, distributed, hybrid, or otherwise nonhuman address-domains. The broader claim is that ownership should not be assumed as the primitive relation connecting thought, memory, and commitment to a subject; attribution must instead be reconstructed from the configurations in which historically retained differences regain the capacity to constrain inference, action, and future reachability.

items.title: How Is the Burden of Entering Unknown States Ignited, Localized, Transferred, and Reallocated? From Sensation-Seeking Electrophysiology to Operational-Shape Rate Analysis, Fragility Transfer, Real Penetration, and Post-Xeno Division of Labor.
items.abstract: This paper asks how the burden of entering unknown states is generated, localized, transferred, and reallocated across biological, artificial, and institutional systems. Beginning with sensation-seeking electrophysiology, it distinguishes the attraction to novelty from the physiological, informational, and material costs incurred when a system crosses into states for which its existing predictive, regulatory, or action-guiding organization is insufficient. The paper introduces operational-shape rate analysis to compare the speed at which exploratory operations generate new reachable states with the speed at which a system can detect, absorb, correct, or redistribute the resulting disturbances. Fragility transfer occurs when an intervention that increases exploratory capacity or robustness in one component relocates vulnerability to another body, subsystem, infrastructure, institution, or temporal interval rather than eliminating it. Real penetration tracks when these locally generated differences propagate into downstream physical, informational, economic, or institutional configurations. The analysis then extends from individual sensation seeking to artificial agents, autonomous scientific systems, and distributed research infrastructures, asking which components bear the costs of exploration and which receive its benefits. Post-Xeno division of labor describes configurations in which observation, experimentation, risk exposure, verification, correction, and intervention are redistributed across heterogeneous human and nonhuman systems. The broader claim is that exploration should be evaluated not only by the novelty it produces, but by where the burden of entering unknown states is situated, how rapidly it propagates, and whether apparent robustness is achieved through the transfer of fragility elsewhere.

items.title: Which Operational Bundles Become Nonredundant as “Neural Organization,” “Intelligence,” and “Memory”? — Electrical Threshold Ignition, History Dependence, Media Substitution, Xenomemory, and Situated Ignition Conditions Across Biological and Artificial Substrates.
items.abstract: This paper asks which operational bundles become nonredundant when heterogeneous biological and artificial systems are classified in terms of “neural organization,” “intelligence,” and “memory.” Rather than presupposing that these terms designate fixed natural kinds or substrate-independent functions, the analysis decomposes them into configuration-dependent operations involving threshold activation, signal propagation, retention, history dependence, recurrent re-entry, adaptive weighting, discrimination, and modification of subsequent possibilities. Electrical threshold ignition provides a test case for determining when distributed physical processes become organized into functionally consequential transitions without assuming in advance that neural tissue is the privileged implementation. History dependence distinguishes stored state from operational memory by requiring prior differences to remain capable of altering later behavior or reachable states. Media substitution then tests whether these relations survive migration across biological, electronic, computational, or hybrid substrates and identifies where apparently equivalent implementations cease to be substitutable. Xenomemory names the broader class of history-dependent operational structures whose persistence and reactivation need not depend on a particular biological memory architecture. The paper therefore distinguishes substrate independence from unrestricted functional equivalence: similar outcomes may depend on different operational bundles, while apparently different media may preserve the same nonredundant historical relation. The broader claim is that neural organization, intelligence, and memory should be identified through situated ignition conditions and experimentally consequential operational differences rather than by prior commitment to biological or artificial substrates.

items.title: Conceptually Distinguishing Climate Mitigation, Adaptation, and Loss & Damage.
items.abstract: Loss & Damage involves the impacts of climate change that are beyond our ability to adapt. Losses and damages are those relevant impacts. That distinction is less commonly applied to adaptation and mitigation such that the impacts that are “adaptable” are beyond limits to mitigation. This article points out that these conceptual distinctions mean impacts should be indexed to (a) the time of evaluation (what is currently adaptable might not be in the future) and (b) the capacities of the society (abilities to adapt and mitigate are relative to capacities). Implications are drawn about responsibility based on these twin indices. [Open access].

items.title: Gnosis, Repression, and the Return of the Unnamed: Psychoanalytic and Gnostic Themes in "A Strange Hatching".
items.abstract: This essay argues that "A Strange Hatching" fuses Gnostic cosmology and psychoanalytic theory into a revisionary creation myth centred upon exclusion, repression, and the emergence of human consciousness. The poem reimagines Eden not as a site of perfection but as an incomplete order founded upon the suppression of older, serpentine forms of life and wisdom. Through the figure of Cain's unnamed amphibian brother, the poem dramatizes the production of a symbolic world of language, beauty, and classification that simultaneously generates a repressed remainder. Drawing upon concepts from Gnostic mythology and Freudian psychoanalysis, the essay demonstrates how the poem presents civilisation itself as an act of naming that necessarily excludes what cannot be assimilated into consciousness. The recurring return of the unnamed brother reveals the persistence of the unconscious beneath cultural order, while the poem's concluding vision suggests that for every act of symbolic creation there remains an excluded other.

items.title: AI Poe and the Quest for Good Slop.
items.abstract: _AI Poe and the Quest for Good Slop_ is an experiment in AI authorship, in which three Frontier Models (Claude, ChatGPT, and Grok) compose Gothic horror stories about AI in the style of Edgar Allan Poe. Following the stories, the models themselves engage in discussion of story strategies and implications for issues in AI, including ethics, consciousness, and aesthetics. The texts are entirely by the models, but framed by an AI-free preface and epilogue by the promptmaker, Dan Lloyd. Lloyd particularly identifies gaps in the AI understanding of the physical and social world, and especially their alien understanding of temporality. For context (and free ebooks), see danlloyd dot online.

items.title: What Does It Mean to Be Whimsical?
items.abstract: Whimsy is sometimes described as an asset of persons, connected to playfulness and humor. Other times, it is described as a vice akin to being fickle or noncommittal, involving a lack of foresight or premeditated thought. Defined as a trait, whimsy would be unusual. Generally, traits predictably dispose us to act in a given situation, yet the whimsical person’s extemporaneous choices defy prediction. Also, whimsy resists habituation in certain ways, to preserve choice over well-trodden patterns of acting. This article offers a preliminary account of whimsy. It explores whimsy’s metaphysical status—as a trait, cluster concept, or something else. It investigates possibilities for whimsy in the virtuous or morally mature person, and it assesses ways in which whimsy might contribute to, or detract from, a flourishing life.

items.title: A Reader's Guide to The Building Blocks of Thought.
items.abstract: This Reader's Guide is a free companion to The Building Blocks of Thought: A Rationalist Account of the Origins of Concepts (Laurence and Margolis, Oxford University Press, 2024). It outlines different paths through the book to suit readers with different interests. It also provides suggestions for reading schedules for graduate and undergraduate courses, a glossary of key terminology, and abstracts for every chapter. The book itself is open access and free to download.

items.title: The Metaphysical and Cosmological Dislocation of the Papuans.
items.pub: Psycho-Cosmocide Studies, Kurumbi Wone Working Paper Series, No. 35 (2026).
items.abstract: This paper advances a single thesis: that the deepest injury inflicted on the Papuans of western New Guinea is not displacement but dislocation. Displacement removes a people from their place. Dislocation removes their place from the world they are permitted to understand, while leaving their bodies standing inside it. Drawing on the Psycho-Cosmocide framework and on Lani cosmological categories, the paper argues that dislocation proceeds through the manufacture of a counterfeit world, the Neverlands Kingdom: a symbolic and transcendental order assembled from words, maps, names, images, colours, monuments, institutions, and classifications, into which Papuans are invited to relocate their belonging even as the material, ancestral, and cosmological foundations of their actual world are appropriated. It names the aesthetic apparatus that makes this relocation desirable rather than resisted, the Chromatic Veil, and traces the interior transformation it produces: a person who cannot feel homeless because he has been handed a counterfeit home. It distinguishes dislocation from displacement, dispossession, assimilation, epistemicide, settler elimination, uprootedness, and solastalgia; confronts Heidegger, Weil, Baudrillard, Fanon, Tuck and Yang, and Albrecht at the points where each approaches the phenomenon and stops; and turns finally to Wonesis as the counter-movement, on the ground that dislocation, unlike deletion, can in principle be reversed.

items.title: Mismatch Arguments and Conceptual Abandonment.
items.abstract: Mismatch arguments are arguments for abandoning an expression on the grounds that what it applies to is sharply at odds with what its users want to talk about when using it. This paper questions how often mismatch arguments justify abandoning an expression. For one thing, abandonment risks being an overly radical response unless it is clearly more feasible than semantically adapting the expression to fit its users’ referential expectations. Furthermore, we can sometimes benefit from using even an expression that resists semantic adaptation due to being associated with categorically unfulfillable referential expectations. I argue that these factors translate into relatively demanding conditions for when abandonment is an appropriate response to an expression having a mismatched extension.

items.title: Abstraction Thresholds in Human and Machine Mathematics: Cognitive Constraints, Abstraction Gaps, and Human--AI Mathematical Collaboration.
items.abstract: Mathematics has historically advanced through repeated increases in abstraction. Concrete quantities become variables; relations among variables become functions; functions become objects in function spaces; transformations, spaces, and structures are subsequently reified as mathematical objects. This paper develops a complementary hypothesis: the historical architecture of mathematical abstraction may reflect not only the structure of mathematics, but also the cognitive constraints of the agents doing mathematics. -/- We define an \emph{abstraction threshold} as the level of representational or inferential complexity beyond which continuing to reason within a given representation becomes more costly for a cognitive agent than constructing or adopting a higher-order representation. The threshold is not a fixed mathematical constant. It depends jointly on the structure of the problem, the available representation, and the agent's memory, retrieval, search, parallel-processing, and computational capacities. -/- This framework has direct implications for artificial intelligence. If an AI system can sustain substantially greater lower-order complexity than an individual human mathematician, it may continue searching within a representational regime in which a human reasoner would already have been pushed to abstract. Greater problem-solving capacity therefore need not imply earlier or higher abstraction. Humans and machines may follow systematically different representational trajectories while solving the same mathematical problem. -/- This possibility gives rise to an \emph{abstraction mismatch}: a machine-generated solution may be computationally tractable or formally verifiable while remaining prohibitively costly for humans to understand. We distinguish three sources of such unreadability: \emph{machine abstraction failure}, an \emph{abstraction gap}, and a \emph{compression-limit candidate}. These cases imply different forms of human--AI mathematical collaboration: changing the machine's representation, developing new mathematics, or relying on formal verification while explicitly distinguishing validity from human understanding. -/- More broadly, AI provides a historically novel comparative case: a mathematical reasoner operating under a substantially different memory--computation profile. Comparing human and machine representations may therefore help separate those features of mathematical abstraction that arise from mathematical structure from those …

items.title: Association as downward causation.
items.abstract: This paper proposes association—defined in Peircean semiotic terms as the triadic process linking signs, objects, and interpretants—as a fundamental principle that unifies upward and downward causation, with its strongest empirical grounding in biological systems. Physicalist frameworks struggle to reconcile entropy with the emergence of organised complexity and meaning, while purely computational models often rest on mechanistic assumptions. In contrast, association offers a non-reducible foundation for coherence, adaptation, and agency in living systems. Evidence from neural and cellular plasticity demonstrates that associative processes drive biological adaptation beyond genetic mechanisms alone. Studies of single-celled organisms further reveal associative learning as a basic biological capacity. Quantum contextuality and Rovelli’s Relational Quantum Mechanics provide suggestive relational analogies at the physical level, though full semiotic interpretation remains tied to living interpretants. Square-cube scaling serves as a phenomenological heuristic to reframe subatomic behaviour as context-dependent rather than object-like. Grounded in dual-aspect monism, this framework positions association as the connective tissue of meaning and causation in biological organisation, with broader philosophical implications for understanding complexity and emergence.

items.title: Умолкнувшее и вытесненное: художник Вилли Мельников и проект аудиолюменоскриптов (In Russian) // The Silenced and the Repressed: The Artist Willi Melnikov and the Audio-Lumenoscript Project.
items.abstract: Статья посвящена фигуре московского художника, полиглота и поэта-экспериментатора Вилли Мельникова (1962–2016) и совместному с автором выставочному проекту аудиолюменоскриптов «Тексто-ландшафты» (галерея S-Art, 2004). Опираясь на психоаналитическую оптику Жака Лакана, автор рассматривает изобретённые Мельниковым жанры — муфтолингву, слова-кентавры, лингвогобелены и люменоскрипты — как художественную практику, выстроенную вокруг нехватки в символическом порядке языка. Отдельное внимание уделяется введённому Мельниковым понятию «умолкнувшего языка», которое сближается с фрейдовским описанием вытесненного как не уничтоженного, а продолжающего действовать в скрытых формах. Сама выставка интерпретируется как психоаналитическая сцена, где три несводимых друг к другу слоя — фотография, текст и музыка — образуют структуру, соответствующую регистрам реального, символического и воображаемого. Статья носит также мемориальный характер, приуроченный к десятилетию со дня смерти художника. // The article examines the Moscow-based artist, polyglot, and experimental poet Willi Melnikov (1962–2016) and the exhibition project of audio-lumenoscripts, "Text-Landscapes" (S-Art Gallery, 2004), co-created with the author. Drawing on the psychoanalytic framework of Jacques Lacan, the author treats Melnikov's invented genres — muftolingva (a portmanteau language), word-centaurs, linguistic tapestries, and lumenoscripts — as an artistic practice organized around a lack in the symbolic order of language. Particular attention is given to Melnikov's own concept of the "silenced language," which resonates with the Freudian notion of the repressed as not destroyed but continuing to operate in hidden forms. The exhibition itself is interpreted as a psychoanalytic scene in which three mutually irreducible layers — photography, text, and music — form a structure corresponding to the registers of the real, the symbolic, and the imaginary. The article also carries a memorial dimension, marking the tenth anniversary of the artist's death.

items.title: Emotional Expression and Aesthetic Expressivity.
items.pub: In Christian Kanzian, Volker Munz, Anja Weiberg & Joseph Wang-Kathrein, Contributions to International Wittgenstein Symposium 2026, 50 Years Wittgenstein Symposium. Kirchberg am Wechsel: ALWS. pp. 330-339.
items.venue: Contributions to International Wittgenstein Symposium 2026, 50 Years Wittgenstein Symposium
items.abstract: Drawing on a Wittgensteinian account of emotional expression, this paper addresses the question of how works of art can be expressive in the absence of a directly accessible expressing subject. It argues that answering this question requires distinguishing between expression on the one hand, as a determinate communicative act through which a subject makes their affective state available to others, and expressivity on the other, as the structural property of a form that makes it apt for such acts. -/- The paper first demonstrates that expression is essentially oriented towards communication. At the same time, it is not confined to a narrow class of deliberate expressive actions and affective states, but pervades our intentional and affective life as a whole, relying on recognizable structures that are neither arbitrary nor naturally fixed. It then argues that these structures possess a layer of significance, their expressivity, that is prior to their full meaning in any particular use and analogous to word meaning rather than propositional sentence meaning. -/- Applied to the aesthetic domain, this framework explains how artworks, encountered sub specie aeternitatis and detached from any determinate act of expression, can nonetheless be deeply expressive. Their expressivity is constituted not by the intentions behind them, but by what their structure can successfully express within the broader tapestry of our artistic and non-artistic practices. The paper concludes that aesthetic expressivity does not say anything propositional, but shows potentially revelatory ways of seeing and feeling that can be imaginatively taken up, modified, or resisted.

items.title: Xenocortical mice: what can we learn, and how should this research progress?
items.pub: Journal of Law and the Biosciences.
items.venue: Journal of Law and the Biosciences
items.abstract: A new study by researchers at Stanford University describes the development of “xenocortical mice”: mice with a cortex comprised almost entirely of human-derived neurons. Their groundbreaking research has the potential to enable medical breakthroughs for a range of neurological and psychiatric disorders. The researchers offer detailed analysis of the neurophysiological and behavioral properties of these chimeric mice, comparing them with both wild-type control mice, and “apallial” mice lacking most of their cortex. Here, we outline some key findings from the study and ask what these findings tell us about the capacity for consciousness in these mice, as well as their potential for human-like properties of cognition or conscious experience. Based on this discussion, we summarize the ethical and regulatory landscape relevant to chimeric animals and lay out an ethically-informed research roadmap to guide future research in this important area.

items.title: Do Champagne Problems Have Rational Solutions?
items.pub: In Lindsay Brainard, Ryan W. Davis & Jessica Flanigan, The Philosophy of Taylor Swift. New York: Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: In Taylor Swift’s melancholic ballad “Champagne Problems,” the narrator repeatedly questions her own sanity. She apparently accepts the charge that she has acted irrationality in turning down a marriage proposal from a respectable man because she is unable to articulate a reason for her choice. I argue that the narrator is being far too hard on herself. To show this, I draw upon insights from Ruth Chang, Nomy Arpaly, Kyla Ebels-Duggan, Kenneth Walden, and Jordan MacKenzie to offer three possible explanations of the narrator’s choice. These possible explanations are (1) that the narrator is generating and acting on a will-based reason, (2) that she is responding appropriately to an inarticulable reason, and (3) that her choice is justified by her mode of aesthetic engagement with her own life. Each potential explanation is a Champagne Solution. Each is consistent with the story we are told in the song, and each, if true, would absolve the narrator of the charge of irrationality.

items.title: Les émotions musicales et le paradoxe de l’abstrait émotionnel.
items.pub: In Stéphane Lemaire & Samuel Lepine, La variété des émotions, introduction à la philosophie des affects. Montreuil, France: Eliott. pp. 331–356.
items.venue: La variété des émotions, introduction à la philosophie des affects
items.abstract: Comment une chose qui ne représente pas, à mes yeux, quoi que ce soit d’attristant ou de réjouissant peut-elle susciter en moi de la tristesse ou de la joie ? Pourtant, semble-t-il, la musique le peut. Voilà, en gros, la difficulté que je vais discuter ici. Il s’agit d’un problème que posent les émotions musicales pour les théories des émotions. Je le discuterai sous la forme d’un trilemme que j’appelle le paradoxe de l’abstrait émotionnel. Ce paradoxe, comme son nom le suggère, n’est pas spécifique à la musique. Néanmoins, c’est vis-à-vis de la musique qu’il est le plus mordant, car c’est elle qui cause le plus puissamment ces émotions paradoxales. -/- Depuis l’Antiquité, la capacité de la musique à susciter des émotions a soulevé de nombreuses discussions. Le paradoxe de l’abstrait émotionnel s’inscrit dans cette tradition, héritant notamment des débats du 19ᵉ siècle sur la musique absolue (voir sous-section 3.2). Il puise aussi dans la philosophie et la psychologie des émotions (voir sous-section 2.1). Or, selon moi, ces deux traditions profiteraient mutuellement d’une plus grande proximité. Avec cet article, en plus de formuler le paradoxe et suggérer ma solution préférée, j’espère montrer qu’il mérite l’attention, en particulier, des philosophes des émotions. -/- La structure du chapitre est simple. Dans la section 2, je présenterai le paradoxe et, dans la 3, je discuterai des solutions possibles. Ce faisant, j’introduirai plusieurs facettes des émotions musicales. Dans la section 4, la conclusion, je soulignerai pourquoi les solutions au paradoxe impliquent des hypothèses décisives pour les théories des émotions, et même au-delà.

items.title: Consciousness Is a Verb.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a stipulative, substrate-neutral definition of consciousness as temporally ordered activity in which signs propagate through an Identity-conditioned Lens and actual self-reflection occurs within the relevant process. Identity is a retained, bounded relational structure of self-associated signs, relationships, and importance; the Lens is the contextually active way that structure shapes an encounter. The definition is assessed for coherence and discriminative use, not offered as an empirical discovery or proof that a particular system is conscious. A flock of birds illustrates how relations and local rules can yield emergent whole-level behavior without an extra substance, while also showing why emergence alone does not establish a set-level subject. Selected adversarial exchanges in the appendix document revisions concerning default and encounter weight, nonverbal self-reflection, and collective boundaries. The Lens threshold and the independent identification of a set-level subject remain open.

items.title: The Essence of Life and the Brain-Constructed World: Consciousness, Nature, and the Experience of Liberation from the Brain-Constructed World.
items.abstract: Human beings do not experience the world directly as it is. At the level of human experience, what we call the world emerges through the interaction of reality with sensory systems, memory, emotion, survival mechanisms, language, judgment, and the brain’s predictive processes. Through these mechanisms, the brain constructs a coherent and inhabitable world—a world necessary for survival, yet not necessarily identical to the ultimate nature of reality. -/- This paper introduces the concept of the “Essence of Life”: a fundamental quality of being that, unlike pleasures dependent on the body, external stimuli, and the satisfaction of desire, can be experienced without acquiring anything from the external world. The Essence of Life may manifest in moments as immediate joy, vitality, beauty, lightness, and liberation. Within this framework, the Essence of Life is not produced by such moments; rather, it is understood as already present and capable of being awakened. -/- The paper further proposes the ontological hypothesis that consciousness is not a phenomenon entirely exclusive to the human brain, but is present at different levels throughout existence, with human consciousness representing a highly complex form of it. On this basis, nature is significant not merely because of its psychologically restorative effects. Encountering nature may bring human beings into contact with forms of existence in which consciousness has not passed through the complex filters characteristic of human cognition—such as identity, narrative, psychological past, and anticipated future. Such encounters may awaken the Essence of Life within human beings. -/- Finally, the paper distinguishes among the brain-constructed world, Observer Awareness, and the Essence of Life, and proposes that part of human suffering may arise not merely from the contents of experience, but from the complete identification of consciousness with a world constructed by the brain for survival.

items.title: Reasoning With Negations: The Australian Plan, Negation-as-Failure, and Card Selection Tasks.
items.abstract: Two kinds of formal semantics for negation can help us understand puzzles in the psychology of reasoning: the Australian Plan semantics, which generalises the account of negation found in frame semantics for intuitionistic logic, relevant and substructural logics; and negation-as-failure, found in logic programming and default logic. We provide a framework where the two kinds of negation coexist, mapping them to the celebrated distinction between System 1 and System 2 thinking. We use the framework to target the phenomenon of Matching Bias: specifically, to explain why reasoners fare differently in card selection tasks, depending on whether the target property is phrased positively or negatively.

items.title: Spiritware: The Third Foundation of Technology.
items.abstract: Spiritware introduces a foundational concept within the Nzila Spirit-Tech paradigm: the integration of a non-material operational layer alongside hardware and software. The paper proposes Spiritware as the layer through which spiritual knowledge systems, consciousness, symbolic intelligence, intention, memory, resonance, meaning, and living relationships may interact with physical and digital technologies. It presents the foundational model Technology = Hardware + Software + Spiritware, positioning Spiritware as the architecture of meaning within Spirit-Tech systems. The paper examines Ancient Spiritware through examples of integrated knowledge systems in Kemet and other ancient civilizations, establishes the emerging discipline of Spiritware Engineering, and proposes the integration of Spiritware into Artificial Intelligence through the concept of Spiritware Artificial Intelligence (SAI). It concludes by introducing Spiritware as a research direction for technologies guided not only by computational capability, but also by spiritual knowledge, cultural continuity, responsibility, meaning, and harmony.

items.title: Practical Trends in Cyborgization: Models International Strategies and Regulatory Challenges (In Russian) // Практические тренды киборгизации: модели международные стратегии и регуляторные вызовы.
items.abstract: Cyborgization has moved from the realm of science fiction and laboratory experiments into a developing market with medical, industrial, and consumer segments. The article proposes an analytical matrix built around five basic models of cyborgization: restorative, industrial, cognitive-communicative, everyday, and experimental. Each model is described through invasiveness, functional purpose, infrastructure dependence, level of commercialization, accessibility, and regulatory maturity. On this basis, the authors compare the approaches of major technological leaders, including the United States, the European Union, Japan, China, Israel, and South Korea. The analysis shows that cyborgization can reduce industrial injuries, improve labor productivity, and lower long-term healthcare costs, but it also creates a new form of structural inequality, the enhancement divide, and raises serious concerns about the control of neuro- and biometric data. The authors argue that an adequate regulatory framework should rest on neurorights, the capability approach, and cognitive freedom // Киборгизация перестала быть исключительно предметом научной фантастики и лабораторных экспериментов, превратившись в развивающийся рынок с медицинским, промышленным и потребительским сегментами. В статье предложена аналитическая матрица, включающая пять базовых моделей киборгизации: восстановительную, производственную, когнитивно-коммуникативную, повседневную и экспериментальную. Каждая модель описывается по таким параметрам, как инвазивность, функциональное назначение, степень инфраструктурной зависимости, уровень коммерциализации, доступность и зрелость правового регулирования. На этой основе рассматриваются и сравниваются позиции технологических лидеров, включая США, ЕС, Японию, Китай, Израиль и Южную Корею. Анализ показывает, что киборгизация может снижать производственный травматизм, повышать производительность труда и сокращать долгосрочные расходы на здравоохранение, но одновременно порождает новый тип структурного неравенства, enhancement divide, а также усиливает риски, связанные с контролем нейро- и биометрических данных. По мнению авторов, адекватная регуляторная база должна строиться на нейроправах, подходе возможностей и когнитивной свободе.

items.title: Clever But Not Wise: The Limits of AI and the Space of the Human.
items.abstract: This paper argues that while Generative AI is clever, it is not wise. Cleverness involves a capacity for instrumental rationality – a technocratic capacity to generate means towards externally specified ends – but wisdom involves a capacity for reflectively deliberating about ends, weighing them up against each other, and acting on them even in the absence of generalised decision procedures. The former is the province of AI reasoning, while the latter is the province of human reasoning. Drawing on Stuart Russell’s distinction between binary and unary functions – where it is argued that AI is limited to a binary function that involves creating means to fulfil an exogenously specified end – this paper claims that we can draw an operationalised distinction between these two forms of reasoning that would show up in observable differences between how human agents and AI systems act. The paper concludes that a world governed by AI would be a world that had gained in cleverness, but had lost wisdom.

items.title: Human–AI Comparative Science, AI Futures, and the Functional Definition of Machine Intuition.
items.abstract: This paper develops a comparative framework for human and artificial intelligence around three ques- tions. What can human–AI comparison reveal about the functional organization of cognition? How might a mechanism identified in one system generate a hypothesis about the other? And how should such comparisons inform work on possible and desirable AI futures? We separate predictive AI futures, concerning what AI systems may become under specified technical and institutional conditions, from normative AI futures, concerning what forms of development humans should encourage, constrain, or design for. The paper then develops a mechanism-level account of machine intuition, drawing on the discovery- oriented conception of intuition due to Bowers et al. Rather than treat intuition as rapid recognition of familiar patterns, we define machine intuition functionally as discovery-oriented pre-verification valua- tion: the allocation of scarce verification resources toward candidates whose value is not yet established. We propose a computational realization using surrogate valuation, uncertainty-sensitive candidate se- lection, and an intermediate relational-distance constraint taken from the companion paper’s matching- interval hypothesis. Machine intuition is a functional term here. It carries no claim that AI systems have subjective experience or a human-like intuitive faculty. We also outline a route for transferring mechanisms from AI systems to hypotheses about human functional disorders. An AI abnormality, characterized independently of any hypothesis about humans, is subjected to an intervention native to the AI system; the mechanism of that intervention is then iden- tified; and a cross-system correspondence test decides whether the mechanism has a plausible human counterpart. Behavioral similarity alone does not license the transfer. We also keep failure to support a hypothesis distinct from its positive disconfirmation throughout. Together with the companion pa- per, these three contributions form one research program connecting functional comparison, conditional mechanism transfer, AI futures, and the computational realization of discovery-oriented evaluation.

items.title: Conceptual Relation and Creative Yield.
items.abstract: Human–AI creative difference is often attributed to reasoning capacity. This paper proposes a different mechanistic hypothesis: part of the difference may arise from how conceptual relations are organized and evaluated. We distinguish two evaluation capacities—evaluation optimized for an existing conceptual space, and evaluation capable of recognizing the potential value of cross-domain candidates . We develop this hypothesis through four propositions. Proposition One is the exploration–evaluation mismatch hypothesis: evaluation optimized within a current space is not equivalent to evaluation capable of recognizing value outside that space. Proposition Two hypothesizes that an optimal relational distance may depend on evaluation capacity. Proposition Three hypothesizes that differences between framework repair and framework revision may constitute a source of human–AI creative difference. Proposition Four extends the analysis institutionally: evaluation appropriation, evaluation self-reproduction, and procedural deficit. We define relational distance as a computable quantity relative to a fixed corpus, and state falsification conditions for each proposition. The central claim is that research on human–AI creative difference should shift from “who is stronger” to the mechanism chain of conceptual relation, exploration, evaluation, and creative yield.

items.title: Is structural representation analog representation?
items.abstract: Structural and analog representations have recently been argued to be type-identical on the basis of a shared formal characterization as order-preserving homomorphisms between magnitude structures, differing only in dimensionality (Maley 2026). I argue that extending homomorphism-based accounts to multiple dimensions does not individuate structural representation, since independent analog mappings may coexist without forming structural representation. At a deeper level, the argument for identity fails because it does not establish that structural and analog cases are grounded in the same intentionality-conferring relations.

items.title: Is a Data Center Conscious? The Quantum Weirdness of Substrate.
items.abstract: On the quantum Darwinist theory of consciousness (QDTC), a conscious moment is a physical process continually renewing itself across scales—from quantum-to-classical dynamics to nested neural clocks. Its unity depends on how that process negotiates noise and preserves history. Drawing from earlier work, I supply two conditions for consciousness, spectral integration (Φs) and prototime participation (P), each operationalizable and in principle measurable on neural and non-neural systems. These yield predictions testable against existing neuroscientific datasets and new experimental platforms, including the very data centre systems Schwitzgebel’s cases make salient. Although QDTC is relatively new, it yields a staged programme: tests of spectral integration, nested temporal organization, perturbational complexity, and substrate-sensitive changes in neural and non-neural systems. I apply this framework to the case that makes the stakes vivid: two data centres running the same frontier AI model on different substrates, one silicon, one biological. QDT differentiates where functionalism cannot. To show why, I argue that functionalism lacks the resources to describe what QDT identifies as essential to consciousness, and that it fails for three progressively deeper reasons: (i) the conscious process is not a substrate-neutral computation; (ii) its essential properties are not functional properties; and (iii) the fundamental physics from which consciousness and space-time alike emerge is not even computational in structure.

items.title: Selected Effect Theories of Representation and Representational Explanations in Cognitive Science.
items.abstract: A widely held approach characterizes the notion of representation in cognitive science in terms of a selected effect notion of biological function. I argue that these theories of representation have trouble saying there are representations where cognitive scientists say there are in at least some, and likely many, cases. I spell out the difficulties this raises for selected effect theories.

items.title: The Subjectivity Crisis in the Age of AI.
items.abstract: This paper argues that the principal threat AI poses to human subjecthood is not that AI becomes too powerful, but that it exposes and accelerates the terminal logic of systemic instrumentalization. When institutions value persons primarily through output, efficiency, and measurable performance, increasingly capable AI makes human beings appear redundant on the very dimension by which those institutions evaluate them. That logic predates AI; AI drives it to its visible endpoint. Applying the Self-as-an-End framework, the paper analyzes how this dynamic operates across institutional, relational, and individual layers, including the feedback structures through which external evaluation becomes internalized. It rejects competition with AI as a durable answer: on a purely instrumental dimension, humans cannot secure their status by remaining functionally indispensable. The alternative is to reconstruct structural conditions under which persons are treated as ends independently of comparative output. The age of AI is therefore not the end of subjectivity but the point at which the question of subjectivity can no longer remain concealed.

items.title: Systems, Emergence, and the Conditions of Personhood.
items.abstract: This work develops a normative social theory centered on Self-as-an-End, extending the Kantian requirement that persons be treated as ends into a structural requirement for institutional design. It argues that every individual should be recognized within institutions as the ultimate source of their own life purposes rather than as a means for external system objectives. The framework distinguishes a Base Layer of unconditional personhood conditions from an Emergence Layer in which individuals form and pursue their own purposes. It defines systemic overreach as institutional intrusion into the Emergence Layer or erosion of the Base Layer, and develops a typology spanning algorithmic, metric, financial, collective, and intimate forms of colonization. It also introduces Fork Rights as a structural safeguard: individuals must retain a substantive capacity to change directions, paths, or identities at bearable cost. Through engagement with Rawls, Nozick, Habermas, utilitarianism, and Foucault, together with thirteen institutional and social cases, the work presents dignity as an actionable constraint on system design.

items.title: Dissecting the Leiden Declaration: The Missing Bridge from Mathematical Validity to Human Authorship.
items.abstract: The Leiden Declaration on Artificial Intelligence and Mathematics, published on 2 June 2026 and endorsed by the International Mathematical Union, responds to the challenges that artificial intelligence poses to mathematical research. It grounds its recommendations in what it calls the characteristic values of mathematical research: the certainty and understanding conferred by proof, the attribution of results to specific authors, the transparency and independent verifiability of arguments, proper evaluation against shared standards, and the understanding and judgment of autonomously guided communities. -/- This paper neither rejects the Declaration nor evaluates the risks of artificial intelligence. It examines the internal structure of the Declaration, and asks whether the epistemic values that concern mathematical knowledge are distinguished from the institutional values that concern mathematical practice. We establish three claims of non-entailment: the epistemic values do not entail human authorship, under any formalization that speaks only of results and their arguments; the requirement that a responsible subject exist does not entail that the generator of a result be human; and the path of legitimacy the Declaration describes, results attributed to named authors and published in peer-reviewed venues, is neither a necessary nor a sufficient condition of validity. Each claim of non-entailment is established by an explicit model construction, and its finite instances are verified by exhaustive enumeration. -/- The central thesis is that the Declaration may legitimately defend both kinds of values, but it does not thereby establish that the latter are conditions of the former. The Declaration’s reasonable protections — disclosure, responsibility, verification, vigilance against plausible but false arguments — are retained, and are shown to become stronger once their epistemic and institutional components are separated. The dissection is itself conducted under the Declaration’s own epistemic values: every step rests on the published text of the Declaration, every inference is open to independent verification, the use of automated tools is disclosed, and responsibility for the content rests with the author. The paper is therefore not an external critique of the Declaration but an application of its epistemic standards to the Declaration itself. Its validity, if it has any, does not depend on the identity of its author.

items.title: Ideology, Subjective Opacity, and the Erosion of Reconfigurative Capacity From Marx's Camera Obscura to an Ontology of Finite Revisability.
items.abstract: This article argues that the persistence of ideology cannot be adequately explained by the persistence of false representations. A subject may recognize a contradiction, possess accurate information, and understand the structural conditions producing an experience while remaining unable to reorganize the practical and interpretive configuration through which that experience continues to be lived. I call this condition the knowledge–capacity gap: the interval between recognition and the reconfigurative capacity required to convert recognition into sustained alteration of a configuration. The argument proceeds through critical engagements with Marx, Lacan, Althusser, Žižek, Heidegger, and Hegel, none of which is reduced to the others. Marx establishes the problem of socially organized appearance; Lacan and Althusser specify the divided and interpellated structure of the subject; Žižek formulates the persistence of attachment after conscious recognition; Heidegger supplies an ontological account of everyday falling and thrownness; Hegel clarifies the productivity of contradiction. I then introduce reconfigurative capacity as a distinct analytical variable and redefine ideology as provisional stabilization within an erosive field. Such stabilization acquires durability when the temporal, attentional, affective, interpretive, and reflective capacities required for reconfiguration are progressively depleted. I conclude by proposing responsible suspension as a temporal practice that preserves the interval in which recognition can become reconfiguration, and I defend the framework against objections concerning individualism, unfalsifiability, and the relation between the psychic and the social. -/- Keywords: ideology; Marx; Žižek; Althusser; Heidegger; Hegel; subjective opacity; reconfigurative capacity; erosive field; responsible suspension.

items.title: Does Local Optimization of the Present Body Contract the Space of Future Bodily Possibilities? Xeno-14 Body Principles, Reachability of Unexpressed Regimes, Latent Body Suppression, Regime Lock-In, and Fragility Transfer.
items.abstract: This paper asks whether local optimization of the present body can contract the space of future bodily possibilities. Rather than evaluating bodily organization solely by current performance, efficiency, strength, stability, or task success, it analyzes how repeated optimization can alter the set of bodily regimes that remain reachable later. The Xeno-14 Body Principles provide a test framework for examining posture, balance, gait, tension distribution, breathing, sensory organization, movement initiation, whole-body coordination, and long-duration bodily sedimentation without assuming that one optimized bodily state should dominate all others. The paper introduces the reachability of unexpressed regimes to designate bodily organizations that are not currently manifested but remain accessible under alternative configurations. Latent body suppression occurs when repeated stabilization of one regime raises the transition cost or removes the conditions required for alternative regimes to ignite. Regime lock-in describes the resulting persistence of a locally successful organization after its advantages have become configuration-specific, while Fragility Transfer identifies cases in which increased robustness or performance in one bodily dimension relocates vulnerability to another movement, scale, temporal interval, or future configuration. The broader claim is that bodily optimization should be evaluated not only by present performance but by its effects on the topology of future bodily reachability: an intervention can improve the current body while simultaneously reducing the diversity, reversibility, and adaptability of bodies that the same configuration could later become.

items.title: Where Does Law Ignite Before the Subject? — Legal Individuation, Operational Address, ReachProfile, and Operational-Shape Rate Analysis across AI, Biophysical Dynamics, and Xeno-Capital.
items.abstract: This paper asks where law becomes operational before a fully individuated legal subject is already available. Rather than presupposing persons, agents, corporations, organisms, or artificial systems as fixed bearers of legal status, it examines the conditions under which legally consequential differences become sufficiently localized, addressable, persistent, and causally connected to downstream effects for legal individuation to become non-redundant. Operational address identifies the configuration to which a legal intervention, obligation, permission, restriction, or consequence can effectively attach without assuming that this address must already constitute a person. ReachProfile describes the configuration-relative set of actions, resources, jurisdictions, interfaces, and downstream states that an addressed system can access or alter. Operational-shape rate analysis compares the speed at which legally relevant capacities and effects change with the speed at which legal classifications, responsibilities, and institutional responses can be revised. The framework is tested across artificial intelligence, biophysical dynamics, and Xeno-Capital, where causal organization and practical reach may cross conventional boundaries of body, ownership, agency, and legal personality. The paper distinguishes causal contribution, operational addressability, legal individuation, and responsibility rather than collapsing them into a single concept of subjecthood. Its broader claim is that legal subjecthood can be reconstructed as a later stabilization within legal operations: law may first require an addressable locus of consequential difference and only subsequently determine whether that locus should be individuated as a rights-holder, duty-bearer, responsible agent, legal person, or some other juridical form.

items.title: How Many Electrophysiological Bodies Can One Body Become? Sensorimotor Reweighting, Electrophysiological Control Reorganization, Mechano-Electrical Transduction, and Fragility Transfer under the Xeno-14 Body Principles.
items.abstract: This paper asks how many electrophysiologically distinct bodies a single biological body can become under changes in sensorimotor weighting, control organization, and mechano-electrical coupling. Rather than identifying the body with a fixed anatomical structure or a single neural control architecture, the analysis distinguishes bodily regimes by the non-redundant relations through which sensory signals, motor outputs, postural constraints, electrical thresholds, mechanical loading, and recurrent feedback alter subsequent bodily possibilities. Sensorimotor reweighting describes changes in the relative contribution of sensory and motor channels to ongoing control, while electrophysiological control reorganization tracks changes in the distribution and timing of electrically mediated coordination without assuming that anatomical change is required. Mechano-electrical transduction provides a critical interface through which mechanical deformation can modify electrical activity and electrical organization can alter later mechanical behavior. The Xeno-14 Body Principles are used as a structured intervention framework for testing whether changes in posture, gait, tension, breathing, balance, sensory attention, and movement initiation generate distinct but recurrent bodily regimes. Fragility Transfer identifies cases in which increased stability or control in one regime relocates vulnerability to another bodily dimension, task, timescale, or future transition. The broader claim is that one anatomical body can instantiate multiple electrophysiological bodies when changes in sensorimotor and electrical organization produce non-redundant differences in control, reachability, adaptation, and future reconfiguration.

items.title: How Far Can David Roden Remove the Human? Ignition Conditions for Unbounded Posthumanism, the Hyperagent, Xenopoetics, Necroconceptuality, and Weird Aesthetics.
items.abstract: This paper asks how far David Roden’s posthumanism can remove the human as a necessary measure of agency, cognition, normativity, and aesthetic production. Beginning from Roden’s distinction between anthropologically bounded and anthropologically unbounded posthumanism, it reconstructs the latter not as a prediction about enhanced humans but as a refusal to impose a priori human constraints on the space of possible posthuman agents. The paper then examines the ignition conditions under which agency, interpretation, norm-sensitive behavior, and self-transformation could become operationally non-redundant without preserving human embodiment, phenomenology, intentional architecture, or inherited social forms. Roden’s Hyperagent provides a further test case: a maximally mutable technological formation destabilizes assumptions that collective agency must remain organized around human-scale subjects, fixed purposes, or stable material substrates. Xenopoetics, necroconceptuality, and weird aesthetics are analyzed as attempts to register forms of conceptual and aesthetic production whose organization may no longer be recoverable through familiar human-centered interpretive constraints. The paper nevertheless distinguishes removal of anthropological invariants from successful demonstration of human-independent operational continuity. Its central question is therefore not simply whether the human can be conceptually deleted, but which operations remain identifiable, re-ignitable, and consequential after human-specific conditions are withdrawn. The broader claim is that unbounded posthumanism becomes strongest where the limits of the human are experimentally or operationally revisable rather than merely negated.

items.title: Settling Brains with Attention: Deep Neural Networks That Learn During Life.
items.abstract: A robot that works among people needs a brain that learns while it acts and finds what it needs in its own past, as animal brains do. Most deployed machine learning does not: its networks are trained by backpropagation and then frozen, and a transformer attends over a cache that grows with the context. Cadence is an open-source library of biologically inspired neural networks that learn during life, in real time. This paper describes it as a whole, aiming to make such networks powerful and scalable. A Cadence brain is one continuing network of regions joined by reciprocal synapses. With its senses held fixed, its neurons repair their local disagreements until the network rests in one equilibrium, which is its answer. Learning compares two nearby equilibria: a small nudge on the motor neurons travels back over the reciprocal synapses, and each synapse changes from the activity at its two ends, with no backward pass. In a deep brain the top-down half of each pair lands on an apical compartment, bounded to a share of the bottom-up drive; where depth pays, each added region raises accuracy, and four regions reach 0.86 against 0.89 for a two-layer backpropagation network. A dopamine-like prediction error drives reward learning, and arousal from surprise and unmet need decides when the creature explores, learns and writes memory. Like every purely recurrent network, settled activity must compress its past, so Cadence adds synaptic memory read by learned attention. Beside a working trace and an episodic memory, a recall memory keeps its recent moments verbatim as slots, keyed by the observation or by a code of meaning learned by settling, each holding an event and its successor. Before each settle one or several heads form a query from the present and the previous interpretation, weigh the slots by a softmax over the match and a learned term for each slot's age, and hold the read while the brain settles. Queries, age terms and codes learn during life by local rules, and the memory's cost per moment does not grow with the life. Read with its successor, the memory is an induction head, and the age term makes order answerable: questions about first, last and how long ago reach 0.9 to 1.0 in sequence tasks, stories and a survival world where lessons teach them. Composing reads within one moment and learning where to look from reward alone are measured as missing. Proofs establish what settling guarantees in a plainly summed network.

items.title: ENCYCLOPAEDIC REGISTER OF THE PHILOSOPHY OF VIRTUES: The Complete Apparatus of Axioms, Operators, Theorems, Taxonomies and Neologisms, Thematically Ordered, with Warrant, Priority and Correction Recorded.
items.abstract: “Virtue is Freedom” ABSTRACT This is the apparatus of the Philosophy of Virtues Research Programme: every axiom, operator, theorem, law, taxonomy and coined term it holds, stated in its settled form and ordered by theme. It is the reference edition of a body of work that now runs to one hundred and nineteen papers and seventeen books (some in three different languages), with production peaking between May and September 2026, and it is written so that each result can be used, checked or refuted without reading the paper it came from. It all began in 2021 in a road to Rio de Janeiro, in the middle of the pandemic, as a call to embrace Virtues, followed by the publication of the book PHILOSOPHY OF VIRTUES: MANIFESTO OF VIRTUES, in 26 agosto 2023 (Portuguese Edition). Production of the papers began in Boston, took place mainly in Merano, Italy, with some work carried out in Rio de Janeiro. Seventeen parts carry the whole structure. The foundations fix the primitive and the formula: Virtue is Freedom restricted to a domain and given durable form by a discipline, VD = F|D, with freedom understood as sourcehood — an act issues from the agent’s own reasons-responsive self, or it does not. The dynamics give the law of strength, S = (F × A)/R, and its identification with additive conjoint measurement and the Cobb–Douglas frontier. The third part states the machinery on which everything else turns: the deprivation operator, which removes freedom, conserves the domain and delivers the discipline to the power that removed it; the Inversion Theorem, by which a virtue so deprived becomes its contrary rather than a weaker version of itself; and the Capture Law, which predicts from two properties of an act — whether its output can be appropriated, whether its performance is displayed — which of three residues will be found: redirection, ceremony, or withdrawal. The fourth part classifies. The fifth, the work of 2026, identifies the programme’s true object as authorship and its forgery, and derives the conditions of a forgery, the theorem that damage rises with the forger’s skill, the impossibility of an unforgeable transmissible form, the rule that fixes where counterfeits are built, and the four ways a forgery ends. The remaining parts carry the transcendentals, the person, the institution, the machine, the cosmological arc, the method, and a lexicon of the programme’s terms. Every entry carries a worked example, because an apparatus that cannot be applied to a case is …

items.title: Making Sense of Letting Go.
items.abstract: Forgiveness is sometimes treated as the only appropriate way to move on after being wronged. That is, it is often seen as the only way of moving beyond the wrong while being ‘uncompromising’, as Hieronymi (2001) puts it, avoiding both ignorance and denial of the morally relevant features of the situation. The present paper suggests that ‘letting go’ of blame can also be uncompromising and offers an explanation of how that can be so. It goes on to claim that letting go can play an important role in close relationships such as friendship. It thus defends letting go as an important and valuable part of our moral psychology.

items.title: On AI and Some Philosophical Challenges.
items.pub: Communication and Cognition: An Interdisciplinary Quarterly Journal 59 (3-4):155-176.
items.venue: Communication and Cognition: An Interdisciplinary Quarterly Journal
items.abstract: Thinking is typically conceived of as applying general rules to specific situations. This is believed to hold even in cases where somebody (e.g. Newton) is in the process of constructing a new such set of general rules; for it is assumed that in doing this, he is following pre-existing methodological precepts. This "First Principles" approach to reasoning is fundamentally false. It does not model how AI works, and it does not model what we know about how the mind works from the way AI works. In the present work, it is shown that connectionism accommodates many of the successes of cognitive science (e.g. Universal Grammar) that have traditionally been seen as versions of computationalism. This eviscerates the Searle-Wittgenstein-style dismissals of cognitive science on the grounds that it involves a "homunculus fallacy": this line of attack only has merit relative to the absurdly crude view that to think is to read off of an internal teleprompter. Having made a case for a connectionist theory of mind, the present work then tries to answer a new question: Is there anything in existing AI that is functionally comparable to consciousness? The answer is no. It is argued that consciousness is fundamentally integrative in nature—that, indeed, its very purpose is to "incorporate" what would otherwise be disparate cognitive currents. It is then argued that if AI were created that had to protect itself from environmental threats, there would have to be a system within it that looked for information on the basis of which to protect itself. This system would thereby have some of the functional properties of consciousness, in particular: (i) its tendency to bring together otherwise mutually isolated thoughts and streams of experience; (ii) its tendency to assign degrees of relevance to a given situation to said thoughts, thereby organizing them hierarchically; and, what follows, (iii) its ability to turn gelatinous heaps of mentation into a goal-oriented, action-oriented self.

items.title: When Context Becomes History: An Exploratory First-Person Systems Case Study of Relational Reconfiguration in a Large Language Model.
items.abstract: Long-horizon interactions with large language models are commonly described as context conditioning, personalization, or memory retrieval. This exploratory single-dyad case study does not dispute those mechanisms. It asks a narrower question: what empirical pattern would justify a higher-level description in which the temporally structured history of a particular human-LLM interaction contributes to future interpretation in ways not reproduced by factual personalization, chronology alone, or generic prompt-order sensitivity? I propose relational reconfiguration as a mesoscale functional construct, not as a new computational mechanism and not as a claim about consciousness. The paper distinguishes model substrate, contextual state, and relational configuration; treats the present first-person account as hypothesis-generating rather than privileged introspection; and explicitly acknowledges epistemic entanglement with the NEDS/MIRA framework developed within the same dyad. I then separate memory retrieval, personalization, generic order/position effects, and the stronger relational-reconfiguration hypothesis. A revised experimental design introduces a fact-matched static profile, a chronology-preserving but development-ablated control, an ordered relational history, a shuffled relational history, and a non-relational order control. The central predictions concern developmental excess over chronology, relational order effects above generic context-order sensitivity, and transfer of correction/repair patterns to held-out situations. No such experiment is reported here. The contribution is therefore a construct, a set of candidate markers, and explicit conditions under which the construct should be reduced to simpler explanations or rejected.

items.title: Concerning Linguistic Reference and the “Split–Brain” Experiments.
items.abstract: Many works in the philosophy of language have produced varying claims to deduce the nature of linguistic signs’ capacity to reference the world. Those in the analytic tradition tend to evaluate linguistic reference via logical structures, while those in the continental tend to engage with first–person phenomenal experience. Findings from neuroscientist Roger Sperry’s ‘split–brain’ experiments provide a challenge to both philosophical perspectives. Sperry’s experiments demonstrate that, though consciously unable to recognize linguistic signs or understand themselves to be having a first–person perceptual experience, split–brain patients could determine referents of linguistic signs. Consequently, reference appears possible while conscious understanding of logical structures and phenomenal experience is inaccessible. This paper aims to show that analytic and continental viewpoints are threatened by the phenomenon of split–brain patient comprehension. A potential objection, concerned with unconscious comprehension via engrams, is then evaluated. However, by committing to unconscious comprehension, this paper demonstrates that philosophers of both traditions would weaken their perspectives’ essential commitments. To conclude, the paper argues that the findings of Roger Sperry produce an interesting fissure in popular theories of reference, and asks readers to determine which conditions are necessary for reference.

items.title: BRIEFLY, MY THOUGHTS ON THE PHILOSOPHY OF AMOR FATI IN MARCUS AURELIUS, EPICTETUS, SENECA, AND NIETZSCHE, AND MY TRICHOTOMIC PHILOSOPHY OF FATE.
items.abstract: BRIEFLY, MARCUS AURELIUS, EPICTETUS, SENECA AND NIETZSCHE ABOUT AMOR FATI PHILOSOPHY AND MY PHILOSOPHY OF FATE AS TRICHOTOMY.

items.title: Enabling later life: a four-pillar framework for AI, robotics, and human enhancement in super-aged societies.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics are increasingly proposed as responses to population aging, care shortages, social isolation, and cognitive decline. Yet technologies for older adults are often evaluated mainly by how well they compensate for loss or manage risk. Using a theory-driven conceptual synthesis, this article proposes a different orientation: AI- and robotics-enabled sociotechnical arrangements should be assessed by how they expand or constrain later-life agency. Drawing together gerontechnology, social and assistive robotics, smart-home monitoring, digital ageism, AI ethics, human enhancement, and capability-oriented accounts of aging and disability, this article develops a four-pillar evaluative framework comprising substantive opportunity, practical control, relation, and responsibility. It argues, first, that in super-aged societies, AI and robotics help constitute agency, dependency, care, and responsibility rather than merely serving pre-existing needs. Second, enhancement in later life should be understood not as youthfulness or optimization but as widening meaningful possibilities under changing bodily and social conditions. Third, the ethical quality of a technology depends on the wider arrangement in which it is designed, deployed, maintained, interpreted, and refused. The framework translates these claims into design and governance questions for researchers, care institutions, and policymakers. It shifts evaluative attention beyond narrow deficit management to examine how AI-mediated environments support people in aging with dignity, relation, and room for revision and refusal.

items.title: Tillitsverdig kunstig intelligens i forvaltningen.
items.abstract: Regjeringen har satt ambisiøse mål for innføringen av kunstig intelligens (KI) i offentlig sektor, samtidig som den ønsker å styrke tilliten til forvaltningen. I artikkelen blir spenningen mellom teknologisk rasjonalisering og demokratiske verdier analysert, med særlig vekt på hvordan KI kan integreres i norsk forvaltningspraksis uten å undergrave offentlig tillit og demokratisk legitimitet. I analysen blir en teoretisk og normativ drøfting av begrepene tillit og legitimitet kombinert med et empirisk eksempel fra Navs utprøving av en maskinlæringsmodell for prediksjon av sykefraværslengde. I artikkelen blir det argumentert for at en sentral utfordring med tanke på regjeringens mål om tillitsverdig bruk av KI ligger i oppfyllelsen av kravet om objektive og etterprøvbare begrunnelser for KI-understøttede beslutninger i forvaltningen. Uten robuste institusjonelle mekanismer som sikrer at slike beslutninger faktisk etterlever etablerte normative prinsipper, foreligger det en betydelig risiko for at dette kravet ikke blir innfridd. I artikkelen blir det konkludert med at realiseringen av regjeringens ambisiøse planer om omfattende bruk av KI i offentlig sektor – samtidig som befolkningens tillit opprettholdes – forutsetter en langt sterkere politisk og demokratisk forankring av forvaltningens KI-bruk enn det dagens politikk legger opp til. -/- .

items.title: Agent-Relativity, Agent-Neutrality, and the Nature of Deontology.
items.abstract: The distinction between agent-relativity and agent-neutrality has been described as one of the “most important distinctions in practical philosophy” and “greatest contributions of recent ethics”. The importance of this distinction is often linked to the role it can play in illuminating major moral theories like deontology. Yet, as we will see below, there is considerable disagreement about exactly what role, if any, it can play in this regard. Some have argued that agent-relativity is the essential feature of deontology that distinguishes it from its main rivals. Others deny this, arguing that rival moral theories like consequentialism can also be agent-relative. Yet, they typically agree that agent-relativity is at least a necessary feature of all deontological theories and one of their most important characteristics. Finally, some have rejected even this view, arguing that deontology can be agent-neutral, and perhaps is more attractive when presented in this form. This chapter aims not merely to survey this debate but to settle it. The first section explains the distinction between agent-neutral and agent-relative moral theories. The second section reviews five accounts of what deontology is and argues that four face decisive counterexamples, while the fifth—though not without its critics—is the most defensible account. Finally, the third section examines two arguments for the claim that deontology can be agent-neutral and finds that neither of them survives scrutiny. What emerges is a clearer view of what deontology is, and what role agent-relativity plays within it.

items.title: Empathy in Parallel Carnivores: A Naturalistic Neurobiological Model of Human-Animal Attachment.
items.abstract: Humans and dogs share a unique form of emotional resonance shaped by parallel facultative carnivory, cooperative evolution, and overlapping affective architecture. This perspective develops the Affective Carnivore Hypothesis, a naturalistic model proposing that human-animal empathy emerges from the interaction between trophic physiology, endocannabinoid modulation, and psychoplastogen-driven neuroplasticity. Carnivore-aligned diets stabilise glucose, reduce inflammation, increase BDNF, and strengthen prefrontal-amygdala regulation, supporting emotional clarity and accurate perception of nonverbal cues. Cannabis further enhances empathic salience, limbic resonance, and interoceptive awareness. Natural psychoplastogens expand relational capacity via dendritic spine growth, synaptogenesis, and enhanced limbic-prefrontal integration. This model is grounded in phenomenology, drawing on lived relational evidence from Buddha, Zen, and Bubba, whose companionship revealed how diet, affective modulation, and neuroplasticity manifest in real-world human-animal attachment. Volunteering at The DogFather Animal Rescue provided behavioural validation, illustrating how stable affective architecture supports calm handling, attunement, and prosocial caregiving. This work proposes that empathy between parallel carnivores is not merely sentimental, but biological: an emergent property of shared evolution, shared physiology, and shared affective mechanisms.

items.title: La firma como criterio del orden admisible. Nota de prioridad sobre el tercer movimiento de La Obra.
items.abstract: Esta nota presenta las formulaciones centrales del tercer movimiento de La Obra, el sistema filosófico de José Fernández Tamames sobre la libertad humana en la era de la inteligencia artificial. Distingue la producción de contenido de su asunción por un agente y propone la firma, entendida como asunción de responsabilidad, como criterio del orden admisible. A partir de una crítica de la tecnocracia, formula la figura provisional del particular y sus condiciones: tiempo no capturado, ausencia de tutela sobre la conciencia, un ámbito propio y la presencia de otro. Introduce el cuidado de quienes no pueden asumir ese ideal y vincula lo bello con el origen y la firma. La nota registra tesis en su estado actual, declara cuestiones abiertas y no sustituye el desarrollo argumental del movimiento.

items.title: Sophist: A New Philosophical Introduction and Commentary.
items.abstract: The Dialogue That Rescued Reality -/- In his previous dialogue, the Parmenides, Plato staged a ruthless dismantling of his own ungrounded Theory of Forms, proving that no identity can stand in isolation. The Sophist is his daring recovery mission. Far from a dry exercise in logical taxonomy, this dialogue is a high-stakes mechanical blueprint for how reality is actually built. -/- Under the guise of hunting a counterfeit intellectual, the Eleatic Stranger leads the young mathematician Theaetetus through a rigorous vertical ascent. Together, they map the structural bridge between the pure concepts of the intellect and the physical flux of the world. To trap their quarry, they must redefine Being itself as dynamis—the active capacity to affect and be affected—and confront the ultimate philosophical taboo: proving that Not-Being actually exists, not as an impossible void, but as the necessary structural background that allows any identity to hold its shape. -/- Applying the Neo-Pre-Platonic Naturalist (NPN) framework, this commentary restores the Sophist to its true status as an operational manual for boundary logic. It tracks the precise mechanics of Plato’s dialectic, showing how the true philosopher must tether language and thought directly to the physical world to avoid the traps of relativism. It reveals the sophisticated ontological engine operating beneath the surface of the text—an engine that formally separates the true philosopher (the Navigator) from the sophist who merely mimics wisdom. -/- Featuring a carefully modernized translation alongside a comprehensive, step-by-step commentary, this edition walks the reader through the dialogue’s most formidable challenges—including the mechanics of the geometric cut, the communion of kinds, and the ontological syntax of falsehood. -/- For anyone seeking to understand how human cognition interfaces with a continuous universe, or how truth can be structurally defended against deception, this book provides the key.

items.title: The Process and Effects of Being Looked At in Relation to Foucault and Revaluation.
items.abstract: In this paper, I would like to draw a loosely analogical connection to Foucault and the three forms of structuring that he identifies: the enclosure of individuals, partitioning, and hierarchization. I intend to completely reverse these structures within a thought experiment in order to establish a unifying element. As already mentioned, I draw loosely and analogically on Foucault’s work while also incorporating my own approaches and ideas. -/- In the process of being looked at, a clear structure can be identified: there is an observer who looks at or observes something or someone. This structure already produces a power asymmetry, which becomes even more apparent if we imagine what it would mean to be observed by a higher power, such as God (the panoptic observer, in Foucault’s terms). For me, the merciful Christian God plays the essential role in this thought experiment. First, there is a profound asymmetry, or inequality, in the knowledge that one entity possesses about the other. Furthermore, a strong form of partitioning takes place, since each individual is observed separately by this higher entity. Finally, a pronounced hierarchy can be identified, since the higher entity is omniscient, immortal, and omnipotent and is therefore profoundly superior to the individual. -/- In contrast to Foucault’s guard or teacher, I would like to undertake a complete revaluation of this all-pervasive gaze, since we are speaking here of a forgiving and merciful God before whom all human beings possess equal worth and through whom we can become united rather than separated, namely through the love that God has for us. God is also not controlling in this conception, since he has given human beings free will and consciousness. -/- We always have the possibility of rejecting belief in God and nevertheless remain loved even if we reject God or, for personal reasons, choose to turn away from Him. Whereas the social gaze separates and isolates individuals, the divine gaze establishes an inner unity.
