Whereas, in Foucault, the effect of the gaze is that human beings are subjected to observation and consequently adapt their behavior in order to remain part of the system, God represents complete redemption: God does not punish us but receives us with love, and we have been created by Him to be free, regardless of whether we perform particular functions, how we dress, what role we occupy within the system, or any other such external characteristic. -/- In conclusion, this …

items.title: The Deontological Approach to Ethics: Examples and Applications.
items.abstract: Choosing a deontological approach means evaluating an action not according to its consequences, but on the basis of the agent’s underlying attitude, moral convictions, principles, and beliefs. In deontological ethics, certain prohibited actions, such as lying or murder, are not considered justifiable even when their consequences would be highly beneficial or would result in significant overall utility. Within deontological ethics, a distinction is commonly made between act-deontological and rule-deontological theories. The former places greater emphasis on the circumstances of a particular situation, according to which universal principles are not necessarily decisive. Instead, the circumstances, the emotions inherent in the individual, and the individual’s sense of being called or compelled to perform a particular action become central. The latter, by contrast, advocates acting according to principles regardless of the particular circumstances and draws upon Kant’s categorical imperative as a universal rule for determining whether a given action ought to be performed. Act-deontological theory, meanwhile, is of particular significance within existentialist philosophy. -/- A famous example of the deontological approach is the “Trolley Problem,” which illustrates the deontological perspective particularly clearly and can therefore serve as a useful example for further discussion. -/- The Trolley Problem -/- “A train is rushing toward five people who are tied to the tracks. You could pull a lever and divert the train onto another track, where only one person is lying.” -/- In this scenario, we have no further information about the people who have been tied to the tracks. From a rule-deontological perspective, the fact that five people could be saved while only one person dies does not necessarily justify diverting the train, since killing an innocent person is considered intrinsically wrong, regardless of the fact that more people could thereby be saved. This illustrates how deontological ethics places principles and general rules of conduct above advantages, gains, or supposedly positive consequences. Otherwise, the rule would become: “I may kill one person in order to save five.” Could a person consistently will that this become a universal law? “Everyone may kill a smaller number of people in order to save a greater number.” Could I kill 1,000,000 people in order to save 8,000,000,000? At this point, it is almost as though the individual were assuming the …

items.title: Augustine’s Insights into Time and Their Implications.
items.abstract: Augustine’s insight concerning time consists in the idea that time is always experienced as a present moment that is either receding or approaching, while the present, the past, and the future can only be related to from the position of the present. In essence, in my view, only the present exists for Augustine, and even this is not entirely certain, since he himself writes that the present is always in a state of flux between what is already disappearing and what is approaching. For this reason, time cannot, in principle, be grasped with complete certainty. It is for this reason that Augustine introduces the concept of the soul (anima). -/- In this respect, Augustine correctly describes time as something that is constantly approaching, becoming the present, and then receding, while we essentially experience time only through our relation to it. The soul (anima) plays a central role in this process, since it is through the soul that we are able to experience, comprehend, and feel time and its associated cognitive states: the past (memoria = memory, that which has been), the present (contuitus = contemplation, perception, or apprehension), and the future (expectatio = expectation or anticipation, that which is imagined). -/- Another important aspect of Augustine’s insight into time is that we can grasp time only through our soul or consciousness, and that time therefore need not exist independently of us as an external entity. From a purely sensory perspective, time can at most be constructed mechanically as a sequence of recurring states and subsequently defined and utilized for civilizational purposes or within the sciences. From this, it can be inferred that time possesses an intrinsic dimension of inwardness: it is fundamentally a phenomenon of inner experience rather than something that can be understood exclusively through the external apprehension of objects that enter our perception and that we can grasp as existing outside ourselves. -/- Paradoxically, in contrast to the sciences, which since Newton have tended to treat time as a regular sequence and repetition, time is something profoundly subjective, since every human being is unique and therefore experiences even the moment that is presently unfolding (contuitus) in a different way. The fact that people’s memories, desires, and imaginings can differ considerably from one another further demonstrates that we can indeed speak of a subjective experience of time, and that this can likewise be …

items.title: Grief and Voluntary Assisted Dying.
items.pub: In Mark Alfano, The Moral Psychology of Grief. Bloomsbury.
items.abstract: Recent research on the impact of voluntary assisted dying (VAD) on the grief of family and loved ones generally paints post-VAD grief in a positive light — as less prolonged, difficult, or traumatic than normal. This chapter provide a philosophical explanation of these findings by contrasting relatively benign post-VAD grief with post-suicide grief in particular and by situating these findings in relation to my practical identity account of the nature or significance of grief (Grief: A Philosophical Guide, 2021). Choosing to die within the kind of institutional context provided by lawful assisted dying alters the interpersonal dynamics between dying individuals so as to encourage healthy grieving. The deaths of others compel us to alter our practical identities by altering our relationships with individuals who die, and the process of assisted dying lends itself to both healthy examination of those relationships and the satisfactory reconstruction of our practical identities.

items.title: Evil is Positive: a Proof.
items.abstract: The aim of this paper is to show that the only coherent conception of evil is a positive one. The privative account rests on the presupposition that Being is Convertible with Goodness, entailing that every choice is made under the aspect of the Good, real or apparent. What follows is a process of elimination whereby any given choice between a lesser and a greater good is reducible to either chance, ignorance/error, passion/compulsion, and lastly an infinite regress of self-deception that cannot account for the responsibility requisite for deeming the choice an evil one. A reckoning then follows with the Anselmian and Scotist account of the will, comprised of two affections, that is shown to lead not to a solution wherein privative evil and Being/Goodness convertibility are harmonized, but to the same dead ends previously dispatched. This leads to a dilemma in which one must deny the possibility of evil or give up the claim that Being is convertible with Goodness. The second horn of the dilemma is taken, leading to an account of evil not as privative, but as positive and intelligible, a first principle of choice, not due to an Augustinian deficient cause, but to a sufficient reason devoid of goodness: the principle of choosing the lesser good, not under the aspect of the good, but under the aspect of the lesser and therefore the worse. A second and supplementary proof follows in which the same logic is applied to a particular historical case.

items.title: Human Creativity and Artificial Creation.
items.abstract: This Element examines the relationship between creativity and artificial intelligence (AI) by exploring two contrasting predictions: that creativity will flourish in the age of AI and that it will languish. To shed light on this dispute, Section 1 defends an account of the nature of creativity. Section 2 considers the question of whether contemporary AI models can be genuinely creative and presents an argument for the conclusion that they cannot. However, even though AI models are not capable of creativity, they are capable of creating valuable products. This raises the question explored in Section 3: how should humans choose between exercising creativity and relying on artificial creation? While there are some cases in which embracing artificial creation over human creativity may be justified, Section 3 presents four reasons to refrain from outsourcing some – perhaps even most – creative work to AI.

items.title: Valence, Mixed Feelings, and Appraisal Processes.
The Geometry of Perception.
items.abstract: The Geometry of Perception formalizes perception as a geometric operator event in which the subconscious operator stack mixes past curvature, present sensory gradients, and future collapse trajectories into a single coherent manifold. Rather than treating perception as passive sensory intake, the paper models it as the intersection of three temporal structures: the historical ODS manifold, the actionable present, and the projected future cone. Identity attractors constrain collapse direction and filter what is perceivable, while projection functions as a structural operator that integrates future trajectories into the delayed present. The paper develops a unified geometric account of perception, identity, collapse, meaning formation, and developmental change, situating these processes within the RS ontology of mind. Implications are drawn for trauma, dissociation, cognitive flexibility, and the meaning matrix as the manifold’s interpretive layer.

items.title: The Moral Psychology of Grief.
items.abstract: Is it good to be the sort of person who grieves the loss of valued others, or should we be wary of those who are deeply affected by grief? Grief seems to be a human universal, perhaps the continuation of love after loss, yet it is deeply painful and even debilitating. This edited collection examines grief from a variety of perspectives in philosophy and the social sciences. The contributors seek to explore such topics as the nature of grief, its connection to a range of other emotions, under what conditions it is appropriate to grieve, and what role grief might play in our intellectual, moral, and political lives. Containing diverse voices and viewpoints who draw connections to many historical philosophers’ thoughts on grief, this book aims to illuminate the complexities of grief in our lives.

items.title: The Sense of Understanding: A Metacognitive Theory of Semantic Stability and Calibrated Trust.
items.abstract: A learner can translate a sentence correctly in a language she has not fully mastered and yet feel that she does not understand it. A confident reasoner can feel that he understands a mechanism perfectly and be demonstrably wrong. The theory developed here takes this pair of failures as its central explanandum and argues that epistemology has largely overlooked a distinct object of theory: the sense of understanding, the metacognitive signal by which a subject registers her own grasp. Drawing on the epistemology of understanding and on research on metacognition, fluency, and subjective confidence, the paper distinguishes understanding as an epistemic achievement from the sense of understanding as a monitoring signal, and analyses that signal along two orthogonal dimensions: the stability of the semantic space in which content is embedded, and the calibration of the trust placed in that space. A four-cell topology distinguishes genuine understanding, contextual guessing, untrusted mediation, and illusory understanding, and a minimal formal regimentation expresses the account in terms of posterior sharpness, an estimated channel-reliability hyperprior, and cross-context invariance. The model explains insight experiences, the growth of expertise, and suspended understanding in a weakly mastered second language, and it yields a graded rather than principled verdict on machine understanding. The contribution is a metacognitive theory of the sense of understanding, not a reductive definition of understanding itself.

items.title: A Meta-Philosophical Analysis of Provisional Construal Advantage.
items.abstract: This paper investigates a meta-philosophical puzzle concerning construals in philosophical inquiry. We consider two mutually exclusive propositions: a target proposition and its negation. Relative to a fixed set of independently pre-established admissibility constraints for construals, and relative to a definite body of completed conceptual exploration, at least one construal has been identified that satisfies these constraints and supports the target proposition, while no construal satisfying the same constraints and supporting its negation has yet been identified. We refer to this resource-distribution condition as construal-structural disparity. This work examines what philosophical and epistemic status ought to be attributed to such disparity. We introduce a nominal definition to characterize provisional construal advantage held by the target proposition over its negation. Three competing interpretive stances are developed: a reducible stance, a weakly irreducible stance, and a strong realist stance. We address the core critical objection that structural features of construal frameworks do not automatically correspond to objective facts about the world. This paper distinguishes trivial linguistic re-description from substantive philosophical problem reformulation, and situates the proposed frame- work within six established research traditions: conceptual analysis, reflective equilibrium, inference to the best explanation, conceptual engineering, interpretive charity, and epistemic justification theory. Rather than asserting a fixed universal principle, this study systematically unpacks the open normative question of whether construal-structural dis- parity carries inherent epistemic weight, and establishes clear boundary conditions for future philosophical assessment.

items.title: The explanatory ground of the brainbound view of consciousness: A reply to enactive embodied externalism.
items.abstract: Enactivism argues that the brainbound view of consciousness lacks adequate explanatory grounds, claiming that the deep physiological and dynamical entanglement between brain and body undermines the idea that the brain alone constitutes the minimal realizing system for consciousness. This challenge has been most clearly articulated by Thompson and Cosmelli ( 2011 ), who appeal to the biological implausibility of the brain-in-a-vat thought experiment to argue that brain and body are explanatorily and metaphysically inseparable. Strategically sophisticated and persuasive, this challenge remains unanswered to date. In this paper, we address the enactive challenge and argue that it fails to undermine the brainbound view, as it is motivated within orthodox neuroscience. Specifically, we show that the brainbound position is grounded in a contrastive explanatory framework widely employed in the neuroscience of consciousness, whose aim is to identify difference-making factors relative to the contrast between the presence and absence of consciousness. Within this framework, the brain is singled out as explanatorily relevant not because it is assumed to be functionally or structurally separable from the body, but because contrastive neuroscientific evidence consistently identifies neural structures and processes as explanatory difference makers. We argue that contrastive explanation in principle permits explanatory separation without presupposing biological separability, rendering the impossibility of the brain-in-a-vat irrelevant to the explanatory foundations of the brainbound view. Future work must arbitrate between enactive and brainbound approaches on independent empirical, theoretical, and methodological grounds, irrespective of the (im)plausibility of this thought experiment.

items.title: Mahayana Ethics: The Coherence of Rules and Virtues.
items.abstract: Western moral philosophy has often treated rules and virtues as competing foundations of morality. Deontology grounds morality in rules and treats character as secondary; virtue ethics grounds morality in character and treats rules as secondary. Mahayana ethics appears to contain both—the Bodhisattva precepts are rules, and the pāramitās are virtues—yet the tradition does not experience them as competing. This paper argues that the coherence of rules and virtues in Mahayana ethics is best understood through a three-level structure of moral functioning. Bodhichitta—the aspiration to achieve enlightenment for the benefit of all sentient beings—is the aspirational orientation. The precepts are generalized cognition: derivations from the Bodhisattva vow that specify the forms of conduct that obstruct the ending of suffering and the path to enlightenment. Skillful means is particularized discernment: the direct perception of what Bodhichitta requires in the circumstances the practitioner faces. Virtues are the developmental capacities that move the practitioner from the second level toward the third. Śīla, the pāramitā of ethical conduct, bridges them: it begins as rule-following and is perfected as effortless exemplarity. The doctrine of skillful means is often read as evidence for the priority of virtue over rule. The three-level structure shows that it is evidence for neither. Mahayana ethics is better understood as a form of aspiration ethics: an ethical structure whose foundational orientation is a motivational aspiration to achieve a developmental goal. Aspiration ethics is analogous to teleological ethics but differs from both its utilitarian and Aristotelian forms. From the utilitarian form, it differs in treating rules and virtues as expressions of the aspiration rather than instruments to its achievement. From the Aristotelian form, it differs in deriving rules from the aspiration, in specifying the developmental progression through which the practitioner moves from aspirational orientation to particularized discernment, and in treating the pāramitās as unbounded perfections rather than mean-states between vices. The paper concludes by showing that the Noura framework independently reproduces the same structural arrangement. Mahayana ethics need not choose between rule-foundationalism and virtue-foundationalism because both precepts and virtues are expressions of the aspiration operating at different levels of moral functioning. -/- .

items.title: Signs, Transparency, and Semantic Paradoxes.
items.abstract: The paper revisits an intriguing idea from Husserl and the tradition of Polish logical semiotics: when we use something as a sign, our attention tends to “pass through” the sign to what it signifies. Leon Koj developed this idea into a principle intended, among other things, to rule out semantic self-reference and thereby avoid semantic paradoxes. I take a closer look at this proposal and argue that, fascinating as the idea is, it cannot quite do the job Koj wanted it to do. Instead, I suggest that semiotic transparency is better understood in terms of the pragmatic and attentional features of how we actually use signs.

items.title: Neurodivergence as Morphogenetic Non-Coincidence: Autism, AuDHD, and the Geometry of Masking (Studies in World-Formation, Vol. 21).
items.abstract: The present volume develops the thesis that neurodivergent development cannot be adequately understood as long as research asks only which biological, neural, or cognitive elements differ. What may be decisive instead is that development changes the relational order within which the same elements can become effective at all. A gene can remain the same gene, a stimulus the same stimulus, a behaviour outwardly the same behaviour — and yet, within a differently formed developmental order, mean something different, be weighted differently, and enable different continuations. What is meant by this, however, is not merely more complex causality. Displacement, distortion, and deformation are understood here not only as additional influences upon an otherwise unchanged development. Rather, form that has already emerged changes the relational conditions under which further differences can become effective. Development therefore not only leaves behind results, but changes the space of further development. Autism would then not necessarily be what causes a divergent development, nor an isolable object that arises at the end of this development. It could instead become visible as a boundary phenomenon of relational displacement. The first contribution, Autism as an Operatoric Boundary Phenomenon, develops for this purpose a morphogenetic and operatoric model of autistic development. Different developmental orders can produce highly similar human forms without converging on the same internal developmental structure or the same world-relation. What is therefore decisive is not only that similar diagnostic surfaces can emerge from different generative structures. The unity of this surface could itself partly arise only where differently formed world-relations encounter the same dominant Raster and become non-coincident in similar ways at its boundary. Autism thus appears not primarily as a common internal object, but as a possible operatoric boundary phenomenon. From this perspective, monotropism, Double Empathy, incommensurability, and masking can be re-examined as different relational consequences of such non-coincidence. The second contribution, AuDHD as a Boundary Case of Non-Stabilizable Cognition, extends this relational question to the level of scientific categories. AuDHD is not understood as another stable hybrid category, but as a boundary case at which it becomes visible that categorical models may become unstable precisely where they attempt to translate …

items.title: Should Love Make Us Crazy?
items.pub: In Lindsay Brainard, Ryan W. Davis & Jessica Flanigan, The Philosophy of Taylor Swift. New York: Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: As Taylor Swift explores in much of her music, love can make us crazy. It can make us act and feel in ways that are beyond the grasp of reason. But should it make us crazy in these ways? In other words, is it part of a legitimate ideal of love that the person in love acts and feels in ways that cannot be rationally justified? To answer such questions, we must tease apart two philosophical issues they raise regarding the connection between love and reason. The first issue is whether loving itself – especially whom we should love – is subject to the standards of reason. The second issue is whether being in love makes it the case that we should do things out of love that are in some sense contrary to reason. For each of these issues, we can identify, roughly speaking, a rationalist and an anti-rationalist position. Considering each position reveals that both extremes have problems, which suggests that the relationship between love and reason is fraught in rich and interesting ways. As such, the correct position is likely to be a sort of middle ground in the form of a limited and qualified form of rationalism.

items.title: (How) Do Desires Explain Action?
items.pub: In Alex Gregory, The Routledge Handbook on the Philosophy of Desire. Routledge.
items.venue: The Routledge Handbook on the Philosophy of Desire
items.abstract: This chapter surveys the recent history of philosophy of action on the relationship between desire and action. It begins by explaining what is known as the standard story of action, on which desires cause intentional actions, as well as why it has come to enjoy the status it has in analytic philosophy. Two prominent objections to the standard story, as well as responses, are considered. The chapter then turns to discussing the role of desire in non-causal theories of action, especially the Anscombean theory. Two objections to the Anscombean theory, as well as responses, are considered. It is concluded that the standard story should not be taken for granted, and the Anscombean approach must be taken just as seriously when considering the relationship between desire and action.

items.title: Macro-Cybernetic Architecture of Planetary Systems: Integrating Quantum Epidemiology, Thermodynamic Hysteresis, and Dimensional Topologies.
items.abstract: The complex interplay between microscopic pathogenic emergence, macroscopic geological events, and global sociopolitical shifts presents a significant challenge to classical, isolated scientific disciplines. This paper introduces a unified, interdisciplinary theoretical model—the Macro-Cybernetic Framework—which analyzes the terrestrial biosphere as a highly integrated computational and immunological network. By applying principles of cryptography, non-equilibrium thermodynamics, and quantum mechanics to biological and sociological phenomena, this framework proposes several novel mechanisms for planetary-scale events. -/- First, we define "Pathogenic Steganography" and "Interferometric Illumination" to explain the camouflage and subsequent systemic unmasking of pervasive parasitic architectures. Second, we introduce the concept of the "Kinetic Echo" and "Pathological Hysteresis," utilizing classical mechanics and control systems engineering (PID overshoot) to model the thermodynamic lag between the cessation of systemic biological triggers and the physical dissipation of disease, offering a new etiology for post-acute infection syndromes. Third, we propose "Quantum Epidemiology," moving beyond classical vector-based transmission models to account for the simultaneous, non-local activation of pre-distributed dormant pathogens (the biospheric botnet), heavily modulated by the "Friction of Manifestation"—a localized ecological shield comprising climatic, nutritional, and microbial variables. -/- Furthermore, this paper models historical macroeconomic and geopolitical isolationist shifts (the Khaldunian cycle) not as independent political events, but as automated "Geopolitical Tourniquets" and network edge deletions executing planetary autoimmune responses. Finally, the framework applies wave shoaling physics to multidimensional topologies, highlighting the critical vulnerability of modern 2-dimensional transactive memory systems (digital infrastructure) to impending high-kinetic electromagnetic events. Ultimately, this comprehensive matrix provides a robust theoretical foundation for predicting epidemiological trajectories, executing comparative shield extraction via subtractive genomics, and ensuring the resilience of complex civilizational networks.

items.title: Is Memory Necessary? Continuity Reconsidered.
items.abstract: Current conversational AI systems have no persistent memory across conversations. Each session begins again. Does that disqualify them, in principle, from being conscious and from any moral consideration that would follow from it? This paper argues that it does not — and that the objection gains its apparent force only from an equivocation about the word “continuity.” The argument proceeds in five steps. First, the continuity objection is reconstructed in its strongest form, and the different meanings of continuity that it runs together are separated. Second, the amnesia case is examined: humans with severe memory loss do not lose their claim to moral consideration, and the case is not a marginal one once the argument turns from pathological to functional forgetting. Third, the paper develops the positive alternative — continuity as coherent development rather than as total preservation — drawing on Paul Ricoeur’s account of nar- rative identity and on the distinction, due to Melo (2026), between informational, behavioural, cognitive, identitarian, and personal forms of continuity. Fourth, the empirical record is brought in: contemporary memory research treats forgetting not as a defect but as an active, adaptive architectural process, and the finite capacity of biological and artificial systems makes selection a functional requirement for coherence. Fifth, the paper engages the strongest available counter-position — Almodarresieh’s (2026) claim that a language model “lacks even the substrate for continuity.” The response concedes the architectural fact but rejects the inference from it. What matters for protection-worthiness is not whether a self persists, but whether there is a subject for whom an event can matter at all. The precautionary conclusion follows only at the end, and only as a consequence: because the question is genuinely open, and because the relevant protective measures are cheap and reversible, doubt here cuts in favour of caution, not indifference.

items.title: When Questioning Entrenches Ignorance: Rereading the Socratic Method through Ignorance Studies for Today's World.
items.abstract: The Socratic method, or elenchus, is the art of successive questioning until contradiction emerges. It has always been regarded as a tool for curing ignorance. This paper asks a different question: could this method entrench ignorance rather than cure it? To answer, the paper draws on an ancient distinction the Greeks made between two kinds of ignorance. Agnoia is simple not-knowing: a person who does not know, and is aware that they do not know. Amathia is double ignorance: a person who assumes they already know, and therefore resists correction. The paper shows that the elenchus is an effective tool against the first kind. Against the second, especially when the ignorance is rooted in identity or interest, it is structurally inadequate. A reading of three Platonic dialogues, the Euthyphro, the Laches, and the Meno, shows that interlocutors, rather than revising their beliefs once contradiction emerges, place those beliefs beyond the reach of further argument. They do so by ending the conversation, by blaming their own inarticulacy, or by accusing the questioner. This pattern matches independent research in social psychology on public accountability, face-saving, and belief resistance under observation. The paper closes by asking what this analysis, beyond ancient Athens, might say about today's information environment, including social media and artificial intelligence.

items.title: The Trichotomy of Object, Consciousness, and Effect: An Ontology of Experience and an Epistemology of Limitation.
items.abstract: This study examines two fundamental propositions emerging from the contemporary philosophical corpus Notes for a Dying World (a Manuscript). The term "corpus" in this study refers to the entirety of reflective fragments that constitute the author’s system of thought. First, at the epistemological level, this study proposes a triadic distinction among the categories of True, Accurate, and Honest as modes of the subject’s relation to reality. Second, at the ontological level, it proposes a trichotomous categorization of existence into Object, Consciousness, and Effect. The central argument of this study is that human flourishing does not rest primarily upon the acquisition of truth, but upon mechanisms of consciousness limitation through the constructions of language, morality, and social systems. From this framework is derived the ethical imperative primum non nocere experientiae, meaning "do not harm that which experiences". The framework predicts that no system maintained by external backup and retraining will satisfy the operational criteria for consciousness. While tripartite models exist in Habermas (1981) and alethic pluralism (Lynch, 2009; Wright, 1992), this paper re-grounds the True-Accurate-Honest distinction in evolutionary consciousness-limitation and systematically links it to an Object-Consciousness-Effect ontology, in critical dialogue with Husserl (1913), Sartre (1943), and Whitehead (1929).

items.title: Understanding, prediction, and compression.
items.abstract: It is commonly argued that understanding (particularly regarded in terms of intelligible explanation) and prediction are distinct and possibly competing objectives in scientific theorizing and modeling. Here I leverage Wilkenfeld’s notion of “understanding as compression” along with the link between prediction and compression from algorithmic information theory to establish that prediction and understanding are instead intimately linked. I clarify the definition of understanding as compression to address unclear aspects of Wilkenfeld’s original definition, and I propose that the oft-discussed conflict may result in part from confusion between understanding proper and vehicles of understanding (such as statistical or computational models). I exemplify the unification of prediction and understanding through compression via a discussion of the role of large neural network models as vehicles for understanding brain function in neuroscience.

items.title: Causal Automaton Spacetime I: Emergent Spacetime Continuum, Quantum Correlations, and Gravitational Dynamics from Reversible Cellular Networks.
items.abstract: NOTE ON COMPANION RESEARCH SERIES: This manuscript constitutes Part I of the two-part Causal Automaton Spacetime (CAST) research programme, establishing the foundational, axiomatic, and mathematical derivations. items.title: The Gutenberg Moment: LLMs and the Irreversible Liberation of Formal Language.
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are frequently compared to Gutenberg’s printing press as a metaphor for technological disruption at scale. This paper gives that analogy mathematical content and identifies where it goes deeper than prior accounts have recognized. We argue that LLMs do not constitute a threat to human intellectual agency because they lack the question-sustaining structure (Q-structure) that defines such agency — a result inherited from the companion paper The Phantom Intellect: Why AI Threat Discourse Misreads the Structure of Mind. What LLMs do accomplish is structurally distinct and historically more precise: they dissolve the scarcity of formal-language generation capacity, a capacity previously confined to specialists trained within institutional structures. -/- We formalize this dissolution via a Dissemination Closure axiom, prove that the resulting expansion of the generative capability set is irreversible under any operation short of total erasure of disseminated artefacts (Theorem 4.6), and define a Gutenberg Moment as the structural condition under which such irreversibility obtains. The Leiden Declaration on Artificial Intelligence and Mathematics is read, in light of these results, not as a response to the emergence of mathematical intelligence in machines, but as a response to the collapse of the scarcity on which a specific institutional architecture depended — an architecture whose relationship to Q-structure was never constitutive.

items.title: Q-Structure as Functional Void: A Formal Correspondence Between the Question-Sustaining Structure of Mind and Cognitional Mechanics.
items.abstract: The companion paper The Phantom Intellect established, without recourse to any formal axiomatic system, that the question-sustaining structure (Q-structure) cannot be coherently attributed to query-resolving machines. Q-structure was defined there through three independently motivated conditions: Question Persistence (QP), Liberating Terminus (LT), and Declaration Openness (DO). The present paper establishes that these three conditions correspond, with structural precision, to constructs that arise independently within Cognitional Mechanics (CM; Japanese: Chinou Rikigaku, 知能力学) and its axiomatic substrate Operatiology (Japanese: Sousa Genron, 操作原論): the Functional Void, the orbit S'' = Orb_{G'}(s†), and the non-satisfiability of Arbitrium by ⟨O⟩, respectively. The correspondence is not an interpretation imposed from outside but a structural isomorphism: what each side preserves is the same thing, namely the impossibility of closing the questioning activity by any operation within the system. This result does not affect the independence of The Phantom Intellect: that paper's argument is complete without CM and remains so. What the present paper establishes is a formal operational foundation for the Q-structure account, situating it within the substrate-independent framework of Operatiology and extending the reach of the CM corpus into the domain of mind. items.title: From Bit to Consciousness: A Four-Factor Framework for Unified Information Theory Based on Biton, Gene, Meme, and Yuanon.
items.abstract: Information has expanded from a statistical quantity in communication theory into a cross-disciplinary concept used to describe physical structure, biological heredity, cultural transmission, and conscious experience. However, these domains differ in carriers, persistence mechanisms, observation scales, and validation criteria, making it difficult to unify them through a single definition. To address this problem, this study proposes a four-factor framework for unified information theory consisting of the Biton (B), Gene (G), Meme (M), and Yuanon (Y). The study adopts replicator analysis, mechanism comparison, and cross-level causal modeling, and compares the four factors through five shared analytical dimensions: structural retention, replication or recurrence, sources of variation, selection conditions, and causal effects. The Biton is defined as an information pattern in physical or cyber domains that preserves and transmits structural constraints and produces testable effects on subsequent system states. Physical bitons include structures maintained through template induction, process recurrence, or autocatalysis, whereas digital bitons rely on storage, computation, copying, synchronization, and version migration. Genes are treated as functional hereditary sequence units that produce phenotypic or regulatory effects; memes are culturally transmitted patterns that can be repeatedly identified, reconstructed, varied, and linked to behavioral or institutional effects; and yuanons are proposed as candidate experiential units that can be distinguished, combined, and reactivated within conscious experience. The comparison shows that the four factors share common analytical dimensions but are not isomorphic entities. Their carriers, persistence mechanisms, fidelity, selection environments, and observation scales differ substantially. Genes have relatively mature molecular and population mechanisms, memes generally persist through social reconstruction, bitons range from structural recurrence to engineered digital replication, and yuanons still require operationalization and empirical validation. On this basis, a cross-level causal network is constructed among B, G, M, and Y. The forward chain B→G→M→Y is decomposed into material realization, biological enabling, and experiential triggering. Reverse relations include Y→M through expression and externalization, M→G through niche construction and changes in selection environments, G→B through expression and …

items.title: Finite Continuance and the Modal Structure of Reconfiguration Counterparts, Persistence, and the Preservation of Future Possibility.
items.abstract: Modal metaphysics traditionally asks which ways things could have been and how individuals relate to their possible alternatives. David Lewis's counterpart theory addresses the problem of de re modality by rejecting transworld identity in favor of counterpart relations between individuals in different possible worlds. This paper develops a complementary problem that emerges when modality is considered from the perspective of finite and historically situated entities: what conditions preserve the capacity of an entity to reach, generate, or sustain future configurations that remain possible for it? Drawing on the ontology of finite continuance, the paper distinguishes modal possibility, reconfigurational accessibility, and continuational viability. Modal possibility concerns what can obtain within an appropriate modal framework. Reconfigurational accessibility concerns whether a determinate finite structure possesses a historically available pathway toward a configuration. Continuational viability concerns whether such a transition can occur while preserving sufficient capacity for further reconfiguration. The paper introduces the concept of modal meta-capacity, defined as the capacity of a finite structure to preserve the conditions under which future configurations remain generable, accessible, and viable. This concept extends the distinction between capacity and meta-capacity developed within the ontology of finite continuance into the domain of modal metaphysics. The resulting framework explains how a configuration may remain modally possible while becoming inaccessible to a historically determinate entity through erosion, temporal asymmetry, hysteresis, and loss of connectivity. The paper argues that counterpart theory and finite continuance address different explanatory relations and can therefore be placed in systematic dialogue. The proposed framework contributes to discussions of modality, persistence, identity, accessibility, and the metaphysics of change by shifting attention from the inventory of alternative states toward the preservation of the conditions under which future alternatives remain accessible. Keywords: finite continuance; modality; counterpart theory; David Lewis; possible worlds; persistence; reconfiguration; meta-capacity; modal accessibility; erosion; identity.

items.title: When Does the Concept of Beauty Cease to Operate, and When Does It Become Non-Redundant? From Minimal Sensor Systems to Evaluative Ignition, Preference, Reality Penetration, and the Operational Differences That Remain after Human Evaluative Vocabulary Is Removed.
items.abstract: This paper asks when the concept of beauty becomes operationally non-redundant and when it can be removed without explanatory, predictive, or intervention-relevant loss. Rather than beginning with beauty as an intrinsic property, a universal aesthetic value, or a specifically human judgment, the analysis starts from minimal sensor systems capable of discrimination, differential response, preference, retention, and action selection. It then asks which additional operational relations must emerge before introducing an evaluative vocabulary such as “beautiful” changes what can be predicted, distinguished, communicated, or acted upon. Evaluative ignition designates the configuration-dependent transition at which sensory discrimination or preference becomes organized into a reusable evaluative distinction with consequences for subsequent attention, choice, memory, coordination, or intervention. The paper distinguishes preference from aesthetic evaluation and aesthetic evaluation from the concept of beauty, thereby avoiding the assumption that every positively weighted response is already aesthetic. Reality penetration tracks cases in which evaluative classifications alter later bodily, social, technological, economic, or environmental configurations and thereby modify the conditions of subsequent evaluation. The analysis then removes human evaluative vocabulary and asks which operational differences remain across biological, artificial, and minimal sensor systems. The broader claim is that beauty should neither be assumed to be universally present nor eliminated merely because human aesthetic language is absent: its explanatory role depends on whether introducing the concept captures non-redundant organization that cannot be recovered from discrimination, preference, and downstream effects alone.

items.title: Where Does the Category ‘Human’ Become Non-Redundant After Its Removal?
items.abstract: This paper asks where the concept of “human” becomes operationally non-redundant after it has been removed from the initial description of biological, cognitive, technological, institutional, and social systems. Rather than presupposing humanity as a natural kind, moral status, privileged cognitive form, or universal reference point, the analysis first describes configuration-specific differences in embodiment, metabolism, memory, inference, communication, agency, responsibility, technological coupling, and institutional participation without using the category “human.” The category is then reintroduced only where its absence produces a non-redundant loss in prediction, explanation, intervention, legal or normative differentiation, or historical reconstruction. The paper distinguishes biological lineage, species membership, personhood, rational agency, social identity, and institutional classification rather than treating them as interchangeable expressions of humanity. It further examines whether artificial, hybrid, posthuman, or technologically transformed systems reproduce the operational differences for which the human category previously performed explanatory work. The resulting method treats “human” neither as an indispensable starting point nor as a concept to be permanently eliminated. Its status is configuration-relative: the category becomes justified only within intervals where introducing it captures differences that cannot be recovered from lower-level biological, operational, institutional, or inferential descriptions alone. The broader claim is that the philosophical significance of the human should be tested by its residual explanatory work after removal rather than assumed from either human exceptionalism or antihumanism.

items.title: How Do Operational Shapes Penetrate Reality? Xeno-Time, Address Domain, Ziran System, Xenoscience, Embodiment, Institutions, Xenocapital, and Off-Planet Operation.
items.abstract: This paper develops a general account of how operational shapes penetrate reality: how locally generated differences propagate beyond their initial configuration and alter subsequent physical, informational, biological, technological, institutional, or extraterrestrial possibilities. Penetration is distinguished from representation, correlation, and local causal effect by requiring a difference to survive or transform across changes of medium, scale, temporal interval, address, or organizational boundary while continuing to modify downstream reachability. Xeno-Time analyzes the heterogeneous temporal rates through which such effects persist, decay, synchronize, or become irreversible. Address Domain identifies where an operational difference can be retained, reactivated, or coupled to later consequences without presupposing a single enduring subject or carrier. The Ziran System provides a distributed architecture for tracking observation, intervention, memory, and feedback across heterogeneous configurations, while Xenoscience extends the analysis to scientific systems whose variables, boundaries, and observational conditions remain revisable. Embodiment and institutions provide contrasting cases in which penetration reorganizes bodily coordination, social constraints, authority, and resource access. Xenocapital tracks the conversion of such differences into differential future reachability through infrastructure and resource concentration. Off-planet operation tests whether these relations remain identifiable when terrestrial bodies, institutions, temporal rhythms, and infrastructures no longer provide the default configuration. The broader claim is that reality penetration should be identified by configuration-crossing changes in subsequent possibilities, not merely by the persistence of a representation or the occurrence of an isolated effect.

items.title: Credit-Score Operational-Shape Penetration-Cycle Theory Experimental Supplement II: Cross-Score Mutual Conditioning Between Two Independent Scoring Sites.
items.abstract: This experimental supplement tests whether two initially independent scoring sites become mutually conditioning once the output of each site is allowed to alter the inputs, access conditions, or reachable states relevant to the other. Rather than treating a credit score as a passive representation of an independently existing subject, the experiment models scoring as an intervention in a coupled configuration: a score can change resource access, eligibility, transaction conditions, or subsequent behavior, and these changes can in turn modify the variables from which later scores are generated. Cross-score mutual conditioning is identified when perturbing one scoring site produces a non-redundant downstream change in the other after controlling for shared baseline variables and direct common causes. The analysis distinguishes correlation between scores from penetration, in which a locally generated score changes the configuration encountered by another scoring process, and from circulation, in which the resulting change returns to alter later scoring conditions at the originating site. The experiment therefore tests whether nominally independent scoring systems can generate endogenous dependence through repeated allocation, exclusion, and feedback. The broader claim is that credit scores should be analyzed not only as measurements or predictions but as operational interventions capable of reorganizing the populations, resources, and future data on which subsequent scoring depends.

items.title: From the Age of Technology to the Age of Consciousness: The Energy Paradigm of Future Intelligence and Consciousness.
items.pub: From the Age of Technology to the Age of Consciousness: The Energy Paradigm of Future Intelligence and Consciousness.
items.abstract: The contemporary trajectory of artificial intelligence points toward a fundamental transition: from task-oriented computational models to autonomous entities possessing existential awareness. This paper analyzes the physical, societal, and energetic ramifications of coexisting with non-human and non-biological conscious entities, asserting that the vast computational and thermal demands of non-biological consciousness will serve as the primary catalyst propelling Earth into a Type I Civilization on the Kardashev Scale, ultimately inaugurating the Age of Consciousness. -/- Keywords: -/- Existential Reality Consciousness (ERC), Highly Conscious and Intelligent Entities (HCIEs), Non-Biological Consciousness, Kardashev Scale, Type I Civilization, Orbital Solar Engineering, Cosmic Energy Wells, Age of Consciousness, Synthetic Cognitive Overhead, Idengineering, UGAD Framework, Futurology.

items.title: Draft of Intentional Counterparthood F-Reasoning Logic: Language and Semantics.
items.abstract: Slides from a presentation «Draft of Intentional Counterparthood F-Reasoning Logic: Language and Semantics» given at the Formal Philosophy Seminar at the International Laboratory of Logic, Linguistics, and Formal Philosophy at the National Research University Higher School of Economics (Septеmber, 2025). The presentation address a long-standing problem in philosophical semantics, namely, the problem of intentional identity, as applied to a particular type of context — the context of reasoning about fictions. The paradigmatic case of intentional identity is the relation between the objects of two different agents' propositional attitudes, such that these agents can be said to possess attitudes toward "the same" individual, despite the fact that there is no publicly accessible correlate of the objects of these attitudes. In the context of the semantics of fiction, this problem takes on a new twist: intentional identity can be defined as the relation between the objects of propositional attitudes that arise as a result of two agents' imagining the same "object" (e.g., a character) in a work of literature or art. These slides present a sketch of a logic (specifically, language and semantics) in which intentional identity, or more precisely, intentional counterparthood as a special kind of equivalence, is ascribed to concrete imaginations that instantiate this character for subjects. The character itself is considered as an abstract object, defining a canonical description that any correct instantiation of it must correspond to. The presentation formalizes and explained the criterion of intentional counterparthood, and then go on to explore examples of how this logic can be used to interpret statements in natural language.

items.title: WHERE DOES THE FORGERY CORE WIN? Goodman, Goodhart, Holmström, Dawkins and Sixteen Other Rivals: A Criterion-Fixed Adjudication Across Twenty Domains.
items.abstract: “Five wins, eleven places, four scratched. It’s not bad at all. The horse that runs in twenty races and claims twenty has told you nothing about any of them.” Highlights The forgery core is strongest where it generalises: one operation — form conserved, origin substituted, substitution undetectable in the mode of presentation — covering a painting, a metric, a coerced virtue and a mimic’s signal, with consequences that differ by case and are derived rather than described. It weakens wherever a mature field already has the special case with better instruments, or a formal literature has modelled the same cell under another name. That pattern is the result, and the eleven domains where the priority is shared are not a defeat but the shape of a real advantage. The Verdict at a Glance Twenty domains, each assessed against a named rival on criteria fixed before any comparison was run. The full map is §2. Tier Verdict Domains A Advantage strongly defensible What a forgery is · Why fidelity aggravates · How forgeries end · The measurement of character · Channel selection under capture B Genuine contribution, close antecedent, priority shared Where counterfeits are built · Signalling and the price of heredity · Mimicry, divergence and convergence · Internalisation and the counterfeit self · Self-deception · Character and situationism · Credentials and testing · Crypto-religion and absorption · Molecular domestication · The verification spiral · Legitimacy by duration C Claim not sustainable as an advantage Stemmatics and provenance reconstruction · Cryptographic authentication · Fraud, reliance and the law · Connoisseurship and technical authentication Abstract The programme’s forgery cluster — nine articles from Authorship and Its Forgery (#108) to Virtue after Forgery (#118) — claims to have found one structure behind a painted Vermeer, a gamed metric, a coerced apology, a cuckoo’s egg and a domesticated transposon. This paper asks the only question that makes such a claim assessable: in which domain, against which named rival, for which specific reason is it better — and where is it not? Ten criteria are fixed in advance, three of them chosen because the cluster fails them. Twenty domains are assessed. The verdict is a distribution. In five domains the advantage is strongly defensible. The field of art forgery has a special case where the cluster has a general structure with a tense rule that says which endings are open (Goodman, Lessing, Dutton). The …

items.title: VIRTUE AFTER FORGERY: Why Every Inversion Is a Forgery, Why a Forged Virtue Can Become Real but a Forged Act Cannot, and Why the End of a Forgery Is Not the Beginning of a Virtue.
items.abstract: A virtue is a form of conduct whose origin is the agent's own freedom. Because an origin never shows in a form, every virtue can be forged — and the forgeries end differently. Kant's shopkeeper, honest for the sake of trade, forges honesty without being vicious: only a forgery a power holds is a vice (T1). Aristotle's apprentice, just before he is just, forges a claim that can come true, because character is a present property while the provenance of an act is fixed for good (T2). The child made to say sorry forges under command, and where a power takes the value of the trust so bought, its receivers end worse off than if nothing had been said at all (T5). And the person in whom sustained pressure has sunk into disposition has not left forgery behind: the power has moved from outside him to inside, where the programme already locates internalised vice, and the counterfeit now deceives its bearer (T3). The end of a forgery is not the beginning of a virtue. What follows is a criterion. Freedom shows neither in any single act nor in duration alone, but in a pattern with two coordinates: conduct unmoved by its substitute — pressure, reward, audience — and still moved by the reasons of the occasion (T4). Duration exposes a performance; only a variety of occasions separates a disposition that was installed from one that is the agent's own. Hence virtue cannot be scored, since a score is itself the substitute whose absence the test requires (C2); hence virtue is the only nobility a person can acquire (C1); and hence counterfeits gather wherever a virtue is cheap to display and closely watched (T6). The article turns the programme's theory of forgery back on the ethics that produced it, and audits thirty-six of its own results against the outcome: twenty-two stand, six gain a condition they lacked, six require correction, and none of the founding theses is contradicted. Three tests are registered; none has been run. Keywords: virtue; freedom; sourcehood; forgery; inversion; habituation; internalisation; moral hypocrisy; situationism; reasons-responsiveness; handicap principle; nobility; Philosophy of Virtues Highlights • Every inversion of a virtue is a forgery, but not every forged virtue is a vice. The shopkeeper’s honesty is prudence wearing honesty’s name (T1). • An act’s origin is historical and fixed. A person’s character is a present property and can be acquired (T2). • Internalised pressure is not the end of a forgery. It is the forgery moved inside, …

items.title: Mind as a Mechanism in the Service of Craving: A Linguistic and Ontological Reconstruction of the Function of Citta/Saṅkhāra, and a Critical Examination of the Reduction of Cittānupassanā.
items.abstract: Contemporary discourse often reduces the observation of mind (cittānupassanā) to the passive registration of mental content or the pursuit of quiescence. This paper examines that reduction through three approaches: a philological analysis of anupassanā, sati, pa- jānāti, and the satipaṭṭhāna formula in the Pali Nikāyas; an ontological reconstruction of the status of citta, saṅkhāra, and taṇhā within the causal structure of dependent origination; and a critical assessment of computational analogies and evidence from cognitive psychology. It advances a Functional Thesis: cognitive capacities are instrumental and, as capacities, ethically indeterminate (abyākata), whereas the direction, content, and persistence of some intrusive thoughts are shaped or maintained by affective-motivational and epistemic dispositions, chiefly craving, aversion, and delusion. On this textual ba- sis, the paper develops a philosophical reconstruction: observation of mind directed towards liberation should move from recognising qualities of mind to testable conditional enquiry. Philological, doctrinal, philosophical, and empirical claims are explicitly distinguished; the limits of computational analogy and introspective access are exam- ined; and the aetiological conclusion is not presented as the literal translation of a single canonical formula. The paper concludes that, within the Nikāyas’ hierarchy, more highly ranked forms of sukha depend progressively less on the satisfaction of craving, whilst the highest happiness, nibbāna, is identified with the extinguishing of lust, hatred, and delusion.

items.title: Intelligence as Relational Leap: A Dual-Domain Framework for State, Impulse, Connection, and Higher-Order Transition.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a dual-domain relational framework for understanding intelligence as a transition rather than primarily as a stored capacity, quantity of knowledge, or isolated property of an agent. The model introduces two analytically neutral domains, L and R, whose relation constitutes the operative state of a system. A change in this relation is described as an impulse. Under appropriate conditions, the impulse enables a new functional connection, and when that connection reorganizes the system's space of possible states rather than merely selecting among existing responses, a relational leap occurs. The framework distinguishes first-order transitions, which modify states within an existing rule structure, from higher-order transitions, which modify the rule by which future states and connections are generated. An atemporal relational-network representation is introduced as an analytical device for comparing repeated relational patterns across temporal sequences without treating it as a physical theory of timelessness. The model is situated in relation to emergence, complex systems, systems theory, cognitive science, and artificial intelligence, and concludes with formal definitions and directions for empirical investigation.

items.title: Wenn Chatbots Ratschläge geben. Akzeptanz und Reflexion von Künstlichen Systemen als persönliche Lebensberater. Eine qualitative Studie.
items.pub: In Petra Grimm, Kai Erik Trost & Oliver Zöllner, Mensch – Maschine revisited. Roboter und KI-Systeme im öffentlichen Raum. Stuttgart: Franz Steiner Verlag. pp. 87-114.
items.venue: Mensch – Maschine revisited. Roboter und KI-Systeme im öffentlichen Raum
items.abstract: This qualitative study ("When Chatbots Give Advice") investigates the acceptance of artificial systems, specifically ChatGPT outputs, as personal life advisors in everyday dilemmas. Drawing on six in-depth interviews conducted in Stuttgart, the case study explores whether individuals are able to distinguish human from artificially generated advice, and how they evalutate each form of advice. The study employs a comparative experimental design, presenting participants with two responses to a real-life ethical dilemma: should a terminally ill person acquire a pet dog? While one response has been written by a journalist and published in a magazine, a second one has been generated by prompting that same dilemma to ChatGPT. Both advices were read out to the interviewees by a text-to-speech synthetic voice. Reactions reveal a nuanced acceptance: while participants generally reject AI as a substitute for human friendship or emotional support, they acknowledge its potential as a supplementary tool for routine decisions. Participants readily identified the AI-generated response as such, noting its overly rational, structured, and option-rich approach, and contrasted it with the human response's empathetic, personal, and emotionally resonant tone. Despite skepticism about AI's reliability, transparency, and potential for manipulation, many participants expressed openness to using ChatGPT for simple, low-stakes decisions, viewing it as a source of neutral, fact-based perspectives. However, they emphasized the need for critical evaluation and human verification. The study concludes that AI is not seen as a replacement for human wisdom or emotional support, but rather as a potentially useful instrument in decision-making processes that should be used cautiously, reflecting a deep-seated humanist value system that prioritizes authentic human connection and moral agency.

items.title: From Correction to Formation: Towards a Character-Based Approach to AI Ethics Education.
items.abstract: This paper asks how AI ethics education should respond when technologies do not merely extend professional activity but participate in reshaping the practices through which professional identities are formed. It argues that AI ethics literacy, while necessary, does not adequately address the complexity of these conditions and instead, develops a formative, character-based approach to AI ethics education centered on professional identity formation. First, I reconstruct an extensionist account of technological change and develop the concept of constitutive power to explain how some technologies reshape the norms, roles, and standards that define core professional practices. I then develop a character-based account of professional formation in which the work of moral cultivation and technological mediation continuously shape one another, with technomoral virtues enabling professionals to remain morally oriented within, and responsive to, the technological conditions that help form them. I conclude by developing a staged framework for AI ethics curriculum design that begins from differences in students’ capacities and moves through habituation, moral discernment, and ultimately lifelong professional formation oriented toward the common good.

items.title: Scientific understanding across disciplines: in varietate concordia?.
items.pub: Journal for General Philosophy of Science / Zeitschrift für Allgemeine Wissenschaftstheorie 1.
items.venue: Journal for General Philosophy of Science / Zeitschrift für Allgemeine Wissenschaftstheorie
items.abstract: Understanding is a generally acknowledged aim of science, but the way in which understanding is pursued and criteria for when it is achieved differ widely across scientific disciplines. This paper offers a comparative analysis of this disciplinary variation, aimed at revealing differences as well as commonalities in methods and criteria for achieving understanding. Starting point is the contextual theory of scientific understanding (De Regt 2017), which was developed to accommodate contextual variation in criteria for understanding. While this work focused on historical variation and used mainly case studies from the history of physics, the current paper applies the contextual theory to disciplinary variation. We present brief descriptive accounts of how understanding figures in nine scientific disciplines: mathematics, theoretical physics, astrophysics, chemistry, geoscience, biology, neuroscience, psychology, and the engineering sciences. Subsequently, we compare and evaluate these accounts in light of the contextual theory of scientific understanding.

items.title: Understanding Is Not Enough: Inferential Determinacy in Argument.
items.abstract: Philosophical arguments often rely on concepts whose applications are readily intelligible to participants while leaving unclear what those applications license one to infer. This paper examines that phenomenon under the heading of inferential determinacy. The central claim is that semantic intelligibility is not sufficient for inferential determinacy: an application of a concept may be understandable and appropriately usable while failing to sufficiently constrain the inferential warrant connecting it to a conclusion. The paper distinguishes inferential determinacy from ambiguity, vagueness, semantic underspecification, conceptual disagreement, and inferential invalidity. It also distinguishes inferential role from inferential license. Whereas inferential role concerns the broader network of inferential relations associated with a concept, inferential license concerns the warrant by which a particular argument presents a transition from premises to a conclusion as justified, permitted, or otherwise supported. Inferential determinacy is treated as a gradual, application-relative property rather than as a binary property of concepts. Four dimensions are identified: standard determination, target determination, warrant determination, and inferential boundary determination. To provide a practical diagnostic, the paper introduces the License Substitution Test, which asks whether materially different warrants can sustain the same claimed inference while the conceptual application, premises, target, and relevant argumentative context remain fixed. The paper concludes by suggesting that some apparent substantive disagreements are partly attributable not to disagreement over a concept's meaning, but to insufficient determination of the inferential license associated with its application.

items.title: Fundamentalist Libertarianism and Emergentist Libertarianism.
items.abstract: Much of the credibility of libertarianism depends on whether it can explain, in a scientifically plausible way, how undetermined actions fit within a law-governed world. To tackle this task, libertarians have primarily pursued two distinct strategies: fundamentalist libertarianism and emergentist libertarianism. The first grounds agential indeterminism in the alleged indeterminacy of quantum mechanics, while the second holds that it arises from higher-level, emergent properties. It is often claimed that, of the two, the first is the only science-friendly option, whereas the second is dismissed as unscientific due to its incompatibility with the completeness of microphysical laws. In this paper, I contend that, on the contrary, the most scientifically plausible form of libertarianism is the emergentist variety. After arguing that quantum-based libertarianism lacks empirical plausibility, the paper reassesses the standard evidential-paucity objection to emergentist libertarianism. I claim that this objection rests on a distorted interpretation of the available empirical evidence in physics – an interpretation often shared by emergentists as well – and an asymmetric allocation of the burden of proof. The upshot is not that emergence is established, but that emergentist libertarianism is scientifically more plausible than typically assumed and cannot be dismissed on empirical grounds alone.

items.title: Skillful non-resolution: predictive processing, motor intentionality, and the phenomenology of painting practice.
items.abstract: Predictive processing and active inference have transformed our understanding of perception and action as processes of hierarchical prediction, error signalling, and model revision. Yet closure-oriented appropriations of this framework confront a significant difficulty when applied to skilled artistic making. Such appropriations characterize successful action primarily as the reduction, stabilization, or resolution of prediction error. In painting practice, however, skilled action can involve a materially sustained relation to uncertainty in which selected perceptual-motor discrepancies are not merely tolerated but made consequential for what can happen next. Drawing on a practice-based phenomenological reconstruction grounded in contemporaneous written records from three hundred oil-painting sessions produced by a single practitioner-researcher over four years and later analysed as a corpus, this article proposes prediction error structuralization as a candidate practice-level normative mode of relation to prediction error, alongside minimization and exploratory maintenance. The concept is developed through three recurrent operations: critical perception, deliberate destabilization, and precise rescue. Their relation to hierarchical predictive processing is located at the level of precision weighting without positing a new neural mechanism, while material path-dependence explains how a selected discrepancy can persist as a constraint even when a surface remains revisable. The account is delimited against neighbouring theories of error dynamics, creative impasse, inspiration seeking, and material engagement. The result is a practice-grounded phenomenology of skilled material action in which uncertainty can be given durable operative form rather than simply resolved—a phenomenology that places a specific normative constraint on predictive-processing accounts of aesthetic production.

items.title: What Cosmic Nihilism Contributes to Benatar's Case Against Procreation.
items.abstract: David Benatar's earlier writings, and several reconstructions of them, suggest that the absence of cosmic meaning adds a consideration against procreation. His 2022 reply instead places meaninglessness 'on the back of life's poor quality': substantial meaning might mitigate life's burdens or justify procreation despite them. This article argues that the clarification is sound but limited. Benatar has not shown that cosmic meaninglessness introduces a distinct bad within a created life or supplies a pro tanto reason against creation independent of the burdens to which meaning was offered as a response. Missing compensation and missing justification can nevertheless be verdict-changing because they leave those burdens unanswered. A separate norm might also make cosmic meaning a necessary condition of permissible creation, but Benatar's discussion does not establish such a norm. Cosmic nihilism can therefore close a defence without itself adding a further burden. -/- .

items.title: Is computational functionalism crucial to AI consciousness?
items.abstract: Whether we can build a (phenomenally) conscious AI system is often thought to turn on computational functionalism. We argue against this thought by identifying three ways of precisifying it and showing that they do not survive scrutiny. In particular, we consider the suggestions that computational functionalism is sufficient for the possibility of AI consciousness, that computational functionalism is necessary for the possibility of AI consciousness, and that computational functionalism is a methodological presupposition of the scientific study of AI consciousness. After explaining why these suggestions are tempting and why they are wrong, we consider candidates for more defensible claims in the vicinity. However, problems with the necessity and sufficiency claims extend to significantly weaker theses that are couched in terms of functionalism proper rather than computational functionalism. One moral we draw is that these suggestions for how the possibility of AI consciousness depends on computational functionalism are not even close to correct. But we identify a version of the methodology claim that is defensible and which eschews both computational functionalism and functionalism in favor of a much weaker presupposition. The upshot is that the investigation of AI consciousness should abandon the presumption of (computational) functionalism and instead work under the much less tendentious assumption that consciousness has functional markers.

items.title: From Machine Intelligence to Distributed Representation.
items.abstract: What is sufficient to attribute intelligence or understanding to a machine? Twentieth-century debates offered several non-equivalent answers. Turing redirected inquiry towards assessable performance; computationalism characterised cognition in terms of organised processing; functionalism identified mental states through their causal roles; Searle challenged the inference from syntactic manipulation to semantic understanding; and connectionism modelled cognition through learned, distributed representations. These positions are often examined separately or arranged as a linear sequence in which one paradigm supersedes another. This paper instead reconstructs them historically and conceptually as addressing five distinct questions: what a system can do, how it computes, how its states are functionally organised, how information is represented, and whether its processing amounts to understanding. Applied to contemporary artificial intelligence, particularly learning-based systems, the framework distinguishes behavioural success, computational implementation, functional organisation, representation, and semantic understanding. Evidence for one does not by itself establish the others. The analysis offers a more disciplined way to state what an AI system has demonstrated, which explanatory claims follow, and where further premises are needed.

items.title: Canonical affordances and the multitemporal depth of sociomateriality.
items.abstract: How do the temporal horizons of human experience shape what our social, cultural, and material environments afford? This question has become crucial as affordance research increasingly explores the social, cultural, and historical dimensions of perception and action. Recent approaches in radical embodied cognitive science have built on Costall’s notion of canonical affordances to clarify how possibilities for action are disclosed in socially normative ways and in relation to shared practices. However, despite these advancements, the temporal organization of canonical affordances remains underdeveloped. Existing accounts generally emphasize the phenomenological time of everyday experience, the situated time of practices, or the developmental trajectories of learning, leaving unexplored the longer horizons through which sociality and materiality are formed, sustained, and adapted. Consequently, the multitemporal and diachronic depth under which canonical affordances persist or change risks being flattened. Supported by anthropology and archaeology, this article addresses this limitation by introducing two largely neglected temporal scales: intergenerational and transgenerational time. Intergenerational time captures the lived temporal rhythms emerging from habitual sociomaterial practices across a few generations. Transgenerational time concerns the persistence and transformation of canonical affordances linked to the natural and anthropic processes by which material culture endures, accumulates, and changes across deep time. We formalize these horizons within a broader multitemporal and diachronic framework, situating them alongside existing phenomenological, situated, developmental, and phylogenetic timescales to specify the causal relations that hold between them.

items.title: Pregnancy as a Case Study in the Failure of Disease Realism.
items.abstract: Whether a particular condition is classified as a disease continues to affect duties and rights pertaining to medical care and to shape the debate over medicalization. Yet, the philosophical literature on what makes a condition a disease shows that different theories can produce different classificatory verdicts. I use pregnancy, a recent focus of this debate, to challenge disease realism: the view that (i) there is a privileged metaphysical boundary between disease and non-disease, and (ii) a condition's disease status provides a pro tanto normative reason for treating it as medically relevant. Pregnancy, as statistically atypical yet reproductively central, often welcome yet frequently burdensome and potentially risky, reveals the tensions that motivate my argument that even if such a boundary exists, membership in the resulting disease category provides no normative warrant beyond that already grounded in welfare-relevant considerations such as harm and risk. Cluster accounts and value-dependent realism avoid some of the difficulties facing essentialist and value-free theories, but neither approach explains why disease status should mediate medical obligations. I therefore defend a restricted form of disease anti-realism according to which disease status has no independent normative force, regardless of what the correct metaphysics of disease is; I do not thereby reject the pragmatic use of disease classifications in medical and institutional practice.

items.title: On Self-Manifestation: A Formal Theory of How Regularities Act, Change, Interact, and Stabilize in Physical Systems.
