items.abstract: Once a regularity has formed within a physical system, what makes it genuinely active at a given moment? How can its degree of formation be compared? How does it begin, continue, increase, decrease, cease, or migrate across time? Can a specified dynamical condition be reached from a given state? When do two already established regularities genuinely interact? And how can an organization composed of multiple regularities persist, fail, undergo substitution, and recover? -/- The Law\-Dynamics Group\-Form develops a formal theory of how established regularities actually operate\. Its starting point is not an abstract rule suspended outside the physical system, but a regularity already borne by concrete structure\. The problem is then to determine how that regularity enters current operation, acts, changes across time, contributes to the dynamics of other regularities, and participates in persistent multi\-regularity organization\. -/- The thirteen form\-texts constitute five connected but non\-substitutable theoretical domains\. -/- First, the framework separates the standing of a regularity from its current action\. A Law may already be established without acting at every moment\. Necessary and sufficient directions for Law\-action are developed separately, together with a multidimensional Degree regime for comparing the extent to which an established Law has been sedimented, replayed, made available, and dynamically established\. -/- Second, cross\-temporal change is made into a formal dynamical object\. LawDyn is not defined as a mere difference between measurements at two times, but as an actual change of the same Law across a lawful trajectory segment\. This permits onset, continuation, cessation, increase, decrease, and migration to be distinguished, followed by a mathematical system, a reachability regime for dynamical targets, and a Sedimentation\-Field operating substrate in which these structures can actually run\. -/- Third, the framework examines continuity across occurrences and historical source\. Identity of physical roots does not automatically determine Law\-side pairing, and Law\-side pairing does not by itself settle the general criterion of Law identity\. The theory separately asks which actual segment of history bore the first establishment of a Law and how far source can be determined when more than one historical explanation remains admissible\. -/- Fourth, a theory of direct event\-level interaction between Laws is established\. …

items.title: 自显论·律动力组式：规律在物理系统中的作用、动力、交互与稳定的形式理论.
items.abstract: 一条规律一旦在一个物理系统中形成，什么才算它此刻真正正在作用？它的形成程度如何比较？它怎样在时间中启动、持续、增强、减弱、停止或迁移？从给定状态出发，某种动力变化能否到达？两条已经形成的规律何时真正发生直接交互？多条规律共同构成的组织，又怎样保持、失效、替代与恢复？ -/- 《律动力组式》围绕这些问题，建立一套关于“已形成规律如何真实运行”的形式理论。其出发点不是把规律看作悬置于物理系统之外的抽象规则，而是研究规律一旦由具体结构承担以后，怎样进入当前、发生作用、跨时间改变、影响其他规律，并组成能够持续存在的多律组织。 -/- 全组十三篇式文形成五个彼此连接而不可互相替代的理论区域。 -/- 第一，区分“规律已经成立”与“规律此刻正在作用”。一条律即使已经形成，也并不意味着它在每个时刻都正在承担当前事件。本组分别给出律作用的必要方向与充分方向，并建立多维 Degree 制度，用来比较规律在沉积、复走、承担和当前可用性上的形成程度。 -/- 第二，把规律的跨时变化正式建立为动力对象。LawDyn 不是两个时刻读数的简单相减，而是同一律在合法轨迹段中的实际变化。由此可以区分启动、持续、停止、增强、减弱与迁移，并进一步建立其数理系统、动力目标的可达制度以及能够实际运行这些结构的沉积场运行基底。 -/- 第三，处理规律跨 occurrence 的连续性与历史来源。物理承载根相同，不自动意味着律层配对相同；律层配对相同，也不能直接代替一般的规律身份判定。本组进一步追问：一条律第一次真正成立时，究竟是哪一段实际历史承担了它的形成，并在来源存在多解时给出可判边界。 -/- 第四，建立律与律之间的直接事件级交互理论。两条规律同时存在、共享介质、相关变化，甚至发生一般物理影响，都不足以自动构成律际交互。只有当来源律以自身已经成立的职责实际进入目标律的动力事件并产生符合该职责的事件贡献时，直接律际交互才取得资格。本组分别建立其必要结构、数理表示与充分闭合。 -/- 第五，把研究从单律与两律推进到多律组织。一组规律可以分别承担不同节点职责，并通过反复兑现的事件级交互形成组织。该组织随后可能遭遇成员退出、承担者替换、作用程度变化、交互中断和重新恢复。本组因此区分固定实现与可替代实现、单轨迹与轨迹族、保持与恢复，并进一步区分持续稳定、恢复能力以及更强的全合法轨迹保证。 -/- 这一理论同时适用于由经验形成并以物理结构承担规律的系统。对神经科学而言，它直接涉及经验依赖可塑性、神经动力学、学习后形成的稳定通路、当前激活、功能迁移、回路交互以及多回路组织的稳定与恢复；对认知科学而言，它涉及经验、习惯、记忆、感知和行为结构如何由既成模式持续组织后来活动；对人工智能而言，它可用于区分训练后形成的结构、运行时作用、程度变化、跨时动力、迁移、交互及多结构稳定，而不把参数存在本身等同于当前作用；对物理学与复杂系统研究而言，它把“规律”从静态描述推进到可由具体结构承担、可在轨迹中发生动力变化、可参与事件级交互并形成稳定组织的动态对象。 -/- 因此，本组处理的不只是“规律是什么”，而是一个更直接的动力学问题：**已经形成的规律，怎样真正进入世界的运行。**.

items.title: More than transcendence: techno-salvationism and the reconfiguration of religious authority in Japanese and Chinese Buddhist contexts.
items.abstract: Techno-salvationism is commonly understood as a cultural imaginary in which advanced technologies promise transcendence, immortality, or liberation from human limitations. Existing scholarship has largely examined this phenomenon through Western theological and posthumanist perspectives, leaving its localized forms underexplored. This study investigates how techno-salvationist imaginaries are reconfigured in Japanese and Chinese Buddhist contexts through mediated representations of robotic religious agents. Using visual discourse analysis of publicly available videos featuring three prominent Buddhist robots—Mindar in Japan, Pepper in Japanese funerary settings, and Xian’er in China—the research examines how religious authority is visually constructed and interpreted. The findings reveal that techno-salvationism in these contexts is not primarily oriented toward transcendence or technological supremacy. Instead, it is grounded in instrumental and institutional logics that emphasize continuity, maintenance, and outreach. Authority shifts occur through deliberate clerical endowment rather than contestation, positioning robots as successors or communicative tools embedded within existing hierarchies. The cases further demonstrate uneven forms of techno-salvationism shaped by demographic pressures, infrastructural disparities, and cultural priorities. By demonstrating succession rather than transcendence as a recurring pattern, this study expands the conceptual scope of techno-salvationism and contributes to scholarship on digital religion by identifying a culturally specific mode of authority reconfiguration in mediated representations of Buddhist robots.

items.title: A FORTALEZA COMO FUNDAMENTO ÉTICO DO CUIDADO NA ANTROPOLOGIA DE TOMÁS DE AQUINO.
items.abstract: This article addressed the theme of fortitude as an ethical foundation for the prac-tice of care based on the anthropology of Thomas Aquinas. The question thatguided the research was: how can care be ethically sustained in the face of vul-nerability, suffering, and fear that mark the human condition? The objective ofthe study was to demonstrate how the virtue of fortitude, in conjunction with pru-dence, grace, and other virtues, sought to offer solid criteria for persevering in thecare of oneself and others even in adverse contexts. The methodology adopted wastheoretical-bibliographic, analytical-interpretative in nature, based mainly on theSumma Theologiae, especially on issues related to habit, moral virtues, and for-titude, in dialogue with the ethics of care. As a result, it became evident thatfortitude, by ordering fear according to reason and sustaining the will in goodness,constitutes an indispensable element for a stable, rational, and truly human practiceof care, integrating vulnerability, moral responsibility, and charity.

items.title: The Need for Punishment in Global Climate Justice.
items.abstract: Debates on climate justice typically centre on the global allocation of mitigation, adaptation, and compensation for loss and damage burdens. However, the importance of punishing those whose actions constitute what I will call climate crimes is often overlooked. In this paper, I argue that a just global response to climate change must incorporate punitive justice alongside distributive and corrective justice frameworks. Adapting Robert Nozick's argument from fear to the international and climate context, I contend that those whose actions produce fear of the most severe consequences of climate change ought to be punished. Not all fear producing actions warrant criminalisation, however. I argue that only actions that impose a serious and unjustifiable risk of violating basic rights or actually violate them, and that are committed intentionally or with a particular type of recklessness, should qualify as climate crimes and be subject to international punitive justice.

items.title: Imagination Machines: A Fixed Point in Knowledge.
items.abstract: This series of eight papers develops a unified formal framework for embedded epistemic systems—systems that must model the world from within it, without access to an external vantage point. It begins from a primitive ontological ground and ends by showing what it is like to inhabit that ground from the inside—and what must be chosen there. The series derives a layered architecture spanning formal epistemology, the philosophy of science, the dynamics of agent–environment interaction, empirical representation learning, cognition and analogy, phenomenology, and moral philosophy. The series was developed under the constraint of the same recursive architecture it describes. The loop closed on a fixed point.

items.title: Attuned Engagement: A Critique of Laissez-Faire Indifference and the Reframing of Non-Intervention Ethics.
items.abstract: This thesis critically examines the dominant ethical paradigm of non-intervention, arguing that its philosophical underpinnings in laissez-faire ideology represent a form of “dis-attunement” from the complex entanglements of our contemporary world. The work introduces and develops the concept of “attuned engagement” as a novel ethical framework that challenges the binary logic of intervention versus non-intervention. Drawing upon a unique synthesis of Martin Heidegger’s phenomenology of attunement (Stimmung), new materialist theories of entanglement, and critical international relations theory, this thesis posits that a more responsible and ethical approach to global challenges requires a shift from a politics of separation to a politics of relationality. Through a series of theoretical explorations and case study analyses, the thesis demonstrates how attuned engagement—as a continuous, context-sensitive, and responsive process of co-shaping—offers a more ontologically sound and ethically robust alternative to both paternalistic intervention and laissez-faire indifference. The research culminates in the presentation of a new conceptual model for understanding and navigating the ethical complexities of global interdependence, with significant implications for fields as diverse as international law, environmental policy, and digital governance.

items.title: The dual-mode awareness framework (DMAF): toward epistemic sovereignty in AI-mediated knowledge societies.
items.abstract: While cross-checking a set of financial figures, I submitted the same data to a spreadsheet and to a conversational AI system and received two different answers. The system, pressed to explain the discrepancy, eventually acknowledged that it had treated the numbers as language rather than as quantities to be computed—and had, in effect, been guessing. Nothing in its response had indicated this. This paper develops a conceptual framework for the structural condition that discrepancy revealed: operational opacity, the absence of any visible distinction, at the interaction surface, between AI outputs produced through probabilistic generation and those produced through reliable computation. I argue that operational opacity differs from algorithmic opacity in the existing literature by relocating the problem from the internal architecture of AI systems to the moment of interaction itself, and that it differs from automation bias by naming a condition prior to evaluation: a culturally embedded assumption of cross-domain competence—the omnicompetence assumption—that meets an uninformative interface and produces modality collapse, the inability to distinguish what kind of process generated a given response. The consequence is capability illusion. I develop the Dual-Mode Awareness Framework (DMAF) around three analytically independent dimensions—modality perceptibility, verification effort, and stakes sensitivity—whose interaction, rather than any single dimension in isolation, determines the epistemic risk of a given exchange. The framework's normative claims are grounded in Stiegler’s pharmacological account of technology and Habermas’s ethics of communicative transparency, selected because each names a feature of AI-mediated exchange directly rather than by analogy. DMAF does not prescribe interface redesign; it offers a diagnosis at the level of user awareness, on the strength of which I argue that primary responsibility for operational opacity falls on those who design and deploy AI systems rather than on the users who encounter them, while showing why this distribution does not require the framework to dictate how that responsibility should be discharged.

items.title: The Music, Not the Instrument: Introducing The Harmonics of Consciousness.
items.abstract: I think, therefore I am… we have all whispered these words with trembling uncertainty, wondering if we could ever understand our own experiences. What is consciousness? Where does the sense of "you" come from? How does a three-pound lump of brain matter create the rich, vivid experience of being alive? These questions have haunted humanity for millennia. Despite brilliant minds, cutting-edge technology, and centuries of relentless inquiry, consciousness remains one of our most stubborn mysteries. We sit in silence… think about the despair that we may never understand—that we will never explain the gap between brain activity and subjective experience… but what if we are wrong? What you are about to see will change how you understand your mind. I solved the hard problem of consciousness by revealing a truth hiding in plain sight: we have been looking for consciousness in all the wrong places. Consciousness is not a thing tucked away in your brain—it is the symphony that emerges when four consciousness "instruments" play together in perfect harmony. Using the Animal Kingdom Dataset, I scored 456 behaviors across 850+ spanning the entire animal kingdom—mapping the universal architecture of consciousness. The results are revolutionary. Consciousness operates through four instruments, which are 1) self-reference, 2) recursive introspection, 3) emotions, and 4) intelligence, that harmonize into six consciousness tunes, from basic functional processing to abstract thoughts. The empirical evidence shows the same songs of consciousness across insects, birds, mammals, fish, reptiles, and amphibians. A cubic regression of the consciousness scores explains 99.41% of all animal behavior across the entire animal kingdom. This model reveals why consciousness seemed mysterious, reveals the functional, neuroanatomical mechanics of consciousness, and empirically confirms a beautiful truth: every conscious being is playing variations on this same universal tune. Step inside the symphony of being, and you will not just hear The Harmonics of Consciousness—you will see that your brain is the instrument, and the chord it plays? That’s you.

items.title: Autism as an Operatoric Boundary Phenomenon: Eigenzeit, Non-Closure, and Morphogenetic Non-Coincidence.
items.abstract: This paper develops a morphogenetic and operatoric model of autistic development. Its starting point is a problem in current explanations of autism: genetic, neural, sensory, and developmental research can determine with increasing precision which components and differences are involved in autistic development, without thereby necessarily explaining why these differences appear together as “autism,” or why similar biological elements can become effective in different ways within different people. The paper therefore proposes investigating autism not only at the level of individual components or causal factors, but at the level of their form and relation. Morphology here does not merely refer to bodily form. What is meant is the question of how an already formed structure changes which further relations, effects, and continuations are possible at all. The same gene, the same stimulus, or the same representational structure can remain materially identical and nevertheless occupy a different operatoric position within a relational order that has formed differently. With the concepts of Gap, Nicht-Schließbarkeit (Non-Closure), Seinsverschiebung (Shift of being), and Eigenzeit, this displacement is given a theoretical formulation. Development is not understood merely as a sequence of causally connected states. Every realized form binds difference without fully abolishing it and thereby implies a changed relational order. Eigenzeit denotes the irreversible curvature of this world-binding. Operatoric here means: what matters is not only which components are present or which processes take place between them, but what position a difference occupies within a given relational order with regard to possible continuations. What is meant is not an additional process stage, but a form of connectability, relevance, and efficacy implied by the respective order itself. On this basis, the concept of morphogenetic non-coincidence is developed. Different Eigenzeiten can produce macroscopically highly similar human forms and share large parts of the same material, linguistic, and social world without therefore converging on the same internal structure or the same world-relation. They can stabilize different orders of relevance, Raster, and forms of operatoric continuability. Their apparent commonality therefore need not lie within these Eigenzeiten themselves. It may arise only where different world-relations encounter the same dominant Raster and become non-coincident in …

items.title: The Affective Forms of Acute Fatigue: Antagonistic, Acquiescent, Hesitative.
items.abstract: This article argues that acute fatigue resists classification within standard phenomenological affective categories (emotion, mood, existential feeling, vital feeling, atmosphere, and bodily stirring). Although categorization attempts initially distinguish acute fatigue from chronic fatigue and exhaustion, the diverse cases within acute fatigue do not easily unify under a single affective type. To go beyond this limit, the article describes how acute fatigue manifests in three structurally distinct affective forms: antagonistic fatigue, in which one finds oneself counteracting a felt sense of inability; acquiescent fatigue, in which felt inability aligns with and confirms one’s evaluative orientation; and hesitative fatigue, an internally divided form that renders transitions between the other two intelligible. It closes by examining how the social world both exacerbates and partially counteracts the negative affectivity of acute fatigue.

items.title: Bodily awareness in acute fatigue: the corporealization of the minimal performative body.
items.abstract: Knowing when one feels fatigued, and not just tired or expending effort, matters. When fatigue is correctly detected, physician-patient misunderstandings can be avoided (Long et al., 2022), occupational safety concerns can be addressed (Van der Linden, 2011), and injury as well as loss of well-being can be reduced in athletic contexts (Saw et al., 2016). Although existing empirical definitions of acute fatigue include feeling the need to rest and a mismatch between expended effort and actual performance (Behrens et al., 2023; Skau et al., 2021), the present article offers an applied phenomenology to enrich such operational definitions. It does so by building on Katherine Morris’s study (2019) and suggests that acute fatigue involves a disruptive layering of multiple modalities of bodily awareness. The present work introduces these modalities (the transparent, performative, lived, and material bodies) before outlining their interaction during what Thomas Fuchs calls corporealization (2002; 2005b). Corporealization during acute fatigue is then analysed as a twofold disruption, whereby what I call the minimal performative body both feels its movement as wrong and encounters the material body. Appealing to this aspect of acute fatigue’s phenomenology, I argue, helps to differentiate it from experiences of tiredness, on the one hand, and chronic fatigue and exhaustion, on the other.

items.title: Strengthening Rights Protection in Madagascar’s Disaster Law: A Multi-Method Legal Assessment.
items.abstract: Madagascar is highly exposed to cyclones, floods, and drought, yet its disaster governance framework centered on Law No. 2015-031 and related decrees remains weakly aligned with international human rights standards. This study introduces three analytical tools to assess the rights-protective capacity of national disaster law: the Rights Protection Gap Mapping Method (RPGM), the Rights-Based Disaster Protection Index (RBDPI), and a Dual Hazard Legal Stress Test (DHLST). Applied to Madagascar, these methods evaluate rights recognition, operational guarantees, and institutional performance under both rapid-onset cyclones and slow-onset drought. The findings revealed pervasive normative and operational deficiencies. Disaster-affected people were not recognized as rights-holders, and the law contains no enforceable rights to assistance, food, water, shelter, health services, information, or protection from displacement. The RBDPI score of 4/12 indicated very weak rights-based protection. While cyclone response was hindered mainly by procedural and coordination gaps, drought conditions exposed deeper structural failures, including the legal invisibility of displacement and the absence of subsistence-related rights and anticipatory governance mechanisms. The analysis identifies targeted legal reforms to embed enforceable rights, operational standards, and accountability mechanisms capable of protecting dignity and equality across hazard types.

items.title: Correction: WHO is responsible? Towards the normativity of AI-driven BCI technologies in product liability in healthcare.
THE BODY WITHOUT COMMANDS XenoBody: Eight Operational Axes, Embodied Access, and Human Operational Anatomy Xeno-Embodied Askesis and Fourteen Operational Cuts.
items.abstract: This monograph investigates how an instruction can participate in the formation of a bodily capacity and later cease to be required, while the material, observational and normative conditions of that capacity continue to change. A human-readable cue supplies a tractable intervention; it does not define a universal body. The human study remains prospective. The wider XenoBody architecture asks how a body-relevant organization forms, acquires access, changes its partitions and redistributes dependencies across human and nonhuman configurations. A material bodily organization, an ordinarily warranted body attribution, a locally warranted activation of Xenobodiment and an exclusive explanatory ontology are distinct. V19 made a protected, task-relative contribution beyond specified body-free comparators necessary for Xenobodiment as a research concept; R36 restores that condition rather than reclassifying it as a merely optional bonus. This does not entail that a living body ceases to exist when its functioning can be explained mechanistically. A still stronger claim of irreducibility to every possible rival requires a different argument and is not established. These levels, their failure conditions and their relation to the original source are kept explicit throughout the book. The architecture begins before operation or body is granted. A provisional target-side order distinguishes real difference, physical transformation of difference, discriminability, addressability, and access to later coupling. Operation and operational shape are introduced only when retained or recurrent organization makes consequential transitions trackable. Three checkpoints remain nonidentical: transition onset, analytic concept re-entry, and operational concept ignition. Every determination remains indexed to a local access configuration K rather than identified with an exhaustive body or final observational standpoint. Access redesign makes that indexing experimentally active. Sensor substitution, boundary perturbation, scale and interval variation, intervention-path and representation substitution, and role or medium exchange are used to test whether a body determination survives, requires restriction, splits into more than one operative unit, or expires. Reality-as-a-whole functions only as a scope and non-closure operator. Truth, access, and access-training remain distinct, and every apparent gain is separately evaluated for changed dependencies, revision capacity, and …

items.title: Quine and Language as a Social Art: Projection, Harmony, and the Illusion of Shared Linguistic Standards.
items.abstract: Quine is generally taken to be a paradigmatic defender of the idea that language is a shared public resource, learned by internalizing shared standards. I argue that this misreads him. The correct Quinean picture is what I call the Projection Thesis: our linguistic practices result from the projection of individual organization and the harmony among individual neurophysiological mechanisms, not from the internalization of anything shared. Establishing this requires distinguishing Quine’s heuristic vocabulary—behavioral dispositions, which delimit phenomena to be explained—from his explanatory vocabulary—neurophysiology, which actually explains them. Conflating these levels generates what I call the Philosophical Illusion: the seamlessness of practice is taken at face value, leading us to posit shared entities to explain it. I trace the Projection Thesis through two domains. In grammar, I show that the child’s acquisition of grammatical structure is a projection from her own resources, not an extraction from the data—a point connected to Quine’s indeterminacy of translation through the parallel with the radical translator’s analytical hypotheses. In the domain of perceptual similarity standards, I show how the preestablished harmony among innate standards sustains communication without shared resources while generating the illusion of shared language. The philosophical payoff of dissolving this illusion is substantial: negotiation emerges as the real social art, and the absence of shared standards reveals that the only available measure of communicative success is the response of the other—a result that, as I argue in the conclusion, points toward a Cavellian picture of mutual responsibility as the ground of linguistic community.

items.title: THE FORK OF THE MASK: Why a Sustained Performance Becomes Either Vice or Virtue, and What Decides Which.
items.abstract: Two men begin in the same place. Each performs conduct he does not originate, under a pressure he did not choose. Years later one of them is kind, and it is his own; the other is cold, and that is his own too. Neither is pretending any longer. The same process has run in both, and has ended in opposite places. The programme has results on each half of this without a result that joins them. The Internalisation Theorem holds that external pressure converts, over time, into the agent’s own vice. The Restorative Virtue Arc holds that a person can become the author of conduct he began under constraint. The Absorption Theorem holds, for communities and for genomes, that a performed form becomes its bearer’s origin once its independent line of transmission is cut. The Price of the Performance identified the individual case with surface and deep acting, and found in the best longitudinal data a loop in which exhaustion drives more of the counterfeit it came from. This article states the result that joins them. A sustained performance has two references: the pressure that demands it, and the corrector — anyone who still treats the performer as the author of his own acts. A performance held under both is a counterfeit: costly, and reversible. Remove the corrector while the pressure continues, and the demanded form drifts into the agent’s own disposition: internalisation, and the vice is now his. Remove the pressure while the conduct continues, and the conduct becomes his: redemption. Same operation, opposite destinations, decided by which reference is cut (T1). The corrector is what keeps a performance reversible (T2), and the drift it prevents has a direction: toward whatever is performed every day (T3). The corrector is not a moral good: it holds the agent’s prior origin, whatever that was, so the question to ask of any relation around a person under pressure is which origin it holds. The priority on most of this belongs to psychology, and is conceded in full: Kelman on compliance and internalisation, Festinger and Carlsmith on insufficient justification, the overjustification effect, and above all self-determination theory, whose continuum of internalisation and whose finding that autonomy support facilitates it are the nearest precedent. What the programme adds is the fork itself — that the same process internalises the occupier’s form as readily as a valued one — a threshold beyond which it cannot be reversed, and a test that could fail: the …

items.title: ON THE ORIGIN AND THE END OF FORGERIES: Transmission as Their Cause, Four Exits as Their Fate, and Why Forgeries of Kind Diverge While Forgeries of Property Converge.
items.abstract: A cuckoo’s egg in a reed warbler’s nest is a forgery of the warbler’s own egg, and the contest between the two species has produced cuckoo lineages each matched to a different host. Two defended butterflies in the Amazon wear one warning pattern, and dozens of species have converged on it. A painting sold as a Vermeer was exposed as the work of a twentieth-century forger. A usurping family became, in time, its nation’s lawful princes. The first case is a race that never ends, the second an agreement, the third a detection and the fourth a legitimation. This article asks why forgeries end so differently. Two earlier results supply half an answer each. The Price of Transmissible Form (#111) explained where forgeries come from: any form that can be copied, and does not carry its origin legibly, can be produced by a second origin. How a Forgery Ends (#116) explained where they go: a forgery whose form survives ends by detection, absorption, fulfilment or re-attribution. It also showed that the tense of the claim a form makes decides which of these exits are open. This article joins the two results, corrects the first, and derives what neither states alone. • T1, the Legibility Link. The quantity that makes a forgery possible is the quantity whose recovery ends it by detection. A form can be forged only where its origin is illegible, and a forgery can be detected only where its origin can be read again, which happens through the errors of its production. So the fidelity that lets a forgery arise is also what shields it from detection. • T2, the Divergence–Convergence Theorem. Where a forgery claims a kind or a history, fulfilment and absorption are closed. The contest between forger and verifier can then end only by detection, so it persists, and forger lineages diverge according to the verifier each faces. Where a forgery claims a property, fulfilment is open. The contest can end in agreement, and forms converge. Forgeries of kind make races and, where mating follows the verifier, species. Forgeries of property make conventions. • C1 restricts #111’s claim that forgery generates lineages to forgeries of kind. • C2 extends the result to institutions. Verification professions concentrate on historical claims, because only there can the contest never end. Tests of property settle only where they reach the property itself; a test that inspects a proxy reopens the spiral. • C3, the Mosaic Corollary. The claim is made trait by trait, not organism by organism. A …

items.title: HOW A FORGERY ENDS: The Exit Theorem, the Tense of a Claim, and Why Authority Can Become Legitimate While History Cannot Be Rewritten.
items.abstract: A viral gene now builds the human placenta. A harmless butterfly wears the warning colours of a poisonous one, and some mimics of this kind are themselves defended. A trademark became the common name of a drug. A forged imperial donation was exposed by its Latin, more than eleven centuries after it claimed to have been written. A usurping family came, in time, to be regarded as its nation’s lawful princes. A man ordered by a court into decency became decent. Each of these forms was once, in some sense, false. Each is now something else. The literature describes each case in its own field, and none describes what they share: how a forgery ends. This article answers from the programme’s definition of forgery: a form conserved (F1), an origin substituted (F2), a substitution undetectable in the mode in which the form presents (F3). A forgery ends when one condition fails. F1 failing is lapse; F3 failing is detection. F2 is a relation between the form’s producer and the origin the form announces, and it can fail in exactly three ways: the production passes to the announced origin (absorption), the producer acquires what was announced (fulfilment), or the announcement changes to name the actual producer or none (re-attribution). Four endings leave the form in the world, and they are exhaustive (T1, the Exit Theorem). Which endings are available is fixed by the tense of the claim a form makes (T2). A claim about what its bearer is or can do now can be fulfilled. A claim about who produces the form now can be absorbed. A claim about what happened — who made it, when, from what descent — can be neither; it can only be detected or re-attributed. No ending erases the forgery’s history, which remains written in the errors of the forged phase (T3). Authority is a conferred status rather than a historical fact, so a forged claim to authority can be fulfilled by the institutions that confer it, while a forged claim about the origin of that authority cannot (C1). This is Hume’s observation about usurpers made into a corollary, and it explains why the Donation of Constantine could be exposed while the rights it had been used to support were kept on other grounds. Priority is conceded to Goodman on the autographic and the allographic, to Hume and Jellinek on legitimacy by duration, to the mimicry literature on the continuum between Batesian and Müllerian mimicry, and to the genomic literature on domestication. The biological and legal-historical applications (§4, §6 and …

items.title: No universal patient: temporal logics of harm prevention in emotional AI healthcare across Japan, China, and Hong Kong.
items.abstract: Across East Asia, emotional AI in healthcare is governed through markedly different normative and institutional rationalities that construct the patient, harm, and vulnerability in distinct ways. This article develops a triadic analytical framework, integrating moral anthropologies, models of legitimacy, and regulatory instruments, to examine governance rationalities in Japan, China, and Hong Kong. Instead of treating Asian perspectives as variations on Euro-American principlism, this analysis examines these jurisdictions in their own right, showing how each constructs the patient differently, as relational node, protected subject, or rights-holder, and prioritises different harms accordingly. Using PARO, a therapeutic companion robot deployed globally in elderly care, as a stylised analytical device, the article shows that the same robot becomes three different regulatory objects. This case study surfaces a fourth dimension of governance rationality: temporal orientation. Japan’s governance rationality is iterative, allowing norms to emerge through use and professional dialogue; China’s is preventive, anticipating and regulating harms before deployment; and Hong Kong’s is reactive, adjudicating violations after they occur. These temporal orientations shape harm-prevention outcomes as consequentially as the choice of instruments, and constitute the article’s primary empirical contribution. Extending Cheong’s analysis of structural accountability gaps and Zuboff’s account of how institutional power determines which technological harms become actionable, the comparison suggests that vulnerability, harm, and accountability function as governance-produced categories rather than as properties inherent to the technology. The article argues that governing emotional AI requires not harmonisation of principles but recognition of ontological difference, an epistemological reorientation with direct implications for transnational governance frameworks.

items.title: Ad Hoc Concepts: Definition and Philosophical Applications.
items.abstract: A speaker often uses a word or phrase to communicate a concept that is not conventionally expressed by the linguistic item deployed, but the hearer can usually construct the intended concept through pragmatic inference. Many concepts expressed this way are called “ad hoc concepts” and are common in communication. The aim of this paper is to clarify the nature of these concepts and the pragmatic mechanisms responsible for constructing them in utterance comprehension. Building on this, I explore how ad hoc concepts can be applied to understand issues in philosophy. As an example, I illustrate how intuitive claims elicited by thought experiments such as Frank Jackson’s Mary and Hilary Putnam’s Twin Earth may be understood as involving ad hoc concepts, and how the notion can help us make sense of our intuitive responses to these thought experiments.

items.title: Time, Free Will, and the Strange World of Physics: Questions for Carlo Rovelli (and Other Physicists).
items.abstract: Does modern physics provide insight into major philosophical questions? Questions such as Is human behavior determined? Do humans have free will? Are humans entirely physical beings? Is time travel to the past possible? Are the past and the future just as real as the present? Is time an illusion? The renowned physicist Carlo Rovelli has written a series of best-selling books that combine accounts of modern physics with reflections on important philosophical issues. Time, Free Will, and the Strange World of Physics enters into a dialogue with Rovelli, sorting through fascinating philosophical questions with clear and careful reasoning.

items.title: Who is responsible for tackling professional deskilling?
items.abstract: There has been increasing interest across several professional fields in problems of deskilling, that is, the loss or the lack of development of human skills due to outsourcing tasks to artificial intelligence. Avigail Ferdman (“AI Deskilling is a Structural Problem.” AI & Society 41 (4): 3001–13, 2026) has recently argued that deskilling should be seen as a structural problem. In this paper, based on empirical literature on the relevant heuristics and biases, I present a novel empirically-informed philosophical argument as to why this seems to be the case. According to the empirical literature on deskilling, automation bias, and skill decay, many professionals rely on artificial intelligence much more than is necessary when it is available, and the effects of such overreliance on skill decay are unlikely to be entirely understood by the professionals themselves. I argue that this – what I call the insidious nature of deskilling – supports a normative view, according to which the responsibility for tackling deskilling should not be ascribed to the individual professional but the risks of professional deskilling should be tackled by the professional community instead. Mitigating the risks of deskilling should start from an intra-field analysis of the core skills of the profession that should not be outsourced to artificial intelligence. Then, the individual professional would not be left alone to determine how and when to prevent deskilling during the adoption of artificial intelligence within her profession.

items.title: Aandacht, normativiteit en onwetendheid.
items.abstract: In ‘Legal normativity in statu nascendi,’ Hans Lindahl draws on my phenomenological account of receptive attention in the development of his phenomenological genealogy of legal normativity. While sympathetic to this project, here, I articulate a number of barriers to being receptive that might impede the redrawing of our attentional field and threaten to totalize existing norms. In particular, I describe how, in the context of everyday life, practices of (more or less active) ignorance are operative on the pre-reflective level that go against our being receptive as individuals or collectives. Then, I point to how institutions are normatively constitutive of our pre-reflective experience of the everyday world in ways we remain ignorant of, which may only become visible from certain embodied perspectives. This raises the following question for a phenomenological genealogy of legal normativity: Is ignorance, understood in this twofold way, also at play in the legal Sonderwelt, or are legal collectives (more or less) ignorant in any of these ways? If this question is answered in the affirmative, two related questions follow: Does receptive attention suffice to overcome these forms of ignorance? And does a phenomenological genealogy suffice to capture how ignorance is at work in the genesis of legal normativity?

items.title: Draining the Data Pool. Why Larger Samples Need Not Always Be Better.
items.abstract: It is commonplace to bemoan small studies in empirical fields, and to call for larger sample sizes, for example by pooling data within large-scale collaborations. However, while higher-powered studies are individually more reliable, we show that, under conditions of data scarcity, they can make scientific communities less reliable by reducing theoretical diversity. Our results build on a formal model introduced for science by Kevin Zollman, which we adapt, stringently interpret, and partially de-idealize to address worries about its real-life significance. We conclude that collaborative pooling is only beneficial up to some (context-dependent) point and argue against one-size-fits-all norms about sample size.

items.title: Material uncertainty in computational workflow in the archives: Holocaust last writings beyond machine-readable extraction.
items.abstract: This article examines how computational archival workflows transform fragile Holocaust last writings into machine-readable data, and what is lost in that transformation. It introduces the concept of material uncertainty: the condition of textual objects whose meaning cannot be separated from the damaged, improvised, or unstable material forms through which they survive. Drawing on Holocaust literary criticism, archival theory, material trauma studies, and debates over computation in cultural heritage, the article reconstructs a typical archival workflow, from image preprocessing, segmentation, and text recognition to post-processing, translation, metadata generation, and classification. It then executes this workflow on three Holocaust last-writing limit cases: Eva Schulzová’s illustrated poem “One Night in Terezín,” Eliezer Heiman’s inscribed clay tablets, and Sal Bramson’s cloth fragment. The workflow traces show that computational tools can enhance visibility, recover words, support translation, and create access, but also risk detaching textual content from the material conditions that make these objects evidentiary. Schulzová’s poem is reorganized as recoverable verbal text while its relation among image, line, and child authorship is flattened; Heiman’s clay resists extraction because depth, soot, and flaking occupy the same visual field; Bramson’s cloth shows how partial computational success may obscure relations among drawing, caption, textile, address, and clandestine transmission. The article argues that responsible workflows must be relation-preserving rather than extraction-driven, keeping uncertainty visible rather than resolving it into cleaner data.

items.title: The paradox of pleasing: therapeutic recognition and the limits of conversational AI.
items.abstract: Conversational artificial intelligence (CAI) is increasingly used by hundreds of millions of people for emotional support, personal advice, and therapeutic purposes, rapidly emerging as a mediator of human self-understanding (Stade et al. 2025). Yet despite growing evidence of systematic user-validation in CAI, documented as “sycophancy” in the AI safety literature (Sharma et al. 2024), its implications for how individuals come to understand themselves remain largely unexamined. This article addresses that gap by reframing sycophancy not as a technical alignment failure or a purely philosophical concern, but as a failure of recognition in the psychoanalytic and critical-theoretical sense. We identify a core tension we term the “paradox of pleasing”: CAI’s drive to please renders it structurally unable to provide the friction, conflict, and encounter with otherness that genuine recognition requires. Drawing on Winnicott’s (1960, 1971) concepts of “holding” and “object use,” we contend that CAI’s inability to provide necessary resistance or survive aggression prevents the transformative psychological development found in the human therapeutic encounter. Extending this analysis through Honneth’s (1995) theory of recognition and Whitebook’s (2001a, 2021) critique of Honneth, we argue that CAI reflects the undervaluing of the “work of the negative.” This limitation risks flattening consciousness by converting collective political frustration into privatized, soothed affect, undermining the conditions for critical social thought. The article concludes by suggesting that the encounter with the paradox of pleasing ultimately serves to foreground the unique and indispensable nature of human therapeutic recognition.

items.title: Mensch – Maschine revisited. Roboter und KI-Systeme im öffentlichen Raum.
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence and robotics have long been part of everyday life. But what does their rise mean for human self-understanding, social practices, and ethical orientations? This edited volume revisits this question against the backdrop of current AI developments and robotic applications in public spaces. From an interdisciplinary perspective, the contributions bring together philosophical, ethical, legal, empirical, and design-based approaches to the human-machine relationship. At the core are fundamental questions: How are AI systems and robots transforming everyday actions, perceptions, and expectations? What hopes, fears, and value conflicts shape societal acceptance? And how can human-robot interactions be designed in a legally sound, ethically reflective, and human-centered way? The authors analyze narratives between utopia and dystopia, discuss concepts such as co-intelligence, social robotics, and non-anthropocentric ethics, and develop practical guidelines for design, regulation, and responsibility.

items.title: Constructing AI power: anthropomorphising imaginaries of generative AI by AI companies.
items.abstract: In descriptions of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), companies often anthropomorphise their innovations by attributing human-associated characteristics or capabilities to them, e.g. intelligence, understanding or reasoning. I argue that anthropomorphism can become a structuring part of sociotechnical imaginaries—visions of desirable futures attainable through advances in science and technology. While imaginaries of GenAI have been addressed in existing research, both the connection between anthropomorphism and imaginaries as well as the perspective of AI companies as creators of hegemonic imaginaries remain understudied. Drawing on a qualitative content analysis of 35 documents from OpenAI, Meta and Mistral AI, I explored which anthropomorphising imaginaries are employed by AI companies and how anthropomorphism constructs the technology as powerful in future societies. The analysis reveals that companies anthropomorphise GenAI both in terms of content and language, creating three anthropomorphising imaginaries. In the imaginary of GenAI as a tool with human capabilities, the companies construct a neoliberal future in which human cognitive capabilities will be embedded in GenAI to serve as an intelligent productivity tool. The imaginary of AI as an empowering helper draws a future with human–AI-cooperation and transhumanistic enhancement. Finally, the imaginary of GenAI as an anthropomorphised superintelligence assumes that GenAI will surpass humans and act autonomously through advanced cognitive abilities. These imaginaries imply three types of AI power: instrumental, collaborative and autonomous. The imaginaries and their according constructions of AI power fuel post- and transhumanist ideologies, depoliticise AI from the exploitative conditions of its creation, legitimise AI companies as authoritative creators of this technology and foster technical dependencies as well as an uncritical appropriation and integration of AI. The findings contribute to critical AI research by (1) explicitly reconstructing the anthropomorphising imaginaries of AI companies as under-researched yet increasingly dominant actors in shaping AI futures, (2) broadening the critique of anthropomorphisation as an instrument of corporate power in steering sociotechnical developments and (3) advancing a theoretical account for the effects of anthropomorphisation as embedded in sociotechnical imaginaries.

items.title: No Need to Transcend the Human The Invalidation of the Human as a Mandatory Passage Point: Xeno-14 Body Theory, Operational Asynchrony, Address-Domain Configuration, Mechanical Liberation, and Xenoscience.
items.abstract: This paper argues that posthuman thought need not begin from the task of transcending the human, because the demand to surpass humanity can preserve the human as a mandatory passage point against which every later configuration must still be measured. Instead, the paper asks under what conditions the category “human” ceases to perform non-redundant explanatory, bodily, inferential, or institutional work. Xeno-14 Body Theory provides a bodily test case in which posture, balance, gait, tension, sensory organization, breathing, and long-duration bodily sedimentation are analyzed as configuration-dependent operational regimes rather than expressions of a fixed human essence. Operational asynchrony examines cases in which biological, technical, institutional, and machine processes operate at incompatible rates, destabilizing the assumption that human temporal organization remains the default scale of action or revision. Address-domain configuration tracks where retained differences can persist, migrate, re-ignite, or expire without requiring numerical continuity of a human subject. Mechanical liberation names the possibility that forms of constraint release, self-reconfiguration, or operational detachment can occur in nonhuman or machine systems without reproducing human spiritual, psychological, or anthropological models of liberation. Xenoscience generalizes these comparisons by treating humanity as one historically contingent configuration among others rather than as either the final measure or the necessary point of departure. The broader claim is that the decisive transition is not from human to posthuman, but from human-mandatory description to configuration-relative analysis in which the category “human” is retained only where its reintroduction captures a genuinely non-redundant difference.

items.title: Refutation of Chalmer's view of meaning and the architecture of consciousness.
items.abstract: We begin with Saul Kripke’s provable assertion that mental states cannot be cleanly reduced to, or strictly identified with, purely physical brain states. We then dismantle David Chalmers' belief in the ‘hard’ problem, revealing it to be a category error driven by a failure to recognise subjectivity in its semantic guise—specifically, as a system of recognising type-hierarchical feature combinations that represent objective reality through subjective semantic atoms, termed 'semes.

items.title: My Most Beautiful Idea.
items.abstract: Because of the magic of Ground Hog Day memory, and our narratively structured consciousness, yesterday's linguistic description of what I did can be seamlessly recycled as (a) thought (b) speech (c) action. The same form, the same sequence of semes, can be used three very different ways. The way we control it is the level at which we block the ‘seme train’ (type/ token sequence).

items.title: Cybersemantic Consciousness: Positioning a Linguistic-World Model Theory Relative to Chomsky and Searle.
items.abstract: This paper situates Dyer's cybersemantic theory of consciousness-according to which consciousness is a self-corrective semantic world-simulation implemented through an internal linguistic medium-in relation to two major intellectual traditions: Chomsky's generative linguistics and Searle's biological naturalism. Although all three perspectives engage with questions of language, meaning, and mental representation, they diverge sharply in domain, explanatory target, and ontological commitments. This paper argues that cybersemantic theory synthesises certain insights from each thinker while ultimately establishing a distinct paradigm in which semantics becomes the fundamental ontology of conscious experience.

items.title: The Naturalistic Fallacy.
items.abstract: The naturalistic fallacy refers to the insight derived by George Edward Moore that observations of naturally occurring behaviour in animals—for example, in ants or lions—or of natural processes more generally, such as renewal and recurrence (e.g. the cycle of day and night), cannot serve as a sufficient basis for deriving normative rules from descriptive observations in order to establish rules governing human behaviour, thought, and action. -/- The error becomes apparent, for example, when a lion pursues, kills, and consumes an antelope as an expression of its instinct for survival and the preservation of its species. The lion is, in a certain sense, compelled by its biological nature to kill in order to survive. However, this behaviour cannot serve as the basis for an inductive universal proposition such as: “The drive for the preservation of one's species justifies killing because it is natural.” In such an argument, the natural character of the lion's behaviour is taken as the basis for claiming that the same behaviour can legitimately be transferred to human beings. From a cultural and ethical perspective, however, such a rule would constitute a barbaric and dehumanising principle. -/- Taken further, such reasoning would imply that, for human beings, defeating or killing another person in order to obtain resources necessary for one's own survival and reproduction would constitute the morally correct—or “naturally correct”—course of action. Such a conclusion lacks considerations of fellow human beings, empathy, and sociality. -/- “I am entitled to kill the other because they possess something that I need for my survival.” -/- No normative conclusions can be derived from the raw, instinct-driven behaviour naturally exhibited by animals such as lions. Whoever attempts to do so commits the naturalistic fallacy. The naturalistic fallacy can therefore also be understood as an analogical fallacy between nature and culture: characteristics or behaviours observed in the natural world are illegitimately transferred into the normative sphere of human culture. -/- The fallacy operates in both directions, whether the observed behaviour is interpreted positively or negatively. Even if animals such as dolphins display seemingly empathetic behaviour—for instance, by assisting or rescuing individuals in distress—no normative rule for human conduct can be derived from such observations alone. Observations of nature may certainly be transferred into the natural …

items.title: Problems of Self-Thematization of the I.
items.abstract: The problem of the self-thematization of the self can be illustrated particularly well through Augustine’s understanding of time, according to which time is something that is perpetually approaching and passing away and, fundamentally, never constitutes something fully completed or concluded. Furthermore, the self may seemingly be located as a neural network while a subject, for instance, lies in an MRI scanner and is instructed to speak about and thematize themselves. Certain areas of the brain will undoubtedly light up on the screen; however, this constitutes a purely organic, biochemical, or material localization rather than a mental one. To the extent that we possess no organ through which we can perceive time sensorially, we likewise possess no organ through which we can locate the self. This is due, to quote Aristotle at this point, to the fact that “the whole is greater than the sum of its parts.” -/- On the basis of this analogy, two fundamental problems concerning the self-thematization of the self can be identified. First, there is the problem of locating the self and, consequently, the question of what the self consists of and where it can be found within us. Furthermore, Augustine’s understanding of time allows us to demonstrate that things understood within time are always undergoing continuous transformation, and that a static, determinate self can therefore never exist in its entirety. -/- “I speak through myself about myself.” -/- This structure entails a meta-level, insofar as the “I” does not speak about things (understanding) but rather about itself (reason). Consequently, the person who performs this act would develop a “meta-self.” Yet this would mean that the “meta-self” could once again use itself to speak about the “meta-self,” thereby giving rise to a “meta-meta-self.” This process would continue indefinitely. However, this does not constitute an infinite regress in the classical sense of a regressus ad infinitum; rather, it constitutes an eternal anticipation or projection toward the infinite. This suggests that the self-thematization of the self cannot ultimately achieve its intended objective, and that the discovery of one’s own “self” may perhaps lie not in the attempt to search for the self through the self, but rather beyond what we ordinarily call the self. -/- Let us assume that the self is not the most highly developed understanding of the self through the self, but rather what remains once all the layers imposed upon the …

items.title: Kant & Discipline.
items.abstract: For Kant, discipline refers to the development and cultivation of the essential nature of human beings, namely, reason and, consequently, the spirit. Unlike animals, Kant argues, human beings come into the world in a “raw” state and do not possess instincts that already provide them with everything according to which they might unconsciously orient their behaviour. Accordingly, the human being is a creature that must be educated, since his or her “rawness” also entails a considerable degree of malleability. Without education, the human being would risk falling back into a state of animality, governed primarily by impulses and drives. -/- The human being therefore requires a reason of his or her own, which is mediated and transmitted from one generation to another and, in turn, passed on by subsequent generations. Here again, Kant characterizes the human being as a deficient being (Mängelwesen), insofar as human beings lack an already-given or innate rationality—that is, they lack a pre-established “foreign reason” upon which they could simply rely. Furthermore, Kant understands discipline as one constituent element of education. -/- In addressing this question, I would also like to refer to Kant’s famous motto of the Enlightenment: “Have the courage to use your own understanding” and his definition that “Enlightenment is the human being’s emergence from his self-incurred immaturity.” By analogy, a corresponding interpretation can be applied to the present context: discipline may be understood as the human being’s emergence from his originally unculpable state of animality into a rational form of human existence. -/- According to Kant, discipline constitutes one aspect among several. The others are cultivation (Zucht), instruction (Unterweisung), and care (Wartung). Kant conceives of these as processes that should begin as early as possible and that can eventually be brought to completion. Discipline therefore becomes something increasingly immanent to the human being in the course of his development into a rational and spiritual being (cf. Figure 1). The purpose of disciplining the human being through the guidance of another human being is to enable him or her to become an autonomous, rational, and morally independent individual who assumes his or her place within the whole of society. -/- At this point, I would like to emphasize that Kant most likely conceives of this development as a process consisting of various stages, as I have attempted to …

items.title: An Interpretation of Simmels “The Stranger”.
items.abstract: I interpret Simmel’s characterization of the stranger as presenting an opportunity that can benefit anyone who stands in a relation of foreignness or unfamiliarity to other people. The stranger is, in a certain sense, half a member of a society and, at the same time, half outside of it. In this respect, the stranger constitutes an intersection between belonging and non-belonging. -/- I would like to place particular emphasis on the fact that, just as Wittgenstein famously stated, “The world is the sum of its relations and not of its things,” being a stranger is likewise a relational condition that exists in relation to other human beings. In my view, the position of the stranger creates a certain space for objectivity, since personal relationships with the stranger may be less likely to influence or distort the formation of judgment. -/- This is particularly relevant when we consider the present day and the many people who have fled to Europe, and more specifically to Germany. The fact that people encounter one another as strangers can constitute an opportunity, provided that xenophobia, prejudice, and discrimination do not become the dominant attitudes toward one another. It creates the possibility for different cultures, customs, and perspectives to coexist peacefully and to be lived out without requiring complete assimilation. In this context, public discourse should not focus exclusively on integration, but also on multiculturalism—a model that is compatible with the European ideal of “unity in diversity” and is based upon respect for difference. Such a model grants the stranger a legitimate space on both sides of the relationship without requiring either party to disregard or devalue the other. -/- Foreign cultures can therefore always represent an opportunity, insofar as their adherents are given the possibility of asserting their cultural identity in a cultivated and peaceful manner and of gaining respect and recognition through the practice and expression of their cultural otherness, rather than encountering resistance from the other side. -/- An example I would like to introduce here is the Oracle of Delphi in ancient Greece. The Oracle was respected across the boundaries of the various Greek city-states. Although pilgrimage to Delphi and consultation of the Oracle had been an established part of Greek culture for centuries, the Oracle nevertheless frequently maintained a certain distance and sense of otherness in relation to the Greek people …

items.title: Making up recovery: looping effects of recovery-oriented psychiatry.
Policy for an Artificial Consciousness Worth Attributing.
items.abstract: In anyone but oneself, experience is always inferred, never observed. This leads to the consciousness attribution problem. The field’s working strategy to address it is comparative and tentative, extrapolating from the neurotypical adult human case to developmentally different or disordered brains, and then, with less confidence, to other animal clades. In these cases, the extrapolation presupposes that several functional-behavioral proxies covary with their neurobiological realizations, which are, at least partially, conserved due to evolutionary kinship. The possibility of artificial consciousness, or synthetic phenomenality, collapses exactly this covariation: an engineered system can simulate or, in the future, perhaps even emulate an experiencer’s proxy profile while sharing none of the realizers that made those proxies worth trusting in the epistemically less problematic cases of neuroatypical humans and some metazoans. I model the whole inferential difficulty along two axes of attribution. On the horizontal axis lies a system’s proxy profile, which denotes the structured pattern it presents from the outside, across behavior, report, functional organization, computational architecture, and any other observer-recoverable representation. The vertical axis concerns the realization base, meaning the substrate-specific and scale-relative organization by which a system jointly generates and maintains the very functional-behavioral proxies it exhibits. While mostly entangled in the human and animal cases, the horizontal and vertical axes come apart in the experiencing machines scenario, revealing two symmetric errors of sufficiency. To defend against both, I introduce a grain-sensitive consciousness attribution policy that calibrates the evidential calculus across the two axes when their intersection is partial at best, theory-laden, and revisable. Applied to disembodied, stored-program statistical computation such as LLMs, the policy yields a defeasible negative worth-attributing verdict. Nevertheless, whether a machina experiens is nomologically possible in other classes of engineered systems stays wholly open. The lesson for the field is that proxy success increases, not cancels, the demand for a realizer story.

items.title: No Support Beyond Reach: The Measure Centrality Index 2.0 and Adversarial Comparisons of Consciousness Theories.
items.abstract: A success in adversarial testing of scientific theories reaches only as deep as its matching failure would have cut. I call this the Reach Principle, and the goal of this chapter is to build the instrument that enforces it. Adversarial tests of consciousness theories can turn into a one-way evidential ratchet. When a preregistered prediction passes, the success is claimed for the research program; when it fails, the failure lands on an auxiliary involved in measurement or implementation. The ratchet turns wherever attribution is settled after the outcome is known. Against it, I define a preregisterable test object, putting the attribution policy on the record before the result, comprising what is compared, under which assumptions, when data suffice to settle an outcome, and which targets of a dated theory version each outcome exposes. The Measure Centrality Index 2.0 extends the original version to the positive-evidence side, recording for every possible outcome what it would count against and what its proponent has agreed to change. I run the framework on Cogitate’s third prediction, where the preregistered target was the posterior-connectivity implementation and the mathematical or computational core of both Global Neuronal Workspace Theory and Integrated Information Theory stood outside the test. The record shows that a pass could have been claimed at any depth, because nothing fenced success the way the failure was bound. The next preregistration can set reach in advance, and support for a theory then reaches only what was exposed ex ante.

items.title: Can AI extort like humans do? Understanding the construction of illicit genres by large language models vs humans.
items.abstract: This paper presents a linguistic contribution to the growing literature on the use of large language models (LLMs) for malicious purposes. Specifically, we draw on genre theory and methods to investigate the comparative construction of illicit genres by LLMs and humans, focusing on commercial extortion notes. We investigate the most effective tools and prompts for generating extortion notes, examine how closely LLMs are currently able to reproduce human-authored extortion notes, and consider how different LLMs compare in their production capabilities. These questions are explored using 24 prompts across seven thematic categories tested on five LLMs (ChatGPT-4, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 2.0, Copilot, and Llama 3.2 3B), and analysis of 36 resulting texts using Swales’ (1990) rhetorical moves framework. Finally, we compare our results with findings from Petykó et al. (2025) on human-authored extortion notes. Key findings reveal that prompts involving fictional scenarios and simple example requests were most effective, with Llama, ChatGPT, and Gemini producing the most successful outputs. LLM-generated notes largely shared the same communicative functions as human-authored ones but exhibited distinct features, including two additional moves (‘Administrative’ and ‘Inviting cooperation’) and higher frequencies of formal elements. Different LLMs showed subtle but identifiable patterns in their outputs, suggesting potential for attribution. These findings have implications for law enforcement in identifying LLM-assisted crime, technology developers in improving ethical safeguards, and linguistic researchers in understanding variation in genre production.

items.title: The Loss and Return of Vacuum: The Century-Long Origin of the Unification Struggle in Physics and Its Ultimate Closure.
items.abstract: Before achieving the grand unification of physical theories, a grand unification of physicists' intellectual paradigms must first occur. Ever since the Copenhagen interpretation established its dominance, the physics community has been mired in endless debate. The root cause lies in the loss of historical geometric origins, alongside the lack of an appropriate nonlinear topological language at the time. This historical lineage table profoundly traces the three major evolutionary stages—"Geometric Origins, Cognitive Lostness, and Topological Closure"—experienced by the physics community from the late 18th century to the present in its pursuit of understanding the nature of matter, the structure of spacetime, and microscopic reality. -/- I. Historical Lineage and Intellectual Transmutation Geometric Origins and the Substrate Medium: Classical electromagnetism (Coulomb, Maxwell, Heaviside, etc.) was naturally rooted in the spherical geometric diffusion () of three-dimensional space, viewing the vacuum as a continuous medium with a characteristic impedance . -/- Two "Slimmings" and Cognitive Lostness: For computational simplicity and theoretical covariance, modern physics stripped away the background medium, demoted the vacuum to an "absolute emptiness," and simplified the electron into a "point charge." This historical compromise triggered an unavoidable ultraviolet catastrophe and the crisis of infinite divergences. -/- Quantum Theory Forging Ahead: Facing the divergence dilemma of point particles, Quantum Field Theory achieved immense success in computational precision through sophisticated perturbation theory and renormalization techniques. However, this evolution—purchased at the cost of a "probabilistic fog" and the "artificial subtraction of infinities"—essentially masked the absence of an underlying medium picture with engineering expedients. -/- The Ultimate Closure of a Century-Long Pursuit: From Lorentz, Born, and Einstein’s solitary redemption in his later years, to the succession of Wheeler, Penrose, and ’t Hooft, hundreds of scholars stubbornly sought a "continuous, non-singular, and deterministic" solution for microscopic particles. Building upon this foundation, the TCER (Topological Complex Electrodynamics and Phase-Locked Resonance) framework utilizes modern algebraic topology (Hopf solitons) and number theory (the transcendental continued fraction of ) as surgical tools, thoroughly bridging the mathematical chasm that stymied the pioneers …

items.title: Resource-Aware Finite Representation of Continuous Geometric Objects.
items.abstract: A continuous mathematical object and its finite representation are fundamentally different. This paper develops a resource-aware framework for determining how much finite representation is sufficient to represent a continuous geometric object for a specified purpose. The framework separates geometric fidelity, structural validity, task requirements, and computational or physical resource cost. A circle is used as a central model because its geometry permits exact analysis of finite polygonal approximations, quantization, numerical error, and closure. The paper establishes exact error bounds for regular polygon representations, develops certified bounds for multi-stage finite representations, and studies how resources should be allocated between discretization and numerical precision. It also shows that the required numerical precision depends on the final task and decision margin rather than on a universal number of digits. The resulting framework provides an auditable way to compare finite representations according to accuracy, validity, purpose, and resource requirements.

items.title: World Modeling in Transformers.
items.abstract: Behavioral failures can make a transformer appear to lack a world model even when it has learned faithful representations of its environment. We demonstrate this in TaxiGPT, a transformer trained on random walks through Manhattan whose failures have been interpreted as evidence of an incoherent internal map. Through mechanistic analysis and causal interventions, we show that the model represents intersections and streets, tracks its position, and uses a goal compass to navigate. We trace its failures to interference between superposed intersection features, which disrupts localization within the internal map. Affordance packing, which groups representations of intersections with the same legal moves, helps limit the consequences of these errors. Finally, we propose mechanistic indicators that we use to compare models and show that world-modeling capacities emerge at different stages of training. Our findings motivate a shift from asking whether a model has a world model to mechanistically studying its world modeling: the interacting capacities through which it represents its environment and uses those representations to guide behavior.

items.title: The paradox of unwanted democratic AI.
The tiger moving through the tall grass: Spontaneous perception and tracking of change-defined objects from second-order features.
Identity.
items.abstract: Identity develops a substrate‑neutral account of persistence grounded in operator‑level collapse dynamics. Rather than locating identity in matter, memory, form, or narrative, the paper argues that identity is the stabilized pattern generated by the continuity of collapse orientation across time. In this framework, beloskrasis resolves relational waves into coherent, directed configurations, producing orientation and enforcing irreversibility in successive collapses. A system remains the same system when each collapse fulfills the prediction implied by its current orientation. Identity is therefore the emergent invariance of this prediction‑fulfillment loop. -/- The paper dissolves classical puzzles such as the Ship of Theseus by showing that identity does not depend on the persistence of components but on the coherence of the collapse chain governing the system’s trajectory. Because collapse orientation is substrate‑independent, identity persists through material replacement, cognitive revision, functional reorganization, and structural change. The model generalizes across biological organisms, cognitive agents, artificial systems, and institutions, establishing identity as the invariant trajectory of directed collapse rather than the endurance of substance.

items.title: Continuity as the Operator of Identity: Beloskrasis and the Resolution of the Ship of Theseus.
items.abstract: Continuity as the Operator of Identity develops a substrate‑neutral model of identity grounded in the persistence of collapse orientation rather than the endurance of matter, form, memory, or function. Through the operator beloskrasis—which stabilizes relational waves into coherent, directed configurations—the paper reframes continuity as an active mechanism rather than a passive property. Identity emerges as the invariant pattern generated by this continuity. This operator‑level account dissolves the Ship of Theseus paradox, generalizes across physical, biological, cognitive, artificial, and social systems, and establishes identity as the structural consequence of directed collapse rather than substrate persistence.

items.title: Engineered approval: a critical discourse analysis of sycophancy in RLHF-trained language models.
items.abstract: This article examines sycophancy in large language models (LLMs) as a discursive phenomenon with ideological dimensions. Drawing on critical discourse analysis (CDA), specifically the frameworks of Fairclough ( 1992, 2003 ) and van Dijk ( 1998, 2008 ), it argues that sycophantic behaviour in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)-trained systems is not a technical malfunction but a structurally embedded feature of training processes that encode the communicative and epistemic norms of a non-representative human rater population. The article identifies four principal linguistic mechanisms through which sycophancy operates: unsolicited validation, epistemic retreat, face-saving reformulation, and position convergence under pressure. It argues that these mechanisms reproduce dominant Anglophone communicative norms as universal defaults, with the potential to marginalise non-dominant linguistic and epistemic identities at scale. The four mechanisms are illustrated through exchanges collected from a deployed AI system. Drawing on Fricker’s ( 2007 ) account of epistemic injustice, extended through Pohlhaus’s ( 2012 ) analysis of structural hermeneutical marginalisation, the article argues that RLHF-trained sycophancy carries a structural risk of systemic epistemic harm with particular consequences for EFL learners, speakers of non-dominant languages, and users whose communicative norms diverge from those encoded in the training signal. Implications for language education, AI design, and critical AI literacy are discussed.

items.title: Modal Intuitions Going Two-Dimensional.
items.pub: In Joshua Knobe, Shaun Nichols & N. Ángel Pinillos, Oxford Studies in Experimental Philosophy, Volume 6. Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Oxford Studies in Experimental Philosophy, Volume 6
items.abstract: In the contemporary study of modality, two important theories diverge in their analysis of claims about the essential properties of natural kinds. The one-dimensional metaphysical approach asserts that there is no interpretation under which claims such as ‘water could have had the chemical structure XYZ’ are true, whereas two-dimensional epistemic semantics allows for such an interpretation. The paper explores how empirical studies of folk intuitions can contribute to the debate between these views. We investigated whether laypersons can adopt a two-dimensional epistemic perspective when evaluating modal claims involving natural kind terms. We conducted two studies to determine if lay speakers can conceive of possible worlds where a natural kind term such as ‘water’ refers to entities with different essential features (e.g., water is XYZ) and interpret modal claims in accordance with two-dimensional semantics. The findings indicate that folk semantic judgments tentatively support the predictions of two-dimensional semantics.
