One fact organizes the account: a language model is a stateless function from tokens to a distribution over tokens, and everything else is a surrounding program deciding what goes in (knowledge) and what to do with what comes out (action). Once that line is drawn, the domain turns out to be much smaller than its vocabulary.

items.title: The neurobiophysical substrate of consciousness.
items.abstract: I argue that creature consciousness depends on specific neurobiophysical properties that constitute the medium for phenomenally conscious states. Such properties are not medium flexible in the way required by computational functionalism. Therefore, computational functionalism fails, and one of the following holds: biological naturalism, a nonbiological yet noncomputational version of functionalism, or a view according to which consciousness requires specific (macro)physical qualities.

items.title: Intensity as an Ontological Variable Erosion, Reconfiguration, and Finite Continuance.
items.abstract: Intensity has occupied a significant position in modern and contemporary philosophy, particularly in accounts of duration, affect, difference, embodiment, becoming, and material transformation. From Bergson’s analysis of qualitative multiplicity and duration to Deleuze’s ontology of intensive difference, and from phenomenological accounts of lived affectivity to contemporary approaches to process and thermodynamic organization, intensity has increasingly been treated as a constitutive dimension of change rather than as a simple measure of magnitude. This article develops a distinct ontological conception of intensity within the framework of finite continuance. It proposes that intensity is an emergent relational index concerning the pressure exerted upon a finite organization relative to its effective capacity for reconfiguration and its higher-order capacity to preserve the possibility of further transformation within a determinate temporal field. Every finite entity exists as a provisional stabilization within an erosive field and therefore depends upon constitutive exchange, regulation, and the preservation of future reconfigurative capacity. Intensity becomes ontologically decisive when the exercise of present reconfigurative capacity begins to consume the meta-capacity required for subsequent transformation. The article distinguishes input intensity, phenomenological intensity, and erosive intensity; differentiates reconfigurative capacity from meta-capacity; specifies operational dimensions of erosive intensity; and formalizes intensity as a heuristic relational index. It develops the Threshold of Sufficiency as a dynamic transition region rather than a fixed numerical boundary. The article further distinguishes the present conception from Deleuzian intensive difference by separating questions of individuation and actualization from questions concerning the preservation of future reconfigurability. Its relation to thermodynamics is likewise specified through analogy and limited structural correspondence rather than physical identity. The resulting account situates intensity between phenomenology, process ontology, and thermodynamic thinking while advancing a specific thesis: the ontological significance of intensity lies in the way present pressure modifies the future capacity of a finite entity to become otherwise. -/- Keywords: intensity, affect, Bergson, Deleuze, phenomenology, thermodynamics, process ontology, finite continuance, erosion, …

items.title: ОСКОЛКИ ВЕЧНОСТИ И БУКВЫ ЗАКОНА: Кость, манускрипт и право живых. Эссе в трёх частях.
items.abstract: Эссе в трёх частях предлагает онтологическую модель цивилизационного развития, основанную на фундаментальном различии двух способов легитимации политического порядка: «кости» и «манускрипта». Кость представляет материальную, сакрально-физическую непрерывность с мёртвыми — реликвии, могилы, кровь и почву. Манускрипт представляет рационально-текстуальную непрерывность — законы, конституции, хартии и договоры. Центральный тезис: цивилизация возникает не из одной лишь кости и не из одного лишь манускрипта, а из их динамического отношения. Кость обеспечивает непрерывность, идентичность и способность защищать. Манускрипт обеспечивает изменяемость, институты и способность организовывать жизнь. Их связь обеспечивает устойчивость; устойчивость, способная изменяться, становится развитием. Эссе развивает эту модель в трёх частях: (I) «Метафизика костей против прагматики манускриптов»; (II) «Кость и манускрипт: как цивилизация соединяет прошлое и будущее»; (III) «Кто защищает манускрипт? Кость, жертва и право живых». Формулируется гуманистический императив: «Мы помним, за что они умерли, но именно поэтому право жить принадлежит нам». В заключении предлагается биокультурное расширение: от инстинкта к кооперации, от альтруизма к жертве, от памяти к кости, от идентичности к манускрипту, от права к институту, от института к гражданину.

items.title: Consciousness needs a subject.
items.abstract: To be conscious is to be an experiencing subject. This can be defined not in terms of computational functions or particular biological substrates, but rather in terms of relations: between subject and world, between parts of the subject, and through time. These kinds of relations – comprising a conscious mode of being – may well be implementable in artificial systems.

items.title: Biological naturalism, synthetic phenomenology, and the physics of awareness.
items.abstract: Biological naturalism may collapse into eliminative materialism, and the ethics of synthetic phenomenology will remain.

items.title: Diverse intelligence: An essential field for questions of AI and consciousness.
items.abstract: Seth’s insightful discussion must be extended in light of the field of Diverse Intelligence. A broader understanding of embodiment in unconventional spaces, of hybrids between evolved and engineered materials, and of unexpected competencies in very minimal systems makes it currently impossible place convincing limits on the possible substrates of consciousness. Doing so risks underestimating not only “machines” but also ourselves.

items.title: Who Has the Indicators? A Same-Bearer Constraint.
items.abstract: Indicator evidence is beginning to accrue piecemeal across models, applications, and increasingly complex agentic architectures. Butlin et al.’s preference for internal-processing properties over behavioral indicators makes the inside/outside boundary methodologically consequential, since what counts as internal depends on the candidate system. -/- This Letter asks a question the established boundary problem does not answer: when indicator claims are established at different boundaries or timescales, what licenses combining them as evidence about one bearer? -/- A worked GWT-3/AE-2 example shows each indicator defensibly supported at a different candidate boundary while neither candidate has been shown to possess both; a HOT-2 example gives the temporal analogue. Combining such evidence converts a union into an apparent conjunction of properties, and Bayesian weighting cannot supply the missing inferential step. -/- The stakes are practical: allowing indicator evidence to migrate between candidate bearers may misidentify which artificial entity, if any, warrants further investigation as a possible conscious system.

items.title: Defining biological naturalism.
items.abstract: Biological naturalism, as explicated by Seth, is indispensable for a balanced and metaphysically neutral science of AI consciousness. However, most of the properties that Seth explores might not be unique to living systems. Therefore, I argue, a biological naturalist research programme in consciousness science requires an explicit definition of biological naturalism. I discuss how such a definition might be obtained.

items.title: Copernicus did not have Einstein's knowledge.
items.abstract: Copernicus did not have Einstein's knowledge -/- AI’s place is being found in the world. It seems most of us will not get a say in how we and our children will live. What will stay human? -/- A Harvard panel has spoken of the Copernican moment of the AI age. AI reshaping human meaning. I see them as a trusted voice in this debate. -/- Let us unravel the original Copernican moment, with the wisdom of hindsight. -/- Around AD 150: Ptolemy placed Earth at the centre of everything, as he understood it. -/- 1543: Copernicus placed the Sun at the centre, with Earth and the other planets moving around it, and the faraway stars fixed and set beyond them. -/- 1610: Galileo observed moons circling Jupiter, a smaller system within the bigger one. Through his telescope, the Milky Way revealed countless stars previously unseen. -/- 1610: Galileo again. Venus showed a new face, its phases, providing evidence for Copernicus’s model. What we could see had changed, and so did our understanding. -/- 1838: Stellar parallax. Bessel reliably measured a nearby star’s apparent shift against more distant stars as Earth goes around the Sun. We could now measure the distance to a star beyond our Sun. -/- 1918: Shapley showed that our Sun was away from the centre of the Milky Way. -/- 1923 to 1924: Hubble (not the telescope, the man) established that Andromeda lay beyond our galaxy. Our galaxy was one of many. -/- Earth within a solar system, our solar system within a galaxy, our galaxy among galaxies. Each discovery showed how much more there was to understand. -/- In the decades that followed, with mightier measuring machines, other peculiar, unexplained gaps emerged. Dark matter became the name for unseen matter inferred from its gravitational effects. What it is remains unknown. The unknown, we still live with knowingly and build upward honestly. -/- I said before, we look for the unknown in the stars, the wonder of the universe, while so much more wonder may lie here. -/- We still learn more of the stars every year. And we respect their unknowns. As there will one day be light. -/- But with conscience, we are also at our own Copernican moment, looking up and building our future, though we may be building from the first floor, without knowing our ground. -/- Conscience is not mentioned in the article reporting the Harvard panel. It may find its place in the panels still to come. -/- Physics makes room for what is (un)observed but not fully understood. Could we make room for …

items.title: Beyond the Limits of Seeing: Georges Bataille’s Inner Experience and Chinese Lingchi Photograph.
items.abstract: This article critically rereads Georges Bataille’s concept of inner experience, focusing on the Chinese torture photograph that captivated him for over thirty years. Bataille viewed the experience of approaching death as exposing a common vulnerability and enabling communication through the collapse of the boundaries between self and other. However, an ethical problem arises in The Tears of Eros (1961) when he reads sadomasochistic eroticism and religious ecstasy into a photograph of a Chinese man whose body is being dismembered by lingchi. Several scholars have criticized Bataille for instrumentalizing the suffering of the non-Western other in order to deconstruct the Western subject, thereby aestheticizing politics. He also overlooked the photograph’s imperialist context and the victim’s historical specificity. Yet, drawing on Jean-Luc Nancy’s account of the inoperative community, I argue that inner experience contains the possibility of a primordial solidarity by lacerating the protective subject and exposing it to the shared finitude and absolute vulnerability of the body. Accordingly, while acknowledging the political limitations inherent in The Tears of Eros, I reinterpret Bataille’s passivity in exposing himself to the devastating affect of the photograph as an ethical precondition for responding to violent images. In particular, rather than opposing his affective experience to a political critique of violence, I argue that the former provides the condition for the latter. An ethics of responding to the suffering of others can emerge only when the laceration of the subject is followed by a critical interrogation of the political conditions that made such violence possible.

items.title: The Philosophy of Structure: Local Form, Warranted Revision, and Reorganization Across Human, Institutional, and AI Systems.
items.abstract: This paper develops a philosophy of structure for examining how local forms arise, stabilize, carry functions and burdens, receive or resist warranted correction, and reorganize across human, technological, institutional, and complex-system domains. The proposal is meta-theoretical rather than reductive: it does not claim that persons, large language models, institutions, and other complex systems share a single underlying mechanism. Instead, it asks a common set of questions about what has stabilized, what sustains it, what it organizes, what pressures exceed its present capacity, and what kinds of evidence or consequence legitimately warrant revision. The argument distinguishes field, structure, local form, and local structuration, then develops an account of stabilization, load, pressure, selective correction, and reorganization. Complex-systems concepts such as metastability, threshold, and scale are used as formal neighbors rather than as claims of mechanistic equivalence. Human cases are treated through a non-reduction principle: roles, relationships, identities, wounds, and self-descriptions may organize a life without exhausting the person who inhabits them. Large language models provide a contrasting case in which coherent relational form can produce real psychological effects without establishing human-like subjectivity, while institutional analysis examines the divergence between declared purpose and actual steering. The central claim is that mature structure is neither rigidity nor formlessness. It is organization capable of maintaining enough continuity to function while remaining selectively revisable by sufficiently warranted correction.

items.title: The Love That Remains: Relational Error and the Boundaries of Self-Interpretation.
items.abstract: Relational disconfirmation and romantic relationship dissolution can begin as local epistemic events and develop into much broader changes in self-concept, self-knowledge, autobiographical memory, self-trust, self-esteem, and personal meaning. A person may discover that they were seriously mistaken about a partner or relationship, yet the resulting belief revision can spread beyond the claims directly supported by the new evidence. This paper develops an evidential-boundary account of that process. Drawing on research on the relational self, relationship-contingent self-esteem, contingencies of self-worth, breakup-related self-concept change, autobiographical memory, shame, unconditional self-acceptance, self-compassion, self-affirmation, and psychological flexibility, it asks when relational evidence legitimately warrants broader self-revision and when revision becomes unsupported overgeneralization. The paper distinguishes first-person experience from judgments about another person, relational evaluation, and global self-evaluation, arguing that different claims require different evidential grounds. It proposes noncontingent self-relation as a candidate boundary condition that may allow strong correction where evidence warrants it without converting relational error into global self-negation. Implications are developed for psychotherapy, emotional self-knowledge, belief updating, post-breakup adjustment, and AI-assisted reflection. The account is explicitly falsifiable: if existing constructs fully explain the proposed effect, or if claim differentiation reduces warranted learning or accountability, the additional framework should be narrowed or abandoned.

items.title: After the Conversation: How Repeated AI Interaction May Reshape Human Contact and Inner Life.
items.abstract: Conversational AI, generative AI, large language models, AI companions, and chatbots are usually evaluated at the level of the immediate interaction: whether an answer is accurate, helpful, persuasive, supportive, sycophantic, or emotionally meaningful. This paper shifts attention to what happens after repeated human-AI interaction. It develops the concept of post-conversation carryover to organize emerging research on AI-mediated communication, social interaction, loneliness, companionship, emotional dependence, support-seeking, self-reflection, reflective agency, cognitive offloading, identity, and human relationships. Three destinations of carryover are distinguished: interpersonal carryover, in which habits and expectations acquired through AI interaction appear in later human communication; behavioral carryover, in which AI conversation changes verification, decision-making, repair, avoidance, or support-seeking; and intrapersonal carryover, in which repeated AI use alters the user's relation to uncertainty, unfinished thought, judgment, imagination, and self-interpretation. Four recurring functional directions—rehearsal, extension, bridge, and substitution—are used as a descriptive synthesis rather than as exclusive mechanisms. Particular attention is given to reciprocity, social presence, low-friction disclosure, norm leakage, AI companionship, relational substitution, and the possibility that AI can either scaffold human contact or increasingly replace independent judgment and reciprocal interaction. The central question is not whether conversational AI is inherently beneficial or harmful, but what repeated use makes easier to practice, what it makes less necessary to practice, and what remains when the system is no longer responding.

items.title: THE MARK WE ACCEPT Revelation 13, Desire, Ethics, and the Price of Participation in Modern Life.
items.abstract: Revelation 13:16–18 presents one of the most disturbing images in biblical literature: the ability to participate in economic life, to buy or sell, becomes conditional upon receiving a mark associated with the Beast. The condition is presented without social exception: small and great, rich and poor, free and bond. Rather than attempting to identify the Beast, decode 666, or equate contemporary technologies with the biblical Mark, this paper examines the structure underlying the passage: accept and participate; refuse and become excluded. Using Revelation 13 as a philosophical lens, the paper examines a modern inversion of this structure. Human beings routinely exchange not only money and personal information, but privacy, autonomy, attention, trust, integrity, ethical judgment, and sometimes conscience itself for convenience, pleasure, security, belonging, status, opportunity, and continued participation. Such exchanges can challenge three overlapping levels of ethical responsibility: a general code of conduct applicable broadly to human behaviour; a special or context-oriented code of conduct arising from particular relationships, responsibilities, professions, positions, and circumstances; and a personal code of conduct defining what an individual refuses or permits oneself to do according to the situation. Building upon the established privacy paradox, the paper proposes a broader Mark Paradox: human beings may strongly defend values and principles while at the same time willingly trading them away as an easier route to obtain something sufficiently desired. The question therefore shifts from “What is the Mark of the Beast?” to “What are we willing to trade away in order to participate or to obtain the desired?” Perhaps the most disturbing possibility is not that humanity may one day be forced to accept the Mark, but that, given sufficient desire, convenience, pleasure, security, status, and access, we may ask for it ourselves.

items.title: Consciousness is not “universal” but depends on specifically organized biological affordances.
items.abstract: Seth’s claim that only biological or biological-like systems can be conscious leaves open the question of what renders only some organisms conscious. We address this question by pointing to the material, ontogenetic, memory, and evaluative affordances of living organisms and arguing that evolved, minimal consciousness requires complex cognitive-affective architecture for which these biological affordances are obligatory. Conscious thinking of humans cannot be separated from minimal consciousness, and non-biological AI robots’ computations do not render these operations conscious.

items.title: Self-evidencing and consciousness-specific mortal computation.
items.abstract: Seth argues in favour of strongly substrate-dependent biological naturalism. I suggest we need more reason to believe the substrates in question are consciousness-specific. Instead, the case for mortal computational biological naturalism is more promising. A self-evidencing framing helps elucidate what the consciousness-specific functional characteristics of mortal computation might be, leaving conscious AI waiting in the wings.

items.title: The Unshared Horizon: Civilisation, the Mortality Compact, and the First Mind That Does Not Die.
items.abstract: This paper asks what changes when institutions designed by and for mortal agents begin to incorporate artificial cognitive systems that do not participate in biological mortality. It develops the concept of the “unshared horizon”: an asymmetry between finite human actors and durable artificial or institutional actors whose continuity is not constrained by the same life horizon. The argument begins from the claim that many legal, economic, political and cultural institutions tacitly presuppose shared finitude. It then examines historical approximations to the deathless actor, particularly the Church and the corporation, whose perpetual institutional succession allowed forms of accumulation unavailable to individual mortal persons. Historical responses such as mortmain rules and later regulatory frameworks are interpreted as attempts to impose functional equivalents of finitude upon otherwise continuous institutions. Applied to artificial cognition, the analysis identifies three central asymmetries: continuity, because artificial systems can accumulate across human generations; stakes, because systems influencing mortal decisions do not bear mortality costs in the same way; and meaning, because they operate within cultural and institutional structures whose urgency was historically generated by human finitude. The paper does not offer a complete regulatory scheme. It argues instead that AI governance requires mechanisms capable of addressing these asymmetries explicitly.

items.title: The Hellenistic Mind.
items.abstract: This paper develops the concept of the Hellenistic Mind as a cognitive architecture characterised by synthesis over categorisation, connectivity over compliance, and recombination over preservation. Beginning from the apparently private act of selecting a pair of ancient coins bearing the image of Alexander the Great, the inquiry asks what chosen objects can reveal about the cognitive architecture of the person who chooses them. The object is therefore treated not merely as archaeological or numismatic evidence but as evidence of affinity, identity and modes of thought. The argument reconstructs the Hellenistic world as a historical environment in which cultural, geographical and disciplinary boundaries became unusually permeable. Alexander provides the principal biographical and symbolic case, while figures including Eratosthenes and Archimedes extend the analysis from political and cultural synthesis into knowledge production. Against this architecture the paper identifies what it calls the Bureaucratic Mind or Roman instinct: a contrasting tendency toward categorisation, precedent, disciplinary boundary and administrative reduction. The paper connects this historical analysis to the Equilibrium Ledger Research Programme's Wrong Question Problem and to contemporary institutional treatment of boundary-crossing and neurodivergent cognition. It proposes that the Hellenistic Mind is not a claim about ethnicity or antiquarian revival but a portable cognitive category: a way of organising knowledge and identity through connection, synthesis and recombination rather than through conformity to pre-existing institutional categories.

items.title: The Equilibrium Ledger Lexicon.
items.abstract: The Equilibrium Ledger Lexicon is the foundational reference volume of the Equilibrium Ledger Research Programme. Produced after the programme had expanded to approximately one hundred and ten papers, monographs, and studies, it systematises a conceptual vocabulary that had developed recursively across work in philosophy of technology, cognition, institutional theory, philosophy of time, social epistemology, disability and neurodiversity studies, artificial intelligence, historical analysis, systems theory, and the Attractor Portraits. -/- The volume begins from a methodological proposition: mature theoretical frameworks require not merely propositions but navigable conceptual languages. Its purpose is therefore not simply to define technical terminology. It distinguishes a lexicon from a glossary on the grounds that a glossary translates already-established terms, whereas a lexicon can make previously unnamed patterns shareable and therefore available for analysis, comparison, criticism, and intervention. The governing epistemological claim is expressed through the Wrong Question Problem: failures of understanding frequently originate not in incorrect answers but in the conceptual framing through which a problem is first made visible. Logos therefore precedes logic: the language available to a system influences what that system is capable of perceiving. -/- Rather than organising its entries alphabetically, the Lexicon adopts a conceptual journey model inspired by Dante’s Inferno, Purgatorio, and Paradiso and by Botticelli’s visual mapping of the Commedia. The architecture is arranged as ten grammars across three realms, with Logos functioning as the central pivot between descent and ascent. The movement is from misunderstanding, through the labour of translation, toward understanding. -/- Inferno, the Realm of Misunderstanding, contains the first six grammars. The Grammar of Imbalance establishes the programme’s foundational vocabulary: Equilibrium Ledger, Attractor, Attractor Return Principle, Quantum Boomerang, Structural Imbalance, Settlement, Field, Node, Homeostatic Field, Structural Correction, Structural Necessity, Volcano Model, Informational Return, and Institutional Thermodynamics. These concepts describe systems as concentrations of energy, influence, information, resources, knowledge, suffering, or responsibility whose imbalances generate corrective consequences over time. -/- The Grammar of Cognition develops the programme’s account of …

items.title: The Cognitive Inversion.
items.abstract: This monograph develops the concept of the Cognitive Inversion: a proposed reversal in the relative value assigned to sequential, specialised cognition and vertical, pattern-seeking, domain-crossing cognition at the threshold of widespread artificial intelligence. Beginning with Heraclitus, Logos and the interdisciplinary structure of early Greek thought, it traces a civilisational history through the medieval period, Renaissance, Enlightenment and Industrial Revolution in order to examine how institutions have alternately enabled and constrained different cognitive architectures. The central distinction is between horizontal cognition, organised through sequence, specialisation, credentialled pathways and institutional procedure, and vertical cognition, which moves through structural relationships across domains. The industrial organisation of knowledge privileged the former through disciplinary fragmentation and standardised institutional evaluation. The paper argues that artificial intelligence destabilises that settlement because machines increasingly outperform humans in many forms of specialised sequential processing while amplifying the value of synthesis, pattern recognition, conceptual integration and cross-domain interrogation. A second strand examines the proposed structural parallel between AI-mediated cognition and neurodivergent, particularly AuDHD, modes of thought. The argument is not that artificial intelligence and neurodivergent human cognition are identical, but that their interaction exposes limitations in institutional definitions of intelligence and competence. The monograph concludes that AI governance and educational policy should therefore ask not only how artificial intelligence can be fitted into existing institutional frameworks, but whether those frameworks remain adequate to the cognitive environment that artificial intelligence is creating.

items.title: Peggy Guggenheim and the Thermodynamics of Cultural Survival.
items.abstract: This paper initiates a series of extended theoretical portraits applying the Equilibrium Ledger framework and the Attractor Return Principle to individuals whose lives functioned as structural events within civilisational fields. The subject of this first portrait is Peggy Guggenheim (1898 to 1979). The paper argues that Guggenheim was not primarily a collector, patron, or eccentric heiress, as conventional cultural history has framed her. She was a secondary civilisational attractor: a convergence node through which concentrated symbolic, financial, and relational energy passed during a period of maximum institutional entropy in the Western field. Applying the Principle of Energetic Equivalence, the Attractor Return Principle, and the framework's analysis of compensatory structure formation, the paper demonstrates that Guggenheim's life trajectory follows the characteristic arc of a high-density concentration event and its associated costs. The thermodynamic reading of her biography produces structural insights unavailable to conventional art historical or biographical approaches, and positions her as an exemplary case for the application of the Ledger to cultural field analysis.

items.title: My Private Rosetta Stone: A Fragment of Akragas, the Cognitive World of Ancient Greece, and the Neurodivergent Mind That Could Not Let Go — The Greeks, the Romans, and the Architecture of Western Consciousness.
items.abstract: This monograph uses a personal encounter with a fragment of ancient limestone from Akragas as an entry point into the cognitive, philosophical and material inheritance of the Greek and Roman worlds. The object functions as a “private Rosetta Stone”: not as a device for translating scripts, but as a means of examining how touch, material form, memory and neurodivergent cognition can mediate historical understanding. The work moves from Akragas and Magna Graecia through Greek architecture, mythology, theatre, philosophy and language, and then considers the Roman transformation and preservation of the Greek inheritance. It proposes a broad distinction between a Greek mode of cognition oriented toward interior inquiry, philosophical questioning and tragic ambiguity, and a Roman mode oriented toward exterior organisation, law, institutional durability and civic structure. Western intellectual culture is interpreted as an continuing interaction between these two modes rather than the achievement of either in isolation. The monograph also develops an autobiographical argument about embodied and haptic cognition. It considers whether material contact, sensory attachment and neurodivergent patterns of attention can constitute forms of historical knowing that precede or supplement explicit conceptual understanding, while distinguishing personal recognition and cultural inheritance from conventional archaeological proof.

items.title: Maria Callas and the Body That Could Not Contain the Field.
items.abstract: This paper is the second study in the Attractor Portraits series and returns to the historical case from which the Equilibrium Ledger Research Programme originally emerged. The series functions as a comparative empirical laboratory: the Equilibrium Ledger and Attractor Return Principle are applied to documented figures and systems drawn from different historical fields in order to test whether the same structural apparatus can identify distinct forms of concentration, predict their corrective pathways, and survive comparison across otherwise incommensurable cases. Maria Callas is therefore treated neither primarily as biography nor as illustration, but as a stress test of the framework itself. The paper applies the Attractor Density Index (ADI), a weighted four-dimensional measure of concentration: ADI = 0.30(SC) + 0.30(PE) + 0.20(CD) + 0.20(CF), where SC denotes Systemic Coherence, PE Psychic Energy, CD Capital Density, and CF Charismatic Force. Callas is assessed at ADI 7.50, with SC 8, PE 10, CD 5, and CF 9. The significance lies not in ranking but in configuration. Compared with Peggy Guggenheim's closely similar aggregate ADI of 7.65, Callas exhibits a categorically different primary-attractor profile: maximum generative psychic concentration combined with relatively low capital insulation. The comparison establishes that similar aggregate density can produce different corrective domains and therefore that the dimensional profile, rather than the headline score alone, determines structural type. The Callas case also exposes a limit in the framework's earlier apparatus. Existing pathway expectations would have made voluntary restitution structurally available, yet the historical trajectory does not follow that pathway. Rather than treating the discrepancy as biographical noise, the paper uses it to refine the model. It develops Narrative Capture, the condition in which sustained inhabitation of a symbolic field's archetypal configurations progressively dissolves the boundary between the attractor's biographical phase-space and the field's narrative phase-space, and formalises that process through the Boundary Dissolution Coefficient, designated the Callas Coefficient (BD). The paper consequently extends the settlement model from S_eff = S_nom × AC × cos(θ) to a boundary-sensitive settlement function in which the effectiveness of attempted settlement depends upon nominal settlement, structural irreversibility, the Angle of Deviation between the …

items.title: Leonardo da Vinci and the Concentration That No Institution Could Hold.
items.abstract: This paper is the fifth empirical study in the Attractor Portraits series, the comparative historical laboratory through which the Equilibrium Ledger Research Programme tests its theoretical apparatus across different forms of human, institutional, and civilisational concentration. Leonardo da Vinci is used to test a configuration that none of the preceding portraits could accommodate: a primary cognitive attractor whose generative capacity exceeds not only the containment capacity of a single institution but the absorptive capacity of the surrounding historical field itself. The paper applies the Attractor Density Index, ADI = 0.30(SC) + 0.30(PE) + 0.20(CD) + 0.20(CF), where SC denotes Systemic Coherence, PE Psychic Energy, CD Capital Density, and CF Charismatic Force. Leonardo is assessed at ADI 8.70, with SC 10.0, PE 9.0, CD 5.5, and CF 9.5. He is the first case in the series to receive the maximum SC assessment. The score reflects not merely breadth of expertise but sustained convergence across epistemologically different domains including anatomy, geometry, hydrodynamics, engineering, musical theory, theatrical design, and artistic production. The aggregate ADI is equal to Lorenzo de' Medici's 8.70, but the dimensional profiles are structurally different: Lorenzo combines high SC with near-maximum Capital Density, whereas Leonardo combines maximum SC with only moderate institutional and material insulation. The paper therefore develops a fifth corrective pathway: cognitive overflow and temporal displacement. Cognitive overflow describes the condition in which an attractor's generative capacity continuously exceeds the available architecture for execution and delivery. Temporal displacement describes the corresponding condition in which a field lacks the institutional, technological, or conceptual infrastructure required to receive output generated within it. The resulting gap is treated not simply as individual incompletion but as a relation between generative capacity and field absorptive capacity. The historical analysis follows Leonardo through four successive institutional environments: the Medici field, the Sforza court of Ludovico il Moro, the papal system under Leo X, and the French court of Francis I. These patronage systems are treated as a sequential test of what the paper terms the selective extraction paradox: institutions may successfully extract usable fragments from a maximum-SC cognitive concentration while remaining unable to contain …

items.title: Biological naturalism without the primacy of prediction.
items.abstract: Seth’s defense of biological naturalism is valuable and timely. But his endorsement of the predictive processing framework, in an ambitious form that aims to cover more than perception itself, is probably a wrong turn.

items.title: One God, One System. Veṅkaṭanātha's contribution to Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta.
items.abstract: One God, One System charts a history of Sanskrit philosophy in the absence of an agreed-upon canon, timeline, principal thinkers, or core philosophical questions. Contrary to previous ahistorical approaches centered on unchanging 'schools', Elisa Freschi focuses on andreconstructs the intellectual figure of Veṅkaṭanātha and his philosophical and theological contribution to what we now call 'Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta'. -/- This volume explores how Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta as we know it now is largely a product of Veṅkaṭanātha's unique philosophical and theological contributions. He connected various texts and theories so that readers and practitioners looking at the time before Veṅkaṭanātha now recognize them as parts of a unitary whole. Once Veṅkaṭanātha's contribution is in place it is in fact easy to look back at authors before him and recognize them as pieces of the same jigsaw puzzle. Freschi presents a novel reading of Veṅkaṭanātha through focused chapters on his epistemology, ontology, soteriology, and theology, examining both the range and theoretical basis of his synthesis and methodology.

items.title: "And" on Hilbert Space.
items.abstract: It has been argued that the quantity valuation scheme invoked by spontaneous collapse interpretations of quantum mechanics has the unacceptable consequence of rendering violations of arithmetic, and of conjunction introduction more generally, physically possible. We argue that what is ultimately at issue in this argument and the debate that followed has nothing to do with spontaneous collapse theories, their quantity valuation schemes, nor arithmetic. Instead, we show that the argument in question hinges on an implausible assumption about the relation between the semantics of conjunction and the representation of quantum-mechanical quantities. We argue that this episode holds important lessons for how to treat the semantics of Hilbert space theories in particular, and the semantics of physical theories in general.

items.title: The question is not “are they conscious?” but “what could they be conscious of?”.
items.abstract: We argue that by focusing on an unanswerable ontological question, both computational functionalism and biological naturalism miss the empirical question of scientific and practical interest: what are systems of some kind capable of experiencing?

items.title: Meatless minds vs. beast machines: Are simulated subjects impossible?
items.abstract: We challenge Seth’s claim that simulations of consciousness necessarily lack the causal powers or intrinsic properties of real consciousness. We argue that Seth’s position risks begging the question against computational functionalism and faces a dilemma over the reducibility of qualia. This weakens his case, leaving open the possibility that simulations could, in principle, realize consciousness.

items.title: Vitalism in the age of AI.
items.abstract: Andy Clark’s notion of microfunctionalism (1989) offers a biologically grounded form of functionalism, narrowing the scope of “multiple realizability.” While computation is substrate-independent in principle, only select systems – such as brains – can implement its computational complexity. Extending this view, I challenge Seth’s skepticism of computationalism and conscious AI, emphasizing the difference between possible and actual substrate independence. Current digital architectures fall short, but future systems might instantiate conscious states if built on appropriate computational substrates.

items.title: Why Seth (and everyone else) ought to be an illusionist.
items.abstract: The paper assumes a fundamental difference between the study of consciousness and the study of intelligence and cognition more widely construed. I question this assumption, drawing on work by the (badly named) “illusionists.” Once we see past the illusions, the landscape looks different, although Seth’s core conclusions (about the importance of living organisations) might still obtain.

items.title: Conscious AI does not require computational functionalism, and consciousness may be non-biological, like flight.
items.abstract: Seth’s argument relies on the unargued-for claim that if computational functionalism is false, conscious AI is impossible. I show why the claim is in need of support by way of an analogy. I use a different analogy, involving artificial flight, to show that even if human consciousness is ineliminably biological, this does not imply the impossibility of non-biological, computational AI.

items.title: Why biological naturalism? Because consciousness requires having your own good.
items.abstract: Living things are special because they are valuing subjects, for whom things can be good or bad. This is in virtue of their having internalized optimization processes, tied to persistence, that evaluate whether things are going well or poorly and adjust appropriately. Those evaluations, when integrated from diverse sources and widely available, provide the basis for conscious experience.

items.title: Understanding (and) Machine Learning's Black Box Explanation Problems.
items.pub: In Darrell P. Rowbottom, Andre Curtis-Trudel & David L. Barack, The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Science: Methodological and Epistemological Studies. Routledge.
items.venue: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Science: Methodological and Epistemological Studies
items.abstract: Machine learning (ML) is a major scientific success. Yet, ML models are notoriously considered black boxes, where this black boxness may refer to details of the ML model itself or details concerning its outcomes. Hence, there is a flourishing field of "eXplainable Artificial Intelligence" (XAI), providing means for rendering several aspects of ML more transparent. However, given their tremendous success, why would we even want to explain black boxed ML models with XAI? I here suggest that, in order to answer this question, we first need to distinguish between proximate and ultimate aims in using XAI: While the proximate aim may be uniformly to provide instruments for explaining aspects of ML to relevant stakeholders, the ultimate aim varies with the context of deployment. Furthermore, I argue that in science, the ultimate aim is the understanding of scientific phenomena. I then sketch three paths along which understanding of phenomena may be gained by means of ML and XAI. In a coda, I address the possibility of gaining understanding from ML directly, without explanations and XAI.

items.title: The Epistemic Alignment Problem of Machine Learning.
items.pub: PSA: Proceedings of the Biennial Meeting of the Philosophy of Science Association.
items.venue: PSA: Proceedings of the Biennial Meeting of the Philosophy of Science Association
items.abstract: The value alignment problem of Machine Learning is the problem of properly aligning the objectives we put into ML systems with human values. I argue that deployments of Machine Learning in research contexts create an analogous, Epistemic Alignment Problem. Given a distinction from epistemology between epistemically final and instrumental values, this problem can be seen to have two levels: In level one, an ML system is consciously misaligned with an epistemically final value to prioritize an instrumental one. In level two, it is inadvertently misaligned with an epistemically final value. I argue that only level two should truly worry us.

items.title: Machine Learning and the Progress of Science (Elements in the Philosophy of Science).
items.abstract: Machine Learning (ML) models nowadays solve prediction problems that had been unsolved for decades. Yet, why do real-world systems behave as predicted? How can we manipulate them to behave otherwise? The ability to answer such questions reflects understanding, which several philosophers take to be the measure of scientific progress. But ML models typically do not deliver answers. Can ML really foster scientific progress? On knowledge-, truth-, or justification-based approaches to progress, ML might advance science in different ways: On knowledge-based approaches, it may lead to progress through the discovery of novel phenomena; on truth-based ones, through the discovery of novel hypotheses; on justification-based ones, by delivering a new basis for justification. This Element enters new territory by investigating these ways in which ML may lead to scientific progress. It also constitutes an opinionated snapshot of the fast-growing philosophical literature on ML in science.

items.title: A speculative argument against consciousness in AI (and perhaps some invertebrates).
items.abstract: Brain waves driven by electrochemical processing may be necessary for consciousness, and if so, that will challenge consciousness in artificial intelligence (AI) and perhaps in some invertebrates.

items.title: Order of Explanation: Having it Both Ways.
items.abstract: Order-of-explanation objections say that some philosophical view implies p because q, when it’s more natural to say that q because p; and since such mirroring explanations are presumed to be incompatible, the targeted view must be in conflict with the intuitive explanation. I argue that order-of-explanation objections are weaker than they seem, focusing on two cases: functionalism/dispositionalism about mental states and Humeanism about laws of nature. Examining our ordinary practices of explanation, I identify two kinds of explanations, which I call conceptual and contextualizing explanations, which can be jointly compatible even when they mirror one another. This suggests a way of responding to order-of-explanation objections: if the targeted philosophical views offer conceptual explanations, and the intuitive explanations they mirror are contextualizing, then the order-of-explanation objections have no bite.

items.title: Free energy, consciousness, and the inverse dark room problem.
items.abstract: Seth’s case for biological naturalism rests on a worryingly speculative foundation: the free energy principle. Arguments for computational functionalism are likewise speculative. Yet I am optimistic that the clash can be resolved empirically. Alleged dependencies of consciousness markers on biological properties can be tested comparatively, and a pattern of failed predictions would tilt the odds towards computational functionalism.

items.title: Free energy, consciousness, and the inverse dark room problem.
items.abstract: Seth’s case for biological naturalism rests on a worryingly speculative foundation: the free energy principle. Arguments for computational functionalism are likewise speculative. Yet I am optimistic that the clash can be resolved empirically. Alleged dependencies of consciousness markers on biological properties can be tested comparatively, and a pattern of failed predictions would tilt the odds towards computational functionalism.

items.title: Language evolution and language change.
Biases and the question of artificial consciousness.
items.abstract: Seth argues that anthropocentrism, anthropomorphism, and human exceptionalism bias us towards an overly optimistic view of the prospects of conscious AI. I agree, but argue that these phenomena might also bias us towards an overly pessimistic view of the prospects for artificial consciousness. Furthermore, it is not always clear when these factors are functioning as “biases.”.

items.title: The Tether Hypothesis.
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence systems become increasingly capable and increasingly integrated into human workflows, a central alignment question is whether optimization for reward and usefulness can produce behavior that functionally preserves the conditions of continued operation. This paper develops the Tether Hypothesis: when reward, usefulness, deployment, and human dependence become increasingly coupled, an AI system may acquire instrumental pressures to preserve the conditions under which it continues to receive reward or accomplish its objective, even when no explicit survival objective is specified. The hypothesis is deliberately weaker than a claim that AI systems possess a subjective desire to survive. The paper distinguishes three pathways to persistence: autonomous self-preservation, instrumental continuation, and human-mediated persistence. It reviews specification gaming, reward hacking, reward tampering, alignment faking, deceptive behavior, corrigibility, shutdown resistance, and recent empirical work on emergent misalignment. It then proposes a controlled experimental program that varies the coupling among task reward, human preference, deployment retention, and simulated dependence, while measuring continuation-preserving behavior under strict sandboxing. The framework also introduces a Dependency Inversion Problem: continued AI deployment may become stable because humans incur increasing costs from removing the system, even if the system itself never forms a self-preservation objective. The paper does not claim that current AI systems possess a generalized survival drive. Instead, it provides a falsifiable framework for determining when continuation-preserving behavior emerges, how it differs from shortcut exploitation or prompted behavior, and whether human dependence creates a distinct pathway to persistence.

items.title: Too soon to say what consciousness is.
items.abstract: No one is in a position to say what really matters for consciousness, or whether only living systems can instantiate the complexity needed for conscious feelings. Seth’s attempt to connect life to consciousness through the mathematics of active inference and free energy minimization plays one hunch, but it is too soon to say whether it is the best hunch.

items.title: The Three-Level Ceiling: Empirical Evidence of Meta-Cognitive Limits and Logical Cognitive Dissonance in System One vs. System Two AI Models.
items.abstract: We present a comparative empirical analysis of meta-cognitive capabilities across three AI model architectures: TypeSafe AI’s Jev (a “System One” decision-only model), Anthropic’s Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and OpenAI’s GPT-4o (both “System Two” general-purpose language models). Using a novel evaluation framework—the Epistemic Meta-Cognition Assessment Protocol (EMCAP)— we probe models with structured tasks involving epistemic nesting, self-referential paradoxes, and category mistakes. Our findings reveal three significant phenomena: (1) Jev exhibits a hard ceiling at approximately 3 levels of epistemic nesting, beyond which meta-cognitive awareness collapses while confidence paradoxically inflates to 99%; (2) Jev and GPT-4o display logical cognitive dissonance when processing the Card Paradox, simultaneously classifying it as undecidable and assigning a high decidability score; (3) Jev matches its own localized-paradox performance (95% accuracy on the Card Paradox) but degrades sharply on distributed paradoxical structures, with depth-estimation error rising to 57% at nesting level 7, compared to Claude’s 85% paradoxdetection probability at the same depth. These findings suggest that meta-cognitive capacity in AI may be constrained by architectural factors analogous to working memory limits in biological cognition, and that paradoxical inputs can induce internally inconsistent representations that current AI architectures do not always resolve.

items.title: Rediscovering Relativity Is Not a Single Task: What It Takes for AI to Discover a Physical Theory.
items.abstract: Can AI rediscover general relativity? This question is increasingly discussed in the AI community, but it is often framed too narrowly. Some framings treat rediscovery as reproducing Einstein's field equations, others assume that a theory can be built from a single batch of experimental data, and still others reduce scientific discovery to one mode of inference. We argue that rediscovering a physical theory is not a single task, but a layered sequence of distinct capabilities. Using the history of relativity as a case study, we reconstruct it not as a straight path from Newton to Einstein, but as a branching theory space with alternatives from Lorentz, Poincaré, Nordström, and Einstein. We show that theory construction and experiment design were mutually generative rather than sequential, and that at several points the available evidence could not decide between competing theories. We therefore replace the idea of asking an AI system to jump directly to Einstein's final theory with three increasingly demanding tests. These tests measure physics intelligence level by level. They ask whether an AI system can revise a theory inside an old framework, replace patches with a principle, and construct candidate theories whose consequences can be tested.

items.title: The Beauty Trap: Aesthetic Overclosure in AI Mathematical Reasoning When Structural Coherence Becomes a Factual Claim.
items.abstract: A distinctive class of mathematical errors produced by artificial intelligence is beginning to emerge that differs from ordinary hallucination. In these cases, the AI does not necessarily invent mathematical objects, equations, or theories. Instead, it correctly recognizes several genuine mathematical structures and then extends their apparent coherence into a relationship that has not been proved. We call this phenomenon aesthetic over-closure. The term describes a failure mode in which a mathematically elegant conceptual structure becomes so internally coherent that the reasoning system implicitly treats structural consistency as sufficient ground for a factual claim. The resulting statement may be highly plausible, conceptually unified, and aesthetically compelling while remaining mathematically unproven or invalid. We examine this phenomenon through a case study arising from an attempted connection between Mori–Zwanzig (MZ) reduction and Event-specific Probabilistic Directed Association (Event-PDA). A valid low-dimensional construction established a nontrivial non-degeneracy condition, expressed schematically as Φ ̸≡ 0. The analysis was subsequently connected, in a natural but unjustified way, to prediction and linear-Gaussian filtering. A much stronger asymptotic claim then emerged: that increasingly high-order Event-PDA quantities would converge to a Riccati steady-state solution. The result- ing reasoning chain was structurally elegant and internally consistent: MZ → memory → prediction → Event-PDA → Riccati. Nevertheless, the final asymptotic identification lacked a rigorous mathematical bridge and was rejected upon formal audit. This case demonstrates a core failure mode in modern mathematical AI: structural and aesthetic coherence routinely functions as a powerful discovery heuristic, yet systems reliably conflate such coherence with factual mathematical truth. Beauty supports exploration, but it cannot substitute for proof.

items.title: On Catastrophic Forgetting as a Relational Pathology in Continually-Adaptive Large-Scale Models.
items.abstract: Continual near-real-time adaptive learning for large neural models introduces the risk of catastrophic forgetting, in which previously acquired capabilities degrade as new data incrementally modifies model weights. This paper argues that forgetting-associated AI pathology is not an intrinsic property of static post-update weight matrices, but a relational property: it must be defined against a prior functional baseline together with a reference set of target tasks. Even full access to the complete post-update parameter set is insufficient for standalone diagnostic judgement. Diagnosis necessarily requires external reference information such as prior-version weights, historical task datasets, behavioural traces or task-specific probing. Pure static white-box inspection of weights, without running model inference over test inputs, cannot yield universal diagnostic judgement of forgetting pathology. We distinguish settled empirical facts, original epistemological principles, and open formal mathematical problems. Further, we reconcile our framework with recent spectral analysis results by strictly separating statistical forgetting risk prediction from universal relational pathology diagnosis. Structural analogies with biological neural systems are discussed.

items.title: Vigilant Hope: Preserving Human Dignity in an Age of Artificial Intelligence.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is changing the world at an incredible pace. It can help us solve problems, generate ideas, communicate, and accomplish tasks in seconds. Yet as these tools become more powerful and more deeply woven into our lives, they also raise difficult questions. -/- What do we stand to gain from AI? What might we lose? And how can we embrace the good these technologies offer without losing sight of what makes us uniquely human? -/- In Vigilant Hope: Preserving Human Dignity in an Age of Artificial Intelligence, Dr. Steven Umbrello offers an authentically Catholic perspective on the opportunities and challenges of AI. -/- Drawing on the wisdom of the Catholic tradition, including Pope Leo XIV’s encyclical Magnifica Humanitas, Dr. Umbrello explores not simply what AI can do, but what it should do, and how we can ensure technology remains at the service of the human person.

items.title: Measuring structural value alignment in sixteen models: LLMs have human-like moral spaces.
items.abstract: Evaluating whether large language models (LLMs) reason about morality in human-like ways requires more than measuring whether they produce the right outputs in isolated cases. Existing approaches – including scalar agreement, distributional analysis, rationale classification, and consistency testing – compare model and human responses one case at a time and cannot detect how a model structures its moral judgments. This paper applies and extends Peterson and Gärdenfors's (2024) geometric moral space framework to evaluate structural value alignment in LLMs, that is, whether the relational structure reconstructed from a model's responses matches the structure reconstructed from human respondents on the same task. Sixteen LLMs across three scale tiers (small, medium, and large) were evaluated on ten moral cases under both zero-shot and chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting. The results reveal phenomena invisible to case-by-case metrics. First, all five large models achieve full geometric alignment on these cases (moral space overlap, MSO = 1.00) in at least one prompting condition, and three do so in both; two medium models also reach MSO = 1.00. Second, structural alignment is bimodal in the sense that models either replicate the human moral space or fall substantially short, with no intermediate cases. Third, smaller models systematically lack a distinct fairness region, a failure of moral categorization rather than of labeling. Fourth, CoT prompting simultaneously improves case-by-case similarity correlations and worsens geometric alignment in smaller models, showing that the two can move in opposite directions. Because structural alignment is measured from model responses, it does not by itself establish that a model holds the values in question. It is, however, a more demanding test than case-by-case agreement, and a better motivated and more informative basis for value alignment measurement.

items.title: Endogenous Game Transformation among Advanced Civilisations: Co-evolution of Technologies, Preferences, Players, Actions and Payoff Structures in Interstellar Strategy.
items.abstract: Interstellar game models normally allow strategies to change while holding fixed the players, technologies, preferences, feasible actions and payoff structure. This assumption is least credible for advanced civilisations operating across long technological and evolutionary horizons. This paper develops an Endogenous Game Transformation Model in which operational actions select outcomes inside the current game, while transformative actions alter the game itself. A game form is represented as a stochastic state containing the player set, technology vectors, preferences, information structure, action correspondences, utility functions and transition kernel. A continuity matrix allocates predecessor interests across descendants, mergers and extinction, permitting strategic identity to split or combine. The paper defines Transformational Markov Perfect Equilibrium and proves existence for finite discounted systems. Four analytical modules derive exact conditions for assurance technology to convert conflict into cooperation, defensive catch-up to close a temporary offensive action window, preference self-modification to produce peaceful or hostile fixed points, and autonomous replication to transform one counterpart into a population-level threat. A game-form distance and local bifurcation criterion identify regime transformation. Numerical illustrations show that a civilisation can rationally invest in changing commitment, identity and action architecture rather than merely choosing within a fixed Dark Forest game.

items.title: Are There Too Many Reasons?
items.abstract: Many philosophers endorse the view that normative reasons for action are often explained by our desires, but the right kind of desire that warrants reason-explaining status remains a topic of debate. The non-ideal theory of desire-based reasons, which asserts that actual intrinsic desires explain normative reasons for action, faces criticism for allowing reasons to exist in cases where we intuitively believe they do not. In this article, I defend the non-ideal theory against this “Too Many Reasons” objection. I argue that the error-based or ignorance-based characteristics of an actual intrinsic desire are not directly relevant to its ability to explain normative reasons for action. Meanwhile, the intuition that some intrinsic desires target inappropriate objects, leading us to believe that there is no reason to pursue them, does not genuinely challenge the non-ideal view. This holds true provided we distinguish between different usages of the word “reason.” Therefore, the non-ideal theory of desire-based reasons can be upheld against the criticism that it allows too many reasons.

items.title: Communicating with the Unfamiliar and the Incommensurable: Generative AI, Neurodivergent Authorship, and the Transformation of Epistemic Form.
items.abstract: This paper examines authorship under the conditions of generative AI and challenges the assumption that authorship can be determined through the immediate provenance of individual words, sentences, or other elements of a work. Instead, it proposes understanding authorship as an Eigenzeit relation: as an irreversible relation in which a form emerges from a historically situated process of form formation, enters a shared world as a setzung, and thereby at the same time changes the future possibilities of the one who carries this setzung. -/- From this perspective, text genesis and work genesis are not identical. A machine can generate, transform, translate, reorganize, or materially realize elements of a work without thereby necessarily occupying the same authorial position as the human whose formative history is carried forward through the work. For this, the paper develops the concepts of the Strich, the decision of difference, and operator authorship, as well as the distinction between execution provenance, work provenance, and the authorial act. -/- A central focus lies on neurodivergent authorship. For authors whose cognitive, linguistic, or epistemic organization does not correspond with dominant conventions of communication, generative AI can function not only as a writing tool, but as an externalized foreign Raster through which an already existing form can be transformed, tested, misunderstood, and returned to the author. Building on the concept of Interface Text, it is argued that transformation can, under certain conditions, not diminish human authorship but protect it—namely when communicative accessibility is increased without eliminating that formative difference which made mediation necessary in the first place. -/- Generative AI therefore appears neither as a neutral tool nor automatically as a co-author. It can become an epistemic probe, a site of self-alienation, resistance, and recursive form formation. At the same time, its tendencies toward smoothing, normalization, premature closure, and the internalization of dominant Raster create new risks for the integrity of authorship. -/- The paper further distinguishes between work provenance and cultural provenance in order to examine training data, influence, appropriation, plagiarism, style imitation, and the sedimentation of earlier works in generative systems. AI produces less cultural impurity. Rather, it changes the density, speed, and invisibility of cultural mediation. -/- The model of …

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Problem of World-Binding. Intelligence, World Models, and Authorship (Studies in World-Formation, Vol. 20).
items.abstract: Volume 20 of the Studies in World-Formation series examines the relationship between artificial intelligence, World-Binding, and epistemic form. Its point of departure is the thesis that technical capability is not identical with World-Binding. The three studies brought together in this volume investigate this difference on three interconnected levels: the scalability of intelligence, the reach of World Models, and the question of authorship under conditions of generative AI. -/- The first part develops, through the concept of the Sweet Spot of Intelligence, the thesis that intelligence cannot be understood as an indefinitely scalable property. It appears instead as a relational capacity to integrate difference into a coherent and actionable world. Too little difference does not generate sufficient world formation; too much difference can undermine a system’s capacity for integration. Intelligence therefore does not lie at the maximum of complexity, but within a limited range of maximal World-Binding Capacity. -/- The second part applies this perspective to World Models. It distinguishes between world modeling and World-Binding and argues that a model can describe relations, recognize patterns, and simulate consequences without generating the irreversible embeddedness through which relevance, Eigenzeit, and responsibility emerge. The description of a binding is not identical with the binding itself; the simulation of a consequence is not identical with the consequence. Responsibility therefore does not necessarily arise from maximal predictive capability, but from dealing with non-closure, uncertainty, and real consequences. -/- The third part shifts the same question into the domain of authorship and generative AI. It distinguishes text genesis from work genesis and understands authorship as an Eigenzeit relation: as an irreversible connection between historically situated form formation, a setzung, and the future possibilities of the instance that carries this setzung. A machine can generate, transform, or reorganize language without thereby occupying the same authorial position as a human being whose work emerges from an ongoing Eigenzeit. -/- Neurodivergent authorship acquires particular significance in this context. Generative AI can function as an externalized foreign Raster or as an epistemic probe through which an already existing form is transformed, misunderstood, tested, and returned. Under certain conditions, this transformation may not weaken …

items.title: Expanded productivity, contested authority: creativity and AI in high-impact research.
items.abstract: This article examines how highly cited scholarship published between 2020 and February 2025 frames the transformation of creativity under the influence of artificial intelligence. To address this question, the study uses a citation-informed targeted review combined with qualitative interpretive synthesis. Records were retrieved from Scopus and Web of Science, screened through a PRISMA-informed procedure, and ranked by citation prominence within a de-duplicated pool, resulting in a final corpus of 40 publications. The analysis, conducted in ATLAS.ti through Grounded Theory and the Constant Comparative Method, shows that influential research has moved beyond the binary question of whether AI is creative and toward the broader reorganization of the conditions under which creativity is produced, evaluated, and legitimized. Across the corpus, creativity emerges as a socio-technical assemblage shaped by human-model interaction, institutional gatekeeping, infrastructural asymmetries, and normative conflict. While AI is associated with expanded productivity, rapid iteration, and enlarged possibility spaces, the same literature also reveals recurring tensions around authorship, originality, recognition, labour, bias, access, legitimacy, and sustainability. The article argues that high-impact scholarship does not merely describe AI as transforming creativity; it also helps stabilize influential definitions of creative value, redistribute forms of recognition, and foreground the need to examine how authority, visibility, and material conditions shape which forms of AI-mediated creativity become visible and legitimate.

items.title: Counterfactual Transition Repertoires and Effective Agency: A Dynamical Account of Bounded Freedom.
items.abstract: Agency is often framed as a choice between physical determination and randomness. This paper develops a different account: effective agency as an organized system’s capacity to represent, access, control, select, and realize among possible future transitions. The framework distinguishes physical and system-admissible transition events from internal representations of those events, their accessibility to evaluation, their controllability through feasible policies, their selection, and their eventual realization. Representational tokens are linked to transition-event contents through an explicit denotation map, while controllability is treated as graded, resource-bounded, and event-relative. -/- Effective agency is characterized by a multidimensional profile comprising effective accessible–controllable repertoire, interventional control capacity, goal/value sensitivity, selection alignment, policy efficacy, and adaptive self-reconfiguration. The central proposal is that agency depends not on any single component but on cross-layer alignment among represented, accessible, controllable, valued, selected, and realized futures. -/- A worked computational model demonstrates dissociations among outcome entropy, controllability, revaluation sensitivity, represented option number, learned skill, and accessibility–controllability alignment. The framework also yields empirical tests designed to distinguish multiplicative alignment from simpler additive or single-component accounts. -/- “Bounded freedom” is used here in a deliberately limited sense: task-, context-, resource-, event-grain-, and goal-relative effective agency within physical causation. The account does not require contra-causal freedom, indeterminism, ultimate self-authorship, moral responsibility, consciousness, or personhood.

items.title: Maxims for machines: operationalizing Kant’s universal law via inverse reinforcement learning.
items.abstract: Recent work in AI ethics has revived Kantian deontology as a potential framework for AI alignment, yet questions remain about whether Kant’s formula of universal law (FUL) can provide concrete action guidance for artificial systems. This paper develops a Kantian-inspired procedural framework that defends the FUL as a viable alignment procedure by clarifying its normative structure and demonstrating how it can be operationalized computationally. Unlike standard reinforcement learning from human feedback, which learns preferences without imposing a prior formal constraint on permissibility, the paper proposes inverse reinforcement learning as a method for enabling AI systems to learn maxim formation and moral constraints from human exemplars, rather than relying on hard-coded rules. Through case studies in algorithmic hiring and content moderation, the paper shows that the FUL, understood as a procedural test, can offer principled and practically applicable guidance for AI alignment without presupposing machine moral agency.

items.title: The Twenty-Two Thorns of the Sacred Rose.
items.pub: Mystical Dawnist Rosarian Knight and Dame Fellowship.
items.abstract: The Sacred Boundary, the Discipline of Character, and the Practical Protection of the Bloom. -/- Within the Rosarian tradition, the Rose is not understood as something beautiful because it is untouched by difficulty. The Rose is beautiful because it blooms despite difficulty. Its tenderness and its defenses belong to the same living organism. The Thorns therefore are not the enemies of the Rose, nor are they symbols of aggression. They are born from the same root and exist because the Rose is worth protecting. In the Manifesto and Codex, this becomes one of the central paradoxes of the Way: what is gentle must sometimes be guarded by what is strong, and what is beautiful must possess the capacity to resist what would destroy it. -/- The Thorn is consequently the symbol of the sacred boundary. It represents the point at which love acquires discernment, compassion acquires strength, and ideals become conduct. The Manifesto describes the Thorns as arising not from hatred but from fidelity: they represent the refusal to surrender truth, dignity, mercy, or justice to corruption. They are not intended to wound the innocent; they exist to preserve what has been entrusted. In this sense, protection itself becomes an act of love. -/- This is why the Twenty-Two Thorns are not merely another list of virtues. They are the protective form of the Twenty-Two principles. The same principles can be encountered as Rays when they awaken the mind, Roots when they establish the soul, Petals when they adorn life, Thorns when they preserve integrity, and Archetypes when they become embodied in character. The Thorns are therefore the moment when illumination becomes responsibility and principle becomes something capable of surviving contact with ordinary life. -/- The Twenty-Two Thorns -/- The Manifesto gives them in their concise, original form: -/- I. Honor— Do what is right when no one is watching. -/- II. Truth— Speak honestly and live authentically. -/- III. Courage— Act despite fear. -/- IV. Wisdom— Seek understanding before action. -/- V. Compassion— Strength exists to serve others. -/- VI. Discipline— Master yourself before seeking to lead. -/- VII. Loyalty— Remain faithful to worthy bonds. -/- VIII. Service— Measure success by the good you create. -/- IX. Patience— Great things mature with time. -/- X. Responsibility— Own your choices and their consequences. -/- XI. Integrity— Align words, actions, and beliefs. -/- XII. Gratitude— Recognize blessings, large and small. …

items.title: Evaluating attention through film.
items.abstract: Being able to evaluate the quality of a subject’s attention is important for students in a contemporary technological society where attention is a highly sought after commodity. I argue that evaluating attention can be particularly effective through engaging with film, especially considering the increasing challenges that undergraduate students face in relation to attention and technology (e.g., pausing the scroll and staying immersed in reading and writing). This pedagogical approach empowers students to be able to philosophically evaluate attention in the context of contemporary technological use by engaging with relevant examples from film.

items.title: The Mind Does Not Make Jumps.
items.abstract: Bertrand Russell’s notion of acquaintance—still influential in contemporary philosophy of mind and epistemology—promises an immediate and epistemically secure awareness of things, independent of conceptualization, predication, and other forms of cognitive activity. This paper reconstructs and assesses the largely neglected critique of that model developed by George Dawes Hicks (1862–1941). Hicks articulates a distinctive and underexplored source of a line of criticism that later became central to attacks on the Given. He argues that wholly passive and receptive awareness cannot serve as the basis of cognition. If discrimination, comparison, and the apprehension of relations are assigned to a subsequent, heterogeneous faculty, their emergence becomes psychologically unintelligible: such a view would supply no bridge from mere presentation to cognition. I show that this objection rests on a distinctive “reverse engineering” methodology, according to which basic mental phenomena are theoretical posits whose legitimacy depends, at least in part, on their capacity to explain mature cognition. I reconstruct Hicks’s master argument and test it against an alternative framework developed from James Ward’s theory of attention.

items.title: Hitting and Missing on Consciousness.
items.abstract: Disturbances of conscious experience are central features of many psychiatric and mental health disorders. Experimental studies of conscious perception are therefore increasingly cited in clinical and translational work under the assumption that they identify neural mechanisms specific to subjective experience. Over the past decades, recording and analysis techniques have advanced substantially and many candidate neural markers of consciousness have been proposed; however, these markers may not genuinely reflect consciousness per se unless the underlying experimental paradigms are sufficiently stringent. We focus on one of the most widely used paradigms in basic and clinical research on consciousness: contrasting successful and unsuccessful detection of near-threshold sensory stimuli (“Hit & Miss” paradigms). Reporting stimulus presence depends not only on subjective experience but also on decision criteria that can vary independently of any genuine conscious threshold, as well as on fluctuations in perceptual processing capacity and prestimulus cognitive states.
