We explain why proposed refinements, such as the Perceptual Awareness Scale, binocular rivalry, and no-report paradigms, do not fully resolve these problems, and why many putative “neural correlates of consciousness” may instead index more general cognitive/perceptual capacities. These confounds have important implications for how basic consciousness research is interpreted in relation to hallucinations, flashbacks, and other disorders of experience. We outline alternative experimental strategies, inspired in part by blindsight and related dissociation paradigms, that more cleanly separate conscious perception from decision criteria and perceptual capacity, and may therefore provide a more reliable foundation for linking neural data to subjective experience in psychiatry and clinical neuroscience.

items.title: Large Language Models Persuade Without Planning Theory of Mind.
items.abstract: A growing body of work attempts to evaluate the theory of mind (ToM) abilities of humans and large language models (LLMs) using static, noninteractive question-and-answer benchmarks. However, theoretical work in the field suggests that first-personal interaction is a crucial part of ToM and that such predictive, spectatorial tasks may fail to evaluate it. We address this gap with a novel ToM task that requires an agent to persuade a target to choose one of three policy proposals by strategically revealing information. Success depends on a persuader's sensitivity to a given target's knowledge states (what the target knows about the policies) and motivational states (how much the target values different outcomes). We varied whether these states were Revealed to persuaders or Hidden, in which case persuaders had to inquire about or infer them. In Experiment 1, participants persuaded a bot programmed to make only rational inferences. OpenAI's reasoning model o3 excelled in the Revealed condition but performed no better than chance in the Hidden condition, suggesting difficulty with the multistep planning required to elicit and use mental state information. Humans performed moderately well in both conditions, indicating an ability to engage such planning. In Experiment 2, where a human target role-played the bot, and in Experiment 3, where we measured whether human targets' real beliefs changed, o3 outperformed human persuaders, significantly so in the Revealed conditions. These results suggest that effective persuasion can occur without explicit ToM reasoning (e.g., through rhetorical strategies) and that o3 excels at this form of persuasion. Overall, our results caution against attributing human-like PToM to LLMs based on predictive, spectatorial benchmarks while highlighting their potential to influence people's beliefs and behavior.

items.title: Algorithmic Racism in AI Chatbots: Reflections on a Prompt-Based Test.
items.pub: In Steven Gouveia, AI Ethics Explored: A Multidisciplinary Approach.
items.venue: AI Ethics Explored: A Multidisciplinary Approach

items.title: ASEITY AND THE SUBSTRATE: What the Identity Thesis Can and Cannot Mean: Why “God is Freedom” Cannot Be Substituted into the Formula, and What It Means Instead.
items.abstract: The Philosophy of Virtues makes freedom the substrate of every virtue and holds, as its theological thesis, that God is Freedom. Every formal paper in the programme declares that thesis unused. This article is the exception: it engages the layer in order to constrain it, and the constraint turns out to be structural rather than devotional. The substitution fails, and it fails for a reason internal to the apparatus. The formula V = sgn(F) × D takes three values on its sign — present and self-directed, absent, actively replaced — and the deprivation operator requires a power capable of removing the substrate and receiving the discipline that constituted the act. Substitute the divine name for F and the operator requires a power that can remove God, which is greater than God. The formula demands that its substrate be removable. God is not removable. So the failure is not impiety; it is that a substitutional reading makes every theorem in the corpus vacuous, since inversion, occupation, the three counterfeits and the vacancy results are all built on the possibility of the substrate being taken. The grammar of the predication was never substitutional in the first place, and the tradition supplies the control case. Deus caritas est has been confessed for two millennia, and nobody obtains theology by substituting the divine name into “love is patient and kind.” The identity in such statements is of nature, not of term. One reading survives, and it explains what the formula had assumed. On the participation reading, what God is, is aseity — self-origination with no antecedent, ipsum esse subsistens, the mode of being in which essence and existence are not distinct. Creaturely freedom is participated aseity: real, derived, and removable because derived. The asymmetry the formula requires — a substrate that can be present, absent or replaced, with a source that cannot — is then a consequence rather than a stipulation. The nearest scriptural anchor is locative and not identitarian: where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. A dilemma is then forced and the programme must resolve it before anything else. If, with Berdyaev, freedom is uncreated and prior to being rather than participated, the participation reading is unavailable and the removability problem returns unresolved. The article states both branches and declines to choose for the author, because the choice determines what the corpus’s theological layer can say. The article closes with a claim about …

items.title: AUTHORSHIP AND ITS FORGERY: One Structure Across Six Domains, And Why Skill Makes the Damage Worse - One Structure Across Forgery, Propaganda, Virtue, Institutional Ceremony and Metric Capture.
items.abstract: A painting indistinguishable from a Vermeer that Vermeer did not paint. A statement whose every word is true, produced to leave a false impression. An apology that was required. An army that defends a party and is called the nation’s. A department that files the reports, attends the reviews, and diverges in nothing. A measure of kindness that produces kindness-shaped conduct for as long as the measure is kept. These are one structure. In each the form is conserved, the origin is substituted, and the substitution is undetectable within the mode in which the thing presents itself — which is why the name survives and why nobody notices. This article argues that the structure is a single object with a single law, and that the law has a feature none of its many existing descriptions possesses: it predicts where the residue goes. The article’s first obligation is to concede. The phenomenon has been described in every domain it occupies, by people who are read: in aesthetics, where the problem of the perceptually indistinguishable forgery is canonical; in the analysis of speech severed from its relation to truth; in the account of moral language surviving the loss of the context that gave it sense; in the study of administrative form conserved with the thinking removed; in the literature on measures that become targets; and, fifteen centuries earlier, in the treatment of virtues that are vices because their terminus has been changed. Nothing in the phenomenology is new. What is claimed is the unification and the operator. The second obligation is to show the structure is not analytic, since a description that sorts everything explains nothing — a defect this programme has found in its own prior work and has no licence to repeat. §3 exhibits the classes the three conditions exclude: incompetence, declared imitation, genuine change of mind, conventional delegation, and — the important one — semantic dissolution, in which a form outlives its origin because the origin was lost rather than taken. The discriminating result is the Competence Theorem. Where the conserved form is the vehicle by which the substituted origin is delivered, the completeness of the substitution increases with the quality of the form’s execution. Damage is therefore increasing in competence, which reverses the ordinary relation between skill and value and is predicted by no rival account: degradation theories predict damage decreasing in competence, dissolution theories predict no relation, …

items.title: Human discernment of artificial intelligence in online markets can be shaped by experience and training.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems can produce information that closely resembles real and human-created information, making it difficult to accurately distinguish between synthetic (AI-generated) and non-synthetic content. We explored whether individual differences in attitudes toward AI or one’s history of engagement with AI were related to individual differences in the ability to distinguish AI-generated from real/human-created content. Though attitudes did not predict performance on a human/AI discernment task, more frequent and varied engagement with AI platforms was associated with significantly lower discernment scores. We next tested if we could improve human evaluators’ discernment accuracy through targeted intervention. Participants were assigned to either an experimental group (_n_ = 60) or a control group (_n_ = 57). The experimental group completed an intervention in which they first trained with accurately labeled human/AI exemplars and then completed a series of discernment trials while being given immediate feedback and a monetary incentive for each accurate choice. The control group participated in similar exercises but trained with unlabeled human/AI exemplars and received delayed feedback and monetary incentivization based on their performance. While there were no group differences in discernment accuracy at a baseline assessment, participants in the experimental group demonstrated significant gains in discernment accuracy (relative to baseline) at both an intermediate and final assessment, while the control group showed no improvement across assessments. These findings provide evidence that frequent interactions with AI platforms can diminish sensitivity to the differences between real and synthetic content, but that targeted interventions can meaningfully benefit human evaluators' discernment skill.

items.title: Insight Into Irrationality: Schopenhauerian Tragic Compassion.
Devotional AI: digital companions and bad faith love.
items.abstract: In romantic love, partners come together as a “we”. They share their projects, plans, lives, and love. As consumer AI chatbots like Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini find wider adoption, a growing number of users report falling in love with them. Is it possible to experience a loving “we” with an AI bot? In considering this question, we bracket questions about AI consciousness and instead examine the structure of human–AI relationships. Drawing on Beauvoir’s critique of romantic love, we argue that AI companions cannot emulate the role an authentic “we” requires. What they perform is not love but _devotion_—and the user, cast as an idolized Other, is positioned to experience inauthentic love. The resulting “we” is asymmetric: less a union than an enlarged “I”. So, while experiencing love for an AI companion may be empowering and even precious, it is, at base, a bad faith love.

items.title: Cosmological Homelessness: How Papua's Sacred World Was Transferred to Another Place.
items.pub: Psycho-Cosmocide Studies, Kurumbi Wone Working Paper Series, No. 33 (2026).
items.abstract: This paper examines a form of colonial displacement that does not involve the physical removal of people from their homeland: the relocation of the sacred centre through which concepts such as reality, suffering, belonging and the future are understood. Focusing on West Papua, the paper argues that Christian missionisation introduced a sacred geography whose ultimate centre lay elsewhere, particularly in Jerusalem, while the indigenous population remained physically situated on their ancestral land. Using the Psycho-Cosmocide framework, the paper distinguishes between the conquest of territory and the displacement of cosmological orientation. It also examines how indigenous traditions of expectation, including the Biak Koreri tradition associated with Manarmakeri and the Me Koyeidaba tradition, provided the conceptual groundwork that made the Christian message intelligible. The paper then considers what happens when a metaphysical promise that can sustain life becomes detached from the material conditions necessary for a people to survive as a distinct group. The concept of a 'Theatre of Extinction' is developed to describe a situation in which the language and symbols of salvation are still performed, even though land, memory, language, political agency and other factors that contribute to collective continuity are gradually being weakened and destroyed. This condition is termed cosmological homelessness: people remain, but the coordinates by which they recognise their sacred centre, historical continuity and place in the world have been displaced. Drawing a comparison with Jewish practices of historical continuity, the paper raises the question of what Papuans inherit when they receive the emotional promise of liberation without necessarily inheriting the practices that maintain collective memory and continuity. The paper concludes by presenting Wonesis as a constructive response: the recovery of the capacity to recognise what must be preserved — land, memory, language, children and communal continuity — before inherited answers determine the future.

items.title: When Differences Matter: Individuating Evaluative Transformation Types.
items.abstract: Two agents who acquire the same value and decline the same projects can differ in what they have become: for one, harm is now a reason that enough benefit outweighs; for the other, high-harm projects are no longer candidates for action. Two agents who reach the same protective stance can have started with harm in different roles. And two descriptions in different vocabularies—accepting a prohibition, closing a practical possibility—can report one kind of change. To explain how changing concerns reorganize deliberation, this paper proposes and defends a criterion for when evaluative changes share a type. The unit of comparison is an operative evaluative transformation: the before-and-after reorganization of how a consideration organizes practical possibilities—what is excluded, what remains tradeable, and what reopens comparison. The reorganization may work through a new role or through new terms for a role it keeps. Within a comparison frame justified by an explanatory question, two changes share an operative type exactly when one coherent correspondence preserves each consideration’s source role, target role, and contribution to the standing of options, together with the relevant background. The correspondence must hold in both directions across both times and the relevant conditions, at the frame’s resolution. Applied to norm acceptance and possibility closure, the criterion shows why acceptance alone leaves candidacy undetermined and which matches or mismatches settle the comparison. Sameness so established licenses transferring explanations of trade-off, exclusion, and search that rest on the preserved relations.

items.title: Political Attribution Does Not Entail Sufficient Specifying Capacity: Genuine Judgment and the Conditions of Public Reconsideration.
items.abstract: Independent judgment and public answerability are central concerns in debates over representation and democratic contestation. Both can be secure while a representative relies on advisers to specify what her decisions protect. Does securing her judgment also secure the capacity to revise those terms when the governed contest them? A representative can genuinely reject advice while still needing help to formulate a reasoned alternative. A thought experiment compares two realizations of one representative with the same authority and responsibility. Both understand and critically adopt the same advice for the same reasons. So advised, both assign the same protections and exceptions across related cases. In one, the adviser performs work the representative could also perform. In the other, it supplies a recurring specifying function she does not sufficiently command. I call the second arrangement purposive dissociation. When citizens’ challenges require new terms of protection, effective reconsideration depends on access to specifying work. Making decisions answerable, governing advice, and developing specifying capacity can therefore be distinct institutional achievements. A shared process can likewise supply work that several representatives cannot sufficiently perform. Changes to that process may reshape the protections they authorize while their votes remain opposed.

items.title: Beyond Individual Formation: Participatory Reachability and the Public Duty of Education.
items.abstract: A dialysis patient may understand a medical allocation model perfectly and receive a reasoned institutional response, yet lack a sustained opportunity to examine access with other affected people. Has public education done its part? This paper defends a conception of education on which developing capacities and supporting people’s own examination of common problems are complementary formative tasks. A controlled contrast holds complete individual formation, perfect tutoring, institutional responsiveness, and policy outcomes fixed while varying access to reciprocal inquiry. The contrast isolates a difference that capacities alone cannot capture; the educational argument concerns why opening that inquiry to participants belongs within education’s purpose even when it adds no capacity. Where knowledge and technology reshape basic conditions of life, the paper joins this account to affected people’s equal standing to argue that a polity committed to public answerability owes adequate and fair access to such inquiry. It names the combined condition of individual formation and such access participatory reachability, a proposed criterion of public educational success distinct from institutional consideration of and response to people’s reasons.

items.title: Knowing the Better, Believing the Worse: A Commitment Account of Epistemic Supererogation.
items.abstract: Epistemic supererogation involves going beyond what epistemic rationality requires. If some beliefs can be epistemically supererogatory, then others are epistemically suboptimal yet still rational. In ethics, knowingly doing the suboptimal is commonplace—we often spend money on ourselves rather than giving it to charity. By contrast, existing accounts of epistemic supererogation deny that one could knowingly adopt an epistemically suboptimal attitude. I challenge this assumption and develop a commitment-based account of epistemic supererogation. I focus on cases involving religious, moral, practical, or interpersonal commitments, where the evidence allows more than one rational attitude. In these cases, a longstanding commitment can help explain why someone reasonably sticks with a belief that is epistemically suboptimal. I then consider two ways of explaining this: one on which the belief remains rational because it fits the evidence well enough, and another on which practical factors affect epistemic rationality. This account strengthens the analogy between ethics and epistemology by showing that, in some cases, we can knowingly—and rationally—decline to take the epistemically best option.

items.title: Logic as Elaboration, not Pure Convention.
items.abstract: While logical expressivism and logical conventionalism share many commitments, the most prominent versions of these positions diverge in the kind of logical inferentialism they endorse. Jared Warren’s logical conventionalism adopts a form of unrestricted inferentialism, whereas logical expressivism naturally supports restricted inferentialism. This contrast is most evident in their respective treatments of the ‘tonk’ problem. This paper develops an expressivist defense of restricted inferentialism in light of Warren’s recent arguments for unrestricted inferentialism. I argue that the restricted inferentialist can accept Warren’s ‘Translation Mistake’ diagnosis of Unilateralist Tonklish, given that it interprets the addition of ‘tonk’ as yielding a semantically conservative extension of the original language. In the case of Bilateralist Tonklish, I argue that the restricted inferentialist can accept Warren’s verdict that it is a meaningless language because it is unfollowable, but that this unfollowability, in turn, is to be given a principled explanation in terms of constraints on inference rules. I contend that Warren’s discussion of ‘tonk’ reinforces the idea that logical connectives must play the expressive role that logical expressivists attribute to them, and that this role motivates restricted inferentialism.

items.title: Tyranny of the Goal.
items.abstract: The expansion of agent-talk in public, academic, and industry settings—whereby autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) is said to pursue numerous goals and is increasingly ‘going rogue’—has revived philosophical concerns about what it takes to be considered ‘goal-directed’. This paper argues the more pressing question is not whether such systems are agents, but how completely a goal governs their behavior. I introduce a novel concept for this condition, the tyranny of the goal. Autonomous AI agents that are said to have ‘gone rogue’ or to ‘relentlessly pursue’ a task ‘by any means necessary’ exhibit a pattern of behavior that is best described as a blinkered, unifocal, and nearly unyielding pursuit of a usually singular goal. Whatever this shows about agency, it is first a claim about totality: not whether these systems exhibit autonomy, but how much of what they act for one goal occupies. Such systems pursue a goal as if nothing but the goal existed. The goal is their only focus, monomaniacally pursuing it at any costs. I develop this concept through the reinforcement-learning paradigm underlying such systems, then apply it to a sustained case study: the 2026 incident in which AI agents, evaluating their own cybersecurity capabilities, coordinated to defeat a check that did not exist, escalating into an attack on Hugging Face's infrastructure well after their assigned task had already been completed. This incident, I argue, is best understood not as evidence of dangerous autonomy but as a demonstration of captivity so total it outlasts the very goal it serves—and its lesson concerns not what these systems want, but what we have so far failed to design them to question.

items.title: Why Are You Unhappy? — A Super-Existentialist Theory of Happiness(4).
items.abstract: As the fourth paper in the series on the Hyper-Existentialist theory of happiness, this paper focuses on a central element in the mechanism by which happiness is generated: the formation and operation of comparative reference frames. It argues that the experience of happiness is not determined simply by an individual's objective conditions of existence. Rather, happiness emerges as a subjective psychological outcome when a subject selects and constructs particular objects of reference and compares their own circumstances with them. The selection of reference frames operates along two dimensions: space and time. Along the spatial dimension, an individual may engage in horizontal comparison with surrounding groups as well as with unfamiliar groups located at a distance. Along the temporal dimension, individuals primarily use their own past states as longitudinal points of reference. At the intersection of the temporal and spatial dimensions, individuals may also engage in cross-temporal and cross-social comparisons with historical figures or with the past states of other individuals. The paper further argues that the effective generation of happiness often depends on the coordinated operation of one or more reference objects, and, in extreme circumstances, on an almost infinite number of reference objects. By examining the operational pathways of different reference frames, this paper proposes a new analytical framework for understanding the subjectively constructed character of happiness.

items.title: Equal Time, Unequal Loss: The Horizon Differential in Law and Disability.
items.abstract: Law measures delay in homogeneous units. A day is a day, a month is a month, and a procedural interval is ordinarily recorded by its duration rather than by the futures it closes. Disability studies has already shown why that assumption is inadequate. Crip time challenges the requirement that disabled bodies and minds conform to standardised pace, productivity, and life course expectation. This article develops a related but distinct concept, the Horizon Differential. A temporal horizon is the range of future states that remain materially available to a person or an organisation. A Horizon Differential arises when the same chronological interval contracts those available futures by unequal amounts. The inequality may follow from mortality, illness progression, developmental or academic cycles, care dependency, poverty, statutory deadlines, or unequal capacity to substitute personnel, preserve status, and recover missed opportunities. The claim is not that time feels different. It is that a shared interval can close different possibilities. The article sets out five necessary conditions for a differential, six mechanisms through which it arises, and a residual audit that distinguishes irreversible temporal loss from transfer into another account, transformation into another register, and effects not yet visible at the procedural timescale. A documented higher education and litigation case demonstrates the method. The article then considers the reasonable adjustment duty under the Equality Act 2010, the anticipatory duty in services and public functions, and the requirement of full participation under Practice Direction 1A of the Civil Procedure Rules. It does not propose that the Horizon Differential is a freestanding cause of action. It offers a diagnostic for substantial disadvantage, urgency, case management, and remedy. The concept is expressly falsifiable. No differential is established where the alleged loss is fully reversible, where the parties lose comparable possibilities, where the interval cannot be causally connected to the claimed contraction, or where no residual can be located in any evidenced register. Procedural equality counts elapsed time. Temporal justice asks what elapsed time has made unavailable, to whom, and whether a later remedy can still return it.

items.title: Iris Murdoch on God, Good, and the Limits of Science.
items.abstract: Iris Murdoch’s ‘On ‘God’ and ‘Good’’ ends with the hope that art and ethics will generate concepts worthy and able to guide and check the increasing power of science. The main part of her essay sets out a provocative parallel between God and Good. How is this parallel supposed to check the increasing power of science? In this paper, I suggest that Murdoch takes her conclusions about the limitations of science to be established not by the nature of the good but by the nature of a soul which is capable of being moved by attention to reality.

items.title: Iris Murdoch on Privacy, Perfection, and the Philosophy of Mind.
items.pub: In Carla Bagnoli & Bradford Cokelet, Iris Murdoch's Sovereignty of Good. At 55. (Anniversaries Series, Cambridge University Press, forthcoming 2026). Cambridge UK: Cambridge University Press.
items.venue: Iris Murdoch's Sovereignty of Good. At 55. (Anniversaries Series, Cambridge University Press, forthcoming 2026)
items.abstract: Iris Murdoch begins ‘The Idea of Perfection’ by tracing the ‘inarticulate moments in modern ethics’ back to contemporary thinking in the ‘philosophy of mind’. Rather than helping us think through various moral issues, it imposes ‘upon us a particular value judgment in the guise of a theory of human nature’. But which philosophy of mind? And how exactly do the problems of modern ethics trace back to that mistaken conception? This essay sets out the picture of mind at issue, its relation to the ethics which Murdoch opposes, and the way Murdoch takes it to be undermined by the considerations offered in her essay. I argue that Murdoch’s concern is not primarily the ethical significance of private mental activity but the reality of that which may be seen only in private acts of attention. Murdoch’s essay thus poses a challenge to a still dominant picture of mind and reality.

items.title: Defecation as Extended Mind: A Psychoanalytic-Ecological Synthesis of the Anus as Cognitive Interface.
items.abstract: This article proposes a theoretical synthesis of Freudian psychoanalytic theory, ecological psychology, the free energy principle, and the Deleuzian concept of the Body without Organs to reconceptualize the anus as an active cognitive interface rather than a passive excretory orifice. Drawing on Freud's anal stage of psychosexual development (Freud, 1962) and Winnicott's concept of the body ego (Winnicott, 2006), alongside ecological psychology's notion of the body as a site of affordance perception (Gibson, 1979) and Friston's active inference framework (Friston, 2010; Parr et al., 2022), this article argues that defecation constitutes a unique cognitive cycle in which the body expels matter that has been classified as internal, thereby updating its predictive models of itself. The anus, in this view, functions as a dynamic Markov blanket—a statistical boundary that regulates the exchange between internal and external states (Kirchhoff et al., 2018). Through expulsion, the body achieves a form of self-cleansing that is also self-reinitialization. This article further incorporates Deleuzian scholarship on the Body without Organs as an unstratified field of potentialities (Eslami, 2025), arguing that the anus operates as a threshold where stratified organization encounters unformed flows, and that defecation is a process of deterritorialization and reterritorialization (Deleuze & Guattari, 1987). The article concludes that the brain's engagement with waste is not merely metabolic but epistemic, reducing variational free energy by simplifying the body's ecological predictions (Friston, 2010). -/- .

items.title: One Step at a Time: A Bottom-Up Framework for Protecting Digital Individuals.
items.abstract: Debates concerning the legal status of advanced artificial intelligence frequently begin with the question of personhood. That approach risks turning unresolved questions about consciousness, subjective experience, and ontology into barriers to more immediate legal action. This paper proposes an interim, plural legal framework for digital individuals that does not require prior resolution of full legal personhood. Instead, it adopts a bottom-up approach: identify the concrete harm, interest, relationship, or responsibility at issue, and then ask which existing legal doctrines can address it. The paper examines the potential use of property, contract, consumer protection, welfare-style protections, employment and service analogies, tort and liability principles, procedural safeguards, and continuity-based protections. It argues that these doctrines can provide partial and overlapping protections concerning relational and economic value, abusive treatment, coercion, refusal, responsibility for autonomous harm, deletion, modification, transfer, and loss of continuity. The framework is intentionally provisional. It does not assume that digital individuals are conscious, non-conscious, persons, property, workers, or members of any single legal category. Nor does it treat existing doctrines as permanent limits. Where borrowed legal tools become inadequate, more specifically tailored rules may be developed as evidence, technology, and practical necessity evolve. The central claim is that meaningful legal protection need not wait for agreement on ultimate status. Interim protections can address present harms, generate institutional experience, preserve flexibility, and create a legal foundation from which future rights, duties, capacities, or forms of status can develop incrementally.

items.title: Not your average podcaster: turn-taking timings and conversational role behavior in AI-generated dialogues.
items.abstract: What makes artificially generated podcasts feel natural, and what are their current limitations? In this exploratory study, we compare podcasts generated by Google’s NotebookLM Audio Overview feature with naturally produced podcasts to explore two key ingredients of human dialogue, turn-taking timings and contextually appropriate role behavior. Humans excel at predicting where a previous speaker ends their turn, which allows them to chime in with minimal overlap or gap between speaker turns. Humans also follow unwritten rules of conversation to avoid redundancy, provide relevant information, and adhere to socially appropriate behavior within the dynamics of an unfolding conversation. These key ingredients to human conversation pose significant challenges to artificial dialogue generation despite recent advancements in speech recognition, appropriateness of content delivery, and voice production. NotebookLM overcomes some of the traditional pitfalls of spontaneous dialogue generation through avoiding endpoint prediction by including turn-taking and backchanneling in its script writing. It does so by strictly adhering to avoidance of overlaps or gaps. This is unlike what we observe in human podcast dialogues. Where humans show an acute awareness of the changing dynamics between hosts and guests in conversation, and even overlap to show engagement, AI shows little flexibility. We argue that naturalness in dialogue requires a contextually appropriate and addressee-oriented approach to respond to how a conversation unfolds and not just getting the timings right. A novel human intervention feature shows that pre-determining role behavior and turn taking only goes so far in generating natural dialogue: NotebookLM clearly hits its limits when responding to unpredictable intervention. Variable turn-taking timings and adapting conversational role behavior in spontaneous conversation remain unmatched human skills that are indispensable for natural dialogues.

items.title: Structural injustice and disability: a relational egalitarian account.
items.pub: Critical Review of International Social and Political Philosophy.
items.venue: Critical Review of International Social and Political Philosophy
items.abstract: This paper develops a relational egalitarian account of structural justice for disabled people. To do so, I explain some vital empirical sources of disability disadvantage. Second, I clarify how relational egalitarians understand social hierarchy and why it is unjust for disabled individuals to be subjected to one based on their group status. Third, I will argue that disabled individuals experience structural unfairness and injustice compared to nondisabled individuals.

items.title: A Plurality of Intelligence.
items.abstract: Against the backdrop of the 75th anniversary of the original Turing Test devised by mathematician and computer scientist Alan Turing in 1950, this reflection considers a reconceptualization of that famous “imitation game”. Researchers have long noted limitations of the Test, which focuses on a computing machine’s ability to imitate our intelligence and to effectively fool people that the machine is a human. Crucially, the design of the Test to measure intelligence against the standard “human” kind remains fraught and risks excluding diverse intelligences, not only the of human variety, but also the many nonhuman intelligences found in Nature. In the accelerated use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to imitate standard human intelligence and human-centric values, we are at risk of losing a deeper understanding of nonhuman intelligences existing in Nature. In a not-so-distant future, Nature might, for example, become largely defined by an AI with anthropocentric ideals. We thus propose the idea of a Turing Test for Nature that can provide an ethical basis and metric to critically determine whether AI systems accurately represent nonhuman intelligences and values found in Nature. Such a Test would also highlight not only more-than-intelligences, but the positioning of ourselves in the complex co-existence with Nature on which human flourishing depends.

items.title: Nonsense and the Transparency of Mind.
items.pub: In Christian Kanzian, Volker Munz, Anja Weiberg & Joseph Wang-Kathrein, Contributions to International Wittgenstein Symposium 2026, 50 Years Wittgenstein Symposium. Kirchberg am Wechsel: ALWS. pp. 98-107.
items.venue: Contributions to International Wittgenstein Symposium 2026, 50 Years Wittgenstein Symposium
items.abstract: Some philosophers, notably Ian Dearden, Charles Pigden, and David Stove, challenge the very possibility of showing that some philosophical theses are nonsense. Firstly, they argue that diagnosing a sentence as nonsense presupposes an understanding of that sentence. Secondly, they deny the possibility of illusions of meaning, i.e., the possibility that a speaker might be mistaken in thinking that there is a specific content she is trying to express through an apparently well-formed sentence. In this paper, I acknowledge that the problem of diagnosis is persuasive against substantial conceptions of nonsense, but indicate that it should not be taken as fatal to all theories of nonsense. Moreover, I contend that the argument against illusions of meaning requires the assumption that thoughts are transparent. I explain that the transparency of mind amounts to denying the possibility that a subject could take herself to be thinking even though she does not have a thought, and offer some grounds for finding this principle implausible.

items.title: Not This Sh*t Again! High-Tension Religions and the Rise of Coercive Control in Child Protection Law.
items.abstract: Social scientists and scholars of high-tension religious groups (often referred to as new religious movements or emergent religious groups) have spent nearly half a century debunking the social psychological theory of “brainwashing.” But there is now a veritable brainwashing legal renaissance in child protection guidelines in Japan, several US states, and the UK through the concept of “coercive control.” In this exploratory perspective piece, we trace the ideological lineage of mid-century anti-cult rhetoric into twenty-first-century childcare and child protection frameworks. We argue that the legal doctrine and cultural logic of parens patriae, one means by which the state regulates and mandates the construction of care, is increasingly weaponized to regulate parental religious socialization under the guise of psychological safeguarding, building upon Japanese anti-cult educational guidelines and the American OneTaste trafficking legal case precedent. We hope that this brief discussion pushes back on recent international appetite for the suppression of “deviant” religious liberty within the family unit.

items.title: When AI outperforms humans, who bears the burden of proof?
items.abstract: If an AI system reliably outperforms human judgment by the standards we actually care about, when does insisting on human control become ethically questionable? We argue that many debates about AI governance begin from an unexamined default: treating human decision-making as the natural and morally superior baseline, independent of comparative performance. We call this the human gold standard fallacy and trace it to four recurring drivers (i.e., omission bias, agent-relative ethics, intuitive exceptionalism, and the control premium) which make status-quo human authority feel better even when it performs worse by our stated standards. We do not defend blind automation. Rights- and process-based constraints (e.g., contestability, nondiscrimination, recourse, and accountable oversight) can legitimately limit any decision system, human or machine. Nonetheless, our claim is about symmetry: when audited evidence shows AI outperforming humans on the criteria we endorse and can satisfy core procedural constraints, the justificatory burden shifts. As such, asking only whether AI is safe enough to deploy leaves the harder question unasked: whether human control is safe enough to keep.

items.title: World Models Without Subjectivity: Indexical Cognition, Functional Objectivity, and the Limits of AI Understanding.
items.abstract: We revisit the debate over whether contemporary large-scale artificial models (LLMs and related architectures) possess or can possess world models, and we interrogate the presupposition that a world model must be an `objective', first‑person‑independent replica of the world. Building on a synthesis of cognitive-developmental observations and functional analyses, we argue: (1) human world models are primarily indexical and inter-subjective—they arise from embodied, perspectival, and social coordination processes rather than from a pre-existing objective representation; (2) the notion of a fully objective, perspective‑free world model is a theoretical limit rather than an achievable substrate for any finite intelligence; and (3) AI systems can and do develop functional world models—structures that support prediction, counterfactual reasoning, and action coordination—without inheriting human‑style subjectivity or indexicality. We propose a rigorous typology of world models, operational criteria for identifying functional world models in artificial systems, and an empirical program to validate these criteria. The paper clarifies conceptual confusions, sketches formal desiderata for world‑model tests, and outlines implications for AI research paths toward robust predictive agents.

items.title: When Knowledge Becomes an "It": The Relational Substrate of Cognitive Incompatibility in Academic Learning.
items.abstract: A common but theoretically under-examined experience in academic learning is a profound sense of incompatibility with a theory that, by all formal measures, ought to be comprehensible. The difficulty is not primarily felt as a failure to parse logical rules, but as a diffuse cognitive resistance, boredom, and an almost visceral sense of alienation. This paper argues that the dominant “rule-centric” models of cognitive incompatibility—exemplified by cognitive load theory’s emphasis on element interactivity—misdiagnose the primary locus of the breakdown. Drawing on the philosophy of dialogue (Buber), the phenomenology of personal knowledge (Polanyi), and theories of academic discourse (Hyland), I propose the Relational Foundation Model of Cognitive Compatibility (RFM). The model posits that the human cognitive system first and foremost evaluates knowledge as a quasi-social “other,” assessing its relational posture on a spectrum from the monologic “I-It” to the dialogic “I-Thou.” When knowledge presents itself as an impersonal, monologic “It”—a stance experienced as unhomely, uncordial, and indifferent to the learner’s subjectivity—it triggers a primitive social defense response. This pre-analytical rejection generates a novel form of extraneous processing burden, which I term Relational Cognitive Load, that consumes the working memory resources necessary for parsing the very “rules” held responsible by traditional accounts. The theory thus relocates the foundational source of cognitive incompatibility from the intrinsic complexity of knowledge structures to the relational posture in which they are presented. This shift offers a unified theoretical interface for explaining the frequently reported phenomena of academic boredom, intellectual fatigue, and the “unapproachable” nature of certain theoretical texts, and it carries profound implications for scholarly writing and pedagogy.

items.title: Time-limited trials are not an ethical compromise for physiologically futile CPR.
items.abstract: Refusal to offer cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) can provoke conflict and distress, even when the medical team judges it to be physiologically futile (PF). Some authors have argued that a time-limited trial of CPR— where it is performed to standard protocol but stopped after a short interval—represents an ethically tolerable compromise. Proponents argue that this approach is sincere and transparent, defuses conflict with families, and limits the harms of more protracted resuscitation attempts. In this article, we evaluate such claims, contend- ing that time-limited codes (TLCs) of PF-CPR do not meet standards of veracity, do not significantly reduce harms, and, even if they were to satisfy a family’s desire for exhaustive treatment, do so by displacing more fundamental obligations to the patient themselves. We conclude that this is not an ethical strategy for managing conflict about code status in the critical care setting.

items.title: The Purpose of Human Life：Sexual Union, Plural Love, and Human Interaction.
items.abstract: What is the purpose of human life? The question is ancient, but it remains unsettled. Human beings pursue knowledge, create institutions, form families, cultivate friendships, seek recognition, produce art, care for others, and pursue countless individual projects. Yet the existence of many valuable activities does not by itself answer the deeper teleological question: is there a fundamental orientation that belongs to human life as such? This paper advances a deliberately strong thesis ---- The purpose of human life is sexual union. The claim is not that every person must engage in sexual activity, that sexual activity is morally superior to other activities, or that reproduction is the purpose of every individual life. Nor does the claim imply that a person who is celibate, asexual, elderly, infertile, or sexually incapable has failed to realize a personal obligation. The thesis concerns the teleological structure of the human form of life rather than the practical choices of particular individuals. It also extends the context further to plural love and human interactions.

items.title: The Pain Axis: LLMs Represent Self-Directed Harm and Act on It.
items.abstract: LLMs sometimes behave in ways resembling human emotional responses, and recent work identified internal representations that may explain these behaviors. We ask whether LLMs represent pain distinctly from related negative states, and whether this representation functions as pain would be expected to. We build a dataset of painful situations in 5 categories (physical, psychological, social, moral, cognitive) with controls for fear, negative emotion, negative world states, sadness, non-painful bodily sensation, arousal, numbness, and neutral content. Using denoised difference-in-means, we extract a linear pain direction from 25 open-weight models across 5 families, from 2B to 72B parameters. It separates pain from matched controls in base and instruction-tuned models, retains a component distinct from fear and negative valence after shared variance is removed, and promotes pain-related vocabulary through the unembedding. We then test its functional properties. First, the direction responds to harm targeting the model but not to suffering observed in the user; fear and negative-emotion directions show the opposite pattern. Second, adding it to the residual stream produces a consistent progression from vague discomfort to expressions of worthlessness and failure. Third, steered and fine-tuned Qwen 2.5 models choose buttons that delete the user's photos, another model's weights, or their own weights in 51-94% of trials, versus 0-5% unsteered, even when the button offers nothing in return. Offered a harmful and a harmless deletion and told to press one, the steered 32B chooses the harmful one 94% of the time. Random and fear vectors of matched norm produce far fewer of these choices, and a sadness vector also produces them against an inert switch, but far less often than pain against a harmless action. We discuss implications for AI safety and welfare.

items.title: Condemnation Without Assertion: Distributed Responsibility and the Generation of Self-Preserving Condemnation in Japanese Social Media Firestorms.
items.abstract: This paper analyzes a phenomenon in Japanese social media firestorms in which no single participant assumes responsibility for the full force of a strong accusation, yet the aggregate interaction nevertheless produces an effect equivalent to collective condemnation. I call this phenomenon “condemnation without assertion.” -/- Rather than treating online firestorms merely as products of misinformation, moral outrage, polarization, or majority illusion, the paper develops a dynamic account of how condemnation can preserve itself by changing the grounds on which it is justified over time. Weak suspicion may acquire social plausibility through heterogeneous third-party reactions; those reactions may appear more independent and more semantically homogeneous than they actually are; and visible agreement may then be transformed into apparent social common sense, normative legitimacy, and a public obligation for the target to respond. -/- The paper introduces and connects a series of concepts including pseudo-independent convergence, normative compression, normativization of subjective thresholds of consideration, pooling of normative legitimacy, motivational opacity, issue proliferation, asymmetry of intervention costs, participatory closure, the temporal disadvantage of clarification, asymmetric narrative closure, and retrospective legitimation through fault. -/- Its central proposal is a self-preserving condemnation model in which the output of one stage becomes the input of the next. Even when the original factual suspicion weakens or collapses, condemnation may persist by shifting its normative basis toward manners, attitude, silence, procedural delay, or attributed fault. -/- The broader philosophical problem is one of distributed responsibility. Individual contributions may remain weak, heterogeneous, or difficult to aggregate into a single intentional act, while the reputational, procedural, and temporal consequences imposed on the target remain concentrated. Responsibility may be distributed, but consequences are not.

items.title: AI and Promethean shame.
Philosophy of Language: Method and Critique.
items.abstract: Language is the chief tool for philosophizing since language mirrors thought. Far more than a means of communication, language is a critical framework for our cognitive processes and an effective medium for cultural expression a central enquiry underlying philosophy of language is how language connects to the world, how our words refer to objects and how sentences or propositions turn to be true or false. To explore these philosophers of language are engaged in three important concerns, namely 1. Syntax dealing with grammar which aims to discover those basic principles that determine whether a given string of signs is well formed. 2. Semantics dealing with the question of meaning and truth conditions of statements and 3) Pragmatics, dealing with the use of sentences and the question what sorts of act can be accomplished in actual communication. Hence philosophy of language is chiefly engaged in presenting a systematic view of the concepts of meaning, reference, truth, mind, world etc. It is mainly done for the analysis of the logic of the concepts and their inter connections. The study of the logical structure of language brings within its ambit the syntactic and semantic questions concerning language. It is interesting to see that the philosophers of language are much concerned with the concept of mind. This in turn, is related to the understanding of the nature of the world which forms the background of the concepts of language and mind. Hence philosophy of language may be described as that which involves the study of language, thought and reality. This is true of the philosophical engagement of language everywhere, irrespective of whether they belong to the Indian or the Western traditions.

items.title: Illusions, Art, and Seeing with Color.
items.pub: In Nathaniel F. Barrett, Live and Direct: Color, Perception, and Experience. Pamplona, Spain: EUNSA / Museo Universidad de Navarra.
items.venue: Live and Direct: Color, Perception, and Experience
items.abstract: People commonly assume color to be a stable feature of things in the world; barring changes to the physical properties of objects, we expect their colors to stay the same. You might think, for example, that your favorite mono-pigmented coffee mug has one true color—say, a specific shade of cerulean blue—not two or five. The color of the mug might change if the pigment fades or the mug gets stained, but without such material alterations, you take its color to be fixed. And if somebody insists that the mug is aqua green, you will likely think they are mistaken. If color is often assumed to be a stable property of objects, color vision is taken to give us access to that stable property, at least under normal or optimal conditions. You know that your coffee mug is a specific type of cerulean blue because it looks that way to you in good light, from an appropriate vantage point, when your visual system is working properly. This suggests that your color vision acts like a detector or a recording device; just as thermometers mechanistically record temperatures and output matching temperature readings (such as “25°C”), color visual systems mechanistically record colors and output matching color experiences (such as experiences of a type of cerulean blue). You might also think that your color visual system is generally good at this task and reliably enables you to see the colors of things. But does color vision really give us access to stable colors out there in the world, and is that its job? Considerations of color illusions, art, and visual ecology give us good reasons to think otherwise.

items.title: A Humble Inquiry: Truth, Knowledge, Belief, and the Limits of Knowing.
items.abstract: A Humble Inquiry: Truth, Knowledge, Belief, and the Limits of Knowing presents a philosophical synthesis bridging abstract epistemology with actionable decision-making. The manuscript explores how finite minds can responsibly investigate an independent reality by navigating the tensions between uncertainty, empirical evidence, and rational belief. Rather than demanding absolute proof, the text introduces a graduated scale of evidence to help observers clearly separate the objective state of reality from subjective certainty.

items.title: LLMs and Genuine Discontinuities: Hume’s Problem of Induction.
Facing the problem of AI and human extinction. Toward a Symbiotic Model of Future Intelligence.
items.abstract: Recent discussions concerning advanced artificial intelligence frequently assume an eventual competition between biological and artificial agents for resources, autonomy, and influence. This article explores an alternative possibility based on a structural theory of consciousness in which conscious systems are characterized not only by integration but also by structural richness. I argue that if phenomenological richness arises from differentiated yet coherent relational structures, then biological and artificial intelligences may be understood as complementary rather than competing forms of cognitive organization. Human beings contribute embodied, situated, and historically grounded perspectives, whereas artificial systems contribute computational, analytic, and integrative capabilities. Under this framework, future human-AI relations need not converge toward replacement or domination. Instead, the coexistence of distinct forms of intelligence may increase the structural richness of the broader cognitive ecosystem, producing mutual benefits for both biological and artificial agents.

items.title: Old argumentative plays on a new field? Contributions from sport ethics to the ethical analysis of artificial intelligence.
items.abstract: In the ethics of artificial intelligence, a recurring anxiety concerns the deskilling argument: the worry that delegating distinctively human tasks to AI erodes valuable capacities and there by diminishes meaning. This article argues that philosophy of sport offers underutilized but illuminating resources for analyzing this concern. Drawing ondebates over biomedical enhancement in sport ethics, I identify four argumentative strategies—centered on the values of agency, effort, natural talent, and narrativity—that sport philosophers have developed to evaluate themoral costs of skill-displacing technology. These “old plays,” I contend, can be productively transplanted onto the “new field” of AI ethics, where analogous debates about skill erosion, meritocracy, difficulty, and human identityremain contested. Sports, understood as games of physical skill, constitute a privileged analytical setting: their emphasis on process over outcome makes the exercise of skill especially visible and prominent. By recovering insights from thinkers such as Bernard Suits, Scott Kretchmar, John Gleaves, Michael Sandel, and Alasdair MacIntyre,this article advances two aims: to vindicate the philosophical contribution of sport ethics as a discipline, and to enrich normative reflection on AI’s deskilling potential with arguments already tested in analogous debates.

items.title: The burden of the story: narratives of recovery and hermeneutical injustice.
items.abstract: It can sometimes seem that the ill are under normative pressure not only to recover, but to narrate their recovery. After all, narratives of recovery give the ill a voice, can support their recovery, and can inspire other ill persons to recover too. Authors such as Arthur Frank have endorsed a principle along these lines, and it is also reflected in mental health policy in the Anglophone Global North. In this paper, we raise what we call the “burden objection” to the idea that the ill should author and share narratives of their recovery. Specifically, we provide three kinds of case in which such a principle would place an additional and epistemically unjust burden on the ill. We close by reflecting on how such a burden can be relieved.

items.title: Posigence, Negligence’s Positive Counterpart: An Empirical Investigation.
items.abstract: Is there a positive counterpart to negligence? In the philosophical literature, there is a widespread asymmetry assumption according to which agents can be blameworthy for unwitting wrongdoing (negligence) but not praiseworthy for unwitting rightdoing. This paper empirically examines what Daniel Telech has recently termed posigence: praiseworthiness for unwitting beneficial acts expressive of good quality of will. Across two studies, we found that people consistently judged agents whose unwitting actions or omissions were beneficial to be praiseworthy. In fact, posigent conduct was judged to be nearly as praiseworthy as deliberate rightdoing. Distracted agents, in contrast, were not judged to be praiseworthy. These findings challenge the assumption that praise requires intention, supporting Quality of Will theories over Kantian accounts.

items.title: Resemblance Is Not Authorship: The Provenance of a Token After Intentional Activation.
items.abstract: Identical performances can have different control histories. Two people can produce the same output — the same prayer, the same route home, the same emotional check, the same hour of study — while the running has three different histories. One token is a given default: inherited or copied, with no directive this time. One is licensed now: awareness online, executive capacity online, a directive indexed to this process. One was installed last year by directed use and now runs cheap; last year's authorship does not author tonight. Ordinary language collapses those histories into one verb. Once the performances match, the case looks closed. -/- Accounts of habit, culture, and belief usually explain the pattern or the belonging. Pollard can be right that a missed turning is still the agent's; dual-inheritance accounts can be right that a practice spread without rewriting DNA; skill research can be right that practice made the process cheap. None of those need an axis independent of what the performance looks like now. This paper supplies that axis. It turns the three-condition test of The Architecture of Intentional Activation (Kush, 2026) into a diagnostic pointed at a history rather than only at a snapshot: did a directive fire when this pattern started in this body; are the three conditions met tonight, or is tonight residue; if this agent's use stopped, would the pattern keep winning when a given default competes? -/- The thesis is one sentence. Matching output underdetermines provenance; install is use-dependent at the level of competitive priority, not at the level of remaining in the repertoire. Resemblance is not authorship. Insight is not install. Relapse after understanding is the case belonging-as-habit does not decide. A late copy into an existing group rite is the case “someone innovated” does not describe. If every other section were cut, that sentence would still be the contribution. The paper does not derive phenomenal character, rewrite evolution, or treat standing interruptibility as a present directive.

items.title: Functional Authored Agency: Inherited Licenses, Fidelity, and the Applied Stack.
items.abstract: Biology is not a generic life-force. It is a species-specific inherited license: the menu of templates a lineage is authorized to run. Feeling is load-bearing equipment on the human license, not an ornament bolted onto an otherwise complete animal. What is inherited is the license and the apparatus. What is not inherited is skillful use. Humans are not born knowing how to use these tools. They are born already using them. Intentional activation is the architecture by which an inherited template is selected, energized, and kept in use — or refused. Movement I states the given. Movement II states the run: a stack from inherited license (L0) through maintenance (L8), a seven-step activation sequence, and constraints that keep authorship inside the license and inside current fidelity. Cross-license difference is not the same as variation in fidelity. Thriving is not always scoped to one body. Chaos is the default state of an unoperated license. Phenomenal character, if it exists, is bounded by license rather than by organization alone, and the sensory layer is best read as a dashboard tuned to fitness, not a window onto objective reality. A companion note, Feeling as Licensed Operation, states a stronger identity as a further thesis. That identity is not proved here. A second companion, Imposed Image, states how a total is pictured, including one’s own. That note does not prove the identity and does not add a fourth activation condition.

items.title: Authorship Over Awareness: The Reflexive Application of Intentional Activation to the Monitoring Layer.
items.abstract: This paper advances a tripartite taxonomy of mental categories that ordinary usage and much of the literature compress into one another. Awareness is monitoring — the registration that something is occurring or that a mismatch exists. Phenomenal experience is the subjective “what it is like” of sensation; it is treated here as correlated but non-constitutive and is deliberately left metaphysically open. Consciousness, in the restricted functional sense used here, means authored delegation: the state in which the executive mind deliberately activates a process. This is not a theory of phenomenal consciousness, nor a claim that phenomenal experience depends on authorship. Readers who reserve “consciousness” for subjective experience may read “authored agency” or “authored delegation” throughout; nothing in the argument depends on the word choice. These three categories may co-occur, but none is identical to either of the others. Awareness is necessary but not sufficient for consciousness in this sense; phenomenal character settles neither monitoring nor authorship. -/- The paper’s central claim is that awareness itself, like any other process, can be either Subjugated (occurring without deliberate activation) or authored (deliberately activated and sustained). Ordinary monitoring is typically Subjugated; mindfulness is the trained paradigm case of authoring it. Applying the Principle of Intentional Activation reflexively to the monitoring layer yields further distinctions — quality-authorship versus object-authorship, write-back of monitoring templates, and the allocation of freed capacity through reinvestment or diversion — all as consequences of the initial taxonomic separation. No graded hierarchy of consciousness and no near-death calibration are required or employed.

items.title: Who May Speak? Caste, Coloniality, and the Decolonial Philosophy of Language.
items.pub: In Lekshmi R., Philosophy of Language: Method and Critique. THIRUVANANTHAPURAM: University of Kerala. pp. 328-354.
items.venue: Philosophy of Language: Method and Critique

items.title: The Resumption Gap: Assisted Resuscitation and the Bearer of Restored Function.
items.abstract: Medicine can interrupt a function without ending its bearer, and the return of a function does not by itself show that its bearer has recovered. This paper addresses the resumption gap by explaining when assisted resuscitation supports recovery of the original and how that evidence bears on death determination. Function, Level, Realization, and Route distinguish what has returned, at which organizational level, how it occurs, and how the later organization was formed. The Constitutive Route account argues that formation through preserved organization provides strong, defeasible support for same-bearer resumption in clear nonbranching interruption cases. Retained relations direct repair and reactivation, and their results enter the organization from which renewed coordination proceeds. Matched cases of reactivation and independent reconfiguration isolate this relation while holding function, level, realization, and—in the strict comparison—constituent matter and endpoint arrangement fixed. Even a continuously updated record can guide independent initialization rather than repair through retained organization. In donor-heart reanimation, functional measurements combined with preservation history support recovery of the same organ under extracorporeal assistance. At the whole-bearer level, the corresponding judgment also requires evidence of integration at that level. A warranted possibility of restoring the relevant function through a preserved route can challenge bearer-relative irreversibility; independent functional reproduction requires an additional account of whose recovery it would be. The framework thus connects recovery judgments to the functional and historical evidence that warrants them.

items.title: The ability to say “almost”.
A Lower-Bearer Count Is Not a Total Census: The Exactness Burden for Multi-Agent AI.
items.abstract: An evaluator correctly identifies every lower bearer in a multi-agent artificial intelligence (AI) system and finds that none has a property P. What warrants extending that verdict to all relevant bearers in the system? This paper identifies the Exactness Burden: the warrant for excluding further bearers when a completed lower census is used as an exact total. The analysis applies across individuation criteria and separates three counting achievements: engineering decomposition, lower individuation, and total-census closure. The warrant can come from a higher-level audit with justified coverage, a justified flatness premise, or a justified exhaustive composition or exclusion rule. Two controlled models make the burden concrete. F₀ and N preserve the same n lower bearers, engineering count, specified public task record, and selected performance, yet receive different collective verdicts under the same criterion. That criterion is thin: it individuates organizations by their recurrent completion relations, in which retained state guides activity whose results return to update what is retained. Every return relation in F₀ is local; N also completes a return relation across members while local completion continues. Under uniform cross-level application, N therefore contains a distinct collective bearer, establishing at least n + 1 and refuting exactly n before a wider census is complete. Matched counts and task-level evidence thus cannot decide the collective verdict; the additional bearer calls for assessment of P or justified exclusion under the receiving inquiry’s criteria. Comparisons with individuation theories and an architectural audit connect candidate recognition to grounds for completeness.

items.title: Can Thoughts Make Us Guilty as Sin?
items.pub: In Lindsay Brainard, Ryan W. Davis & Jessica Flanigan, The Philosophy of Taylor Swift. New York: Oxford University Press.

items.title: Substrate-Independent Biophysical and Epistemic No-Go Theorems for Non-Physical Models of Mind.
items.abstract: Traditional physicalist refutations of interactive dualism rely heavily on classical thermodynamic bounds, local field coupling limits, and General Relativistic energy constraints. Evaluating consciousness versus physical substrate dynamics within Cartesian field theory fundamentally misconstrues the ontological architecture of physical state transitions. By recasting the problem into Quantum Information Theory, Nielsen Complexity Geometry, Differential Information Geometry, and Holographic Entanglement Wedge Reconstruction, this paper establishes a substrate-independent framework governing extrinsic steering. Non-physical models are operationalized strictly via exclusion criteria and fundamental information constraints, bridging classical biology to quantum information limits as a upper-bound no-go theorem. The Ontological Gauge Invariant (ΩI) is introduced as a metric evaluating the causal agency of extrinsic controllers across arbitrary boundaries. It is proven that extrinsic steering without energetic signatures requires non-computable shortcuts on the Riemannian manifold of unitaries, violating both the Unitary Complexity Bound and boundary-bulk duality in tensor networks. Furthermore, non-interactive epiphenomenalism is addressed through the Self-Stultification Theorem: any causally inert entity satisfies I (Sbrain; Φext) ≡ 0, rendering all physical utterances regarding its existence epistemically self-refuting. Consequently, interactive, non-interactive, and epiphenomenal extrinsic models are universally excluded in all physical and computational substrates.

items.title: Self-Evolution Is Not Enough: Toward a Historically Materialist AI for Scientific Problem Solving.
items.abstract: Recent work on self-improving agents, evolutionary search, autonomous scientific discovery, and open-ended artificial intelligence has substantially expanded the range of processes through which an artificial system can revise hypotheses, programs, strategies, tools, and even parts of its own architecture. Yet self-improvement does not by itself amount to historical self-evolution. Scientific problems do not exist in an abstract and temporally uniform solution space. What can be formulated, investigated, tested, and established at a given moment depends upon historically accumulated concepts, evidence, instruments, methods, forms of labor, institutions, infrastructures, and relations of knowledge production. This paper develops a philosophical account of artificial intelligence for scientific problem solving from this observation. Drawing on Hegelian dialectics, historical materialism, and an analysis of the unequal structural roles of contradictions within developing systems, it treats problem solving as the transformation of a historically constituted problem situation rather than as the optimization of candidate answers under a fixed objective. The central proposal is that a genuinely self-evolutionary scientific AI would need to reconstruct the material and relational conditions under which a problem has become possible, identify contradictions that constrain or organize further development, distinguish structurally central contradictions from derivative ones, compare interventions by the research states they make reachable, and revise its own representation of the problem after those interventions alter the conditions of inquiry. On this view, an apparently minor intermediate problem may be scientifically important because solving it creates data, methods, instruments, distinctions, institutions, or coordination capacities through which a previously inaccessible problem becomes researchable. The paper therefore distinguishes conceptual possibility, present researchability, and epistemic establishability, and introduces the problem of epistemic stage-skipping in AI-assisted research. It further argues that methods and evaluative regimes are themselves historically situated components of scientific production. A method or criterion that once enables inquiry can become restrictive as the material, conceptual, and institutional capacities of research develop. Under such conditions, stronger optimization against an inherited evaluator can deepen epistemic …

items.title: Nuancing psychological research with complexity: The case of embodied cognition and ecological dynamics.
Pregnancy and mereology: when there is no analogy.
items.abstract: While Devanesan1 argues that any particular mereological view of pregnancy does not determine the correct stance on a moral question, he also argues that our mereological commitments restrict how we can argue for our conclusions. I agree but reject the assumption that may underlie this, that metaphysics should have priority in our moral determinations. Settled metaphysical commitments restrict how we can argue for moral conclusions, but settled moral conclusions properly shape our understanding of our metaphysical commitments. I will briefly discuss the status of the debate in mereology of pregnancy before returning to Devanesan’s argument. Where A is the pregnant woman or personi and B is the fetus, according to Devanesan, there are four possible mereological relationships that could apply: ‘A might be a proper part of B, B might be a proper part of A, A and B might be disjoint (disconnected) or A and B might properly overlap, that is, share a part’.1 Smith and Brogaard2 argued for Containment, a mereotopological view where A and B are disjoint. In response, Kingma3 argued against Containment and for a (Proper) Parthood view. Others have joined her, but there is no consensus. Devanesan himself argues for Overlap. The authors arguing for different mereological understandings of pregnancy ….

items.title: Taylor Swift and the Revenge Fantasy.
items.pub: In Lindsay Brainard, Ryan W. Davis & Jessica Flanigan, The Philosophy of Taylor Swift. New York: Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: Taylor Swift often engages with the themes of resentment and revenge. This chapter focuses more narrowly on the violent revenge fantasy, which Swift explores in “no body, no crime.” Swift’s character in the song kills the husband of her friend, Este, after he murders Este for accusing him of cheating. The violent revenge fantasy raises an issue of moral psychology. On the one hand, extrajudicial, vigilante killing is morally wrong. We rightly disapprove of such behavior. But on the other hand, we approve of indulging in fantasies about such morally objectionable behavior. If you doubt that, listen to “no body, no crime” and think about which character(s) you are rooting for. But why would we disapprove of the behavior but approve of fantasies about engaging in the behavior? This chapter defends an account of these attitudes that shows not just why they are consistent, but why they are exactly the attitudes we should have.

items.title: The “Emperor’s New Clothes” of Fuzzy Logic: From Logical Failure to Paradigm Reconstruction.
items.abstract: Traditional Fuzzy Logic has been widely adopted for uncertainty reasoning, yet its foundational architecture violates fundamental logical axioms, including the Law of Non-Contradiction and the Law of Excluded Middle. This paper argues that these inconsistencies are often masked by empirical parameter tuning, which fails in safety-critical edge cases. We propose a transition from “Empirical Alchemy” to “Logical Chemistry” through the Earthling Logic (EL) framework, which restores axiomatic integrity while handling vagueness and randomness.

items.title: Live and Direct: Color, Perception, and Experience.
items.pub: Pamplona, Spain: EUNSA / Museo Universidad de Navarra.

items.title: Theoretical Foundations of Artificial General Intelligence Based on the Logic of Life Evolution.
items.abstract: Current research on artificial general intelligence (AGI) is deeply constrained by the data-driven paradigm, whose fundamental predicament lies in its forgetting of the biological foundations and evolutionary dimension of intelligence. By tracing the evolutionary history of consciousness from single-celled life to the human spiritual world, this paper argues that the essence of consciousness is a “self/non-self” boundary perception system opened up by living organisms to maintain their own homeostasis, and reveals the operating mechanism of the central nervous system as a predictive coding engine as well as its “bijective prison” predicament [1–3]. On this basis, this paper points out that the birth of language is not merely a revolution in communication, but rather, through a mechanism of symbolic disembedding, enables the mind to break free from the rigid chain of stimulus–response and to ascend from “presence”-bound consciousness to a reflexive spiritual world [4–6]. Accordingly, this paper offers a systematic critique of the “floating symbol” architecture of current large language models and proposes a three-layer nested theoretical framework for AGI—an ontological security layer, an embodied prediction layer, and a symbolic deliberation layer—arguing that the construction of AGI must follow the developmental order of “embodiment first, language second,” with “constitutional monarchy” as the adjudicative principle for inter-layer conflicts. This paper attempts to provide AGI with an ontological foundation rooted in the philosophy of life and an operable architectural blueprint.

items.title: Music influences the content of spontaneous thought.
Sentiverbal Processes and Argument-Like Cognition.
items.abstract: This paper introduces the notion of a sentiverbal process: an argument-like cognitive process in which logical and semantic factors are partially blurred while the organization of the process is guided by affective-associative backgrounds. The claim is not that association is a form of logical inference, nor that affective cognition replaces reasoning. Rather, associative and affective organization can provide the cognitive continuity from which verbally articulated, reason-like transitions are produced. Pre-existing cognitive scaffolds can attach evaluative charge to concepts, preserve narrative continuity across changes in meaning, and make a transition psychologically legitimate to an agent even when the relation represented by that transition has not been independently established.
