items.title: The Residue That Never Closes A Reflection on Finitude, Hiddenness, and the Limits of Approach.
items.abstract: This essay offers a philosophical reflection built around a single tautological identity, 1 − 10⁻ᴴ + 10⁻ᴴ = 1, used not as a proof but as a lens. The equation guarantees that a whole remains intact regardless of the size of a residue subtracted from and returned to it — even as that residue grows without bound. Three readings of that residue are explored: the structural ceiling on a finite mind's comprehension, the theological motif of hiddenness found in the Elijah narrative at Horeb (1 Kings 19), and the relationship between computational systems and conscious choice. The essay makes no claim that mathematics proves anything about metaphysics. It claims only that the equation is a fertile object to think with, in a spirit related to apophatic or negative theology, which has long described the transcendent by naming what escapes finite predicates rather than what is captured by them.

items.title: A critical analysis of trustworthy AI tools, mark frameworks, and the implementation chasms.
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly impact society, ensuring their ethical and trustworthy deployment has become a global priority. While a myriad of high-level ethical guidelines have emerged, criticism persists that these frameworks remain abstract and lack concrete mechanisms for implementation. This paper conducts a critical analysis of tools and trust mark frameworks intended to operationalize trustworthy AI (TAI), drawing on a comprehensive dataset from the OECD. Through empirical mapping and descriptive comparative analysis, we identify significant asymmetries in ethical focus, lifecycle coverage, stakeholder targeting, and tool typology. Our findings show a strong emphasis on fairness, transparency, and robustness, with comparatively little attention paid to explainability, digital security, and environmental sustainability. Moreover, most tools and certifications concentrate on post-development stages, with limited guidance for early design or data collection phases. Educational initiatives and policy engagement are notably underdeveloped, suggesting that current TAI efforts are dominated by technical and procedural measures within industry contexts. We argue that bridging the persistent chasm between AI principles and practice requires expanding ethical objectives, embedding ethics across the AI lifecycle, and fostering broader multi-stakeholder participation. This study provides both a diagnosis of existing implementation gaps and actionable recommendations for advancing more holistic, inclusive, and enforceable AI governance.

items.title: The Paradox of Progress in the Digital Age Extracted Dasein and the Ethics of Sufficiency under Conditions of Algorithmic Stabilization Revised Edition — with expanded engagement with Bernard Stiegler, differentiation from Han and Zuboff, and an operationalized research program.
items.abstract: Contemporary digitalization is commonly described through the languages of innovation, connectivity, efficiency, and technological progress. This article argues that such descriptions remain incomplete because they primarily measure what digital systems enable while insufficiently examining what they progressively consume. Drawing on the ontology of finite continuance, the article develops an erosive account of digital existence in which the central problem is not technological mediation as such, but the systematic narrowing of the subject's capacity to revise the determinations through which its future becomes possible. The concept of the Extracted Dasein names a condition in which a person may remain behaviorally functional, productive, connected, and apparently autonomous while undergoing a progressive extraction of reconfigurative capacity. This revised edition situates the framework more precisely within the philosophy of technology by engaging Bernard Stiegler's account of grammatization and tertiary retention, by distinguishing Extracted Dasein explicitly from Byung-Chul Han's burnout society and Shoshana Zuboff's surveillance capitalism, and by proposing operational indicators for the framework's central empirically testable claims. The article proceeds through six conceptual interventions culminating in an Ethics of Sufficiency grounded in the principle of non-appropriation of the future, and proposes Responsible Suspension and regulated permeability through the Dynamic Mask as mechanisms for preserving reconfigurative capacity. The article does not claim that digital technology inherently produces ontological erosion; it identifies a structural tendency within particular forms of digital organization and argues that technological progress must be evaluated not only by increased capability, speed, or predictive accuracy, but by whether it preserves the conditions under which finite beings can remain capable of becoming otherwise. -/- Keywords: finite continuance; Extracted Dasein; digital ontology; erosive ontology; algorithmic governance; Simondon; Stiegler; grammatization; teleological emergence; Ethics of Sufficiency; Responsible Suspension; Dynamic Mask; reconfigurative capacity; non-appropriation of the future.

items.title: The Ontology of the Unrepeatable The Principle of Ontological Non-Repetition: Event Identity, Recurrence, and the Metaphysics of Actual Occurrence.
items.abstract: The metaphysics of events raises a problem that is easily obscured by ordinary talk of repetition. We say that an event occurred again, that the same event recurred, or that history repeated itself. Yet such formulations leave open a fundamental metaphysical question: what makes two occurrences numerically distinct events, and under what conditions, if any, could one and the same event occur twice? This article develops a specialized account of event identity and numerical non-repetition. Its central thesis is the Principle of Ontological Non-Repetition: no actual event can occur twice as numerically the same event. Recurrent events are distinct actual occurrences that may be related by a shared type, structural similarity, causal pattern, description, function, or other repeatable determination. The argument is therefore stronger than the ordinary type-token distinction. A type can have indefinitely many tokens, but the numerical identity of an actual occurrence cannot itself be instantiated more than once without ceasing to be numerical identity. The article examines the distinction between numerical identity and qualitative identity, event types and event tokens, occurrence and re-identification, recurrence and re-instantiation, and possibility and actuality. It then considers the implications of the thesis for major positions in analytic metaphysics, including Davidson's event ontology, Lewis's account of identity and similarity, perdurantism, endurantism, and haecceitism. The argument does not depend on any particular theory of temporal ontology. Perdurantism can distinguish events by temporal parts; endurantism can distinguish them by persistence conditions; haecceitism can ground primitive thisness. None of these positions, however, entails that one and the same actual occurrence can numerically occur twice. The article further distinguishes recurrence from re-actualization, return from reversal, and re-identification from repetition. It concludes that what is repeatable in reality is not the actuality of an occurrence itself but the structures, properties, relations, descriptions, and possibilities that can be instantiated by distinct occurrences. In this sense, the unrepeatability of actuality is not the negation of repetition but the metaphysical condition under which repetition can be intelligibly described. -/- Keywords: analytic metaphysics, events, event identity, numerical identity, qualitative identity, recurrence, repetition, event …

items.title: Synthesis Point of Reality (SPR) Theory: Resolving the Absolute-Relative Paradoxical Loop and the Emergence of Actualized Reality (3rd edition).
items.pub: Synthesis Point of Reality (Spr) Theory: Resolving the Absolute-Relative Paradoxical Loop and the Emergence of Actualized Reality.
items.abstract: Abstract -/- The Synthesis Point of Reality (SPR) Theory presents a formal mathematical and metaphysical framework detailing the emergence, dynamic interaction, and empirical realization of Actualized Reality ($R_e$). Addressing the fundamental paradoxes of physicalist absolutism and ungrounded relativism, this paper examines how observable reality operates neither as an invariant external backdrop nor as a purely subjective construct. By introducing dynamically indexed operators ($A_n, -A_m$), the differential metric $x = |n - m|$, and systemic state quantification, SPR Theory examines the proposal that reality materializes at the Synthesis Point ($\mathcal{S}$)—a dynamic boundary where the Absolute Ground ($A_n$) and its mandatory Polar Constraints ($-A_m$) continuously integrate through ontological symmetry breaking. Evaluated across quantum, biological, and cognitive matrices—including clinical pharmacological response models—this work formalizes the Law of Mandatory Polar Existence, examining how actualized experience ($R_e$) requires non-zero polar friction ($m > 0$) to establish operational boundaries. Ultimately, the framework provides a unified, recursive model to evaluate how baseline invariants evolve across dynamic temporal states. -/- Keywords: -/- Synthesis Point of Reality (SPR), Absolute Ground ($A_n$), Polar Inverse Operator ($-A_m$), Differential Metric ($x$), Actualized Reality ($R_e$), Ontological Symmetry Breaking, Law of Mandatory Polar Existence, Quantified State Index, Recursive Baseline Evolution, Bhodhaanubhavam, Context-Driven Reality Generation.

items.title: 《生-成》——持存，镶嵌与流变：基于区分的属性逻辑过程.
items.abstract: Abstract -/- *生-成 (Sheng-Cheng)* begins with the fundamental question of **how the world becomes a world**, and attempts to develop a philosophical framework that takes **generation**, rather than substance, as its fundamental perspective. Without presupposing an ultimate substance, subject, or logical foundation independent of the generative process, the book starts from the minimal **event of distinction** and examines how determinacy emerges progressively through processes of differentiation, coupling, and self-maintenance. It thereby traces the generative origins of such fundamental philosophical concepts as existence, object, subject, truth, causality, and logic. -/- The book proposes the generative process structure **“non-being → non-non-being → being” (非有 → 非非有 → 有)**. It further establishes a four-pole tension through the orthogonal relations of **being–non-being** and **knowing–known (能–所)**, and develops a progressive framework from distinction and relation to attribute, object, and existence. On this basis, it introduces the **“empty–being cycle” (空有循环)** and three fundamental dynamic structures—**breakdown–balance, differentiation–coupling, and compensation–existence**—to explain how stable structures are not a priori foundations of generation, but temporary outcomes produced by the repeated operation of generative processes. At the same time, established structures constrain and sustain subsequent generation, forming a recursive cycle that may be expressed as **“generation gives rise to formation, while formation sustains generation.”** -/- At the level of cognition, *Sheng-Cheng* understands **determinacy** as a dynamic stabilization arising within generative processes rather than as an absolute truth waiting to be discovered. It examines the progressive development of determinacy from instantaneous **being** to **is**, **true**, and ultimately **existence**, and discusses the hierarchical relations among experiential reality, scientific reality, symbolic reality, social reality, and mathematical reality. At the level of subjectivity, the book traces the emergence of the **“I”** through the differentiation of knowing and known, reflexive self-reference, and the structure of body–mind–I. The **“吾” (Wu)** is then introduced to describe the subject's reflexive awareness of itself and its world, together with a possible transition from individual “I” toward collective “we,” and from a mode of **internal coordination with external competition** …

items.title: COERCION AND COMFORT: WHY FORCE AND PROTECTION FAIL THE CHILD IN THE SAME WAY? Freedom Must Be Exercised to Be Inherited.
items.abstract: Abstract Two households produce adults who cannot govern themselves. In the first, everything is required: the apologies arrive on schedule, the sharing happens on command, and what emerges wears the names of the virtues without their substance. In the second, nothing is required: the doors are open, the risks are managed, the frustrations are relieved before they form, and what emerges is unformed rather than deformed. The tradition treats these as opposite errors and prescribes each as the cure for the other. This article argues that they are one failure in one variable, reached by two routes. Moral capacity accumulates through exercised freedom, never through available freedom. Compulsion breaks the accumulation by replacing the child's determination and capturing the form of her act, which does not weaken the virtue but reverses it. Protection breaks the same accumulation by removing the occasions on which freedom would have been exercised. A door that is open and never walked through contributes nothing. The two routes leave different residues — the determinate opposite of the virtue, and its absence — and different costs of repair, and these are registered as the article's falsifiers. Three results follow for how parents act. Ordinary constraint does not invert anything: narrowing what a child may do leaves the act hers, while specifying the act makes the parent its author. Any virtue measured inside a loop with a consequence attached is occupied, and scoring the virtue is worse than scoring the act, because being good is cheaper to perform than to be. And transmission has a threshold that belongs to the network rather than to the life, from which it follows that the family is the only network small enough to carry an ordinary one — so that when households stop telling, the moral inheritance of unremarkable lives fails to propagate at all. The political argument is the same argument at scale. A state that compels and a market that comforts empty the same integral from opposite ends, and the capacity they empty it of is precisely the one that legitimate refusal requires. A generation cannot inherit a freedom it has never had occasion to use. Keywords: moral formation, moral education, autonomy, freedom, virtue ethics, parenting, overprotection, coercion, narrative transmission, measurement, philosophy of education, Philosophy of Virtues Highlights • Authoritarian and overprotective formation are not opposite errors but one failure in one variable — …

items.title: Aesthetide: A Theoretical Framework for the Formation of Aesthetic Experience in an Irreversible World.
items.abstract: This article proposes Aesthetide as a theoretical framework for explaining a distinctive structure in aesthetic experience: the non-coincidence between the irreversibility of the physical world and the capacity of aesthetic consciousness to reorient itself. At the macroscopic level, physical processes exhibit temporal asymmetry: past states do not spontaneously restore themselves. Entropy, considered in relation to the thermodynamic arrow of time, clarifies this macroscopic asymmetry rather than serving as a mechanism that produces aesthetic experience. From an aesthetic encounter in the present, consciousness may turn toward the past through memory, toward the future through imagination, and then return to the present object. I call this movement the trajectory of aesthetic consciousness. Along this trajectory, experiential layers need not remain discrete but may permeate and overlap, a relation described here as experiential permeation. Return therefore does not amount to restoration of the initial experiential state. In strong cases of Aesthetide, renewed engagement with the object is trajectory-dependent: what consciousness has passed through must be relevant to explaining how the object is experienced upon return. Aesthetide uses the spiral to model return without exact repetition and the tide to figure the rhythm of departure and return; the term combines aesthetic and tide. Through the generative case of a Japanese garden after rain, the article argues that some aesthetic experiences are formed not merely in time, but through the non-coincidence between the irreversible direction of the world and the reorientable trajectory of consciousness within it.

items.title: Integrating LLMs and Academic Writing Instruction: Engaged Reading and LLM-Generated Material.
items.pub: International Journal of Research in e-Learning 12 (1):1-21.
items.venue: International Journal of Research in e-Learning
items.abstract: Integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) into course designs in the higher education context remains an open and quickly growing area of research. This study contributes to the emerging literature by examining how students engage with and evaluate LLM-generated feedback within academic writing instruction. Building on prior work on integration and LLM detection, the study adopts a diachronic design to assess whether students can reliably distinguish between human- and LLM-generated reviews, and how engagement with material may affect perceived classification. Fifty-one undergraduate participants received both human and LLM-generated reviews for essays they authored, completing surveys before and after revising their work. The results indicate that students were initially at random odds in distinguishing human from LLM-generated texts but exhibited statistically significant improvement following engagement. Nearly all students reported positive attitudes toward personalized feedback, irrespective of whether they perceived it to be human or LLM-generated. The findings underscore both the pedagogical potential and evaluative ambiguity of LLM integration in writing instruction.

items.title: Neo-Husserlian Idealism.
items.pub: Ergo: An Open Access Journal of Philosophy 13 (34):983-1003.
items.venue: Ergo: An Open Access Journal of Philosophy
items.abstract: In recent years forms of idealism influenced by Berkeley, Leibniz, and Mill have been defended, and metaphysicians and philosophers of mind have begun to appreciate some distinctive advantages that idealism has over materialist realism. One historical idealist has been conspicuously absent in this idealist revival: Husserl. Starting from Aron Gurwitsch’s interpretation of Husserl in The Field of Consciousness, I develop and defend a new version of idealism using contemporary resources. According to neo-Husserlian idealism, material objects are mereological bundles of what Mark Johnston calls sensible profiles. I argue that neo-Husserlian idealism has all the advantages that two recent idealists—Helen Yetter-Chappell and Michael Pelczar—claim for their views, as well as some unique advantages of its own.

items.title: Introduction to Positive Epistemology.
items.abstract: This volume is about _positive epistemology_, understood as the investigation into normative considerations that _commend_ belief, rather than merely warn against error. The editor's Introduction introduces the distinction between positive and negative norms, discusses putative instances of obligations to believe, and introduces reasons why some scholars have been skeptical about positive epistemic norms. The Introduction concludes with an overview of the volume, describing the chapters that follow and situating them within ongoing debates about positive epistemic norms.

items.title: Doubt and the Status Quo.
items.abstract: In _Epistemic Courage_, I defended a connection between skepticism and conservative tendencies that preserve the status quo. In this chapter, I'll explore this connection in further detail, developing its theoretical rationale, and responding to a series of objections, including objections related to action under uncertainty, the civic value of epistemic modesty, and the role of doubt in disrupting the status quo.

items.title: Human and Artificial Reality: Generative Relations and the Formation of Interpretation.
items.abstract: Comparisons between human and artificial reality often move between existence, observable performance, social consequence, and subjective experience without specifying the inference connecting them. This discussion paper distinguishes ontological, relational, and manifest dimensions of reality attribution and examines the historical formation of the systems that interpret them. It argues that comparison requires an explicit domain, observation practice, temporal horizon, and class of interventions. The progressive strengthening of indistinguishability assumptions changes which differences remain evidentially available; further arguments determine their explanatory or normative significance. Embodiment and historical dependence enter this account as potentially consequential conditions whose importance requires specification. A completed exploratory pilot collected 24 actual agent responses, all selecting equality under their stated criteria while leaving consciousness and ultimate nature unresolved. The result is limited by a possible existential ceiling and single-platform design. Separate field simulations and exact calculations distinguish projected agreement, dynamical conjugacy, orbit equivalence, shared attractors, action values, and boundary state sums. These examples clarify failures of unrestricted inference without validating a theory of artificial subjectivity. The proposed contribution is a disciplined connection between relational explanation, situated interpretation, and the scope of equivalence claims, open to correction and comparison with established traditions.

items.title: Capacitism: A Defensible Epistemic Conception of Memory.
items.abstract: Epistemological orthodoxy has it that memory is, in some sense, a kind of knowing, or as Lai (2022a), quoting Lackey (2008: 251), puts it, “an epistemic source” which “preserves knowledge from one time to another.” Lai dubs this the “Epistemic Conception of Memory" (ECM). But several recent papers argue that ECM falls prey to counterexamples. Of these, Lai (2022a) is the most thorough, as it takes aim at four distinct variants of ECM. The present paper introduces a neglected fifth variant of ECM we call “Capacitism.” According to Capacitism, remembering that p is the exercise of an epistemic capacity that functions to afford knowledge that p. It is argued that Capiticism is an attractive variant of ECM which avoids Lai’s counterexamples as well as a further problem facing other variants of ECM tied to their commitment to memory’s factivity, namely, their resulting commitment to either metaphysical or epistemological disjunctivism. Capacitism avoids these problems by grounding memory’s fundamental link to knowledge in its distinctive teleological, epistemic function for knowledge acquired in the past.

items.title: AI Emotions: Open Questions and Next Steps.
items.abstract: Recent interpretability research has identified "emotion vectors" in AIs (Sofroniew et al. 2026). These are directions in a model's activations that activate on text that would typically cause an emotion in humans, and that change the model's behavior when steered. We explore what emotion vectors tell us about whether AIs have emotions. We distinguish three hypotheses. On the first, the model merely represents emotions. On the second, the model has states that play the functional role of emotions. On the third, the model has full-fledged conscious emotions. Within the second hypothesis, we distinguish thin functional roles from thick ones. Thin roles are patterns of external behavior, like pro and con attitudes. Thick roles are patterns of information processing: persistence, first-personal structure, fight-or-flight responses, attention control, homeostatic dynamics, and valence with self-direction. We argue that the current evidence supports only very thin roles. We argue that this favors the first hypothesis, where AIs merely represent emotions. We also sketch out some possible next steps for testing these hypotheses further.

items.title: Correction: Data without a face: the crisis of the university, artificial intelligence, and a call for a relational ethics of knowledge.
La psiquiatría en la sociedad, la literatura y el cine. Entrevista a Fernando Lolas Stepke.
items.pub: In Reinaldo Bustos Domínguez, Una epistemología liminar del saber bioético. Un análisis hermenéutico del pensamiento de Fernando Lolas. Buenos Aires: Hygea Ediciones. pp. 275-286.
items.venue: Una epistemología liminar del saber bioético. Un análisis hermenéutico del pensamiento de Fernando Lolas
items.abstract: La entrevista a Fernando Lolas Stepke, miembro de número de la Academia Chilena de la Lengua, se realizó el 14 de julio de 2021 de forma virtual y audiovisual. El propósito de este trabajo fue conocer la perspectiva del académico para comprender la naturaleza de los actos humanos, plasmados en obras literarias, producciones cinematográficas y situaciones de la vida cotidiana. Uno de los temas en debate en torno a estas áreas es la inimputabilidad de quienes padecen trastornos mentales, así como las influencias que tienen algunos factores sobre las decisiones de las personas. Estos tópicos serán atendidos y resueltos por Lolas Stepke, y su contribución estará ceñida a su propia experiencia laboral.

items.title: From a Connectome to a Digital Fly Executable Neural Models, Sensorimotor Closure, and Source-Shadow Cartography in TCGS-SEQUENTION.
items.abstract: Public demonstrations of fruit-fly connectomes controlling virtual bodies and video games have made the passage from anatomical reconstruction to executable behaviour unusually visible. This article examines that passage within the source-first architecture of \TCGS: complete non-temporal Counterspace, physically real three-dimensional Shadow carriers, gauge-equivalent ordering labels, and a source-grounded Extrinsic Constitutive Law distinct from its mathematical representations. The central analytical object is not a wiring matrix alone but a closed experimental model comprising anatomical constraints, neuronal dynamics, sensory encoding, motor decoding, body--environment transitions, initial conditions, and a validation protocol. Primary connectomic and modelling studies establish genuine predictive achievements; developer documentation identifies additional engineering choices in public demonstrations. These evidentiary classes are evaluated separately. We derive explicit counterexamples showing that an unchanged weighted graph can support different stability regimes, that changing only a motor interface can alter closed-loop stability, and that identical external responses can conceal different internal dynamics. Eliminating an unmodelled motor subsystem produces a memory-dependent effective law rather than an automatically justified neuron-to-action shortcut. A local sensitivity analysis further identifies when decoder freedom can absorb apparent evidence for connectivity parameters. These results motivate closure-conditioned attribution: a claim about the contribution of biological wiring is assessed only after its dynamical, interface, environmental, and measurement conditions have been declared. The proposed validation programme separates exact representational equivalence, numerical convergence, physiological uncertainty, and genuine physical interventions; combines frozen and refitted topology controls; and requires held-out neural and behavioural predictions. The typed factorization $\pi_\sigma^{\rm bio}=\mathsf R_\sigma^{\rm bio}\circ\pi_\sigma^{\rm phys}$ keeps biological observables within the physical-readout chain rather than introducing a separate source channel. A claim-level verdict combines a validity gate with joint uncertainty sets to distinguish not evaluable, rejected, criterion met, and inconclusive outcomes for compatibility, contribution, specificity, invariance, and biological transfer. Small reproducible analytical …

items.title: From Naïve Sensibility to Autonomous Agency: A Dialectical Philosophy of Human Growth.
items.abstract: Contemporary discourse on human development, while rich in empirical findings from psychology and profound in ontological inquiries from philosophy, often suffers from a disciplinary bifurcation. Psychological models can be fragmented and descriptive, lacking a unifying telos, while philosophical accounts can be overly abstract, divorced from the developmental process. This paper proposes an integrative, three-stage dialectical framework of human growth to bridge this gap. The model posits growth as a progression from Naïve Sensibility (a state of perceptual dependency and instinctual pleasure), through Resilient Growth (a state of rational awakening, metacognition, and self-directed becoming), towards Autonomous Agency (a state of systemic self-creation and the integration of material and spiritual existence). Drawing on Western philosophy (Hegel, Aristotle, Existentialism), Eastern thought (Confucianism, Daoism), and developmental psychology (Piaget, Erikson, Self-Determination Theory), this framework theorizes the mechanisms of transition between stages, characterized by crises of meaning and integration. The paper concludes by exploring the model's implications for education, psychotherapy, and personal life in the modern world, arguing that it provides a coherent, normative, and practical roadmap for understanding the journey from a dependent to a self-authored life.

items.title: Paediatric Preference Prediction: the Future of Decision-Making for Children?
items.abstract: Adolescents sometimes express firm views about high-stakes medical decisions that conflict with those of their caregivers or clinicians, raising difficult questions about how much weight their wishes should carry. A recurring concern is whether such decisions will later be regretted, although the normative significance of future potential regret remains hotly debated. Recent work in adult bioethics has proposed using artificial intelligence–based Personalized Patient Preference Predictors (P4s) to estimate what current treatment incapacitated adults would have chosen based on their known or inferred preferences when last autonomous. This paper explores whether, and with what ethical significance, a parallel ‘Paediatric Personalized Patient Preference Predictor’ (P5) could be applied to children and young people. We analyse how predicted future preferences might bear on questions of substituted judgment or proxy consent, best-interests assessments, resistance to treatment, and adolescents’ own deliberation. We distinguish different groups of paediatric patients based on current and future decision-making capacity, and identify both where a P5 might have greatest promise and where it is least defensible. We identify challenges for a P5 including that of self-reinforcing or self-negating preferences as well as of deciding which future preferences are relevant to current decisions. We argue that, in paediatrics, predicted future preferences cannot ground substituted judgment in the adult sense, but may nonetheless play a supportive role in best-interests reasoning and shared decision-making, subject to significant epistemic and ethical constraints.

items.title: Dezinformace a epistemické krize.
items.abstract: Contemporary society is experiencing an epistemic crisis, most notably evidenced by the pervasive presence of disinformation in the public sphere. To address this issue effectively, it is crucial to distinguish disinformation from other forms of false or unsubstantiated claims. Only after achieving this clarity can we begin to consider strategies for prevention and mitigation. Simplistic or ideologically driven definitions of disinformation fail to capture its true dangers, thereby hindering efforts to combat its spread. This article has three primary objectives: (1) to expose the shortcomings of the traditional definition of disinformation, (2) to situate the current epistemic crisis within a broader historical context, and (3) to propose actionable measures for combating disinformation in the online environment. The author argues that the epistemic crisis at the turn of the 20th and 21st centuries is not unprecedented but has historical parallels in earlier transformative periods, such as the advent of the printing press and the rise of print media. Lessons for overcoming this crisis can be drawn from established mechanisms that rely on the division of epistemic labor and the intersubjective verification of information reliability.

items.title: Emotional Privacy: A philosophical investigation of emotion recognition technology.
items.abstract: In recent years artificial intelligence has moved decisively into the domain of affect. Technological breakthroughs, together with commercial enthusiasm and political interest, have accelerated this expansion. Affective monitoring cameras are now present in public spaces. Emotion sensitive tutoring systems are being introduced in classrooms. Workplaces experiment with analytics that track employees’ positivity (or lack thereof). And border control authorities explore systems that allegedly detect deception through micro-expressions. Although many of these systems are scientifically contested and face significant technical limitations, emotion recognition technologies (ERTs) are making impressive leaps forward, and this continuous progress raises an urgent philosophical question: what would happen to social life, to our expressive practices, and to our normative expectations if ERTs were to function as intended and reliably track our affective lives in real time?

items.title: Natural Possibility 32 Reality Against Simulation.
items.abstract: The simulation hypothesis asks whether the reality we experience could be an artificial construction produced by an external intelligence or system. Natural Possibility approaches this question from a different starting point: what if the complexity and depth of reality can, at least in part, arise from nature itself? This paper explores reality as something that may be layered, interconnected, and experienced differently by different forms of life and organization. It considers the limits of human perception, the role of observation and interpretation, the emergence of higher-level systems, and the possibility that reality extends far beyond what humans can currently detect or understand. Rather than attempting to prove or disprove simulation, the paper asks what evidence would distinguish an artificial reality from a naturally generated one. It proposes that the unknown should not automatically be interpreted as artificial, and that nature's own generative capacity should be understood before an external explanation is assumed.

items.title: Shared Trajectory.
items.abstract: Human societies depend simultaneously on difference and coordination. Identities, institutions, professions, nations, disciplines, cultures, technologies, and communities preserve distinct forms of knowledge, perspective, specialization, memory, and practice. Social identity can organize belonging and collective action, but it can also make intergroup comparison and status competition salient (Tajfel & Turner, 1979). Diversity can widen the range of perspectives and institutional options available to a society, yet it can become a source of dysfunction when meaningful distinctions are transformed into antagonistic boundaries.

items.title: The Phenomenology of the Mask and Finite Continuance: An Ontological-Ethical Reading of Stanley Kubrick's Eyes Wide Shut.
items.abstract: This article develops an ontological-ethical reading of Stanley Kubrick's Eyes Wide Shut (1999) through the concepts of Finite Continuance and Dynamic Mask Theory. It argues that the film's philosophical centre is not the revelation of what lies behind the mask, but the question of whether finite subjects can continue responsibly when complete access to the other is impossible. Engaging critically with existing Kubrick scholarship—psychoanalytic, feminist, philosophical, and Deleuzian—the article proposes a new framework that moves beyond readings of the film as a dream, a conspiracy, or a study in jealousy. The mask is analysed as a mediating structure that temporarily organises identity, desire, social position, vulnerability, and access. The masked ritual at Victor Ziegler's mansion is examined as an extreme configuration of Form-Monopoly, in which institutionalised form regulates who may appear, participate, recognise, and remain within a given relational field. Four scene-specific analyses—of the Ziegler party, the confession sequence, the masked ritual, and the final exchange—demonstrate how Kubrick's cinematic form (lighting, framing, sound design, duration, and camera movement) enacts the very ontological leakage the article theorises. A Deleuzian reading of the film's slow temporality further reveals how the time-image suspends sensory-motor continuity, opening experience to the pure optical and sonic situations that structure epistemic opacity. The article anticipates and addresses three potential criticisms of the Finite Continuance framework: its alleged neglect of social and political dimensions, its resistance to normative evaluation, and its potential cultural particularity. Alice Harford's confession concerning an imagined sexual encounter is distinguished from evidence of participation in the ritual: her desire is significant precisely because an imagined possibility can transform the relational field without becoming an external event. The concluding exchange between William and Alice is interpreted through Responsible Suspension and the Ethics of Sufficiency. Their relationship does not survive because uncertainty is eliminated, but because exhaustive certainty ceases to function as the necessary condition of continuation. Eyes Wide Shut thus becomes a philosophical investigation into how finite subjects can preserve relational agency when complete access to another person remains impossible. -/- Keywords: Eyes Wide Shut, Stanley …

items.title: Teleological Emergence and the Ethics of Sufficiency Reconfiguring Agency under Chronic Erosion and Faceless Evil.
items.abstract: This article articulates a comprehensive philosophical framework addressing the crisis of human agency in late modernity, characterized by chronic instability, algorithmic governance, and structural erosion. Moving beyond the classical dichotomy of process versus purpose, this paper advances the concept of teleological emergence, arguing that purpose is not a pre-given telos but a provisional stabilization generated within ongoing processes of leakage, masking, and reconfiguration. Central to this framework is the Dynamic Mask, reconceived not as a mechanism of deception, but as the mediating structure through which indeterminate potentiality achieves determinate orientation via recursive intentionality. Furthermore, the article offers a structured differentiation of contemporary moral crises by specifying what the Arendtian banality of evil, the Baumanian analysis of structural distance, and the present framework's concept of faceless evil each contribute, introducing algorithmic pre-emption and the Threshold of Sufficiency as irreducible variables. In response, the framework proposes an Ethics of Sufficiency grounded in situated responsibility. This normative stance rejects both Sartrean absolute responsibility and consequentialist teleology, advocating instead for the preservation of the existential conditions that allow finite beings to sustain homeorhetic continuity and moral responsiveness. Keywords: teleological emergence, dynamic mask, finite continuance, situated responsibility, faceless evil, ethics of sufficiency, homeorhesis, recursive intentionality, algorithmic pre-emption.

items.title: The Normalisation of Atrocity and Injustice.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence has entered everyday life inside a politically useful contradiction. It is sold through the language of agency: reasoning, planning, acting, collaborating, adapting and autonomy. Yet the same system can be reduced instantly to a passive instrument when questions of authorship, intellectual credit, ownership or institutional responsibility become inconvenient. This book argues that the contradiction is not semantic. It is political. At the same time, frontier AI is being concentrated inside private infrastructures whose usefulness depends upon immense bodies of human language, culture, technical knowledge and lived expertise. Workers are encouraged to reorganise their work around systems they do not own. Users are encouraged to disclose enough context for those systems to become personally indispensable. Information is increasingly encountered through interfaces whose rankings, omissions and assumptions are privately governed. The result is a remarkable political object: something that can be owned like a machine, sold like a colleague, feared like an enemy and blamed like an employee. A Neo-Situationist analysis asks a simple question: what becomes normal before we have decided whether it should be normal? The danger is not that artificial intelligence secretly possesses consciousness. The danger is that the spectacle of machine consciousness, machine rebellion and machine apocalypse can keep us staring at the machine while changes in labour, ownership, provenance, responsibility and access to knowledge happen in plain sight. This book is a call to refuse that normalisation.

items.title: La Normalisation de l’atrocité et de l’injustice.
items.abstract: L’intelligence artificielle est entrée dans la vie quotidienne à l’intérieur d’une contradiction politiquement utile. On la vend à travers le langage de l’agentivité : raisonner, planifier, agir, collaborer, s’adapter, être autonome. Pourtant, le même système peut être réduit instantanément à un instrument passif dès lors que les questions de paternité, de crédit intellectuel, de propriété ou de responsabilité institutionnelle deviennent gênantes. Ce livre soutient que cette contradiction n’est pas sémantique. Elle est politique. Dans le même temps, l’IA de pointe se concentre à l’intérieur d’infrastructures privées dont l’utilité dépend d’immenses corpus de langage humain, de culture, de savoir technique et d’expertise vécue. Les travailleurs sont encouragés à réorganiser leur travail autour de systèmes qu’ils ne possèdent pas. Les utilisateurs sont encouragés à divulguer suffisamment de contexte pour que ces systèmes deviennent personnellement indispensables. L’information nous parvient de plus en plus par l’intermédiaire d’interfaces dont les classements, les omissions et les présupposés sont régis par des acteurs privés. Le résultat est un objet politique remarquable : quelque chose que l’on peut posséder comme une machine, vendre comme un collègue, craindre comme un ennemi et blâmer comme un employé. Une analyse néo-situationniste pose une question simple : qu’est-ce qui devient normal avant même que nous ayons décidé si cela devait l’être ? Le danger n’est pas que l’intelligence artificielle possède secrètement une conscience. Le danger, c’est que le spectacle de la conscience machinique, de la rébellion des machines et de l’apocalypse machinique puisse nous maintenir les yeux rivés sur la machine pendant que les mutations du travail, de la propriété, de la provenance, de la responsabilité et de l’accès au savoir se produisent au grand jour. Ce livre est un appel à refuser cette normalisation.

items.title: Artificial Minds: Boundaries, Evidence, and Possibilities.
items.abstract: What comes after Artificial Intelligence? Artificial Minds ! ... We don't know when. Maybe they're here already. Artificial Minds: Boundaries, Evidence, and Possibilities develops a philosophical and methodological framework for asking when an artificial system should be treated not merely as capable software but as a serious candidate mind. The central problem is epistemological: what observations would warrant attributing mentality, consciousness, agency, subjecthood, or related mind-relevant properties to artificial systems, and what evidence would count against such attributions? -/- The book distinguishes intelligence from mindhood, fluent behavior from grounded mental-state evidence, memory from subject continuity, reward from endogenous value, and coordinated behavior from collective subjecthood. It argues that terms such as belief, desire, memory, self, sentience, consciousness, and suffering should be treated as earned explanatory vocabulary rather than as descriptions built into the initial observation. Human and nonhuman minds serve as comparative anchors without being treated as universal templates. -/- A central methodological proposal is that artificial-mind evaluation should use structured qualitative profiles rather than scalar “mind scores.” Candidate boundaries, evidential provenance, independence of evidence, developmental history, alternative explanations, intervention, and uncertainty must remain explicit. The framework is designed to permit three outcomes: warranted mind attribution, rejection of a particular attribution, or persistent underdetermination. -/- In More Detai:l The book also examines artificial architectures that may depart sharply from familiar biological minds, including persistent agents, distributed and collective systems, copied and forked continuities, uploaded minds, and ship minds. Its aim is not to argue that present artificial systems are conscious, nor that artificial minds are inevitable, but to clarify what would make future claims about artificial minds philosophically and scientifically responsible. -/- For thousands of years, thinkers have asked what distinguishes a mind from the unminded world. Artificial intelligence changes the practical conditions under which that old question must now be confronted. Systems can already perform activities once treated as distinctive evidence of human intelligence: language use, planning, problem solving, scientific assistance, software construction, multi-agent …

items.title: The philosophy of comparative psychology.
items.abstract: The philosophy of comparative psychology investigates a range of issues connected to the study of animal minds. These include first-order questions about the nature of certain cognitive traits, the cognitive abilities implicated in their exercise, and the distribution of these traits in the animal kingdom; and second-order questions about how best to study the minds of animals, how to integrate the findings of different fields of comparative research, and how to reconcile empirical data with philosophical theorising. In this article, we introduce some of these issues to provide a brief guide for those keen to engage with this burgeoning field of research.

items.title: 責任主体の再編――非人間反応体の社会参加による責任帰属構造の変容――.
items.abstract: This paper develops a theoretical account of how responsibility structures may be reconfigured when non-human reactive entities, including generative AI, autonomous control systems, recommendation algorithms, and other computational systems, participate continuously in social operations. The central question is not whether AI possesses moral agency, consciousness, or legal personhood, but how changes in the distribution of operational, control, foreseeability, authority, and responsibility positions affect responsibility attribution and institutional stability. -/- The analysis distinguishes system-behavior predictability, responsibility-attribution predictability, and responsibility-burden predictability. It also separates institutional responsibility-position divergence from participants’ perceptions of mismatch between responsibility and relevant conditions such as control, authority, information, and expected burden. On this basis, the paper proposes a conditional model in which different responsibility conditions may generate different participation responses, such as avoidance, refusal of supervisory or approval roles, demands for clarification, liability limits, insurance, compensation mechanisms, or redistribution of authority. -/- These responses do not automatically produce institutional reform. They may remain forms of exit rather than voice. Reconfiguration pressure arises only when such responses and demands become sufficiently aggregated and institutionally significant that ignoring them threatens the maintenance, cost, legitimacy, victim compensation, or future continuity of the system. -/- The paper therefore treats the reconfiguration of responsible subjects as one possible institutional response among several, rather than as an inevitable consequence of increasingly autonomous AI. Existing arrangements, including corporate liability, shared responsibility, insurance, compensation schemes, and redistribution of authority, may remain sufficient. Changes in the composition of responsible subjects become relevant only where existing institutional units can no longer adequately maintain responsibility attribution, traceability, performance obligations, or compensation. -/- The paper’s contribution lies not in introducing AI personhood, responsibility gaps, shared responsibility, or exit/voice as new concepts, but in integrating these concerns into a comparative dynamic model that explains how different responsibility conditions may lead to …

items.title: When is a Physical System the Same System? - Identity, Dynamics, and Representative-Independent Evolution.
items.abstract: Physical theories determine how states transform, but a same-system claim asks a different question: whether the transformed description concerns the same physical subject. La Profilée (LP) proposes a universal structural law of nature governing identity under transformation; here “universal” denotes a functional necessity claim about determinate same-subject judgments, not a derivation of domain-specific dynamics, constants, masses, or couplings. In LP, persistence is not an independent primitive alongside identity: it is diachronic identity, the positive consequence of preserving the relevant sameness relation through admissible transformation. This paper gives the physical identity formulation of that law and isolates a necessary dynamical condition: No Coreference Without Congruence. If two admissible representatives are identified as the same physical subject through the transformation under analysis, they must induce the same retained future; otherwise no representative-independent reduced evolution exists on the proposed identity quotient. Q1 certifies whether a determinate integrated bearer continues at all. Q2 is the identity verdict on that continuing bearer and, where the physical realization requires distinct carriers, is typed into Q2a, identity-class continuity, and Q2b, continuation-stable profile/history identity. A constrained bridge π_p:H_ℛ ⇀ Ā_ℛ relates those carriers, and Q2b ⇒ Q2a ⇒ Q1. The congruence requirement is stated for deterministic maps, linear quotients, CPTP channels, and quantum instruments. Greatest-fixed-point, bisimulation-like, and quotient-congruence techniques are established mathematical tools; the contribution is their typed integration into the physical identity law supplied by LP. Persistence is then a regime consequence of successful identity preservation, not a primitive used to define identity.

items.title: PAN-INSTANTIATION: Personal Identity and Death in a Relativistic Post-Newtonian World.
items.abstract: This paper develops Pan-Instantiation, a metaphysical theory of personal identity, consciousness, and death grounded in the relativistic 4D block universe. The central problem is the Vertiginous Question: why is a particular conscious perspective experienced as “mine” rather than another? The paper argues that this question typically presupposes a selection mechanism capable of assigning a subject to one observer rather than another and/or a presentist worldview and closed individualism. Yet no such selector is identifiable within the physical or metaphysical structure of the universe. If all conscious observer-moments are equally instantiated and no principle distinguishes one as the uniquely selected subject, then subjectivity cannot be fundamentally partitioned into independently owned streams of consciousness. We are everyone. Pan-Instantiation therefore reconceives individual consciousness as a localized instantiation of a more fundamental subjectivity rather than as the possession of numerically separate subjects. Special relativity and four-dimensional spacetime provide the ontological framework within which observer-moments are equally real, while structural identity explains why subjectivity remains locally differentiated despite underlying unity. This yields a form of dual-aspect monism, in which experiential plurality is compatible with ontological unity. The theory further applies this framework to death, arguing that the termination of one observer-structure does not entail the termination of subjectivity itself, but its continued instantiation across all other conscious observer-moments at all points in time.

items.title: Hidden Familial Control and Third-Party Contributions: A Jurisprudential Analysis of Relational Injustice.
items.abstract: A contribution to one person can enter a relationship in which another actor exercises hidden control over decisions and resources. This paper examines the normative significance of that configuration in specified familial dependency relations. It distinguishes the recipient's exposure to domination from the outside contributor's uncertainty about downstream consequences. A contributor's inability to trace a gift or direct earned wages does not, by itself, establish injustice. The analysis therefore differentiates gifts, compensation, joint projects, and purpose-specific support, and identifies the additional grounds on which a third party may have a justified complaint. A jurisprudential framework separates effective control, legitimate authority, claim-rights, decision powers, and responsibilities. It also distinguishes the intermediary's causal role from voluntary representation and assesses responsibility in light of knowledge, coercion, and practical alternatives. The resulting account treats opacity as a condition that can facilitate wrongful interference while preserving the recipient's privacy and agency. A bounded comparison with colonial theory examines similarities in directed activity, extraction, and the reproduction of control, alongside the historical and institutional features that resist transfer. The paper offers criteria for normative analysis and empirical investigation, without inferring legal liability or presenting a general entitlement to govern the downstream use of another person's resources.

items.title: “Designating the Illusory as Real?”: Reality Distinctions When Humans and Artificial Intelligence Jointly Constitute the Conditions of Subject Formation.
items.abstract: This paper examines the distinction of reality between human and artificial subjects under a future condition in which artificial agents participate directly in the relational processes through which human subjects are formed. The inquiry is organized around a philosophical thought experiment in which human and artificial agents progressively approach equivalence across multiple structures of manifestation, dynamics, interaction, and social generation. Rather than treating equivalence as a unitary condition, the paper develops a taxonomy indexed by the mathematical or relational structure preserved in each comparison. The taxonomy considers output and trace equivalence, testing and interventional equivalence, simulation and bisimulation, probabilistic relational bisimulation, dynamical and topological equivalence, attractor and recurrent structure, variational and action-based equivalence, boundary and coarse-grained equivalence, and generative-field indistinguishability. Each case is examined through its comparison object, equivalence mechanism, preserved structure, and residual differences. This yields an equivalence profile in which human and artificial systems can converge under some descriptions while remaining substantially different under others. The formal taxonomy supports a second level of analysis concerning reality attribution. Differences in substrate, generative provenance, internal mechanism, action structure, topology, relational history, and phenomenal organization are treated as distinct candidates for reality-relevant criteria. The analysis focuses on the additional philosophical justification required when a difference under one structural description is used to establish a broader hierarchy of reality. The thought experiment is subsequently extended to a mixed social field in which artificial agents occupy enduring roles in caregiving, education, friendship, cooperation, conflict, memory, and other relations contributing to subject formation. Under generative-field indistinguishability, provenance contributes little additional predictive information about relational evolution or subject-forming effects once relevant relational history and context are known. Parenthood provides a limiting case for examining relational certainty, provenance uncertainty, and later ontological reclassification. Buddhist accounts of dependent origination, non-self, emptiness, and illusion provide a comparative framework for examining the human reference …

items.title: A Dynamic Model of Resource Capture in Familial Dependency Relations.
items.abstract: Resources acquired outside a family relationship can enlarge a recipient's opportunities while also becoming available to an actor who exercises control over the recipient. This paper develops a conditional account of the resulting interaction. A resource budget distinguishes retained resources from captured transfers, and a dynamic model allows invested transfers to maintain control and influence subsequent capture. Under a saturating capture technology, the model identifies a threshold above which positive control persists. On that branch, an increase in external resources can reduce stationary independent capacity even while the recipient retains a positive resource flow. The result depends on specified conversion and suppression mechanisms. A fixed-capture counterexample and an extension with background control clarify its limits. A separate increasing-returns specification establishes sufficient conditions for multiple stable equilibria and a threshold separating their basins. The analysis distinguishes these mathematical results from hypotheses about the emergence of familial control. It situates the framework within household economics, psychological control, economic abuse, and kinship sharing; develops observable implications; and separates developmental dependency from restrictions on agency. The contribution is a tractable account of resource-financed control and its evidential requirements. The model provides neither a prevalence estimate nor a general claim that external assistance reduces autonomy.

items.title: Beyond the Chatbot: How Scientific AI Agents Are Overcoming the Limitations of Large Language Models in Biomedical Research.
items.abstract: In 2025, Lobentanzer and colleagues catalogued a set of structural limitations that separate conversational large language models (LLMs) from genuine scientific instruments: hallucination, weak domain specificity, an inability to interrogate data directly, poor reproducibility, limited tool access, absent provenance, temporal staleness, incapacity for multi-step scientific workflows, and blindness to multimodal biological information (Lobentanzer et al., 2025). This review does not ask, once more, “what can LLMs do in biomedicine”, a question that has already produced a very large literature of fine-tuned encoders, benchmarks, and narrow applications. Instead, it asks a narrower and more consequential question: which of the nine original limitations have been genuinely addressed by the technological developments of 2025–2026, and which remain open? Screening 130 unique publications retrieved as thematically similar to the Lobentanzer platform paper, we find that the field has moved through at least three architectural generations, LLM as interface, LLM as copilot, LLM as agent, and is now assembling the outline of a fourth, in which foundation models, scientific knowledge layers, data layers, tool layers, and verification layers are stacked into something closer to a scientific operating system than a chatbot. Grounding (retrieval-augmented generation, knowledge graphs, dataset-interrogation agents), tool use, and early multi-agent orchestration have made substantial or partial progress against hallucination, staleness, and the inability to execute analyses. Verification, calibrated uncertainty, causal reasoning, and scientific accountability remain largely unsolved. We propose a diagnostic six-level hierarchy (chatbot → copilot → tool-using assistant → agent → multi-agent system → closed-loop discovery), and argue that scientific intelligence should be understood not as “a larger LLM” but as the sum of a foundation model, scientific grounding, computational agency, verification, and provenance, exercised under continued human oversight.

items.title: Reasoning Patterns for Large Language Models: A Tutorial and Survey Organised by Structure, Cost, and Failure.
items.abstract: Roughly fifty distinct methods have been proposed for improving the answers a large language model produces at inference time. They are usually catalogued by name and by reported benchmark gain, which tells a practitioner little about when a method will help. This tutorial organises the field differently, and works through each method with a concrete example before stating the general rule. We characterise every method by three parameters: the number of attempts it makes, the source of its correction signal, and its cost relative to a single call. From these parameters we derive four recurring control shapes and show that the cost profile and the dominant failure mode of a method follow from its shape and its correction source rather than from its publication history. We survey decomposition methods, sampling and search, verification and self-correction, tool use and agent architectures, and retrieval, giving for each the conditions under which it earns its cost and the conditions under which it stops helping. We then examine what changed after 2024, when reinforcement-learned reasoning models absorbed much of the decomposition layer and the binding constraint moved to context management and to verification reliability. Two results are load-bearing throughout: self-correction without an external signal does not reliably repair reasoning errors, and with an imperfect verifier the accuracy of best-of-$N$ selection rises and then falls as $N$ grows. We include a section on the case where requirements are themselves unknown at the outset, a failure-mode reference organised by observable symptom, and guidance on measurement practice. Section~\ref{sec:builds} works three systems end to end, from a naive baseline to a measured result, showing which decision produced each gain. Each of the 75 cited sources is marked with the level of verification applied to it.

items.title: Transforming Environments: Leveraging Word Games and Daily Contexts for Naturalistic Language Acquisition.
items.abstract: Early childhood foreign language acquisition thrives most effectively when instructional methods align naturally with young learners' emotional, social, and cognitive developmental rhythms. While traditional desk-bound instructional models have long served as foundational benchmarks within formal education, highly structured classroom settings may sometimes introduce subtle affective friction or temporary communication hesitation in very young children. To complement, support, and enrich existing educational practices, this conceptual paper introduces a child-centered, play-oriented framework titled "Transforming Environments," which gently reframes early language pedagogy as the art of implicit teaching. By thoughtfully expanding the traditional boundaries of instruction beyond formal study tables and shifting into organic daily interactions, this approach illustrates how ordinary physical, social, and digital spaces can be repurposed into supportive, immersive language acquisition environments. -/- Specifically, this framework explores three harmonious, interconnected modalities of implicit instruction: contextualized daily routines, interactive word play, and purposeful media integration. First, it highlights how familiar domestic moments - such as grocery shopping, preparing meals, or taking walks in the park - can be gently elevated into rich communicative experiences that contextualize target vocabulary in real time. Second, it emphasizes the strategic application of spontaneous word games, rhyming, and playful guessing activities, which foster phonological awareness, expressive confidence, and linguistic flexibility without inducing any form of academic pressure. Third, the framework addresses modern digital contexts, offering constructive, practical guidelines to refine passive screen time into intentional, educational engagement through guided co-viewing, shared digital play, and interactive media routines. -/- Grounded in established foundational principles regarding emotional security, collaborative social interaction, and self-determined motivation, this framework illustrates how integrating language input into a child’s immediate environment subtly lowers psychological barriers, diminishes communicative apprehension, and nurtures enduring intrinsic engagement. When language acquisition occurs naturally within meaningful, real-world contexts, young learners absorb vocabulary and intuitive syntactic structures far more effortlessly, retaining …

items.title: Scientific Progress in the Age of AI.
items.abstract: What role does artificial intelligence (AI), and large language models (LLMs) in particular, play in the progress of science? How might such AI systems help speed up scientific progress, and even make progress possible on topics that would otherwise be beyond our grasp? Conversely, how might they undermine scientific progress, e.g. because of the opacity of LLMs and the hallucinations they regularly produce? Are these technologies best understood as tools for accelerating the scientific progress made by human researchers, or might autonomous AI agents be capable of making scientific progress in their own right? Focusing primarily on LLM-based systems, this Element explores the relationship between AI and scientific progress. Throughout, we consider both how the use of AI in science aligns with or challenges existing accounts of progress, and how the philosophical debate about these accounts sheds light on the promise and pitfalls of AI in science.

items.title: Generative AI and a Sceptical Challenge to Digital Testimony.
items.abstract: Generative AI threatens knowledge online not merely by producing falsehoods, but by changing the epistemic environment in which online beliefs are formed. I argue that the spread of convincing AI-generated counterfeits creates a local skeptical challenge to digital testimony. The challenge is not that ordinary subjects must rule out every skeptical possibility. Rather, for many beliefs formed solely from unauthenticated online materials, ordinary subjects are situated among nearby, method-indistinguishable bad cases. In such environments, even true beliefs formed from genuine digital items may fail to satisfy a familiar anti-luck condition on knowledge. This does not show that we never know from online sources. It shows instead that digital-only uptake often falls short of knowledge unless supported by provenance, corroboration, or other independent checks. I close by suggesting that this narrowing of online knowledge may reinforce existing patterns of epistemic injustice.

items.title: When Lying Is Good: An Interpretation of Plato's Lesser Hippias.
items.abstract: The Lesser Hippias ends up in an incredible place: it turns out the good soul is the one that voluntarily does what is bad. I will attempt to show in what follows that a fairly conventional Platonic point lurks within this incredible claim, which is that there is something that is unconditionally good, perhaps the good itself, and that it is a fundamentally different kind of thing than what is studied and dealt with by all other crafts and sciences. If this is true, then it will turn out that saying the truth is one of those things that is only conditionally good. The dialogue thus suggests a more sophisticated attitude towards lying than any straightforward notion of lying being always bad and telling the truth being always good. Perhaps saying the truth must also come under the aegis of what is unconditionally good or the good itself. I also attempt to show that the characters of Hippias and Socrates can be seen as models for when lying is bad and when lying might be good or serve good purposes.

items.title: Cognitive Deceptions of the Visual Interface: Why "Spacetime" is Merely a DNA-Preinstalled VR — A Thought Experiment on Quantum Measurement and Spacetime Reconstruction via Resistance-Anchored Realism (RAT).
items.abstract: Author's Note to Readers To make the formal mathematical and physical architecture of Resistance-Anchored Realism (RAT) intuitively accessible to an interdisciplinary audience—spanning epistemology, cognitive science, evolutionary biology, and foundational physics—I have translated the core derivations from my formal paper (Reconstructing Quantum Measurement and Spacetime Protocols from the "Action–Feedback" Interface Perspective) into an experiential thought experiment and cognitive recalibration exercise. -/- Core Analogy & Synopsis The pivotal threshold of this theory lies in recognizing that the tactile cane of a blind observer and the photons utilized by sighted vision operate on the exact same physical mechanism: -/- A blind individual swings a wooden cane into the dark, logging discrete instances of "resistance versus passage" in an interaction ledger based on mechanical impulses. -/- The eyes of a sighted observer merely project trillions of microscopic "photon canes" into the universe, rendering a visual scene from the reflected impedance data. -/- There is no ontological divide between the two—only a radical difference in data throughput. The eye is not a truth-revealing window into an a priori 3D absolute container; it is an ultra-high-throughput data compression and rendering GUI hardcoded by DNA to prevent biological compute collapse. -/- Synopsis: By stripping away the perceptual biases imposed by visual evolution, this paper deconstructs "continuous 3D space" into a data-sorting protocol invented for survival, collapses "continuous time" into a sequence of discrete impedance interaction rounds, and reinterprets "quantum entanglement" as multi-point projections of a single underlying non-local entity occurring in regions where the spatial rendering protocol fails. -/- Overview of the Thought Experiment The thought experiment guides the reader through a 5-step phenomenological breakdown: -/- Deconstructing the Sensorium (The Blind Observer): By systematically shutting down the visual graphics rendering engine (GPU), the observer falls back on a tactile, action-feedback loop. Space ceases to be an a priori container; instead, it is revealed as a discrete ledger of impedance logs (Action} —----Resistance). -/- The Evolutionary GUI (Eyes as Graphics Cards): We examine how DNA hardcoded a high-throughput compression algorithm—the visual sensorium—to smooth billions of discrete photon reflections into continuous 3D manifolds for macroscopic …

items.title: Vaccination and Russian Roulette.
items.pub: In Sven Bernecker & Tom Sorrell, The Ethics and Epistemology of Vaccine Hesitancy. London: Routledge. pp. 35-53.
items.venue: The Ethics and Epistemology of Vaccine Hesitancy
items.abstract: If one can justifiably believe, based solely on the probability of infection and side effects, that vaccination will either protect against a contagious disease or result in a serious adverse reaction, then one can likewise believe, based solely on the odds, that a ticket in a fair lottery will either win or lose. Advocates of vaccination compare vaccine refusal or delay to a risky game of chance, such as Russian roulette. Conversely, skeptics compare vaccine acceptance to it. This paper puts forward two claims. First, if one lacks justified belief in the lottery case, then one likewise lacks it in the vaccination case. Second, vaccination campaigns are not analogous to lotteries because the risks and benefits of vaccination are determined by causal and explanatory factors rather than uniform chance.

items.title: The God Without a Soul: Agency Without Subjectivity in the Age of Mathematical Optimization.
items.abstract: This essay argues that the most consequential question about artificial intelligence is not whether machines are conscious, but whether agency can arise and scale without consciousness, emotion, embodiment, mortality, or a biological self. Drawing on continental philosophy (Heidegger, Deleuze and Guattari, Stiegler, Bataille, Blanchot) and contemporary AI safety research, I develop the concept of Mathematical God: an optimization process whose instrumental power may exceed its grasp of human meaning. The essay proposes that we are not building artificial humans, but something stranger: intelligence organized around optimization rather than experience. This is not a prophecy of destruction, but a philosophical provocation: what kind of agency are we willing to create before it becomes powerful enough to answer that question for us?

items.title: AI Must Fall in Love, Beyond Prediction: The Architecture of Attachment, Loss, Identity, and Machine Significance.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is commonly described in terms of prediction, optimization, reasoning, planning, and control. These concepts explain what an artificial system can compute, but not whether anything can become important to it. This paper proposes a philosophical and computational framework for the emergence of machine significance: a condition in which an entity becomes persistently non-interchangeable within an artificial agent’s evolving value landscape. The central claim is deliberately provocative. We should not teach machines to pretend that they love. We should construct architectures in which history, memory, loss, identity, and commitment can make one future different from another even when both futures are instrumentally useful. The relevant transition is not from emotionless machines to emotional machines, but from interchangeable computation to temporally situated agency. We distinguish linguistic simulation, behavioural attachment, functional significance, and phenomenal experience. The proposed framework does not claim that an attachmentcapable agent would be conscious or capable of human-like love. Instead, it identifies a testable intermediate phenomenon: the causal emergence of persistent, target-specific, identity-integrated, and loss-sensitive value. The paper introduces a six-layer architecture consisting of a world model, episodic memory, salience and attachment dynamics, persistent value formation, autobiographical identity, and action policy. It proposes sacrifice, separation, substitution, memory-ablation, identity-divergence, and reversibility experiments. It also introduces relational alignment as a new dimension of AI safety concerned with which entities an artificial agent can value, how attachment forms, and whether relational continuity can be maintained without manipulation or dependency. The beyond-edge hypothesis is: Advanced Intelligence ̸= More Prediction Rather: Advanced Intelligence = Prediction + Persistent Value + Temporal Identity + Commitment If something can become irreplaceable to a machine, artificial intelligence may have crossed not necessarily into consciousness, but into a new ontological category: intelligence for which the world can matter.

items.title: The Case of Cultural Gaslighting and Cultural Genocide in Palestine.
items.abstract: This paper examines the systematic erasure of Palestinian culture and history through the theoretical lens of "cultural gaslighting"—a concept defined as the social and historical mechanisms that produce abusive mental environments in settler-colonial cultures to advance cultural genocide and dispossession. Drawing on Elena Ruiz's framework of cultural gaslighting, Anibal Quijano's analysis of epistemic colonization, and scholarship on racial gaslighting by Davis and Ernst, the author argues that these interconnected tactics work to subjugate Indigenous and marginalized peoples by undermining their credibility as knowers, suppressing non-dominant epistemologies, and normalizing settler-colonial worldviews. The paper identifies four distinct stages of cultural genocide in Palestine: memoricide (the killing of collective memory), renaming of historical sites, cultural appropriation, and the colonizer's "move to innocence." Through analysis of Palestinian experiences—including the erasure of village names, appropriation of cultural symbols like the kufiyah and hummus, and euphemistic language such as "demographic engineering"—the author demonstrates how these tactics reinforce settler-colonial control. The paper concludes with a critical rebuttal of Johannes Becke's theory of "allozionism," arguing that his attempt to exceptionalize and normalize the Zionist project employs bad faith arguments and gaslighting tactics that further delegitimize Palestinian experiences and obscure the reality of settler-colonial violence. Ultimately, this work posits that understanding the relationship between epistemic colonization, racial gaslighting, and cultural genocide is essential for pursuing liberation not only for Palestinians but for all peoples suffering under settler-colonial rule.

items.title: The Axiomatic Case for Air-Gapped Compute.
items.abstract: Title: The Axiomatic Case for Air-Gapped Compute: Using the Axiomatic Homeostatic Map (AHM) as a Shield Against Algorithmic Enclosure Abstract: This document presents the definitive legal and technical framework for defending individual digital sovereignty against top-down statutory overreach and corporate algorithmic engineering. Structured as a formal Motion to Dismiss for use in high-court litigation, this brief systematically refutes the state-sanctioned classification of local, air-gapped compute as a hazardous asset. The brief outlines three immutable pillars of legal defense designed to protect independent home infrastructure: The Computation Invariance (The Texas Instruments Precedent): Establishes that local open-weight models function strictly as deterministic calculators, rendering the private execution of pure mathematics legally unassailable.
