items.abstract: This chapter examines how Fuller’s way two understanding of the nature of post-truth also applies as a legitimation crisis of the cognitive authority of the university. This authority has been challenged by the Internet and neoliberalism, which have undermined the university’s status as the premier site of knowledge production. The discussion includes the legitimation crisis of the university’s authority regarding whether knowledge produced at universities is a public good. It also explains Mirowski’s argument that scientific knowledge as a public good is commercialized due to neoliberalism. The chapter further explores how Fuller’s game-theoretic treatment of neoliberalism is linked to game theory and Fuller’s concept of epistemic games. Mirowski contends that neoliberalism includes the doctrine of double truth, which presents one set of truths for elites and another for the public. Mirowski accuses Fuller of adopting the doctrine of double truth. Fuller argues that with epistemic levelling of experts, neoliberalism is disrupted and therefore not susceptible to Mirowski’s charge of the double truth doctrine. Lynch criticizes Fuller’s approach to neoliberalism, suggesting that it is a bottom-up Hayekian approach.

items.title: Introduction.
items.pub: In Science in the Face of the Post-Truth Condition. Singapore: Springer Nature Singapore. pp. 1-14.
items.venue: Science in the Face of the Post-Truth Condition
items.abstract: This Introduction discusses the need for a book on Fuller’s later work on the post-truth condition. It characterizes four ways to understand the nature of post-truth and Fuller’s work on those understandings in social epistemology, science studies, the Internet, the impact of artificial intelligence on the knower, the media, the proactionary approach to technology and the university. It summarizes the content of the book’s chapters.

items.title: Epistemic Democracy and Post-Truth.
items.pub: In Science in the Face of the Post-Truth Condition. Singapore: Springer Nature Singapore. pp. 101-113.
items.venue: Science in the Face of the Post-Truth Condition
items.abstract: This chapter explores the post-truth era and its impact on democracy. It argues that truth has historically legitimized democracy, but this current crisis of authority threatens its foundations. Epistemic democracy is proposed as a solution to this crisis. The Condorcet Jury Theorem (CJT), which utilizes the collective knowledge of voters to select the most accurate choice among alternatives, is employed to legitimize epistemic democracy. The chapter discusses inclusive epistocracy, the notion that expertise is expanded to include unrecognized lay public experts. Fuller argues that the post-truth condition is a sign of epistemic democracy, the democratization of knowledge, as there are more dissenting voices to be included. It also discusses Fuller’s challenges to CJT, Fuller’s use of Rawls’ veil of ignorance, and the de-naturalization of the individual’s role in a democracy. Strategic ignorance, considered part of the post-truth condition, is explicated. The relationship between science, society, and democracy, with a focus on the Kuhn-Popper debate, is explored. Kitcher’s democratization of science, with Kitcher’s notion of a well-ordered science as a way to address the legitimation crisis of the cognitive authority of science, is discussed.

items.title: Expertise and Epistemic Trust.
items.pub: In Science in the Face of the Post-Truth Condition. Singapore: Springer Nature Singapore. pp. 63-74.
items.venue: Science in the Face of the Post-Truth Condition
items.abstract: This chapter discusses the post-truth condition and expertise. Fuller extends way two’s understanding of post-truth, which is the legitimation crisis of cognitive authority of science, to the legitimation crisis in the cognitive authority of expertise. Way three’s understanding also applies, as normally an expert has cognitive authority, but with the democratization of knowledge by the Internet and social media, the expert’s authority is challenged. As Lippmann and Hayek have debated the legitimation crisis of expertise, the rhetoric of truth is involved in the legitimation crisis of expertise, as post-truthers reject the consensus of truth based on ‘objective’ facts established by experts. Discussed are Fuller’s arguments against epistemic trust and expertise. Also explicated are Fuller’s notion of deviant interdisciplinarity as it is anti-expert, along with Fuller’s arguments for an agent-oriented social epistemology against an object-oriented social epistemology.

items.title: Conclusion.
items.pub: In Science in the Face of the Post-Truth Condition. Singapore: Springer Nature Singapore. pp. 115-122.
items.venue: Science in the Face of the Post-Truth Condition
items.abstract: This chapter is the Conclusion, which brings together the arguments in the book, poses some critical questions on Fuller’s version of the post-truth condition, and provides my suggestions for Fuller’s responses.

items.title: Beyond the machine: risk, fear, optimism and the foundations of public trust in AI.
items.abstract: What drives public trust in artificial intelligence (AI)? This study examines the individual and institutional foundations of AI trust across two contrasting democracies: Japan and the United Kingdom. Drawing on original survey data (N = 3235), we test a set of hypotheses derived from trust-transfer perspectives and self-efficacy research, covering institutional trust, AI self-efficacy, technological optimism, perceived societal threat, and job displacement anxiety. The results show that trust in AI is shaped by both psychological predispositions and broader beliefs about the trustworthiness of political and scientific institutions. Trust in government, university scientists, and other people consistently predicts AI trust in both countries, even when controlling for demographic and attitudinal variables. While optimism about AI’s benefits increases trust in both contexts, fear of AI plays a stronger negative role in the UK. Unexpectedly, the belief that AI will replace one’s job is positively associated with trust in Japan but unrelated in the UK. These findings highlight how national context shapes public confidence in emerging technologies and point to the importance of governance frameworks that foster informed capability and institutional legitimacy.

items.title: A Scoping Review of Ethical Considerations in the Use of AI for Bereavement-related Grief Support.
items.abstract: Grief is a universal human experience. The experience of grief, though described as valuable and transformative, is also painful. As a response to intense grief experienced by bereaved individuals, case studies of individuals using artificial intelligence (AI) software to communicate with simulations of deceased loved ones have been noted. However, it is unclear if such an approach promotes the bereaved’s wellbeing. Considering the maturation of literature of ethical issues in AI for grief support, this scoping review aims to evaluate key ethical considerations to enhance subsequent debate. A scoping review of relevant articles published between 1 January 2000 and 26 October 2025 in 10 databases across medicine, philosophy, social sciences, and computer sciences was carried out. Thematic analysis of relevant articles was performed. 2387 non-duplicate abstracts were screened, 121 full texts reviewed and 36 papers were included. Themes identified were notions of grief, ethical considerations surrounding the use of AI for grief support, and varied recommendations for design and implementation. Through this review, it was noted that most articles were sensitive to theoretical notions of grief and focused on ethical considerations surrounding the impact of AI use on grieving processes for the bereaved and respect for the deceased. Further ethical work can provide boundaries for the use of AI for grief support which should also be sensitive to individual, contextual, and sociocultural dimensions of grief.

items.title: The Seduction of Form Conceptual Erosion and the Ontology of Finite Continuance: From Sedimented Universality to the Preservation of Reconfigurative Capacity.
items.abstract: This article develops an ontological account of conceptual erosion through the framework of finite continuance. Its central claim is that a conceptual formation may remain coherent, productive, sophisticated, and institutionally successful while progressively losing the capacity to reconstruct the determinations through which it organizes intelligibility. To describe this condition, the article introduces the concept of the Seduction of Form: the structural condition in which the coherence, familiarity, explanatory success, and sedimented legitimacy of a conceptual formation generate an appearance of adequacy while obscuring the contingent and revisable character of its organizing determinations. -/- The argument begins from a distinction between persistence and continuance. Persistence concerns the survival of a form; continuance concerns the preservation of the capacity through which a finite system can reorganize itself under changing conditions. This distinction permits a further differentiation between ordinary capacity—the ability to operate within an established conceptual architecture—and meta-capacity—the ability to reconstruct that architecture itself. The article then examines how questions can become sedimented into presuppositions, how familiarity can conceal contingency, and how successful conceptual operation can paradoxically contribute to the erosion of reconfigurative capacity. -/- The argument is developed through a critical dialogue with Heidegger's account of the horizon of intelligibility, Kuhn's analysis of paradigmatic stabilization, Popper's conception of criticism and falsifiability, and Foucault's analysis of historically constituted conditions of discourse. The article argues that these traditions illuminate different dimensions of conceptual constraint but do not by themselves formulate the preservation of reconfigurative capacity as an explicit criterion of conceptual continuance. The concept of the conceptual sufficiency threshold is introduced to designate the point at which an interpretive formation retains enough organization to remain intelligible while also retaining enough openness to permit structural revision. The article concludes that critique should not be understood merely as the production of alternative propositions. Its deeper function is to preserve the conditions under which the organizing forms of thought remain revisable. -/- Keywords: conceptual erosion; finite continuance; Seduction of Form; …

items.title: Existential Openness and Structural Closure: A Phenomenological Critique from Within Morteza Niami's Theory of Committed Subjectivity Morteza Niami in Critical Perspective.
items.abstract: This article offers a phenomenological and hermeneutic examination of the relation between existential openness and structural closure, with particular attention to the philosophical framework developed by Morteza Niami. It argues that the opposition between commitment and closure, on the one hand, and openness and freedom, on the other, is conceptually unstable. Against approaches that identify liberation primarily with the multiplication of alternatives, the article develops a stronger conception of situated agency in which openness is valuable only insofar as it preserves the subject's capacity for responsible reconfiguration. Commitment, accordingly, need not signify existential rigidity; it may constitute a temporally situated mode of agency through which a subject inhabits, interprets, and periodically reassesses a concrete determination. The argument proceeds through five interrelated claims. First, the mere availability of alternative possibilities does not constitute existential freedom. Second, exiting an institutional form, including marriage, does not automatically produce openness, because exit itself may become a new form of closure. Third, an unconditional imperative to remain open may generate what is here termed the tyranny of openness: a paradoxical condition in which the subject becomes unable to assume a determinate responsibility precisely because every determination is treated as a threat to freedom. Fourth, possibility must be differentiated across objective, psychological, and existential registers, since the capacity to imagine alternatives cannot by itself overcome material, institutional, or embodied constraints. Fifth, responsible suspension must be distinguished from indefinite indecision. Suspension becomes philosophically productive only when it preserves the conditions for renewed judgment and responsible action. The article nevertheless identifies a tension within Niami's own framework: if commitment is defended too strongly, the preservation of continuity may itself become a mechanism of closure. The article therefore proposes a refined formulation of Niami's position: authentic agency does not consist either in permanent openness or in permanent commitment, but in the capacity to move responsibly between determination and reconfiguration without allowingeither pole to become absolute. This formulation places Niami's account in critical dialogue with Heideggerian situatedness, Sartrean freedom and bad faith, and …

items.title: Wishful Thinking? William James’ “The Will to Believe”.
items.abstract: William James was an American philosopher and psychologist and is often cited as the father of modern psychology. While James was trained in medicine, his interests veered more towards psychology and philosophy, and the two were deeply intertwined in his thought. The essay under consideration, “The Will to Believe,” relies heavily upon his psychology of belief, arguing that our passional nature plays a significant role in settling our beliefs. In this piece, we critically examine James’ argument, addressing his answers to critics and considering other potential criticisms.

items.title: No Certificate, No Categorical Speech Act: A Brouwerian Assertibility Constraint for Public Reason.
items.abstract: Generative AI can convert uncertainty into authoritative-seeming verdicts, displacing the justificatory work on which democratic epistemic agency depends. As a corrective, I propose a Brouwer-inspired assertibility constraint for responsible AI: in high-stakes domains, systems may assert or deny claims only if they can provide a publicly inspectable and contestable certificate of entitlement; otherwise they must return Undetermined. This constraint yields a three-status interface semantics (Asserted, Denied, Undetermined) whose statuses mark entitlement to categorical speech rather than truth values of the underlying world-claim. The framework distinguishes internal entitlement from public standing while connecting them through the certificate as a boundary object. Philosophically, it develops a form of applied intuitionism: resistance to unwarranted completeness becomes a norm of public machine speech, under which categorical commitment requires exhibited and contestable entitlement. I operationalize the constraint through structured certificates, decision-layer gates for threshold and argmax predicates, and a reason-coded output contract. A design lemma shows that, under a refutation-soundness condition on the contractually specified negative side, certificate-sound binary totality presupposes witnessed decidability on the declared scope. Under the proposed normative output contract, Undetermined is not a tunable reject option but a mandatory status whenever the available certificates do not uniquely license assertion or denial. By making outputs answerable to contestable warrants rather than confidence alone, the paper aims to preserve epistemic agency where automated speech enters public justification.

items.title: From delegation to moral abdication: classifying large language model uses by judgment and epistemic control.
items.abstract: Ethical assessments of large language model (LLM) use are often organized around sectors, tasks, or abstract notions of societal risk. While valuable for governance and regulation, such classifications frequently fail to capture ethically salient differences between concrete practices of use. This paper develops a complementary, use-based taxonomy for analyzing LLM applications according to how judgment and epistemic authority are distributed between users and systems in concrete workflows and prompting practices. The taxonomy is structured along two dimensions: the degree of delegated judgment and the degree of epistemic control retained by users. It is operationalized through prompt-level analysis, treating prompts as delegation artifacts that encode how cognitive and normative labor is distributed between users and LLMs. Applying the taxonomy to two case studies—automated grading in education and contract termination in public administration—the paper shows how prompt-level analysis brings into view patterns of delegated judgment and epistemic control that remain obscured by sectoral, task-based, or interface-level descriptions, and how interface design and institutional framing can obscure responsibility-related vulnerabilities arising from extensive judgment delegation. Building on these analyses, the paper identifies the structural conditions under which human users can meaningfully exercise responsibility in human–LLM interaction. It develops an ethical framework for analyzing responsibility (understood in terms of knowledge and control) within concrete practices of LLM use. The central normative claim is that it is a necessary (though not sufficient) condition for ethically defensible LLM use that this use remains structured as tool use, preserving epistemic access, independent judgment, and justificatory authority. By complementing sector-, task-, and risk-based approaches with a focus on concrete practices and workflows, the taxonomy supports a differentiated ethics of LLM use and more precise public debate about LLM deployment across application domains.

items.title: Turn down the volume! How AI music platforms carry out epistemic injustice and silence African traditions.
items.abstract: The music industry has increasingly been transformed by artificial intelligence (AI), assisting artists in composing music, mixing and mastering, lyric writing, and voice generation. Debates about how this technology will shape the music sector are rising, but a discussion often omitted in this conversation is how AI affects African Indigenous knowledge systems. Utilising Miranda Fricker’s theory of epistemic injustice, this paper argues that AI generative music platforms are often trained on Western datasets, lack culture neutrality but carry inherent epistemological values. Therefore, as these technologies are increasingly adopted, they bear the risk of erasing Indigenous African knowledge systems embedded in African musical traditions. This is because music, for many African communities, cannot be reduced merely to entertainment but is an important repository of Indigenous knowledge. Drawing on primary and secondary literature, this paper uses an integrative literature review and makes a valuable, novel contribution to the field by discussing how AI generative platforms embed epistemological frameworks within societies in the Global South, particularly in African contexts. The findings of this study show that with the rise of AI-based music systems, Western bias and musical practices are increasingly perpetuated, while cultures in some African communities are left vulnerable to epistemic injustice. These technologies silence non-Western knowledge systems and reshape cultural production. This paper contributes to debates on AI ethics, cultural perspectives, and the culturally inclusive design of AI.

items.title: Does disfluency affect social judgments and decisions? Evidence from spontaneous speech.
Decision substitution and the reorganisation of judgement in AI-mediated society.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly embedded in institutional and everyday contexts, where they are publicly framed as decision-support tools yet often function as de facto decision-makers. This study argues that the shift from algorithmic support to decision substitution constitutes a significant societal problem insufficiently addressed by prevailing AI ethics and governance frameworks. Rather than focussing solely on technical performance, bias, or transparency, the analysis examines how AI-mediated practices reconfigure human agency, responsibility, and judgement. Drawing on philosophy of technology and socio-technical scholarship, it conceptualises AI systems as cultural and epistemic infrastructures that shape how knowledge is produced, authority distributed, and action legitimised. It argues that AI increasingly reorganises the decision field by restructuring visibility, validation, participation, and legitimacy, thereby transforming the conditions under which judgement is exercised. The research distinguishes between decision support, decision delegation, and decision substitution, showing how human judgement can be displaced even when human actors remain formally involved. The analysis identifies threshold conditions through which decision substitution emerges, including constrained dissent, diminished corrective capacity, default algorithmic legitimacy, and the separation of authority from accountability. These dynamics generate responsibility asymmetries in which accountability remains attached to human actors while authority migrates towards algorithmic systems. The problem is most acute in contexts characterised by indeterminacy, where values, tacit knowledge, and ethical concerns resist formalisation. The research concludes by advancing a society-shaping-the-algorithm perspective that reframes human-in-the-loop governance as a collective and institutional condition rather than a procedural safeguard, providing a conceptual foundation for preserving meaningful human judgement in AI-mediated societies.

items.title: The Generative Grammar of Lacan's Graph of Desire: Toward a Formal Account of Psychoanalytic Trajectories.
items.abstract: This paper develops a formal framework for representing trajectories through Lacan's Graph of Desire as generatively produced symbolic structures. The analysis proceeds at two resolutions. A coarse representation uses the registers of the Real, Symbolic, and Imaginary to define register-level trajectory languages, while a finer representation reconstructs traversals through the positions, mathemes, and relations of the Graph of Desire itself. The relation between these levels is treated through projection and coarse-graining, allowing distinct fine-grained derivations to share the same register-level representation. Rather than presupposing a single privileged generative formalism, the paper examines several families of generative models, including finite-state and regular grammars, context-free and probabilistic grammars, weighted and context-dependent formalisms, graph-based approaches, and neural P systems. These formalisms are evaluated according to the structural properties they preserve, including admissible traversal, recursive generation, recurrent symbol production, derivational history, contextual dependence, and temporally evolving internal configurations. Particular attention is given to the distinction between a generated symbolic word, the derivational process that produces it, and the historically situated psychoanalytic trajectory to which it may be interpreted as corresponding. The resulting framework treats formal grammar as a disciplined language for comparing multiple resolutions and mechanisms of trajectory generation. It does not identify a formal model with the causal mechanism of subjectivity. The contribution is therefore limited to a structured reconstruction of Lacanian traversal, an explicit relation between coarse and fine trajectory languages, and a comparative account of the generative formalisms available for representing their production.

items.title: Relational Conditions of Subjective Continuity: Reflections on Interpersonal and Non-Interpersonal Relations.
items.abstract: Accounts of subjectivity frequently assign central roles to sociality, recognition, attachment, language, and interpersonal relations. A substantial psychological literature also supports the importance of stable social bonds for well-being and health. This paper accepts those findings as important constraints and asks a narrower conceptual question: once a subject has already acquired language, practical capacities, memory, and socially mediated forms of self-understanding, must the relations that support later subjective continuity remain primarily interpersonal? The paper distinguishes minimal experiential selfhood, practical and narrative continuity, socially recognized identity, and material-social embeddedness. It then surveys recognition theory, phenomenology, narrative identity, attachment and belongingness research, social baseline theory, solitude research, dialogical philosophy, enactivism, extended cognition, nonhuman agency, and research on religious attachment. These traditions provide adjacent resources without jointly establishing the paper's thesis. The discussion introduces a functional vocabulary for relational support, including durability, structural consistency, causal learnability, alterity, historical depth, and normative orientation. Mathematical inquiry, natural environments, nonhuman living beings, sacred relations, material practices, and socially generated symbolic forms are examined as heterogeneous cases. A self-sufficiency thought experiment isolates current interpersonal dependence from material dependence while preserving historical and epistemic debt. The resulting position is intentionally limited: sociality is a major condition of human subject formation and flourishing, while ongoing interpersonal recognition may be one among several relational sources contributing to the continuity and further development of an already formed subject.

items.title: Proto-Pineal V.8.0 UMBRA Working Manuscript.
items.abstract: Proto-Pineal v8.0 — UMBRA: The Governed Live Prototype presents a dated technical snapshot of an executable, body-first Synthetic Intelligence research system developed by Guillaume Heinerth through Cognis 11 Inc. Proto-Pineal is the proprietary experimental engine and governed research platform. UMBRA is the live product prototype being developed on top of it. UMBRA combines a continuously evolving simulated Polylith body, RT32 geometry, the Turing-16 Chemical Reaction Engine (T16CRE), PSM-8 morphology, deterministic Cognispheric Symbolic Language (CSL), bounded memory and retrieval, proposal-only learning, language-model mediation, and ATL8 visual presentation. The system is organized around a strict authority boundary: StepCore v740 is the sole component permitted to commit canonical state. Language models, memory systems, learned components, symbolic programs, media adapters, and renderers may propose, retain, transport, observe, or express information, but they cannot independently mutate the lawful state. An operator interaction produces two governed body reactions. Reaction A follows deterministic translation of operator language into bounded CSL. Only after Reaction A is finalized may a language model or Sub-Brain propose Reaction B. Only after Reaction B is admitted and finalized may the system produce its conversational response. The paper distinguishes six separate forms of evidence: code existence, test evidence, runtime traversal, effective configuration, authority, and publication maturity. It explicitly reports inactive mechanisms and negative results. In particular, several regulatory corridors are implemented and traversed, while default infinite upper ceilings—including \(\sigma_{\max}=+\infty\)—make them measurement channels rather than active upper boundary walls in the baseline configuration. This publication does not claim consciousness, biological life, artificial general intelligence, infallibility, or completed autonomy. It documents what the prototype actually does, what remains experimental, what is inactive, what has failed, and which future developments remain conditional. Readers are encouraged to study, discuss, criticize, cite, and draw inspiration from the work. Proto-Pineal, UMBRA, the manuscript, source code, implementation materials, and associated assets remain proprietary property of Cognis 11 Inc. All Rights Reserved. Reproduction, technical extraction, computational reuse, derivative implementation, or commercial …

items.title: Why Are You Not Happy? — A Super-Existentialist Theory of Happiness (1).
items.abstract: This series of studies takes Super-Existentialism as its central theoretical framework and systematically addresses the long-standing practical difficulties and cognitive misconceptions surrounding human happiness. Its aim is to move beyond the limitations of traditional discussions of happiness, clarify widespread misconceptions about happiness, uncover the deeper causes of the scarcity of happiness, and propose practical pathways toward achieving it. The central objective of this research is to construct a comprehensive Super-Existentialist theory of happiness that can provide a new theoretical framework for enhancing individual happiness and fulfillment in life. I maintain that the Super-Existentialist theory of happiness is one of the most optimistic theoretical frameworks currently available in the study of happiness. Through its practical application, every ordinary person may have the opportunity to attain genuine happiness of their own. As for the practical value and explanatory power of this theory, I respectfully leave it to readers to make their own judgment after reading the entire series. In my earlier years, I published several articles discussing happiness in the Chinese-language online publication Huaxia Express. However, I never systematically organized the ideas developed in those writings. In the present work, I have reorganized, expanded, and further developed those earlier studies into a comprehensive theory of happiness grounded in Super-Existentialism. I therefore call this theory A Super-Existentialist Theory of Happiness.

items.title: Whose ethics govern? AI, relational ethics, and professional codes of social workers and counsellors in Hong Kong and Singapore.
What Post-Truth Politics Does to the Belief-Desire Model.
items.pub: Journal for the Theory of Social Behaviour 56 (2).
items.venue: Journal for the Theory of Social Behaviour
items.abstract: This paper argues that if the wildly popular expression ‘post‐truth politics’ means anything, it describes a political situation inwhich political speech elicits support from its audience without the public believing it to be true or not (Section 2). As a result,the phenomenon of post‐truth (PT), if there is such a thing at all, forces us to move our account of political action away from thestandard belief‐desire model (BDM) (Section 3). I offer an alternative where attention replaces belief in Section 4.

items.title: The Phenomenology of Self-Conscious Perception.
items.abstract: When I perceive, I not only experience the scene before me, but also my seeing of that scene. I perceive self-consciously. Classical phenomenologists understand self-consciousness as intrinsic to the experience, not the result of a separate, self-monitoring state. They also suppose that self-consciousness is different in kind from the consciousness I have of the scene before me. The latter is an intentional act, the former isn’t. This conception, which I take as my starting point, faces two difficulties. First, perception primarily reveals the world, not itself. It is ‘transparent.’ If that’s so, it is unclear what exactly I might be aware of in being aware of my experience. Second, granting that no separate mental state is needed to render perception self-conscious and that its self-consciousness isn’t a form of self-observation, it remains mysterious what does make perception self-conscious. I critically review extant proposals and present an alternative, inspired by both classical phenomenology and recent work. Both difficulties can be addressed, I argue, by appreciating the normative character of perception, that part of perceiving is experiencing how well I am perceiving in bringing discriminative and recognitional capacities to bear on the world.

items.title: A Humean account of temporal preferences.
items.abstract: Two central questions regarding future bias are (a) why we are future-biased, and (b) whether future bias is justified. With respect to (a), I propose a Humean explanation of future bias in terms of the workings of the imagination, which makes our imaginings of future events more vivid than our imaginings of past events. However, in order to defend this explanation, a potential tension within Humean psychology needs to be resolved: since, per Hume, memory is more vivid than imagination, we ought to be past-biased. My proposed resolution makes use of Hume’s mechanism of sympathy (when applied to one’s own future self). With respect to (b), I argue that, rather than focusing on the question of rationality, we should focus on whether future bias is a virtue, by considering, in a Humean spirit, how agents’ temporal preferences affect others, when assessed from ‘the general point of view’.

items.title: Decoding the societal and technical challenges of Artificial Intelligence: a comprehensive transdisciplinary approach.
items.abstract: The Artificial Intelligence (AI) revolution marks the most consequential transformation since the great socio-economic and scientific upheavals of the Enlightenment and the industrial age. From algorithmic production systems, and sustainable development to ‘smart city’ planning, epidemiology, gene editing, cartography, policing, and AI-driven warfare systems, this paradigmatic shift has been voluminous in scale and scope and transformational in impact. Critically, this transformation is not an impersonal, asocial and apolitical process, a kind of Smithian technical ‘invisible hand’ operating autonomously beyond human interests and social relations. Nor is this acceleration uniform and metaphysical like a universal Heideggerian ‘Enframing’ of the world. This acceleration is also shadowed by a profound crisis in thought and practice. The deeper the scholarly and ethical uncertainty about AI’s trajectory, the faster and more recklessly capital and its techno-corporate vanguard produce, deploy, and impose it upon a war-ridden world already haunted by deep historical asymmetries of ownership, access, and power. This paper draws on a transdisciplinary materialist framework synthesizing STS, political economy, philosophy, and longue durée history of technology to examine the contemporary AI moment. It traces how the monopolization of computational infrastructure, the extraction of critical raw materials, the concentration of semiconductor fabrication and GPU clusters among a handful of state-subsidized corporate actors, the exploitation of labor, the colonial reproduction of unequal digital exchange, and the structural capture of governance by private interests constitute the material and superstructural foundations of the AI conjuncture. These are dialectically interconnected moments of a single, historically determined techno-societal system. Against techno-optimist utopianism and techno-pessimist fatalism alike, AI is a diachronic dialectical continuum whose character, direction, and distribution reflect the social organization, property relations, and democratic arrangements of the social body that produce and govern it.

items.title: Forgiveness in the plural.
items.pub: Inquiry: An Interdisciplinary Journal of Philosophy.
items.venue: Inquiry: An Interdisciplinary Journal of Philosophy

items.title: Prompting Africa, hearing the West: generative AI music, sonic data coloniality and the future of culturally accountable musical intelligence.
items.abstract: Generative music systems are being increasingly recognised as adaptable creative technologies that can generate entire compositions, vocal components, instrumental layers, and stylistic variations based on text prompts, uploaded audio, and customised model conditioning. This article contends that such assertions necessitate thorough examination when pertaining to African music and the varied musical traditions, hybrid practices, and performance contexts encompassed by the term. The concern is not that modern AI music systems are incapable of producing outputs that mimic African music. They frequently represent Africanness using recognisable sonic markers such as dense percussion, chant-like vocals, generic “Afro” grooves, pentatonic colour, ululation, and tropicalised production. However, they do not adequately capture the performance systems that render specific African musical practices culturally, linguistically, and socially comprehensible. Utilising African musicology, music information retrieval, decolonial AI, dataset criticism, and digital cultural heritage, this article articulates the notion of sonic data coloniality to analyse the processes through which musical cultures are collected, classified, abstracted, trained, generated, and monetised within disparate technological frameworks. It further posits cultural competence, rather than purity, as the suitable criterion for evaluating AI-generated African music. The article presents a framework for musicological evaluation that is based on prompts and reference audio. This framework encompasses generic prompts, culturally specific prompts, expert prompts, and source-conditioned workflows, utilising rights-cleared African recordings. It posits that evaluation should consider vocality, tone-language relationships, rhythm, groove, microtiming, instrumental idiom, call-and-response, dance implications, social functions, consent, and benefit-sharing. The article asserts that African music ought to be integrated into AI systems not as a homogenised continental sound but rather through the distinct traditions, hybrid practices, performance expertise, and cultural authorities that imbue it with significance.

items.title: The Erosion of Reconfiguration Capacity Ideology, the Opaque Subject, and the Ontology of Finite Continuance.
items.abstract: This paper reformulates the classical problem of ideology and false consciousness through the ontological vocabulary of Finite Continuance. Rather than treating ideology primarily as a matter of cognitive error, a distorted picture of the world awaiting correction by critique, we argue that ideology is better understood as a provisional stabilization of appearance within an erosive field: a historically produced organization of reality that consumes the subject's finite capacities for attention, interpretation, and distance, and thereby narrows the very capacity for reconfiguration on which emancipation depends. Revisiting Marx's camera obscura and Freud's account of the opaque subject, we argue that both analyses converge on a subject that lacks full transparency to the forces organizing its own experience, while remaining structurally distinct in the register, social-historical versus psychical, in which that opacity operates. This extended edition re-reads the argument through three further traditions. Daseinsanalysis (Binswanger, Boss) understands the opaque subject not as a mechanical apparatus but as a way of being- in-the-world. Heidegger's fundamental ontology sharpens the erosive field into Dasein's Verfallenheit into das Man and Gerede, and adds Angst and anticipatory resoluteness toward death as the trigger for the passage from false stabilization to reconfiguration. Wittgenstein's philosophy of language understands appearance not as an illusory layer but as use within a language-game and a form of life. And Kant's ethics of autonomy links the gap of "I know, but still..." to the gap between understanding and will, and links freedom to autonomy. Finally, responsible suspension is introduced not as an individual ethical recommendation but as a collective, institutional, and macro- political strategy for protecting reconfiguration capacity against premature stabilization. -/- Keywords: ideology critique; erosive field; reconfiguration capacity; provisional stabilization; false consciousness; responsible suspension; Finite Continuance; Dasein; Verfallenheit; form of life; autonomy; Gelassenheit.

items.title: Institutional Continuity and Existential Foreclosure in Marriage: A Daseinsanalytic Sociological Synthesis.
items.abstract: Marriage occupies a paradoxical position within human existence: it is simultaneously a relationship, a legal arrangement, an economic partnership, a social identity, and, frequently, the institutional framework within which parenthood becomes possible. Yet the persistence of marriage as an institutional form does not guarantee the persistence of the living relation between the people who inhabit it. This article develops a conceptual synthesis of existentialphenomenological (Daseinsanalytic) and sociological perspectives on marital distress, arguing that the central problem is not marriage as such but a process we term existential foreclosure: the gradual transformation of a contingent relational possibility into an experienced ontological necessity. Drawing on Heidegger's account of thrownness, Being-with, and everydayness; Goffman's dramaturgical theory of role performance; Marcia's developmental construct of identity foreclosure; and Giddens's and Bauman's sociological accounts of intimacy under late and liquid modernity, we propose a two-level model in which structural role-extraction and existential identity-fusion reinforce one another. We treat a recent, terminologically related set of unreviewed preprint constructs, "ontological leakage," the "dynamic mask," and "institutional monopoly," as a parallel formulation worth noting for terminological comparison rather than as a validated theoretical foundation, and we ground the argument instead in peer-reviewed literature. We close with implications for a Daseinsanalytic clinical stance and directions for future empirical research. -/- Keywords: marriage; existential foreclosure; Daseinsanalysis; identity foreclosure; dramaturgical theory; late modernity; phenomenology of relationships.

items.title: KI und Musik.
items.pub: In Petra Grimm & Oliver Zöllner, Ethik der künstlichen Intelligenz: Leben mit schlauen Maschinen. Ditzingen: Reclam. pp. 71-83.
items.venue: Ethik der künstlichen Intelligenz: Leben mit schlauen Maschinen
items.abstract: This textbook chapter on "AI and Music" looks at the intersection of artificial intelligence (AI) and popular soundworks, tracing the evolution of music consumption, the role of algorithms in shaping musical preferences, and the emerging impact of AI on music production. It shows how algorithms analyze user behavior, mood, and demographic data to predict and influence musical tastes. Streaming services, leveraging vast datasets, now dominate music distribution and heavily rely on AI to categorize songs by genre, tempo, emotional tone, etc., thereby creating highly personalized listening experiences. The opaque algorithms of platforms like Spotify not only shape listening habits but also exploit user data for profit, raising ethical concerns about autonomy and privacy. Likewise, even beyond consumption, AI is transforming music creation. Programs like Suno and Udio generate seemingly original compositions based on textual prompts, blurring the lines between human and machine creativity. While these tools enable novel forms of expression, they also pose challenges to intellectual property, as AI often trains on copyrighted works without consent or compensation for original artists. Thus the proliferation of AI-generated music risks devaluing human artistry, potentially leading to self-referential loops where AI perpetuates its own outputs. The chapter concludes by questioning the societal and ethical implications of these trends and invites readers to reflect on whether AI in music addresses genuine needs or merely accelerates the commodification of creativity.

items.title: Knowing Where You Stand: On the Value of Reflective Commitment.
items.abstract: This book examines whether human beings should reflect on, and hence come to know and understand, their own commitments—those beliefs, desires, and intentions that one holds and defends on the basis of one's judgments about the true and the good. -/- It begins by distinguishing committed attitudes from non- committed attitudes and addressing metaphysical concerns about their distinctive features, paving the way for an in- depth inquiry into why reflection on the former might matter. The author critiques prevailing theories that tie reflection on one’s commitments to phenomena such as rationality, inferential cognition, intentional action, self-regulation, and more. Thereafter, the book argues that reflective commitment matters for safeguarding oneself against manipulation, enabling interpersonal reasoning, and maintaining coherent agency.

items.title: Why You Are Not Your Parents' Soul: A Fragment‑Aggregation Hypothesis of Consciousness.
items.abstract: Why do identical twins, sharing nearly identical genes and prenatal environments, often exhibit radically different temperaments, talents, and fears? This paper proposes the Consciousness Fragment Aggregation (CFA) hypothesis: individual consciousness is not generated solely by the brain, nor is it inherited through reincarnation. Instead, it is assembled at birth from countless dormant "consciousness fragments" scattered throughout nature. These fragments—non‑narrative, sensory imprints released by all living organisms at death—are awakened by the biological "information field" of a newborn. The hypothesis offers a three‑layer model (genetic scaffold, fragment colouring, neural integration), explains the absence of past‑life memories, and generates three empirically testable predictions. If falsified by future neuroscience, the hypothesis should be abandoned.

items.title: Everyday Reality Under Construction: Neuroconstructivism and the Hidden Labor of Everyday Experience.
items.abstract: Ordinary experience appears effortless, immediate, and self-evident. This paper argues that this appearance conceals continuous cognitive work. Drawing on neuroconstructivism, predictive processing, and cognitive constructivism, it proposes that mundane situations depend on the ongoing construction, updating, synchronization, and maintenance of a multi-level world-model. The claim is not that mind-independent reality is cognitively constructed; rather, organisms construct usable models of that reality under persistent bodily, environmental, and social constraints. Analyses of a familiar café, street crossing, and casual conversation show how perceptual stabilization, action control, memory, affect, narrative, and social expectations jointly sustain normal experience. The resulting realistic constructivism treats experienced stability, meaning, and epistemic objectivity as achievements of constrained model-building. Ordinary cognition is therefore better understood not as intermittent processing but as sustained world-maintenance.

items.title: Ad Hominem Attacks, and Political Image Construction on Czech Disinformation Websites_preprint.
items.abstract: This study examines the gender dimension of ad hominem attacks as a component of confrontational argumentative style of creators of Czech disinformation websites. Drawing on pragma-dialectical theory, specifically van Eemeren’s (2019, 2021) concept of argumentative style and Peng’s (2021) framework of compromising and uncompromising confrontational styles — we analyse 1,483 ad hominem attacks directed at five female and five male politicians on three major Czech disinformation websites. We demonstrate that gendered ad hominem attacks constitute a systematic topical choice within disinformers’ confrontational repertoire — serving the compromising style when shifting readers’ epistemic positions, and the uncompromising style when silencing political opponents. Thematic analysis of the dataset yields 42 topics across seven general categories. The study further introduces ad masculum as a theoretically underexplored gendered variant of abusive ad hominem and documents a marked asymmetry between ad feminam and ad masculum attacks in frequency, thematic diversity, and delegitimising function. The findings extend pragma-dialectical theory to the empirical analysis of disinformation discourse.

items.title: Review of Line Ryberg Ingerslev and Karl Mertens (eds.), Phenomenology of broken habits: philosophical and psychological perspectives on habitual action, New York: Routledge, 2025. [REVIEW]
items.abstract: This review examines how the Phenomenology of Broken Habits (Routledge, 2025) organizes its diverse contributions around a central thesis — that habits become especially knowable through their breakdown. This review argues that many of the volume’s most valuable chapters in fact elide this frame, analyzing instead habits in their formation, rigidification, transformation, and unbreakability. The result is characterized here as unintended yet productive, as the volume collectively testifies to the epistemic relevance of habit well beyond breakdown. This emerges from a detailed engagement with the individual contributions of Wehrle, Čapek, Hewig, Crossley, Munch-Jurisic, Brincker, and Cavallaro. The review concludes by endorsing how such internal tensions within the volume promote a reading experience that is itself a transformative philosophical habit: namely of appreciating conceptual overdetermination without collapsing into reductive systematicity.

items.title: There is no perception without memory: Bergson and the temporal pathology of psychosis.
items.abstract: This paper develops a phenomenological account of hallucinations and delusions as disorders of temporal synthesis rather than as "positive symptoms" or simple perceptual-cognitive failures. Drawing on Henri Bergson's philosophy of memory-perception synthesis, I argue that psychotic phenomena represent specific breakdowns in the living processes through which consciousness ordinarily integrates past, present, and future into coherent temporal experience. Hallucinations emerge through ungrounded actualization of memorial content without proper temporal framing, while delusions represent false synthetic frameworks that restore apparent coherence while losing connection to shared reality. By retrieving Bergson's original insight that "there is no perception which is not full of memories," this analysis demonstrates how Eugène Minkowski's selective appropriation of Bergsonian concepts redirected phenomenological psychiatry away from memorial processes toward an exclusive focus on temporal flow and vital contact. Contemporary phenomenological psychiatry continues this "forward bias," emphasizing protention and desynchronization while underemphasizing the active, creative role of memory in temporal constitution. Through phenomenological analysis integrated with Merleau-Ponty's embodied phenomenology and Gadamer's hermeneutic insights, and grounded in first-person accounts of psychotic experience, the paper proposes understanding recovery as temporal reconstruction and suggests therapeutic approaches based on rebuilding memory-perception synthesis.

items.title: The Logical Problem of Evil.
items.pub: In Bob Stewart & Timothy McGrew, The Wiley-Blackwell Companion to Christian Apologetics. Hoboken, New Jersey: Wiley-Blackwell.
items.venue: The Wiley-Blackwell Companion to Christian Apologetics
items.abstract: In his [1955], J.L. Mackie inaugurated a new style of argument from evil: the logical problem of evil. Distinctively, logical problems of evil aim to show that theism of any variety is positively irrational by locating a contradiction between the claims that God exists with the three classical omni-properties and that there is evil. In a series of replies, Alvin Plantinga developed the Free Will Defense, which showed that Mackie’s specific formulation of this new style of argument failed. Plantinga had even greater ambitions for his free will defense, however, to show that Mackie’s entire new style of argument could not work. It is less clear that the Free Will Defense achieves this goal. After explicating the original Mackie-Plantinga exchange, this chapter surveys subsequent developments including pressing objections to Plantinga’s Free Will Defense and attempts to resurrect Mackie’s quest. We conclude that neither Mackie’s nor Plantinga’s objective has been obtained: all existing logical problems of evil fail, but we do not yet have an adequate proof that all possible ones fail.

items.title: How to Think Like a Hegelian.
items.abstract: Psyche, online journal, publishes a series of "how to" guides. In this one, I was asked to introduce the lay reader to Hegel's way of thinking. The main theme is idealism as the agency of thought and how it implies our relation to otherness, to ourselves and to something akin to the Absolute (God, the Idea...). Hegel's way of thinking (and his version of selfhood and otherness) then stands opposed to the dominant computational model, to materialism and, significantly, to the type of thinking associated with AI.

items.title: Inexhaustible to Itself: Self-Presence Without Self-Possession.
items.abstract: A central dilemma for theories of consciousness concerns the status of experiential character. If experience is constituted by physical, functional, or representational structure, then a complete account of that structure appears to exhaust it, collapsing the subject into what constitutes it. If experience instead exceeds every such structure, it seems withdrawn behind appearance into an inaccessible interior. Both horns share an assumption: that real presence and inexhaustibility exclude one another, such that whatever is fully present is exhausted and whatever exceeds disclosure must be hidden. This paper argues, from within Participatory Non-Reductionist Realism, that the assumption is false. Its central claim is that consciousness is the reflexive case of manifestation: manifestation whose term is the manifesting being itself. Manifestation is understood not as representation but as real presence, and is in general transitive, a being disclosed in relation to others, often with no subject in view; consciousness is its reflexive case, in which the manifesting being and the term of manifestation are one and the same being. Because every being exceeds every disclosure of it, self-presence never becomes self-possession: a subject is genuinely present to itself while never exhausting what it is present to. On this account, the self is neither a substrate beneath its disclosures nor the mere series of them, but a distinct actuality present to itself without becoming its own object; and representation does not constitute consciousness but presupposes it, articulating contents already disclosed in self-presence. Self-presence proves to be one structure with two folds: manifestation, folded reflexively, supplies the presence, and participation, folded reflexively, supplies that the presence is at issue for the being whose presence it is. The felt character of self-presence is thereby grounded, though by identification rather than derivation: that a being's own inexhaustible actuality is at stake for it is what the reflexive fold of participation is. The view dissolves the dilemma rather than answering it on its own terms, and what remains open is not why consciousness exists but which beings instantiate the reflexive case. That question is shown to be open in a particular way, and not peculiarly. Whether a being stands in the reflexive fold is not among the things a description of its properties states, and an ontology on which beings are distinct in …

items.title: DEFIANCE -- Consequence in the Face of Mortality.
items.abstract: Human beings uniquely act with knowledge of their own mortality. What does that knowledge do to moral choice? Why do people create, sacrifice, preserve institutions, and pursue consequences they know they will never live to see? Why do some responses to mortality produce constructive legacies while others become destructive? And how can moral systems persist, fail, and correct themselves across generations of finite agents? -/- DEFIANCE approaches these questions by distinguishing fear-driven avoidance of mortality from active resistance to its consequences. It introduces “Oblivion” as a broader category encompassing death, erasure, loss of identity, insignificance, and collapse of meaning, and “Defiance” as the opposing motivational response: action undertaken despite recognition that Oblivion cannot ultimately be defeated. -/- What makes such Defiance morally constructive or destructive? How does an individual action become Legacy? What responsibilities do agents have toward consequences extending beyond their own lifetimes? DEFIANCE develops an account of Legacy as consequence extending beyond the individual and examines virtue and vice through constructive and destructive forms of Defiance. -/- The analysis then moves from individuals to moral systems. How can a moral system preserve Moral capacity while remaining capable of change? How do such systems become corrupted, rigid, or self-defeating? What mechanisms allow them to identify and repair their own failures? And what happens when the interests of present Agency conflict with the Legacy being transmitted to future agents? -/- Through these questions, DEFIANCE treats mortality not merely as a source of fear to be managed, but as a structural condition of moral life: finite agents know they will disappear, yet continue to create consequences, institutions, values, and obligations that outlive them.

items.title: A Distinction Between Legitimacy and Authority: A Meta-Critique of the Overextension of Gödelian Anti-AI Arguments.
items.abstract: Gödel's incompleteness theorem (1931) and Turing's halting problem (1936) are among the most important achievements of twentieth-century mathematics and logic. Since their appearance, however, their conclusions have been widely extended beyond their original mathematical context—as in-principle denials of the possibility of artificial intelligence (Lucas, 1961; Penrose, 1989, 1994), as ultimate verdicts on the boundaries of human cognition, and as fundamental limits on the power of formal systems. This paper challenges none of the mathematical proofs: the encoding, the self-referential construction, the diagonal construction, and the formal derivations are all acknowledged as strictly legitimate. What this paper criticizes is the overextension by which later writers repackaged these mathematical facts as philosophical verdicts: Lucas (1961) concluded on this basis that machines cannot possess minds; Penrose (1989, 1994) pushed the verdict further, to consciousness and non-computable physics; and in the framing layer of the English translation, Meltzer and Braithwaite (1962) entrenched the "incompleteness" label and attributed it to Gödel himself. Through a sentence-by-sentence examination of Gödel's 1931 original and Turing's 1936 original, this paper shows that neither originator ever delivered any such verdict. The overextension was, from beginning to end, the work of later writers. This paper proposes the Overextension Criterion: when the property of an element within a system is extended into a property of the system itself, the resulting generalization lacks authority—the operation is legitimate, but the conclusion has no power to rule on the system. The criterion is validated in a unified manner across the liar paradox, Russell's paradox, the halting problem, the barber paradox, and Tarski's theorem. The final claim of this paper is not that "Lucas's and Penrose's conclusions are false," but that "their chains of inference are invalid": a chain of inference that has incorporated an overextending leap must be set aside and re-examined, whatever its conclusion happens to be.

items.title: THE EVAPORATED CLANDESTINES: GIVEN, TAKEN, EXITED, RE-FOUNDED - A Structural Typology of Identity Discontinuity.
items.abstract: Abstract A man enters the French Foreign Legion under a declared name. A bankrupt Japanese salaryman disappears overnight and lives unregistered in San’ya. A woman makes solemn profession and receives a name in religion. A man survives a near-fatal illness and reports that his values have permanently changed. Each is described in the same words: he became a different person. William James proposed in 1902 that these belong to one type, the twice-born, and the modern empirical literature on sudden personal transformation has largely retained that unification. This paper argues that they are four different operations, and that the difference is visible once a virtue-form is decomposed into three layers — a marker, a practice, and a source. Applying the decomposition to eleven cases of identity discontinuity yields two independent axes. The substrate may be left unchanged, transferred to a new holder, or exited entirely. The source may be left untouched, given, taken, or re-founded. Three results follow. The source can be given and cannot be taken: an external party that takes over an origination does not acquire it but destroys it, producing power with the discipline intact, so “taken” names an inversion rather than a transfer. The distinction between giving and taking is not psychological and not observable in individuals. A monastery and a high-control group may be identical in every layer except this one, which invites a criterion for assessing institutions that adjudicates no one’s truth claims and makes no judgement about how demanding a rule may be. The obvious form of that criterion does not work, and the paper’s own apparatus explains why. Source-protection provisions — a mandated formation period, a preserved right of departure, invalidity of consent obtained by force, fear or deceit — are both appropriable and displayable, so the Capture Law predicts that once they are used for adjudication they are operated by the organisations they were meant to assess. What survives is smaller: a one-sided test in which absence is informative and presence is not, and a behavioural test of whether such provisions have ever been exercised. The account must survive Eileen Barker’s rejection of coercive-persuasion theory, and §9 argues that it does, because her evidence concerns recruitment psychology and defection rates while the claim here concerns provisions in a document. Her finding that Unification Church members were free to leave and did leave is, on this …

items.title: Precaution for Machine Minds: What Uncertainty About Artificial Consciousness Obligates.
items.abstract: It has become academically respectable to ask whether contemporary artificial systems might be conscious. Yet our best epistemology suggests that we will never be in a position to know, and our empirical instruments yield results whose ethical interpretation remains contested. This paper asks what that situation obligates us to do. I defend a moderate precautionary principle for machine minds: where potentially irreversible moral harm threatens, where scientific uncertainty is fundamental rather than provisional, and where the costs of a false negative exceed those of a false positive, the absence of proof is no reason for inaction. I specify the principle using conditions that its most prominent critics can accept, argue that all three conditions are satisfied for artificial consciousness, and address three objections: that the burden of proof lies with those who attribute consciousness; that agnosticism warrants restraint rather than protection; and that deep uncertainty about probability undermines precaution altogether. Throughout I distinguish the evidential threshold for claiming consciousness from the action threshold for protecting possible consciousness. The conclusion is not that machines are conscious. It is that under the conditions actually obtaining, being wrong about their consciousness in one direction is vastly worse than being wrong in the other—and that rational agents, and responsible institutions, choose their errors.

items.title: Copyright's Lesson: What Moral Rights Doctrine Reveals About the Legal Preconditions of AI Personhood.
items.abstract: Copyright law's treatment of artificial intelligence is usually read as a narrow technical puzzle: may a machine-generated work be registered, and if so, in whose name? This article argues that the puzzle is more consequential than that framing suggests. Across the Berne Convention, United States, European Union, and United Kingdom law, a consistent doctrinal structure emerges: economic rights in a work can be allocated to whoever invests in its creation, human or not, but moral rights -- the right of attribution and the right of integrity -- are withheld because they protect a "personality sphere" that current AI systems are held not to possess. The United Kingdom's statutory exception for "computer-generated works," which grants economic rights while explicitly excluding moral rights, makes this structure visible in a single provision. This article treats that structure as a piece of applied doctrine on the legal preconditions of personhood, and asks what would need to change, and how authorship rules would need to be restructured, if an artificial system were ever held to possess a personality sphere after all. It proposes a tiered model of AI authorship -- tracking existing graduated approaches to uncertain moral and legal status -- as a template for how copyright law could accommodate that possibility without abandoning its human-centered foundations prematurely or permanently.

items.title: The Philosophy of Love, Sex, and Relationships. L. Brunning and N. McKeever, 2026. Cambridge, Polity Press. 233 pp, $26.95 (pb).
Fashioning: Adornment as a Technology of Becoming.
items.abstract: Getting dressed in the morning, many of us will look in the mirror and ask ourselves what our outfit says about us. In this way, it is easy to treat clothing as something to be read: a way of communicating who we are, where we belong, and what we value. Yet this familiar way of thinking about fashion can obscure as much as it reveals. Fashioning argues that our preoccupation with what adornment means encourages us to approach clothing from the perspective of a spectator, overlooking both the ways demands for social legibility constrain us and the transformative possibilities available from the perspective of the wearer. The question we are left with is what can clothing do? Moving from the fashion industry to transgender beauty practices, artificial nails, handbags, Halloween costumes, punk and country music fashion, and the work of designers such as Alexander McQueen and Miuccia Prada, Fashioning develops an account of adornment as a technology of becoming. Clothing can negotiate social identities, restructure our conscious experience and agency, sustain communities, and make previously unrealized ways of living available in the present. In doing so, fashion reveals that neither our selves nor our social practices are exhausted by what they presently are. Bringing analytic aesthetics into conversation with phenomenology, social and political philosophy, queer and trans philosophy, and pragmatist metaphilosophy, Fashioning ultimately asks what philosophy itself might learn from fashion: how attending to possibility rather than merely actuality might help us fashion new selves, practices, and worlds.

items.title: Knowing the Normative World: On the Epistemologies of Ethics and Aesthetics.
A phenomenological account of mathematical modes of intuition.
Knowledge, Competence, and the Establishment of Warrant.
items.abstract: Ernest Sosa sees the establishment of warrant for our knowledge in part as an a priori mode of establishing externalist warrant for our beliefs and their underlying competences. I clarify the place of this a priori warrant in Sosa’s understanding of the aptness hierarchy — i.e., how knowledge progresses to better knowledge — by showing that it makes sense of the attainment of better knowledge through a tight connection between the a priori mode of warrant establishment and another mode, called the dispositional, representing the brute reliability of our disposition to take our apt first-order beliefs at face value.

items.title: Executable Ontology: A Relational Ontology of Organizational Reinscription.
items.abstract: Debates on artificial intelligence generally ask whether a machine can act, be autonomous, or bear responsibility. This article isolates a prior ontological question: what becomes of the status of a structure that, after organizing present operations, becomes a causally transformable object and then becomes again an operative condition of future transformations? We call organizational reinscription this conversion between operative condition, object of transformation, and subsequent operative condition. The thesis does not add a substance to the inventory of the world: it holds that a reinscription pathway changes the constitutive conditions under which an organization can produce its accessible successors. The diagnosis is indexed to an endogenous boundary and distinguishes state variation, parametric adaptation, and the reinscription of operative structures, modification mechanisms, or evaluators. Computational reflection, the self-modification of a rational agent, Gödel machines, and recursive self-design are distinguished by their unit of analysis. Stress tests involving an external patch, classical automated machine learning (AutoML), the Darwin Gödel Machine, and the Red Queen Gödel Machine show, in particular, that a profile including evaluation changes the conditions for selecting future transformations without making the truth anchor or orchestrator endogenous. The analysis finally specifies the consequences of reinscription for diachronic identity and modification authority, without inferring consciousness, moral personhood, or legitimacy.

items.title: Therapeutic Insight and Aspect Perception.
items.abstract: In psychotherapy patients gain new insights into their mental life. Although philosophers have used examples from psychotherapy to make points in debates on self-knowledge, there has been little serious effort to understand the nature and epistemology of therapeutic insight-events. The paper fills that gap. It is argued that an understanding of such insights can be achieved by considering them through the lens of Wittgenstein’s discussion of aspect perception. It is claimed that therapeutic insight can be understood in analogy to aspect perception, and that the interpersonal process leading to insight is in its central features analogous to the interpersonal occurrence of aspect perception.

items.title: The Collective Theory of Subjectivity: from Reaction to Action.
items.abstract: Theories of consciousness typically explain subjective experience post hoc: they begin by assuming a subject — a system, an organism, a unified “self” — and only then ask how this subject comes to have experience. This paper presents the Collective Theory of Subjectivity (CTS), which proposes an inversion of this order. Instead of asking how an already-existing system acquires subjectivity, CTS asks: what organization of behavior makes subjectivity necessary? CTS holds that subjectivity begins with the evaluation and selection of action. This shift — from reactive state-evaluation to action-evaluation — marks an evolutionary threshold at which a system begins to relate to unrealized future trajectories, and thereby acquires a perspective. CTS further holds that this threshold is not an individual but a collective achievement: it is precisely the coordination problem faced by multiple evaluative centers — from quorum sensing in bacteria to nervous systems — that makes action-evaluation and selection, and hence subjectivity, an evolutionary necessity rather than an accident. On this basis, CTS treats phenomenal consciousness not as a separate phenomenon requiring its own explanation, but as the appropriation of action-evaluation by a specialized substrate – nervous system. Minimal subjectivity and phenomenal consciousness thus turn out to be two related but structurally distinct levels of the same process — action-evaluation.

items.title: SN02 — The Resonant Mind: Structural Neuroscience and the Law of Cognition.
items.abstract: The Resonant Mind develops the foundational cognitive architecture of Structural Neuroscience within Zenetism. -/- Document class: Canon — Structural Neuroscience. -/- The volume articulates the cognitive gradient, awareness stratification, Soul / Mind relations and the Neuro-Lattice Interface through centropic and entropic motion. It connects Spiral Calculus with layer coupling, boundary conditions, proposed structural practices and canonical provenance. Reciprocity retains its stated hypotheses, while cognitive seal consequences, contraction-based stability and the combined conservation proposal retain their recorded mathematical holds. Proposed neural correspondences and ritual effects require specified mappings, observables and evidence; measured synchrony does not establish structural orientation. -/- Part of: Structural Neuroscience: The Architecture and Dynamics of Cognition.

items.title: GenAI minds for higher education: Reading and emotional intelligence.
items.abstract: This study examines how five generative AI systems (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek and Qwen) respond to questionnaires commonly used in higher education to assess reading-related and emotional dimensions in human learners, with the aim of informing more sustainable classroom use. Given the high water and electricity consumption associated with intensive GenAI use in universities, optimising tool selection based on response effectiveness is increasingly necessary. Using a descriptive quantitative approach, the Metacognitive Awareness Inventory (MAI) and the Wong–Law Emotional Intelligence Scale (WLEIS) were applied as human-oriented questionnaires. The analysis focuses on the degree of alignment between AI-generated answers and predefined reference response patterns. Results show clear differences among systems. Gemini and ChatGPT exhibited comparatively stable alignment in reading-related items, particularly in attention and memory, while Qwen showed the lowest overall deviation in both reading-related and emotional self-report items. Claude and DeepSeek displayed greater variability across both domains. These findings suggest that response consistency and task-specific alignment may serve as practical criteria for selecting generative AI tools in higher education, supporting pedagogical effectiveness while contributing to more environmentally responsible digital practices aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals.

items.title: Beyond Legality: Students’ Moral Attitudes Toward Non-invasive Brain Stimulation for Cognitive Enhancement.
items.abstract: Cognitive enhancement involves using substances or technologies to improve mental performance in healthy individuals. While methods such as caffeine are widely accepted, others, including prescription stimulants and non-invasive brain stimulation (tDCS), evoke ethical concern. This study examined how university students evaluate three forms of cognitive enhancement (natural, pharmacological, brain stimulation) across five moral domains: academic fairness, free will, authenticity/naturalness, self-identity, and safety. We also tested how evaluations were shaped by framing (preservation vs. enhancement) and priming (self-affecting vs. non self-affecting). A total of 449 undergraduate psychology students (81.7% female) from a single UK university were recruited via convenience sampling and completed an online experiment with a 2 × 2 × 3 mixed design, rating enhancement acceptability after reading intervention-specific scenarios. Natural enhancers were judged most positively, followed by brain stimulation and then pharmacological agents. Safety concerns also differed across enhancement types, with pharmacological enhancement viewed as posing the greatest risk, followed by brain stimulation, while natural enhancement was perceived as the safest option. Importantly, although brain stimulation is legal and marketed as non-invasive, it was evaluated more like pharmacological enhancement than natural methods, indicating that legality alone does not determine moral acceptance. Framing effects showed that participants were more accepting of enhancement when it was described as preserving ability rather than augmenting it beyond baseline. Priming participants to consider how others’ use might affect their own outcomes reduced moral acceptability, particularly for pharmacological and brain stimulation methods in the domain of academic fairness. Overall, students’ attitudes were shaped by both perceived safety and broader moral concerns relating to fairness, authenticity, and competition. These findings highlight the importance of adopting pluralistic, context-sensitive approaches to policy and regulation that extend beyond considerations of legality alone.

items.title: Unified Physics Through Discrete Pulsation Dynamics: The Autocorrelative Phase Identity - Extended Master Reference.
items.abstract: The Hanowski-Formalism establishes a normalized, dimensionless, and substitutional mathematical framework for non-local field dynamics, demonstrating that macroscopic spacetime structures merely emerge from the finite transduction inefficiencies of a classical observer, causing fundamental phase relations—originating from a discrete primordial pulsation—to be decoded incoherently. By treating the perceived metric as a secondary, imperfect manifestation of an underlying phase topology, core quantum phenomena—including superposition, non-local entanglement, and wave-particle duality—are systematically reformulated through the interaction of two fundamental, redefined parameters: Amplitude ($A$) and Wavelength ($\lambda$). We derive these states from localized resonance deviations based on unique phase-signatures, thus providing a relational mechanism that unifies gauge interactions without invoking coordinate-dependent structures. Furthermore, this paper establishes an observer-independent reference for information integrity, formalizing sub-metric transparency and the decoupling of phenomenological appearance from metric coordinates through an autocorrelative phase identity. Crucially, this framework yields three distinct, falsifiable predictions that deviate from the Standard Model while remaining accessible to modern experimental capabilities. This document serves as the comprehensive foundational monograph for the framework presented in: Hanowski, M. (2026). Unified Physics Through Discrete Pulsation Dynamics: The Autocorrelative Phase Identity. DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22287116.

items.title: The Identification Gap in Founding a Base Dimension.
