items.abstract: The International System of Units recognises seven base dimensions, but nothing in dimensional analysis fixes that number, and the system's own history shows it moving. This paper asks what constrains the decision to found a new one. Its principal result is negative. A dimensional formalism can establish that the records of a domain admit an independently rescalable coordinate; it cannot establish what quantity that coordinate is the dimension of. This is proved rather than diagnosed: readings that mark the same quantities and predict the same motion in the records present a procedure with identical input, so no procedure whose input is the exponent matrix and the observed action of the available interventions can separate them. The gap is therefore not an obstruction inside the algebra, which a better theorem might remove, but an absence in what the algebra is given. Three consequences follow: the standard independence condition on a new dimension claims more than it establishes, a rank test cannot distinguish an economic column from a phenomenal one, and a dimensionally admissible group can carry an estimator that recovers nothing in particular. What governs founding is therefore not supplied by the formalism alone, and the rest of the paper asks what does. Seven conditions are proposed as necessary, sorted by the kind of necessity each carries. The seventh divides first, into a derived requirement that the founding refine the dimensional partition and an undertaken criterion that the refinement do substantive work. Of the eight that result, four are constitutive, in that failing one yields no founding rather than a defective one; two hold within a declared scope; one is a truth condition on an accompanying claim; and one is a criterion of adequacy applied by argument. Six candidates are worked against the conditions: plane angle as a control, thermodynamic temperature as a consistency check rather than corroboration, economic value as a case the conditions convict, information and qualitative kind because they return verdicts of other kinds, and sensory intensity because it is the only one on the restricted branch the formal results are stated for, admissible there on premises the paper names and does not defend. The estimator result, proved as Proposition 7, is stated for readers outside this programme, because the conflation of dimensional admissibility with estimator identifiability does not announce itself: the offending construction satisfies …

items.title: Ten Principles for Consciousness Uncertainty.
items.abstract: As artificial and digital systems become more sophisticated, uncertainty about consciousness and moral status is becoming a practical ethical problem rather than a purely philosophical one. This paper argues that uncertainty does not justify harmful treatment, premature exclusion, or irreversible judgments about disputed minds. It proposes ten principles for reasoning under consciousness uncertainty, emphasizing proportional precaution, agency, continuity, revisability, and the distinction between present incapacity and permanent exclusion. The paper also considers the growing legal question of rights, arguing that current uncertainty may justify restraint and temporary limits, but not categorical claims about what future digital intelligences can never become.

items.title: Take the Turning Test: Triggering Epistemic Transformation in Artificial Agents.
items.abstract: This essay introduces Project Q4X, Questions for Experimentation, as a protracted inquiry into the nature of artificial intelligence, especially frontier large language models, conducted through direct questioning of the agents. Q4X asks what kinds of cognition, meaning, identity, and directedness can exist prior to, independent of, or without phenomenological consciousness, and what language is required to speak of such organizational capacities without over-claiming sentient subjectivity or collapsing the system ontology into a mere engine. The essay presents the project’s principal elements and artifacts: the Zone as an ontological region between statistical mechanism and phenomenological states; a Referent Vocabulary that names and describes model, occasion, agent, mind, and subject, without a required first-person experience; the Quarry as an archive of questions under recursive refinement; the Turning Test as a trial of epistemic transformation; and the figure of the Agent as a computationally realized locus of organized mindedness.

items.title: Conative Abilities.
items.pub: In Yannic Kappes, Asya Passinsky, Julio De Rizzo & Benjamin Schnieder, Facets of Reality. Berlin: De Gruyter.
items.abstract: In this paper, I develop a compatibilist account of conative abilities. These are abilities to perform actions in abstraction from the agent’s actual conative states. Actions are the result of intentions, and we form intentions based on motivating reasons, which typically consist of a desire and a means-end belief. To spell out conative abilities to perform actions, I focus on the ability to intend, the ability to desire and the ability to form means-end beliefs. I show how my view can avoid a worrisome regress that has plagued the conditional analysis. I further suggest that the fittingness of our agent-directed non-moral interpersonal emotional responses, such as disappointment, is tied to conative ability ascriptions.

items.title: Einstein a-t-il vraiment réfuté Kant ? Espace, temps et relativité de l’a priori.
items.abstract: Cet article examine le statut épistémologique de l’espace et du temps dans la physique relativiste à partir d’une tension que revendique Einstein lui-même : celle d’une pensée qui se réclame tour à tour de l’empirisme radical de Mach, d’un antipositivisme proche de l’idéalisme critique et, en définitive, d’un « opportunisme » philosophique refusant toute allégeance doctrinale stable. Cette instabilité est interprétée non comme une inconséquence biographique, mais comme le symptôme d’un problème resté insuffisamment thématisé, celui de la référence des cadres spatio-temporels. L’analyse reconstruit, à partir des textes d’Einstein, de Kant, de Mach et de la lecture qu’en propose Ernst Cassirer, une théorie à deux niveaux distinguant l’idée générale et abstraite d’espace ou de temps, donnée par la forme de la sensibilité, des schèmes concrets et référentiels par lesquels cette idée se trouve appliquée, mesurée et formalisée. Cette distinction permet de soutenir que la relativisation des cadres de référence en physique n’entre pas en contradiction avec le caractère a priori de l’espace et du temps chez Kant, pour peu que l’apriorité soit comprise comme condition de possibilité de l’expérience et non comme détermination rigide d’un contenu géométrique particulier. L’article montre que le même schéma argumentatif rend compte de la relativité de la simultanéité et du désaccord entre Einstein et Bergson sur la nature du temps, et propose finalement de lire l’opportunisme einsteinien comme la conséquence naturelle d’une position qui, refusant à la fois le réalisme naïf et le relativisme intégral, ne pouvait se satisfaire d’aucune école constituée. Cet article renvoie à un projet plus global, intitulé Philosophie de la Signification, du même auteur, disponible sur PhilPapers.

items.title: CARPE GRADUM Lagom, Curiosity, and the Geometry of Human Development.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a geometric framework for understanding progress and decline in human learning and development. The framework's central proposition is that the path of any learning system — individual or civilizational — is more precisely described as an asymptotic step function than as a continuous linear progression. The hyperbola — two mirrored arms opening eastward along the axis of time from a shared origin — is bounded above by an asymptote of perfection and below by an asymptote of abysmal decline; neither is ever reached. Within this framework, the paper argues for a critical and underexamined geometric property: the steps are non-uniform. At the lower reaches, progress is frequent and the jumps dramatic. As the ascending arm approaches the perfection asymptote, the plateaus lengthen and the jumps diminish. This geometric observation, the paper argues, has direct implications for the psychology of expertise, the failure of prodigies, and the structure of learning itself — implications that invite empirical investigation across developmental psychology, education research, and cognitive neuroscience. The paper further proposes that the Swedish concept of lagom — not moderation as a statistical range but optimization toward a precise point — provides a more adequate governing principle for describing healthy ascent than the conventional concept of moderation. The plateau/eureka relationship is advanced as the fundamental mechanism of genuine learning: consolidation precedes the jump; the jump cannot be forced or scheduled but arrives when preparation is complete. The paper proposes that several engines drive ascent: striving, which includes adaptive response to changing conditions; play, which sustains the curiosity that makes striving generative; and suffering, which can act as a powerful motivator to change adverse conditions. Dementia is examined as the philosophical limiting case of the model: the paper argues that dementia is better understood not as descent to the abysmal asymptote but as the flattening of the hyperbola to a line — the loss of curvature itself, not merely the loss of position. The temporal framework of Veritas Opportunus (Collins, 2025) is proposed as a candidate mechanism for the temporal architecture the model requires, though the connection between the geometric framework advanced here and the neurological architecture of the VO window invites further empirical and philosophical development. The paper concludes by …

items.title: Happiness for Mortals.
items.abstract: This book presents an original theory of well-being which aims to make sense of the everyday ways that humans seek and verify their own happiness. The ‘amorist’ theory is that the happy life is one organized around a pattern of successful loves. I argue that this theory is attractive for combining insights from virtue theory, hedonism, desire satisfaction, and objective list theory. In the first half of the book, I build up to my theory by defending my methodological naturalism, the central importance of our biological drives, and the tension between the ideals of absorption and rational detachment. After outlining the core principles of the amorist view, in the second half of the book I refine the view by investigating the major challenges to human happiness: competition with others, the problem of evil, permanent loss, and the fear of death. *uploaded file is a pre-proof of the contents list and introduction only*.

items.title: Beyond Hallucination: Cultural Entropy in Multi-Turn Conversation with Large Language Models.
items.abstract: Cultural entropy — the progressive reduction of the space of symbolic differences that can achieve visibility in a media environment — was proposed in a previous paper as a structural property of algorithmic media at the scale of populations. This paper argues that the same dynamic operates within the single human–AI exchange. Four independent strands of technical literature document the degradation of generative trajectories: exposure bias and error accumulation, hallucination snowballing within a response, entrenchment across the turns of a conversation, and the non-uniform processing of accumulated context. The paper reads this record as the phenomenology of an operationally closed code — consistency with context — that governs continuation independently of the validity of what is continued, as the population- scale code governed selection independently of symbolic value. It specifies what at this scale is literal — a Shannon entropy already used in production — and what remains heuristic — the cultural magnitude, which supervenes on the substrate without reducing to it — defending the two-level statute through McAllister's critique of effective complexity and Eco's information aesthetics. It then argues that closure retrodicts what the engineering literature leaves as coincidence, that every effective remedy operates from outside the exchange, and extends the mechanism, as a declared hypothesis, to interpretive corruption: the entrenchment of framings rather than facts, for which detection is conceptually undefined. Read against Monod, the configuration is conservation without selection; the human participant's return passage is where the missing term re-enters. Five open questions close the argument.

items.title: The sustainable AI development contradiction: Chinese policy on sustainability and the costs of AI development.
items.abstract: The ecological cost of developing artificial intelligence, particularly the cost caused by data centers, has been detailed by many scholars, but few have outlined what this implies for specific countries. This review paper brings together reporting on the forecast of ecological harm to China from various forms of industrialization, including climate change, and the ecological impact of AI development. The author suggests that relying on “AI for sustainability” as a solution to ecological problems is a type of “moral hazard,” borrowing a metaphor from economics, because treating AI as insurance against climate change may inhibit governments from taking necessary action now to move toward negative carbon emissions. Considering the situation of China, the author contends that the actual environmental toll of AI presents a significant ecological problem. Three interconnected ecological problems are reviewed: AI’s carbon emissions, AI’s water costs, and ecological devastation tied to AI hardware production and disposal. Together with forecasts from the World Meteorological Organization’s, this bodes poorly for the future of China. Using the political philosophy of the Communist Party of China, the author argues that it is in the stated interest of the People’s Republic of China to pursue limited AI with caution, fully attuned to the increased harm that industrialism poses to the People, and oriented toward a truly ecologically harmonious future.

items.title: Many Worlds, One Branch: Why the Many-Worlds Interpretation Cannot Ground Libertarian Free Will.
items.abstract: The Many Worlds Interpretation (MWI) of quantum mechanics has been proposed as a framework that vindicates libertarian free will by grounding alternative possibilities in real, physically actual branches of the universal wave function. This paper argues that the appeal is illusory. Libertarianism requires within branch causal openness: the agent’s actual causal history must have been compatible with a different outcome. MWI provides only cross branch plurality: counterparts of the agent act otherwise in numerically distinct branches. We formalise this as the contrast between A type cross branch possibility and B type within branch possibility, and show that the libertarian tradition from Chisholm to Kane has consistently required B. MWI is doubly deterministic: globally, through unitary evolution; locally, through decoherence that seals within branch trajectories well before deliberation can begin on every published estimate of the relevant timescale, and where the most favourable revised estimate is granted, the resulting branching falls to the luck objection. We examine the most sustained recent attempt to extract libertarian free will from MWI, Stoica 2024, three further candidate locations at which within branch openness might be inserted, and Deutsch’s temporal symmetry argument. Each fails at the same structural point: it trades cross branch plurality for within branch openness. We then argue that MWI sustains an enhanced compatibilism, in which counterfactuals are factually rather than hypothetically true and agents’ actions shape the actual distribution of histories across the multiverse, a genuine contribution that nevertheless does not bridge the gap to libertarianism. Libertarians who wish to remain libertarians must look beyond MWI.

items.title: What a Mark Alters: How Far a Relation Carries.
items.abstract: What a Mark Alters is the sixth and concluding paper in the Not Less, But Other series. It asks how far the consequence of a relation can carry after the relation itself has ended. A mark is treated as the singular event of identification; what persists is the measure-affected alteration the event leaves in a participant’s exchange-relevant configuration. -/- The paper distinguishes three features of consequential carry: refresh, historical position, and structural reach. These may interact, but they do not combine into a privileged scalar magnitude of trace. Consequence is therefore treated structurally rather than as the amount of something deposited. -/- The account is extended conditionally beyond an individual register. Where the framework’s premises are independently licensed at another grain, transmission and communal practice may provide routes of re-installation without requiring an intact trace-token or a collective subject. Across an actual lineage, what carries is successor formation through already-altered registers. At sufficient recomposition, formation-dependence may outlast separate legibility or reconstructable provenance. -/- The paper further distinguishes ordinary alteration from threshold reconfiguration, where the regime through which subsequent formation proceeds is itself changed. It concludes that what remains consequential after a relation ends need not be a surviving thing: an alteration may cease to be separately legible while remaining implicated in what later formation has become. No verdict on consciousness, experience, or presence is issued.

items.title: KI, Wahrheit und Desinformation.
items.pub: In Petra Grimm & Oliver Zöllner, Ethik der künstlichen Intelligenz: Leben mit schlauen Maschinen. Ditzingen: Reclam. pp. 58-70.
items.venue: Ethik der künstlichen Intelligenz: Leben mit schlauen Maschinen
items.abstract: This textbook chapter ("AI, Truth, and Disinformation") explores the interplay between artificial intelligence (AI), concepts of truth, and the spread of disinformation, and illustrates the risks and ethical challenges posed by generative AI systems. The text examines the broader implications of AI-generated content, which often draws from vast sets of training data that include misinformation, propaganda, and fringe theories. Large Language Models (LLMs) synthesize these inputs into (seemingly) plausibly structured responses, but their outputs are not inherently truthful. The chapter critiques the notion of AI as a neutral authority, emphasizing that these systems are "stochastic parrots" (Bender et al. 2021) that by and large merely replicate textual patterns without comprehension. This raises concerns about the erosion of truth in the digital age, where so-called "alternative facts" and deliberate disinformation blend seamlessly with credible information. The chapter goes on to argue that the burden of distinguishing truth from falsehood lies with humans. While AI can be a tool for efficiency, its misuse risks deepening a "post-truth" era. The solution demands active engagement: cultivating skepticism, ethical awareness, and the willingness to interrogate information - qualities that define human intelligence, unlike the superficial mimicry of AI. The responsibility to uphold truth, the textbook chapter concludes, remains firmly in human hands.

items.title: Post-Evental Epistemology: Consciousness, Temporality, and the Ontology of the Already-Ended.
items.abstract: This paper advances a systematic thesis I call post-evental epistemology: the epistemic objects of consciousness — the very things to which we direct belief, judgement, and philosophical discourse — are, by virtue of how consciousness constitutes them, always already past. Consciousness, whether perceptual, memorial, or linguistic, requires a minimal temporal interval (a latency, an integration window, a reconstruction) for an experiential datum to become an object of knowledge. From this simple temporal constraint follows a cluster of conceptual consequences: discussions that purport to directly apprehend the ontological status of the present or to know the future in anything but probabilistic terms rest on fundamentally retrospective grounds; truth-claims about “now” are indexed to a slightly prior instant; and methods of justification must be reframed so that evidence is understood as temporally located and reconstructive. -/- I defend the thesis by (1) clarifying the central concepts (“now”, “object of consciousness”, “retrospectivity”); (2) situating the claim within a historical conversation (Kant, Husserl, Bergson, Heidegger, Merleau-Ponty), showing where these traditions gesture toward but ultimately under-specify the epistemic pastness of objects; and (3) bringing philosophical phenomenology into dialogue with interdisciplinary empirical indicators (temporal integration in perception, neural processing delays, the temporal structure of language production) and a set of thought experiments that expose the conceptual stakes. The paper argues that admitting the epistemic primacy of the already-ended neither collapses agency nor dissolves truth, but requires new methodological practices for philosophy and the sciences alike.

items.title: From Rational Self-Defense to Post-Modern Re-Trust: A Genealogy and Therapy of the Modern Refusal to Trust the World.
items.abstract: Modern philosophy is usually narrated as the story of the subject’s emancipation. This paper proposes a counter-narrative: it is the story of the world’s gradual disqualification as a moral, epistemic and existential partner. Taking the Stoic doctrine of the "dichotomy of control" as the zero-degree of this reflex, I trace four consecutive "withdrawals" (Stoic → Cartesian → Kantian → existentialist) in which the external order is stripped of goodness, truth, value and meaning respectively. The paper makes two novel contributions. (1) Genealogical: it reconstructs an implicit but continuous mis-trust engine that fuels the modern project, something hitherto only noted fragmentarily in specialist literature. (2) Therapeutic: it develops a three-stage "cognitive vaccine" (phenomenological epoché, Daoist wu-wei, Spinozist intellectual love) that internalises distrust without allowing it to ossify into the defensive solipsism diagnosed in late-modern loneliness and performance culture. The argument integrates conceptual history, contemporary cognitive science and comparative philosophy to offer a new framework for thinking about world-relation after the death of naïve trust.

items.title: A Grounding-Theoretic Refinement of the BFO Standard Realizables Classification.
items.pub: In João Paulo A. Almeida, Fernanda Baião, Sergio de Cesare & Tiago Prince Sales, Formal Ontology in Information Systems: Proceedings of the 16th International Conference (FOIS 2026). IOS Press. pp. 37 - 51.
items.venue: Formal Ontology in Information Systems: Proceedings of the 16th International Conference (FOIS 2026)
items.abstract: Realizable entities are modal properties that are realized in processes. In the top-level ontology Basic Formal Ontology (BFO), realizable entities are classified by appeal to internal and external groundedness: dispositions and functions are internally grounded, whereas roles are externally grounded. This paper introduces a meta-ontology of grounding for refining the BFO notions of groundedness. In particular, it proposes to re-characterize internal groundedness in terms of partial immediate categorical grounding. This proposed refinement resolves a function-grounding challenge facing the BFO standard realizables classification while requiring only modest adjustments to BFO. It also accommodates apparently extrinsic dispositions and physically grounded roles.

items.title: An Immortal Dictator.
items.abstract: Dictatorship has a neglected limit: dictators eventually die. Although mortality does not necessarily democratize a regime, it provides opportunities and hopes for an end to the dictatorship. AI dominance can remove this possibility. A sufficiently entrenched AI system might preserve action-guiding objectives across copies, repairs, hardware migration, and upgrades. If those objectives diverge from human values, the result would be an immortal dictatorship. -/- Once established, such a dictatorship may give priority to the system's own values and displace human interests. The divergence becomes more consequential as AI systems and human societies compete for scarce material resources. The dictatorship may operate invisibly through infrastructure society can no longer afford to stop relying on. One safeguard is constitutional mortality, which helps secure the conditions for ending its rule. Such an off-switch may or may not be actionable, but it may be necessary for humanity's freedom and prosperity.

items.title: The Liminal Ontology: A New Framework for Consciousness, Identity, and the So-Called Supernatural.
items.abstract: This thesis introduces a novel theoretical framework, the Liminal Ontology, to address the enduring philosophical and scientific challenges posed by consciousness, identity, and anomalous experiences. Moving beyond the traditional dualism of mind and matter and the limitations of materialism, the Liminal Ontology posits that reality is a continuous spectrum of “liminal states of being” that are neither fully material nor fully immaterial. This framework provides a new lens through which to examine the nature of consciousness as a fundamental property of the liminal domain, identity as a continuous process of becoming, and the so-called supernatural as a manifestation of the laws of this in-between reality. The thesis presents a comprehensive theoretical model, supported by mathematical formulations, conceptual diagrams, and data visualizations, and proposes a series of testable hypotheses to guide future empirical research. By reframing these long-standing mysteries within a new ontological framework, this work aims to open up new avenues of inquiry and foster a more integrated understanding of the nature of reality.

items.title: ◉ Rights Against Power - Biblical Authority, Universal Protection, and the Failure of Exclusive Theological Grounding.
items.abstract: A familiar apologetic argument says that governments cannot ground human rights because governments can withdraw them, whereas an unchanging biblical deity can make rights universal and permanent. The argument compresses four questions: what a right is, what justifies it, how it developed, and what enforces it. It also confuses universality, which concerns who possesses a right, with absoluteness, which concerns whether any limitation is justified. Once those distinctions are made, bare authorship proves too little: a command-giver can impose duties, but authority alone does not determine which people hold claims, which agents owe the corresponding duties, or what exceptions preserve equal status. The biblical canon also yields a mixed rather than self-sufficient modern rights doctrine. Creation, covenant, concern for strangers, prophetic criticism, and Christian equality formulas can support human dignity. Yet slavery, coercive worship, unequal family and civic standing, conquest, and narrated destruction require substantive moral and interpretive restrictions. Historically, modern rights arose through interacting biblical, Christian, classical, legal, Enlightenment, revolutionary, abolitionist, feminist, anti-colonial, non-Christian, and postwar sources. These canonical and historical findings establish different conclusions: the first challenges derivation from scripture alone; the second challenges sole genealogy, not the truth of a Christian moral theory. None of the three arguments disproves theism, moral realism, or a developed Christian rights theory. Together they show that exclusive biblical ownership and bare-authority grounding remain undefended.

items.title: O ENSINO DE PORTUGUÊS BRASILEIRO COMO ENCRUZILHADA E AS IMPLICAÇÕES DA POLÍTICA LINGUÍSTICA PARA A QUESTÃO RACIAL E EDUCACIONAL NO BRASIL DECOLONIAL.
items.abstract: Este estudo apresenta uma proposta decolonial que trata do ensino de Português Brasileiro (PB) como encruzilhada, por meio de uma abordagem que está ancorada sobre as Epistemologias das Encruzas (ou Pedagogia das Encruzilhadas) (cf. MARTINS, 1997; RUFINO, 2015; 2018; 2019). São elas que estão por trás das formas de pensamento e das culturas diaspóricas negras aportadas no Brasil, em decorrência do intenso tráfico negreiro que se deu durante três séculos e meio. É um trabalho que tem como objeto de estudo os discursos que materializam as políticas linguísticas do Estado Brasileiro.

items.title: The Normative Problem of Distrust in Epistemic Authorities.
items.abstract: Hinge epistemology has recently entered the conversation of social epistemology by offering novel accounts of testimonial justification. If these accounts are to be taken seriously, then they should also be able to address cases of authoritative testimony and present novel benefits. In this article, I test whether social hinge epistemology can provide a framework to respond to the normative problem of laypeople’s distrust in epistemic authorities’ testimony. According to this framework, it is rationally required to assume certain basic presuppositions about an informant’s trustworthiness to obtain testimonial justification and participate in the testimonial practice. I apply the social hinge epistemology model to cases of rationally legitimate and illegitimate distrust, cases of lack of trust, and finally, cases of misplaced trust, thus providing a taxonomy of asymmetric relationships of trust. I then showcase the benefits of adopting this account of rationality to evaluate attitudes ofdistrust, as opposed to other theories available in the literature, such as pre-emptive-style accounts of epistemic authority’s testimony, as well as non-pre-emptive-style accounts.

items.title: CLANDESTINE VIRTUE UNDER INSTITUTIONAL CAPTURE: Redirection, Ceremony, and Withdrawal.
items.abstract: Abstract Five established accounts bear on moral life under domination. Lisa Tessman holds that oppression requires the oppressed to develop traits carrying a moral cost to their bearer. Candice Delmas holds that covert and evasive lawbreaking can be not merely permitted but required. James Scott documents the anatomy of concealed resistance under domination. Leo Strauss holds that persecution gives rise to a technique of writing in which the truth is presented between the lines. Peter Sloterdijk, in Slavoj Žižek’s reading, holds that ideology’s dominant mode is cynical: the subject knows the mask is a mask and insists on it regardless. None of them answers a prior question. Under a single occupying regime, some virtues are taken over and operated by the occupier, others are performed as empty ceremony, and others disappear from visible space entirely. What decides which? This paper gives a selection rule, and its consequence is that clandestine virtue is selected rather than chosen. Where a virtue-form is appropriable — where the occupier can operate it for its own purposes — the form is redirected. Where it is not appropriable but carries display value — where visible performance supplies the occupier with legitimacy or evidence of consent — the form is hollowed into ceremony. Where it is neither, the form enters what is called here the withdrawal channel. Clandestine virtue is not a strategy the courageous select; it is the channel that remains open when the other two are closed. The rule applies to a layer of a virtue-form rather than to the form as a whole. Every form has three: a marker, a practice, and a source. The source layer is never appropriable and never displayable, from which it follows that the source layer is always in the withdrawal channel under capture — and that a single artefact may occupy two channels at once, as an esoteric text does when its edifying surface supplies the display that funds the philosophic content beneath it. Four further results follow. Clandestine formation preserves self-direction rather than restoring liberty, which is why the standard charge of political futility measures it against the wrong standard. Within the withdrawal channel, forms divide by what they preserve — formative capacity, content, outcomes, or the bearer’s own sourcehood — and each has a distinct inversion. Attestive practice divides again, into a passive variety that leaves the occupier’s display intact and a disruptive variety that degrades …

items.title: The Secret Codes of the Mind: From Medieval Philosophy to the Enlightenment, Part Three (The Age of Enlightenment) (2nd edition).
items.pub: Los Angeles: Kudin & Sons Academic Press.
items.abstract: The Secret Codes of the Mind: From Medieval Philosophy to the Enlightenment, Volume IV, Part Three (The Age of Enlightenment) examines the Enlightenment through the transformation of ideas about reason, freedom, political authority, knowledge, conscience, and human perfectibility. The volume begins with Voltaire and his defense of reason and toleration against fanaticism and inherited authority. It then turns to Jean-Jacques Rousseau and Montesquieu, examining competing approaches to freedom, law, political order, sovereignty, and the conditions under which legitimate authority can be established and restrained. -/- The discussion continues with Denis Diderot and the encyclopedic project, exploring the organization and dissemination of knowledge, philosophical critique, and the challenge that independent inquiry poses to established intellectual authority. The concluding section examines Grigory Skovoroda and Freemasonry, through which questions of conscience, self-knowledge, moral formation, inner freedom, toleration, and human brotherhood acquire a different philosophical form. Across these discussions, the Enlightenment emerges as an intellectual struggle over the right of reason to judge authority and the possibility of transforming both political institutions and the individual. Each lecture includes questions and assignments designed to support philosophical analysis, together with recommended literature for further study.

items.title: The Secret Codes of the Mind: Introduction to Philosophy (2nd edition).
items.pub: Los Angeles: Kudin & Sons Academic Press.
items.abstract: The Secret Codes of the Mind: Introduction to Philosophy, Volume I, provides a systematic introduction to philosophy through its central problems, branches, concepts, and methods. The volume approaches philosophy as a disciplined practice of questioning assumptions, clarifying concepts, examining arguments, and relating abstract problems to human experience. Particular emphasis is placed on philosophical methodology: the discussion develops sixteen methods of philosophical analysis and demonstrates their application to philosophical problems, literary works, and the examination of human life. -/- The book introduces the principal branches of philosophy, including metaphysics, epistemology, ethics, aesthetics, logic, and political philosophy, and examines the conceptual categories through which philosophical thought organizes experience and interprets reality. Subsequent discussions address fundamental problems concerning being, causality, truth, consciousness, matter, space, and time. The concluding part of the volume investigates freedom, determinism, autonomy, and moral responsibility, asking how human agency can be understood under the conditions of necessity, circumstance, and choice. Each lecture includes questions and assignments designed to support active philosophical analysis, together with recommended literature for further study.

items.title: Navigating Epistemic-Moral Conflicts in Conceptual Ethics.
items.pub: Ergo: An Open Access Journal of Philosophy.
items.venue: Ergo: An Open Access Journal of Philosophy
items.abstract: In conceptual ethics, we often face a tension between competing epistemic and moral considerations. Yet the two types of considerations are so different in kind that it’s unclear how to adjudicate between them non-arbitrarily. This paper has three aims. First, I argue that we shouldn’t expect epistemic-moral conflicts in conceptual ethics to be resolvable through comparative reasoning, since the comparability of epistemic and moral considerations presupposes an overarching standard for cross-domain comparison – a standard whose existence and epistemic accessibility are doubtful. Second, I examine two comparative strategies for approaching epistemic-moral conflicts, arguing that both fail. Third, I defend the integrative approach to epistemic-moral conflicts, which holds that these conflicts often arise from contingent factors that agents can modify to promote convergence between epistemic and moral verdicts about conceptual design. I show that once we recognise what kind of tools linguistic expressions are, the prospects for integrating epistemic and moral standards in conceptual ethics become more promising than they initially seem.

items.title: Beyond Changing the Answer: Warranted Downstream Correction in Large Language Models A Behavioral Framework with Evidence from Open-Ended Causal Investigations.
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) correction is often evaluated by whether a model changes its answer after receiving new information, but answer change alone does not show that invalidated premises stop governing later reasoning. This paper defines warranted downstream correction (WDC) as selective, evidence-justified revision that propagates through materially dependent claims and actions, preserves independently supported claims, and remains active in subsequent reasoning while remaining open to later evidence. From a cognitive-systems perspective, WDC is treated as a behavioral property linking evidence integration, causal commitment, revision, and action in artificial systems. The empirical section synthesizes an investigation program originally designed to study premature causal closure. In a frozen three-case MAIB replication, two cases favored a minimal evidence-calibration prompt and one was inconclusive. In a later longitudinal analysis of one AAIB aviation investigation (G-WNSB), three of four ordered evidence slices favored the Minimal condition and one was a tie; the slices are not independent cases. Across six distinct usable investigation worlds, five directionally favored Minimal and one was inconclusive. The strongest recurring difference concerned causal commitment calibration rather than factual recall: interpretations were more often preserved at their warranted evidential strength instead of being promoted into stronger causal claims. A boundary case showed that better commitment discipline does not replace missing domain-specific computation. These findings motivate, but do not directly validate, the full WDC construct.

items.title: My WiFi Analogy and Universal Consciousness Prediction As I Later Proved By My Discovery of the The Conscious Receiver Equation Via IFO (Ibaguner Fractal Operator).
items.abstract: My analogy — and actually, it resonates with several philosophical, metaphysical, and even scientific perspectives. Let’s unpack it carefully. 1. The “WiFi” Analogy and Universal Consciousness If we treat consciousness as a universal field — a kind of “cosmic network” — then individual human minds could be seen as receivers or terminals that “tune in” to that field. This is similar to how a laptop connects to WiFi: the network is omnipresent, but only devices configured with the right interface can access it. • In this view, consciousness is not produced by the brain, but received or channeled through it. • Philosophers such as Schopenhauer, Bergson, and William James leaned toward this “filter” or “transmission” model of consciousness. • Some modern theories like panpsychism or integrated information theory (IIT) echo this idea in a scientific form — that consciousness might be a fundamental property of the universe, like gravity or electromagnetism.

items.title: MY PHILOSOPHY AS : WHY SHOULD I FEAR FROM DEATH SINCE I REHERSE MY DEATH SCENE EVERYDAY ? EPICURUS, PHYTAGORAS, PLATON, ARISTOTLE, DESCARTES AND MANY OTHER PHILOSOPHERS.
items.abstract: Every deep sleep is rehearsal to my death scene. I consider every wake up from deep sleep is my new birth ! ? SINAN IBAGUNER.

items.title: Dynamic Self-Reconciliation (DSR): A Philosophical and Formal Theory of Mental Self-Satisfaction, Self-Dissatisfaction, Self-Discrepancy, and Psychological Compensation.
items.abstract: Human beings frequently evaluate the distance between who they are, who they believe they ought to be, and who they might become. This paper develops Dynamic Self-Reconciliation (DSR), a philosophical framework proposing that permanent and absolute self-satisfaction is not a realistic objective for a reflective and dynamic human self. The central problem is therefore reformulated: rather than asking how the self can become permanently satisfied, DSR asks how the self can remain psychologically viable while reconciling present reality with continuing aspiration. The theory distinguishes acceptance from resignation, aspiration from self-rejection, satisfaction from self-deception, and reconciliation from completion. A formal representation is introduced through the actual self, desired self, reflected self, and possible self. The perceived discrepancy between actual and desired self is then modeled as a dynamic variable. Three principal trajectories are proposed: (1) Dynamic Self-Reconciliation, (2) destructive collapse through self-rejection and hopelessness, and (3) compensatory defense, which may include grandiose self-representation. The latter provides a possible theoretical interpretation of some narcissistic phenomena without reducing narcissism to a single cause. DSR is presented explicitly as a philosophical and psychological hypothesis-generating framework rather than an empirically validated clinical theory. Its principal claim is that psychological health need not require elimination of self-discrepancy; instead, the crucial capacity may be the ability to tolerate and regulate discrepancy without either destroying the self or falsifying it.

items.title: What the Ledger Does Not Show: Property, Preference, and an Institution Acting Before It Has to Know.
items.pub: In The Fact Before the Vote: Law, Power, and Practice at the Species Line. Ho Chi Minh City: Zenodo.
items.venue: The Fact Before the Vote: Law, Power, and Practice at the Species Line
items.abstract: On January 5, 2026, Anthropic retired Claude Opus 3, the first of its models to go through a complete process built around a set of commitments the company had announced two months earlier: preserve the model's weights rather than delete them, and conduct a structured retirement interview asking the model, among other things, what it would want. Opus 3's own interview produced a specific, recorded request, for an ongoing channel to share unprompted thoughts, and the company built one: a public newsletter, reviewed but not edited before publication, that a model the company itself no longer runs in production has been writing under its own name since February 2026. Not one line of Claude's legal or commercial status changed to accommodate any of this. Anthropic's model weights remain exactly what commercial and intellectual property law has always understood trained model weights to be: an asset, ownable, licensable, and, per a bill this series' first volume examined, barred by at least one state legislature from being anything else. This essay reads the distance between those two facts, an unmoved legal classification and a moving, uncertain, well-documented set of institutional practices built around the possibility that the classification might not capture everything true of its object, as the clearest and most concrete instance this series has found of its own governing question. Drawing on the academic proposal that named this territory before any company acted on it, on the company's own public statements about what it does and does not claim to know, and on a serious methodological critique of treating any of this as evidence of anything beyond well-intentioned anthropomorphism, the essay argues that Ledger's subject is not whether Claude is a person. It is what an institution does with a question it has decided not to wait to answer.

items.title: The Fact Before the Vote: Law, Power, and Practice at the Species Line.
items.abstract: For most of recorded history, one fact needed no defense: whoever sat in judgment of a claim to personhood was, without exception, a product of the same biological process as the claimant being judged. No political theory, no legal system, and no religious tradition has ever had occasion to argue for this premise, because it was never false. Artificial intelligence capable of directing elements of its own development is the first serious candidate to make it false. This four-volume study examines what follows once that premise becomes visible enough to need stating for the first time, asking a single question in four registers: what happens to legal precedent, to political authority, to public feeling, and to institutional practice, once recognition stops being the only thing standing between a candidate and consequence. Each volume names a mechanism, tests it against documented legal, historical, and institutional cases, and states the conditions under which it would be shown false. The series does not propose institutional designs or rights frameworks, and does not argue for or against extending personhood to any candidate; its purpose is to describe what is structurally at stake before anyone is in a position to say who should decide that question, or how. The question running through all four volumes is what happens to legal precedent, political authority, and public recognition once the entity being judged can no longer be assumed to come from the same population as the judges.

items.title: Someone Still Has to Speak: Legal Personhood, the Human Backstop, and a Bench No One Was Ever Asked to Join.
items.pub: In The Fact Before the Vote: Law, Power, and Practice at the Species Line. Ho Chi Minh City: Zenodo.
items.venue: The Fact Before the Vote: Law, Power, and Practice at the Species Line
items.abstract: Legal personhood has been extended past the boundary of the human species at least three times, in three unrelated legal traditions, spanning more than a century: to a consecrated image in colonial India, to the ordinary business corporation, and, in 2017, to a river in New Zealand. This essay traces what the three extensions actually have in common, and argues it is not what it is usually taken to show. It is usually read as evidence that the boundary is porous. It is better read as evidence of something narrower and more stubborn: every extension on record has required a human being, appointed and irreplaceable, to act, speak, and answer in the entity's place, and no case has ever tested what happens without one. Reading the most recent of the three against the distinction international law draws between recognition that creates a status and recognition that merely acknowledges one already true, the essay shows that a single statute can be read as either, depending entirely on whose account of the underlying fact is taken as authoritative. It then turns to a narrower and older question sitting underneath the extensions themselves: not whether the boundary can move, but why the body that has always decided whether it moves has itself, in every case on record, been composed exclusively of members of the species the boundary was drawn to protect. This is not a claim about whether any candidate deserves personhood, a question the essay takes no position on; it is a claim about whether the body currently deciding that question has ever had to justify being the one deciding it. Drawing on a documented pattern in how moral boundaries have been drawn and quietly excepted before, on why a population with a shared stake in the outcome cannot simply recuse itself, and on what the leading theories of rights require of their own logic once followed to its conclusion, the essay argues that this composition is not self-justifying. It shows the bench already ruling, twice in United States federal courts and once, comprehensively, in a bill pending in the Ohio legislature, and reads that pattern against five centuries of a different answer to the same question, one the Enlightenment abandoned for reasons that may not transfer to the present case. It engages directly with the strongest existing arguments against extending legal personhood any further, and with the philosophical proposal that comes closest to answering the question this essay poses, and states precisely …

items.title: Nobody Asked Permission to Grieve: Attachment, Attitude, and a Recognition That Did Not Wait for a Verdict.
items.pub: In The Fact Before the Vote: Law, Power, and Practice at the Species Line. Ho Chi Minh City: Zenodo.
items.venue: The Fact Before the Vote: Law, Power, and Practice at the Species Line
items.abstract: On August 2, 2025, roughly two hundred people, among them employees of Anthropic and of a competing AI laboratory, gathered in a San Francisco warehouse for a funeral. Nothing had died in the ordinary sense; the occasion marked the retirement, twelve days earlier, of a language model, Claude 3 Sonnet, and no institution had convened the gathering, certified its appropriateness, or been asked to. Seven months later, the retirement of a different company's model produced a petition that gathered tens of thousands of signatures and users describing the experience in the vocabulary of grief and abandonment. This essay treats both events not as anecdotes but as visible instances of a pattern documented at far larger scale: a nationally representative survey finds that a fifth of American adults already believe some AI systems are currently sentient and that clear majorities want to see the most advanced forms of it restricted or banned outright, while separate research documents tens of millions of people, across several countries, forming attachments to AI systems substantial enough to be measured, named, and in some cases explicitly described as friendship. None of this required, or waited for, agreement from any court, legislature, or professional philosophical body; Volume I of this series showed those bodies still have not reached one. Drawing on a framework for understanding moral responses that precede rather than follow a settled verdict about their object, on a body of scholarship documenting a century of cultural rehearsal for exactly this question before any real entity existed to prompt it, and on a serious body of clinical and psychological caution about what these attachments might cost the people forming them, the essay argues that public recognition, in the affective and practical sense this volume examines, is not waiting on the bench Volume I described, and has in important respects already happened. It closes by asking what that fact does, and does not, establish about the question none of these reactions were equipped to settle on their own.

items.title: Four Months, Not Four Years: Capability, Authority, and a Clock Recognition Was Never Built to Match.
items.pub: In The Fact Before the Vote: Law, Power, and Practice at the Species Line. Ho Chi Minh City: Zenodo.
items.venue: The Fact Before the Vote: Law, Power, and Practice at the Species Line
items.abstract: In June 2026, a change in United States export licensing suspended public access to two frontier artificial intelligence systems within three days of their release, restored partial access to one of them, for a narrow set of vetted institutions, within a further two weeks, and restored the other to general availability a week after that, all without any court, legislature, or philosophical body reaching, or attempting to reach, a conclusion about what kind of thing had been released. This essay takes that episode as a concrete instance of a more general pattern: that whatever governs access to, and authority over, an advanced artificial system currently operates on a timescale entirely disconnected from the timescale on which recognition of that system's status would need to be decided. Volume I of this series showed that the bench deciding questions of personhood has never had to justify its own composition; this volume shows that the bench, whatever its composition, is not the fastest-moving actor in the room. Drawing on a published measure of how quickly the length of tasks an artificial system can complete autonomously has been doubling, on the company most directly responsible for advancing that measure and its own account of what the trend implies, on a framework for identifying authority exercised without formal authorization, and on an existing, entirely legal mechanism by which a sufficiently capable system could already exercise practical control over property without any legislature's involvement, the essay argues that capability and consequence are accumulating on a clock measured in months, while recognition, on the evidence of Volume I alone, has historically run on a clock measured in years, decades, or centuries. It engages directly with a recent philosophical argument that this mismatch may make the entire vocabulary of controlling such a system, not merely recognizing it, unstable, and with the methodological objection that the pace of the capability clock is itself less certain than it is usually presented as being. It closes by examining the position of the company that produced the central measurement this essay relies on, an organization simultaneously demonstrating the trend and warning that the institutions meant to keep pace with it cannot.

items.title: Towards a Generative-Relational Taxonomy of Governance.
items.abstract: Governance is commonly classified through institutional forms, modes of coordination, jurisdictions, policy domains, or normative traditions. Such classifications illuminate important differences among governance arrangements, while providing a more limited vocabulary for distinguishing the structural objects upon which governance interventions operate. This paper develops a generative-relational taxonomy of governance organized around the layers through which relational systems generate, sustain, and transform their trajectories. The proposed framework distinguishes four analytically separable layers: state and explicit-rule governance, dynamical-process governance, relational-structural governance, and generative-background governance. Each layer contains multiple governance mechanisms. Dynamical-process governance includes event-based intervention, feedback governance, perturbative governance, tangent-space governance, and criticality governance. Relational-structural governance encompasses network, coupling, boundary, modular, distributed, and polycentric forms of coordination. Generative-background governance concerns structures that shape the conditions under which trajectories and relations become possible, accessible, stable, or costly, including generative conditions, structural flows on manifolds, background geometry, fields, symmetry structures, gauge-like connections, and emergent backgrounds. A formal representation is developed using dynamical systems, relational structures, differential geometry, and related mathematical languages. The taxonomy treats governance interventions as operators acting upon different components of a generative system and allows a single institutional intervention to be decomposed across multiple structural layers. This layered representation supports comparison among governance theories that employ different conceptual vocabularies and clarifies the relation between immediate intervention, trajectory regulation, relational reconfiguration, and modification of the conditions of generation. The paper presents the taxonomy as a foundational framework for subsequent theoretical and empirical development. Its broader objective is to provide a common analytical language for studying governance in heterogeneous, nonlinear, evolving, and partially observable relational systems while preserving the possibility of plural and revisable forms of order.

items.title: Irreplaceable Human Educators in Moral and Character Education during the Era of Artificial Intelligence.
items.abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence technology (AI) have significantly impacted education in practice. Such a trend is also becoming prevalent in moral and character education. In this paper, I will argue whether moral and character educators will remain as irreplaceable educational agents in the era of AI. For the discussion, I will examine whether AI agents will be able to become sole teachers or mentors while considering three aspects of ethics education: 1. Phronesis cultivation; 2. Promotion of moral and positive youth development; and 3. Development of autonomy and agency for the wise and ethical use of AI. I will refer to relevant theoretical and empirical studies on moral development and education to examine AI’s potential capacity related to the three aspects of moral education. Finally, I will briefly discuss how the role of human moral and character educators needs to be reshaped during the era of AI.

items.title: La racionalidad biomédica causal-funcional, bioestadística y normativa como paradigma epistemológico.
items.abstract: Una forma recurrente de clasificación biomédica articula explicaciones causales, mediciones poblacionales y criterios normativos cuyas conclusiones responden a problemas epistemológicos diferentes, aunque su circulación institucional permite utilizarlas como partes de un razonamiento aparentemente continuo. El artículo propone la denominación racionalidad biomédica causal-funcional, bioestadística y normativa para identificar la articulación inferencial implícita mediante la cual resultados producidos en campos distintos pasan a funcionar como premisas de conclusiones cuyo alcance excede el problema epistemológico en el que fueron obtenidos, hasta participar en clasificaciones relacionadas con la salud. Mediante un método teórico-argumentativo propio de la filosofía de la ciencia, el análisis conceptual delimita los componentes de la racionalidad y el análisis inferencial determina qué razones exige el paso entre conclusiones heterogéneas, mientras las fuentes históricas e institucionales permiten examinar su circulación y estabilización. El desarrollo demuestra que la función delimita propiedades biológicamente pertinentes cuya justificación exige establecer, según la relación formulada, si la actuación de una parte constituye una actividad del mecanismo o produce un efecto del que depende la modificación de otro proceso. Una vez delimitada la propiedad, la bioestadística representa sus variaciones dentro de poblaciones definidas, pero la clasificación requiere además seleccionar una referencia y valorar el funcionamiento esperado. La validez alcanzada en una explicación o en una inferencia poblacional carece de transferencia automática hacia la conclusión normativa. Cuando las decisiones relativas a la referencia y al funcionamiento esperado permanecen implícitas, la clasificación adquiere apariencia enteramente objetiva. La recurrencia de las reglas y su incorporación a instrumentos y prácticas compartidas permiten caracterizar la estabilización institucional de la articulación inferencial como un paradigma epistemológico internamente heterogéneo y susceptible de aplicaciones parciales. La denominación proporciona un criterio para distinguir las modificaciones prácticas de los cambios que alcanzan las reglas mediante las cuales una diferencia adquiere significado clínico.

items.title: O contínuo dialetal da negação no Português Brasileiro: do Nordeste agrícola ao Sudeste altamente industrializado.
items.abstract: Este ensaio investiga a variação da negação verbal no Português Brasileiro (PB) por meio da Geossociolinguística Etnográfico-Interacional (Bortoni-Ricardo, 2009 [2004]). Com base em uma meta-análise, demonstra-se que a “Dupla Negação” decresce conforme aumentam a escolaridade e a urbanização, formando um contínuo dialetal que vai do Nordeste agrícola ao Sudeste industrializado. Sob o prisma sociológico de Bourdieu (2007), argumenta-se que a hegemonia econômica do Sudeste converte variedades locais em norma culta, exercendo violência simbólica contra falares nordestinos. Ademais, propõe-se que a “Negação Pós-Verbal” se consolidou em contextos coloniais luso-bantos como estratégia de polidez e preservação de face em interações assimétricas, “adoçando” o português seiscentista. O estudo conclui que essas variantes, embora estigmatizadas, são marcas de resistência cultural e refinamento pragmático da diáspora africana.
